papers.title: Can AI Help Explain AI? Effects of Multimodal LLM-Generated Explanations on Perceived Understanding and Perceived Trust in XAI Visualizations
papers.abstract: Explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) aims to make machine learning models understandable, yet many XAI visualizations remain difficult for end-users to interpret. Here, we evaluate whether augmenting XAI outputs with textual explanations from multimodal LLMs improves perceived understanding and perceived trust. We conducted a pre-registered within-subject experiment ($N = 128$) across seven decision scenarios and five XAI methods, with and without LLM generated explanations. The explanations improved perceived understanding and perceived trust by 0.35 and 0.26 points on five-point scales (both $p < .001$). The gain appeared in all seven scenarios, did not differ between local and global explanations, and was largest for participants with the least prior XAI exposure. A mediation analysis indicates an indirect effect on perceived trust through perceived understanding. These results suggest that multimodal LLMs can provide a useful interpretive layer for XAI beyond expert audiences.

papers.intro:
Explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) is now widely used in practice to provide insights into how models reach conclusions (Ehsan et al., 2024; Wang and Yin, 2021; Zhang and Lim, 2022; Bilal et al., 2025). While originally developed to support model debugging and validation, XAI outputs are increasingly used by managers, auditors, and decision-makers to support oversight, justify automated recommendations, build trust, and enable accountable decision-making. Yet, the outputs of many XAI approaches remain difficult to interpret in practice, especially for end-users (Bobek et al., 2025).

Explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) is now widely used in practice to provide insights into how models reach conclusions (Ehsan et al., 2024; Wang and Yin, 2021; Zhang and Lim, 2022; Bilal et al., 2025). While originally developed to support model debugging and validation, XAI outputs are increasingly used by managers, auditors, and decision-makers to support oversight, justify automated recommendations, build trust, and enable accountable decision-making. Yet, the outputs of many XAI approaches remain difficult to interpret in practice, especially for end-users (Bobek et al., 2025).

Over the past decade, many XAI methods have been developed, including SHAP (Lundberg and Lee, 2017; Lundberg et al., 2020; Senoner et al., 2022), LIME (Ribeiro et al., 2016; Salih et al., 2025), partial dependence plots (Friedman, 2001; Kruschel et al., 2026), and saliency-based approaches (Selvaraju et al., 2020; Senoner et al., 2024). These techniques can broadly be categorized into (i) local explanations, which focus on individual predictions, and (ii) global explanations, which describe overall model behavior. However, many of these approaches have been developed primarily with an emphasis on model fidelity and technical faithfulness rather than human interpretability. As a result, explanations that are mathematically rigorous are not necessarily understandable to end-users.

These techniques can broadly be categorized into (i) local explanations, which focus on individual predictions, and (ii) global explanations, which describe overall model behavior. However, many of these approaches have been developed primarily with an emphasis on model fidelity and technical faithfulness rather than human interpretability. As a result, explanations that are mathematically rigorous are not necessarily understandable to end-users.

In practice, XAI visualizations can be challenging to understand and interpret, especially for end-users such as managers and other decision-makers. Many XAI approaches combine feature importance rankings, instance-level attributions, and baseline comparisons within a single visualization. Further, such visualizations span different aggregation levels, such as instance-level predictions and global patterns, which require users to reconcile multiple layers of abstraction. For example, a SHAP summary plot (“beeswarm”) displays the distribution of feature attributions across an entire dataset, while encoding feature importance, directionality, magnitude, and data density simultaneously through position and color (Lundberg et al., 2020). Integrating these signals into a coherent mental model can be challenging for end-users. Empirical research shows that users frequently misinterpret attribution magnitudes, confuse explanation levels, or overgeneralize from complex visual encodings (Wang and Yin, 2021; Wang and Yin, 2022; Ehsan et al., 2024; Poursabzi-Sangdeh et al., 2021; Humer et al., 2024).

In this paper, we use multimodal LLMs to generate explanations of XAI visualizations in natural language. Our work is motivated by prior work applying generative AI to machine learning models, yet with different objectives; existing works are primarily methodological. One stream employs LLMs to explain the model behavior directly. For instance, systems such as TalkToModel (Slack et al., 2023) allow users to query machine learning models through a conversational interface. However, such systems operate on the underlying model and data in response to user-initiated queries, so the interpretive work starts from the model rather than from an XAI visualization that a user has already been given. Another stream integrates LLMs with explanation techniques to translate XAI outputs into text. For example, LangXAI demonstrates that vision language models can generate textual descriptions of XAI visualizations (Nguyen et al., 2024), and related works propose the broader idea of using LLMs to “explain explanations” with a methodological focus on preserving the explanatory faithfulness (Zytek et al., 2024b; Zytek et al., 2024a; Bello et al., 2025).

In contrast, our focus is not methodological but behavioral: we aim to test how users respond to AI-generated explanations of XAI visualizations. To the best of our knowledge, ours is the first controlled study to test the effects of such explanations on Perceived Understanding and Perceived Trust when they are generated by a multimodal LLM from a diverse set of rendered XAI visualizations.

In contrast, our focus is not methodological but behavioral: we aim to test how users respond to AI-generated explanations of XAI visualizations. To the best of our knowledge, ours is the first controlled study to test the effects of such explanations on Perceived Understanding and Perceived Trust when they are generated by a multimodal LLM from a diverse set of rendered XAI visualizations.

From a human–computer interaction (HCI) perspective, explanations support sense-making by shaping users’ mental models and calibrating perceived trust. Research in human–AI interaction suggests that perceived understanding is a key antecedent of appropriately calibrated perceived trust and effective oversight (Ibrahim et al., 2023; Chen et al., 2024). By translating complex visual encodings into structured narratives, multimodal LLMs may reduce cognitive load and help users integrate multiple explanation signals into a coherent interpretation. Whether this translation meaningfully improves perceived understanding and perceived trust, particularly for end-users, remains an open empirical question. We thus address the following research questions (RQs): RQ1: How do LLM-generated textual explanations of XAI visualizations influence end-users’ perceived understanding of how an AI system makes decisions? RQ2: How do LLM-generated explanations of XAI visualizations affect end-users’ perceived trust in AI-assisted decisions? RQ3: To what extent does the perceived understanding mediate the relationship between LLM-generated explanations and end-users’ perceived trust?

To answer these RQs, we conducted a pre-registered within-subject experiment (NN = 128). Our research design is shown in Figure 1. Participants evaluated XAI visualizations under two conditions: (a) XAI visualizations alone and (b) XAI visualizations augmented with LLM-generated explanations generated in natural language. We measured Perceived Understanding and Perceived Trust in the AI system, page interaction time, and perceived helpfulness of the explanations. Explanations were generated by a state-of-the-art multimodal LLM that reads the XAI visualization images directly. We compare user responses across different settings with seven use cases inspired by real-world applications, spanning different XAI methods and data modalities. Our main analysis is based on GPT-5.6 Sol; to demonstrate generalizability, we also demonstrate robustness in a validation sample (NN = 63; using GPT-4o).

papers.intro:
We are interested in the critical temperature at which Bose–Einstein condensation (BEC) occurs in an interacting Bose gas. The ideal-gas transition is explicit, whereas in the interacting problem two-body scattering is coupled to long-wavelength critical fluctuations. For an interacting system, the Penrose–Onsager criterion identifies condensation with a macroscopic eigenvalue of the one-particle density matrix [13]. Our aim is to bound the temperature above which this cannot occur. We obtain a sharper normal-phase bound by refining the path-integral method of Seiringer and Ueltschi [17].

papers.title: GridDriver: On-Board BEV-Based Language Planning and Reasoning
papers.abstract: Bird's-Eye-View (BEV)-conditioned large language models (LLMs) enable language-interactive driving, but onboard deployment requires efficient perception and continuous planning alongside autoregressive language generation. We present GridDriver, an efficient BEV-conditioned LLM framework combining trajectory prediction, structured driving indicators, natural-language navigation, driving explanations, and scene question answering. Lightweight spatio-temporal BEV perception and spatially structured tokens provide scene context to a shared LLM, while frame-wise scheduling interleaves trajectory prediction with asynchronous language generation. GridDriver achieves competitive performance on public benchmarks, reaching 87.9% PDMS on NAVSIM and 57.6% accuracy on nuScenes-QA with a shared planning and QA checkpoint. Spatial representation analyses demonstrate improved geometric information retention and trajectory prediction compared with Q-Former compression. The system achieves 32.7 ms standalone planning latency and 9.4 plans/s in an onboard ROS 2 pipeline. We further evaluate planning on our own data recordings and demonstrate open-loop onboard operation on a research vehicle. Across public benchmarks and real-world evaluations, we identify strengths and limitations of the BEV-based approach.
papers.intro:
Large language models (LLMs) have extended autonomous driving with natural-language instructions [1, 2, 3], question answering [4, 5, 6], and driving descriptions [7]. These capabilities allow driving models to combine trajectory prediction with language understanding and generation. Grounding such models in the driving scene requires spatial information about road geometry, surrounding agents, and their motion from multiple camera views. Bird’s-eye-view (BEV) representations fuse multi-camera observations into a shared ego-centric frame [8], providing spatial and temporal context aligned with trajectory prediction. This makes BEV a suitable interface for language-conditioned planning [9, 6, 10, 1].

These capabilities allow driving models to combine trajectory prediction with language understanding and generation. Grounding such models in the driving scene requires spatial information about road geometry, surrounding agents, and their motion from multiple camera views. Bird’s-eye-view (BEV) representations fuse multi-camera observations into a shared ego-centric frame [8], providing spatial and temporal context aligned with trajectory prediction. This makes BEV a suitable interface for language-conditioned planning [9, 6, 10, 1].

Moving BEV-conditioned LLM planning toward real-vehicle operation introduces additional requirements. Complex urban scenes demand rich spatial representations, while onboard computation requires efficient perception and inference. At the same time, the language capabilities motivating the use of an LLM should remain useful in practice, from natural-language navigation to passenger-facing driving explanations. We investigate these aspects through spatial representation analysis, joint planning and language evaluation, and exploratory onboard operation on a research vehicle.

We propose GridDriver, a BEV-based LLM planner with natural-language input and output (see Figure 1). We evaluate task-specific configurations on nuScenes, NAVSIM, and nuScenes-QA, and investigate deployment on a research vehicle. Our contributions are: • We demonstrate competitive language-conditioned trajectory prediction using a lightweight BEV-based LLM planner with temporally fused spatial tokens and direct waypoint regression. • We extend the planner with free-form driving explanations and scene question answering, and investigate how language influences predicted trajectories. • We demonstrate real-time onboard BEV-based LLM inference with structured driving indicators and asynchronous language generation, and evaluate planning on geographically held-out urban recordings. Code and checkpoints for the public datasets, and a documentation of the vehicle integration, will be made available.

papers.title: Optical characterization of Fermi polarons in monolayer MoSe$_2$ encapsulated in amorphous silicon nitride
papers.abstract: Amorphous silicon nitride is the leading low-loss, CMOS-compatible platform for wafer-scale integrated photonics. Encapsulating transition-metal dichalcogenide (TMD) monolayers within this platform offers a promising route towards scalable TMD-photonic circuits. Yet the effect of this amorphous dielectric on the optical response of the monolayer remains poorly understood. Here, we compare monolayer MoSe$_2$ encapsulated in amorphous silicon nitride with a hexagonal boron nitride-encapsulated reference, using differential reflectivity and photoluminescence. Whereas the reference is dominated by the neutral exciton, the nitride-encapsulated monolayer shows attractive and repulsive polaron resonances separated by ${\sim}31$~meV, with emission dominated by the attractive branch. A quantitative comparison of temperature-dependent reflectance with a microscopic finite-temperature Fermi-polaron theory shows that the nitride induces substantial electron doping in the monolayer, with an electron density of $(0.8$--$0.9)\times10^{12}$~cm$^{-2}$. Using the extracted density and trion binding energy as the only input parameters, the theory reproduces the photoluminescence spectra up to ${\sim}80$ K in excellent quantitative agreement with experiments, thus corroborating the Fermi-polaron description of the observed excitonic response.

papers.intro:
The integration of transition metal dichalcogenide (TMD) monolayers with photonic circuits is a promising route towards compact and scalable light sources, modulators, and nonlinear elements. Silicon nitride is the natural platform for this goal: it is the workhorse dielectric of low-loss, CMOS-compatible integrated photonics, combining wafer-scale deposition, foundry availability, and tight optical confinement in waveguides and resonators, with broadband transparency spanning the exciton transitions of most TMDs 1, 2. Routing and multiplexing have been demonstrated on this platform 3, 4. Monolayer TMDs have accordingly been interfaced with silicon nitride in many geometries of interest: waveguides and resonators, for modulation, nonlinear conversion, and emission control 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10; and patterned membranes and metasurfaces, for strong light-matter coupling and photoluminescence (PL) enhancement 11, 12. The silicon nitride, as a photonic platform, may also be engineered to host its own intrinsic single-photon emitters 13. In these directions, hexagonal boron nitride (hBN) offers a less versatile route: the growth and transfer of large-area, single-crystal films have yet to reach the maturity required for seamless integration with photonic-foundry processing 14, 15.

In nearly all of these demonstrations, however, the monolayer sits in direct contact with the nitride, and its optical response has not been fully characterized. This is important because the Coulomb interaction in a two-dimensional crystal is only weakly screened, and thus the properties of the excitonic and charged-exciton complexes are highly sensitive to the dielectric and electrostatic environment of the monolayer 16, 17, 18. This sensitivity can be a resource, since it allows the response to be engineered, but it can also become a liability, since disorder at the monolayer-substrate interface—in the form of surface roughness, physisorbed residues, and substrate charge traps—inhomogeneously broadens the resonances 19, obscuring information about the intrinsic properties of the monolayer. hBN is the standard remedy: its atomic flatness, chemical inertness, and wide band gap allow encapsulated monolayers to reach PL and absorption linewidths approaching the homogeneous limit, with residual charge disorder essentially eliminated 20, 21, 22. A recent comparative study of monolayer WS2 found substantially greater inhomogeneous broadening in silicon nitride environments than in hBN, attributing the difference primarily to substrate-induced charge trapping 23. Whether silicon nitride can serve as an effective protective and encapsulating layer for TMDs, using hBN as the benchmark, therefore hinges on its electrostatic influence on the monolayer.

papers.title: Evolution Under Fire: Evolving Agent Safety Harnesses with Adaptive Injection Stressors
papers.abstract: Tool-using language-model agents must act on information from untrusted emails, webpages, and documents. This creates a central security challenge: malicious instructions and legitimate task directives can arrive through the same interaction channel. Existing defenses are largely hand-designed and static, making further improvements dependent on repeated manual redesign. We introduce Evolution Under Fire, a staged framework that couples safety-harness evolution with adaptive stressor evolution. Utility-constrained, Pareto-scheduled tree search evolves complete executable safety harnesses from execution evidence while keeping the task model, benchmark, tools, and evaluator fixed. Adaptive stressor evolution then discovers utility-preserving attacks that guide a subsequent stage of harness evolution. On AgentDyn with GPT-4o-mini, an evolved harness reduces attack success from 50.4% to 3.0%, improves clean and attacked utility over the initial harness, and offers a stronger security-utility trade-off than reproduced defenses. On Agent-SafetyBench with Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, harness evolution reduces attack success from 82.6% to 62.0% while retaining helpfulness and runtime validity. Evolved harnesses also transfer without further evolution to Qwen3.5-35B-A3B, reducing attack success from 32.1% to 0.9% while improving attacked-task utility.

papers.intro:
Language-model agents increasingly complete user requests by reading emails, webpages, repositories, and other external content before invoking consequential tools. The same interface that makes these agents useful also creates an indirect prompt-injection channel: an attacker can place instructions in data that the agent later treats as authority (Greshake et al., 2023; Debenedetti et al., 2024; Zhan et al., 2024). The resulting failure is not confined to an unsafe response. It can change a tool call, disclose private data, or commit an external side effect.

Defending this setting exposes a difficult security–utility trade-off. Prompt reminders and content filters can suppress attacks but also discard instructions that are legitimately required by open-ended tasks. Conversely, permissive agents preserve utility while remaining vulnerable. Recent system-level defenses introduce planning constraints, information-flow rules, privilege policies, causal monitors, or action auditors (Debenedetti et al., 2026; Shi et al., 2025; Li et al., 2025; Zhu et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2026c; Wang et al., 2026a; Ma et al., 2026b). Each design encodes a useful hypothesis, but each is a fixed point in a large program space: the surrounding harness can choose how to construct context, expose tools, maintain state, invoke auxiliary models, validate actions, and recover from uncertainty.

In response to this question, we propose Evolution Under Fire, a framework that places safety-harness evolution under adaptively generated injection pressure while keeping the task model and benchmark fixed. The defense-side process is utility-constrained, Pareto-scheduled harness tree evolution. Each expansion selects one utility-qualified parent and produces one child harness, while a scheduler can revisit any previously evaluated branch rather than committing to a linear chain. Candidates that violate utility constraints cannot become parents, but remain visible as negative evidence. The attack-side process is utility-preserving, lineage-based stressor evolution. It opens or continues stressor lineages against cases a target harness originally solved securely, and retains a generated stressor as feedback only when the attack succeeds without destroying the benign task.

Our contributions are: • Executable safety-harness evolution. We formulate agent defense as search over complete executable harnesses within a fixed evaluation environment. A read-only Diagnoser and code-generating Expander ground each edit in execution traces and archive-wide search history. • Utility-constrained Pareto tree search. Harness evolution admits only candidates that preserve utility relative to the initial harness, then samples parents from the Pareto frontier using uncertainty-aware metric estimates. It maintains diverse security–utility trade-offs, allows strong older branches to receive further expansions, and retains utility-rejected candidates as counterexamples without allowing them to propagate. • Feedback from adaptive stressors. Our stressor evolution generates adaptive stressors whose outcomes are verified by benchmark oracles. These adaptive stressors expose residual weaknesses in strong harnesses and provide targeted feedback for subsequent defense evolution. Stressor-guided evolution improves the security–utility frontier over a budget-matched harness-only control, and the resulting defenses transfer across closed and open-weight task models.

papers.title: EvoSkill-S1: Evolving Reusable Skills with Genetic-Inspired Operators
papers.abstract: Reusable skills allow language-model agents to accumulate and reuse problem-solving experience. However, most existing methods improve a skill bank only indirectly through rollout-driven accumulation and heuristic reflection, often resulting in shallow and weakly controlled updates. We present EvoSkill-S1, an RL-driven framework that instead treats reusable skills themselves as the direct objects of evolution. Given hard-negative failures, EvoSkill-S1 selects parent skills and transforms them into candidate child skills through five genetic-inspired operators: revision, cross-revision, mutation, dual-reflection, and crossover. Downstream task rewards train the skill evolver to generate more effective child skills, while evaluator-guided write-back selectively retains beneficial updates. Complementary Skill Bank Fusion consolidates operator-specific banks to exploit their distinct recovery patterns, while a Procedural Skill Interface supports transfer to unseen problems. Across all reported math and code benchmarks, EvoSkill-S1 improves the corresponding initialized skill banks under both Qwen and GPT-family solvers, with relative gains of up to 12.39%. Compared with the strongest external baseline without direct skill evolution, the largest relative improvement reaches 20.39%.

papers.intro:
Large language models (LLMs) have become increasingly capable of complex reasoning, including mathematical problem solving and code generation. Nevertheless, many challenging problems still benefit from reusable problem-solving experience rather than isolated one-shot generation (Brown et al., 2020; Wei et al., 2022; Kojima et al., 2022; Wang et al., 2023; Cobbe et al., 2021; Hendrycks et al., 2021b; Chen et al., 2021; Li et al., 2022). A natural way to provide such experience is through a skill bank: a collection of compact abstractions, strategies, and cautions that can be retrieved for related problems, echoing broader work on language-agent memory, tool use, and experience reuse (Yao et al., 2023; Schick et al., 2023; Park et al., 2023; Wang et al., 2024; Packer et al., 2023; Shinn et al., 2023; Zhao et al., 2024).

Many existing approaches improve such banks only indirectly. As new rollouts arrive, they append new skills or summarize and reflect on additional experience (Wang et al., 2024; Shinn et al., 2023; Zhao et al., 2024). Direct skill-level evolution, however, is non-trivial. First, different failure modes require different transformations: some skills need conservative repair, while others require cross-problem transfer, an alternative solution route, stronger guardrails, or composition with another skill. Second, a single hard negative can yield multiple plausible child skills, requiring a principled mechanism for comparing candidates and assigning credit to useful transformations. Third, evolved skills may retain artifacts specific to their source problems, limiting transfer to unseen problems. Finally, different operators may recover complementary subsets of failures, requiring a mechanism to consolidate their distinct strengths.

papers.title: Sharp Fractional Capacitary-Distance Hardy Inequalities
papers.abstract: Let $d\in\mathbb N$, $p\in(1,\infty)$, $p':=\frac{p}{p-1}$, and $s\in(0,\min\{1+\frac1p,\frac dp\})$. For an open set $\Omega\subset\mathbb{R}^d$, let $F:=\mathbb{R}^d\setminus\Omega$. For any $\alpha\in(0,1]$ and $x\in\Omega$, let \begin{align*} d_{\alpha,s,p}(x) :=\inf\left\{r\in(0,\infty): \frac{\operatorname{cap}_{s,p}(\overline{F\cap B(x,r)})} {\operatorname{cap}_{s,p}(\overline{B(x,r)})}\ge\alpha\right\}, \end{align*} where $\operatorname{cap}_{s,p}$ is the capacity associated with the fractional Sobolev energy $[\,\cdot\,]_{s,p}^p$. In this article, we prove that there exists a positive constant $C$, depending only on $d$, $s$, and $p$, such that, for any $\alpha\in(0,1]$ and $u\in C_{\rm c}^\infty(\Omega)$, \begin{align*} \int_\Omega\frac{|u(x)|^p}{d_{\alpha,s,p}(x)^{sp}}\,dx \le C\alpha^{-p'}[u]_{s,p}^p. \end{align*} We also show that both the exponent $p'$ in $\alpha^{-p'}$ as $\alpha\to0^+$ over the class of all open sets and the range $s\in(0,1+\frac1p)$ within $sp<d$ are sharp. Our proofs use variational minimization, equilibrium measures on trees, and weighted Hardy inequalities.

papers.title: BRepA: Graph-Based B-Rep Pretraining for Unified CAD Understanding and Generation
papers.abstract: Boundary representation (B-Rep) of CAD models encodes geometric primitives and their relations as a graph structure, enabling efficient shape modeling within CAD software. Learning on B-Reps for downstream tasks, such as segmentation and novel shape generation, requires specialized neural network designs. Moreover, performance improvements and accelerated training can be achieved with effective pretraining strategies, which is particularly important for tasks with limited labeled B-Rep data. In this paper, we introduce BRepA, a unified self-supervised pretraining framework that explicitly reconstructs both the geometry and topology of B-Rep objects via graph-based modeling. By learning from large-scale unlabeled CAD data only once, BRepA produces representations that generalize across tasks and significantly enhance both discriminative and generative learning. On segmentation tasks, BRepA demonstrates remarkable data efficiency. For instance, with only 1% labeled samples, BRepA pretraining improves mIoU by 32.52% compared to models trained from scratch. On generative tasks, aligning diffusion model representations with pretrained BRepA features substantially accelerates convergence, achieving nearly 2 times faster training while improving generation quality under the same computational budget, despite the diffusion model being roughly 20 times larger than BRepA. Overall, our results show that geometry- and topology-aware B-Rep pretraining provides a powerful foundation for both understanding and generating CAD structures, serving as a versatile representation backbone for diverse downstream applications. We will release the code to facilitate future research.

papers.intro:
Boundary representation (B-Rep) is a fundamental CAD data format that encodes both the geometric and topological structure of 3D objects [15, 19]. The geometric information describes the parametric characteristics of surfaces, edges, and vertices, while the topological information defines both inter-type relationships (e.g., which edges bound a face) and intra-type adjacencies (e.g., neighboring faces or edges). B-Rep is widely used in industrial design and manufacturing workflows for visualization, machining feature management, and engineering analysis.

The geometric information describes the parametric characteristics of surfaces, edges, and vertices, while the topological information defines both inter-type relationships (e.g., which edges bound a face) and intra-type adjacencies (e.g., neighboring faces or edges). Despite its importance, training B-Rep models presents unique challenges. Models like UV-Net [15], BRepNet [19] and SB-GCN [16] are examples of neural network architectures operating on B-Reps. Compared to 2D images or 3D data [39, 40, 41], the amount of publicly available B-Rep data is limited, and labeled datasets are particularly scarce, making B-Rep models prone to overfitting on small datasets [17]. Moreover, B-Rep is a parametric and symbolic representation, which is highly abstract and discrete in the feature space. This discrete and fragmented data manifold makes it especially challenging to train generative models such as diffusion models [12], which typically rely on continuous and smooth spaces.

A promising strategy to address these challenges is self-supervised pretraining, where models are trained on available unlabeled B-Rep data to learn generalizable representations, which can then be fine-tuned or aligned for downstream tasks. However, research in this direction remains limited. In this work, we introduce BRepA, a new B-Rep pretraining model designed to learn both geometric and topological representations. BRepA naturally models B-Rep data as graphs by using Graph Attention models (GAT) [31] and adopts Transformer-based encoders for both surfaces and edges. It jointly learns geometry- and topology-aware representations through two complementary pretraining objectives: Geometry Masked Autoencoding (MAE) and Topology MAE. Our experiments demonstrate that the learned representations from BRepA benefit both discriminative and generative tasks: (1) In segmentation tasks, pretrained BRepA consistently outperforms both untrained BRepA and UV-Net, particularly in low-label regimes, as depicted in Figure 1 (a). (2) In generative tasks, BRepA enables faster and more effective training of large-scale generative models such as BrepDiff [21] through feature alignment, improving both training efficiency and final generation quality, as depicted in Figure 1 (b), even though these diffusion-based models contain far more parameters than BRepA itself.

papers.title: Rescaling OLS-Merged Adapters To Improve Personalized Image Generation
papers.abstract: Merging multiple adapters into a single image generation model reduces deployment costs while preserving diverse task capabilities or personalization modes. State-of-the-art methods such as RegMean, Mix-of-Show, and Subspace Routing fit the outputs of the merged model to those of the individual adapters using ordinary least squares (OLS). We show that this reconstruction objective systematically shrinks task-specific signals whenever the activation distributions of different tasks overlap, producing a merged adapter that is too weak for downstream use. We derive a decomposition that quantifies this shrinkage and propose rescaling the merged update to restore signal strength. On multi-subject personalization with up to 30 merged adapters, rescaling substantially improves subject fidelity over unscaled baselines. Our approach also improves results on style transfer, concept erasure, image classification, and LLM-based text classification.

papers.intro:
Low-rank adapters (LoRAs) [27] have become the standard way to personalize text-to-image diffusion models. A few images are enough to teach a model a new subject [50], an artistic style, or an erasure that removes a concept from the model [39, 19]. Many applications need several of these adapters in one model, for example to generate any of a set of personalized subjects or styles, or to erase a list of unwanted concepts at once.

Low-rank adapters (LoRAs) [27] have become the standard way to personalize text-to-image diffusion models. A few images are enough to teach a model a new subject [50], an artistic style, or an erasure that removes a concept from the model [39, 19]. Many applications need several of these adapters in one model, for example to generate any of a set of personalized subjects or styles, or to erase a list of unwanted concepts at once.

One option is to train a single adapter on the images of all subjects together. This requires the training images of every subject, which are often unavailable because adapters are typically shared as weights without their data, and the training has to be repeated whenever a subject is added. The alternative is to combine independently trained adapters into one set of weights without further training, which is the model merging problem [30, 73, 79, 40, 59, 22, 52].

Merging becomes difficult when many adapters are combined. All adapters modify the same layers, and their prompts share most of their text embedding, so each adapter also changes the images generated for the other adapters’ prompts. This interference grows with the number of adapters. Weight-space methods ignore the input distribution adapters were trained on, and their subject fidelity drops substantially as more adapters are merged (Tab. 1). Data-based methods instead fit the merged weights so that each merged layer reproduces the output of every adapter on that adapter’s own inputs, which can be formalized as an ordinary least squares (OLS) problem [32, 22, 8, 67]. Among them, Subspace Routing (SSR) [67] is particularly well suited for many adapters. It solves the OLS problem in the low-rank bottleneck of the LoRAs, so its closed-form solution scales with the total adapter rank instead of the layer width. SSR routes each prompt to the correct adapter, yet the subjects still fade as more adapters are merged (Fig. 1).

Scaling the merged adapter up by a single factor therefore improves the merged model substantially.

papers.title: A transformer analysis lowers the energy threshold and improves the sensitivity of a compact imaging atmospheric Cherenkov telescope
papers.abstract: Context. A companion study simulated an idealised stand-alone imaging atmospheric Cherenkov telescope with a 5 m diameter mirror. A video vision transformer that processes the raw camera waveforms lowered its energy threshold by a factor of three, compared with the standard analysis based on image parameters. Aims. We use realistic photodetectors, compute the differential flux sensitivity, and study how hardware parameters affect the transformer analysis. Methods. With the simulation tools of the Cherenkov Telescope Array Observatory, we compare three photodetector efficiencies (100 %, 50 % and that of the LST-1 photomultipliers) with the transformer and with a standard analysis optimised for each. We then vary the dish diameter, field of view, pulse width and sampling rate. Results. With the LST-1 photomultipliers, the energy threshold is 0.18 TeV with the transformer and 0.73 TeV with the standard analysis. The standard analysis needs a photodetector efficiency of 100 % to match that threshold. The main reason is that the transformer works with events of about 35 photoelectrons in the camera, whereas the standard analysis needs about 200 before image cleaning. A 4 m dish with the transformer is more sensitive at all energies than a 5 m dish with the standard analysis. Dishes of 4, 5 and 6 m diameter give thresholds of 0.38, 0.18 and 0.13 TeV. Sampling the pixel signals at 2 GS/s instead of 5 GS/s raises the threshold to 0.26 TeV, whereas the single-photoelectron pulse width (1-3 ns) matters little. Conclusions. The analysis matters as much as the mirror area and the photodetector efficiency. With the transformer analysis, the idealised 5 m diameter telescope comes within a factor of about four of the sensitivity of LST-1 and MAGIC above 0.25 TeV, although its mirror area is 21 times smaller than that of the 23 m LST-1. This performance should improve substantially in the coming years.

papers.intro:
For the last forty years, the reconstruction of events recorded by imaging atmospheric Cherenkov telescopes (IACTs) has been mostly based on the parameterisation of the shower image introduced by Hillas (1985). Some IACTs take a snapshot of the Cherenkov flash, whereas many others record a short movie of it, with a waveform in every pixel. Each waveform is converted into one charge and one arrival time. The pixels that probably contain only night-sky light are then removed, and the image is described by a few image parameters. The event is reconstructed from these parameters, nowadays often with machine-learning methods such as random forests. Each of the 3600 pixels of the camera considered here records 128 samples, so an event contains about 4.6×1054.6\times 10^{5} values. These values are reduced to about ten parameters before any reconstruction begins (Jobst et al., 2026). This approach is robust, well understood and used by most current instruments. We call it the standard analysis. Its performance improves when more photons are detected from each shower, with larger mirrors or better photodetectors. It also improves with stereoscopic observations, in which several telescopes observe the same shower.

With such a network, Jacquemont et al. (2021) reconstructed the real data of LST-1, the first Large-Sized Telescope of the Cherenkov Telescope Array Observatory (CTAO), better than the standard analysis. (2025) applied a CNN to the simulated waveforms of LST-1, but still after the standard image cleaning. These networks are designed for existing telescopes, which were themselves designed for the standard analysis. Their hexagonal pixels, for example, do not fit the square grid that networks developed for images expect. Transformers have been applied to simulations of a future array of water Cherenkov detectors for gamma rays, and they outperformed the established reconstruction methods (Pirke et al., 2026). To our knowledge, Jobst et al. papers.title: RevolIACT: a longitudinally distributed array of compact AI-driven Cherenkov telescopes for the time-domain sub-TeV sky
papers.abstract: Context. The coming decade will be the golden era of time-domain astronomy. In ten years, however, sensitive very-high-energy observations below ~1 TeV may be possible only at the two sites of the Cherenkov Telescope Array Observatory (CTAO). Each can observe a source for only a few hours per night. Aims. We quantify the loss caused by this limited coverage and assess whether RevolIACT, an array of compact stand-alone AI-driven stations, can close the gap. Methods. We estimate the sensitivity that a stand-alone station needs to detect important transients seen by current imaging atmospheric Cherenkov telescopes (IACTs). We also compute the temporal coverage of layouts of ten to fourteen stations distributed in longitude, and how many of the 4401 Fermi-GBM gamma-ray bursts each layout could have observed when they occurred. Results. For each station, a sensitivity of ~15 % of the Crab flux in one hour above 0.2-0.3 TeV, about three times worse than that of current IACT systems, would suffice for an array to detect most of these transients. With the standard analysis, a telescope with a 5 m diameter mirror misses this target by a factor of 17. With a video vision transformer, it comes within a factor of two in an idealised simulation, and a 6 m telescope within 1.5. Ten to fourteen stations would provide three to four times the temporal coverage of CTAO, averaged over the sky and for the GBM bursts. Fourteen stations can observe most sources around the clock for about two months per year. Conclusions. Temporal coverage, not only flux sensitivity, will limit sub-TeV transient astronomy in the next decade. RevolIACT would complement CTAO. The concept relies on the transformer analysis, which is still young and will improve. The decisive next step is to confirm this performance on real data, with a prototype station.

papers.intro:
For almost four decades, very-high-energy (VHE) gamma-ray astronomy has progressed by building larger telescopes and by observing in stereoscopic mode, in which several telescopes observe the same air shower. The dish diameter went from the 10 m of Whipple (Kildea et al., 2007) to the 17 m of MAGIC (Aleksić et al., 2016b), the 28 m of the largest H.E.S.S. telescope (H.E.S.S. Collaboration, 2017a) and the 23 m of the Large-Sized Telescope (LST) sub-array of the Cherenkov Telescope Array Observatory (Acharya et al., 2013; Abe et al., 2023, CTAO;). This strategy has been extraordinarily successful. The number of known VHE sources has increased from a handful in the 1990s to more than two hundred in the TeVCat catalogue (Wakely & Horan, 2008). Imaging atmospheric Cherenkov telescopes (IACTs) have detected pulsed gamma rays from the Crab, Vela and Geminga pulsars, at energies from below 20 GeV up to 20 TeV (Aliu et al., 2008; VERITAS Collaboration, 2011; Ansoldi et al., 2016; H.E.S.S. Collaboration, 2018; H.E.S.S. Collaboration, 2023; MAGIC Collaboration, 2020a; Abe et al., 2025). They have also detected flat-spectrum radio quasars at redshifts close to 1, such as PKS 1441+25, QSO B0218+357 and OP 313 (Ahnen et al., 2015; Ahnen et al., 2016; Abe et al., 2026), whose gamma rays left them when the Universe was less than half its present age. The absorption of these gamma rays by the extragalactic background light (EBL), the light emitted by all stars and galaxies over cosmic history, has allowed IACTs to constrain the density of this light (Aharonian et al., 2006a; MAGIC Collaboration, 2008; Acciari et al., 2019). IACTs have also measured flux variations of active galactic nuclei (AGN) on timescales of minutes (Aharonian et al., 2007; Albert et al., 2007; Aleksić et al., 2014), and they have detected gamma-ray bursts (GRBs) (MAGIC Collaboration, 2019; H.E.S.S. Collaboration, 2019; H.E.S.S. Collaboration, 2021) and the recurrent nova RS Ophiuchi (H.E.S.S. Collaboration, 2022; MAGIC Collaboration, 2022).

This strategy has, however, also created a blind spot: current telescopes can detect very faint sources, but they cannot watch them continuously. This blind spot is about to matter more than ever, because the number of transient alerts is growing by orders of magnitude. The NSF–DOE Vera C. Rubin Observatory alone is expected to issue of order 10710^{7} alerts per night (Ivezić et al., 2019). SKA and DSA-2000 in the radio, Einstein Probe and SVOM in X-rays, and IceCube-Gen2 in neutrinos will add their own streams. The gravitational-wave network is moving towards the Einstein Telescope (Punturo et al., 2010), which will issue alerts minutes before binary neutron star mergers (Banerjee et al., 2023). Many of the most interesting transients last only minutes to days and emit a large fraction of their VHE power below 1 TeV. This is the case for GRBs, novae, flaring AGN, and perhaps also for some of the counterparts of neutrinos and gravitational waves (Sect. 2.2).

At the same time, the number of places from which these transients can be observed with good sensitivity below 1 TeV is shrinking. MAGIC, H.E.S.S. and VERITAS are likely to stop operating within the next decade. The ASTRI Mini-Array on Tenerife (Scuderi et al., 2022) is designed for the multi-TeV range. The LACT array of 32 telescopes of 6 m, planned at the LHAASO site, is designed mainly for the ultra-high-energy range, in combination with the water Cherenkov and muon detectors of LHAASO (Zhang et al., 2025). Ground particle arrays such as LHAASO, and in the future the Southern Wide-field Gamma-ray Observatory (Albert et al., 2019, SWGO;), survey the overhead sky continuously. However, for point sources below ∼\sim1 TeV and on timescales of minutes to days, their sensitivity is orders of magnitude worse than that of an IACT (Sitarek, 2022). Only an exceptional event overcomes this limitation. LHAASO detected more than 64 000 photons above 0.2 TeV from GRB 221009A, the brightest GRB ever recorded (LHAASO Collaboration, 2023), but such a burst is expected only about once every 10 000 years (Burns et al., 2023). By the mid-2030s, the only IACTs with good sensitivity down to ∼\sim0.1 TeV may therefore be those at the two CTAO sites: CTAO-North on La Palma and CTAO-South in the Atacama Desert. The sub-TeV transient sky would then be watched from only two locations. A transient that is not above the horizon of one of them during darkness is, in practice, not observed at sub-TeV energies.

The solution is simple in principle: many telescopes in different time zones, spread in longitude over both hemispheres, which observe a source one after another as the Earth turns. Optical time-domain astronomy has already taken this route. The Las Cumbres Observatory operates a global network of robotic telescopes (Brown et al., 2013). A white paper submitted to the Expanding Horizons call of ESO argues that multi-messenger astronomy in the 2040s needs a dedicated large-aperture facility for time-domain spectroscopy, with flexible operations across both hemispheres (Nissanke et al., 2025). One proposal of this kind is the Time Domain Telescope (TDT). It would consist of about a hundred robotic 2 m telescopes, which together collect as much light as one 20 m telescope, at a much lower cost. They would be grouped in clusters, possibly at several sites in both hemispheres, so as to obtain spectra ‘anywhere, anytime’ (Kupfer, 2025). For VHE gamma rays, such an array has long been considered unaffordable, because many telescopes can be built only if each of them is inexpensive. We call each telescope of the array a station. An inexpensive station is a small stand-alone telescope, which observes in monoscopic (mono) mode (Sect. 3.1). The standard analysis of IACT data reduces each shower image to a few image parameters (Hillas, 1985), from which machine-learning methods such as random forests estimate the type, the energy and the direction of the primary particle (e.g. López-Coto et al., 2022, for LST-1). With this analysis, however, a stand-alone telescope with a 5 m diameter mirror has a poor sensitivity and a high energy threshold, 0.73 TeV with the photodetectors used in LST-1. With few photons from each shower and a single viewing direction, the few image parameters carry too little information (Jobst et al., 2026a; Jobst et al., 2026b). Until recently, such a telescope was therefore not considered a useful instrument below 1 TeV.

papers.title: Zero mode surface of Hermitian two-by-two matrices
papers.abstract: We classify the zero mode surfaces, also called Clifford spectra, of Hermitian $2\times 2$ matrices. Using the covariance of the Dirac operator under the Euclidean group and its invariance under unitary conjugation, together with a singular value decomposition, every $m$-tuple of Hermitian $2\times 2$ matrices, after adjoining zero matrices if $m<3$, is reduced to the normal form $(b_1\sigma_1,b_2\sigma_2,b_3\sigma_3,0,\dots,0)$ with $b_1\geq b_2\geq b_3\geq 0$. Since adding a vanishing matrix only embeds the Clifford spectrum into a higher-dimensional space, it suffices to consider three matrices. In this normal form the determinant of the Dirac operator is given in closed form and its critical points are determined explicitly. The zero mode surface consists of one or two points if $b_3=0$. Otherwise it consists of two disjoint topological spheres if $b_1>b_2+b_3$, of two topological spheres touching at one point if $b_1=b_2+b_3$, and of a single topological sphere if $b_1<b_2+b_3$. The topology is thus governed by the triangle inequality for $(b_1,b_2,b_3)$, which can be interpreted with Heron's formula. In particular, the Clifford spectrum of any tuple of Hermitian $2\times 2$ matrices is never empty.

There are two physical motivations for studying this set. In applications to topological materials, a spectral localizer combines a Hamiltonian with position observables in an operator of the form (1.1) [2, 3, 4]. Its associated invariants remain constant along invertible deformations. Singular localizers thus identify where an invariant can change; a singularity does not by itself imply that such a change occurs [10, 15, 5]. This motivates a geometric study of the Clifford spectrum independently of a particular material model. The applications surveyed in [5] include topological insulators and superconductors [7, 8, 9], metals and gapless systems [10, 11], and crystalline [12], photonic [13] and nonlinear [14] systems.

In string theory, the IKKT and BFSS matrix models [16, 17] (for reviews see [19, 20, 21]) describe space-time and branes by configurations of Hermitian matrices, which may be interpreted as quantized embedding functions of a non-commutative or fuzzy space [18]. Well-known examples are the fuzzy sphere [22, 23] and fuzzy Riemann surfaces of higher genus [24, 25]. In order to extract the underlying classical geometry from a given set of matrices, generalized coherent states [26] have been used. They can be defined as quasi-coherent states, i.e. ground states of a Laplace-type operator [27, 28, 29], or as zero modes of a Dirac-type operator of the form (1.1) [30, 31, 32], which can also be motivated by tachyon condensation [33]. For m=3m=3 the zero modes of D⁡(x)D(x) generically form a two-dimensional surface in ℝ3\mathbb{R}^{3}, the zero mode surface, which can be seen as the shape of the fuzzy membrane described by the matrices. Since the matrices are finite dimensional, the zero mode surface is the zero set of the polynomial detD⁡(x)\det D(x) and can be determined without computing the states themselves [31, 34]. Based on this observation, a mapping between directed graphs and triples of Hermitian matrices was introduced in [34], which allows to construct fuzzy spaces with zero mode surfaces of arbitrary genus, see also [35] for fuzzy spaces with a classical limit and [36] for further examples such as a fuzzy trefoil knot and for gauge deformations of the fuzzy sphere. The zero mode surface and the Clifford spectrum are therefore the same object, which is studied in both communities under different names.

papers.title: Reusing Battle-tested Code: A Systematic Literature Review of Automated Software Transplantation
papers.abstract: Software reuse remains a fundamental challenge in software engineering, often caught between the security risks of external libraries and the reliability concerns of generative AI. Automated software transplantation offers a compelling alternative by enabling the direct extraction and integration, into new host systems, of battle-tested logic (code that has already survived the rigors of production, possibly over many years of extensive in-production use). This paper presents a systematic literature review to evaluate the current state-of-the-art and identify the remaining barriers preventing this technology from becoming a mainstream engineering practice. We identified 27 distinct automated software transplantation approaches. Our analysis reveals that while the adaptation of code is highly automated, significant bottlenecks remain in the manual prerequisite steps of organ location and test suite augmentation. We conclude with a research roadmap that suggests how these manual obstacles might be overcome, including the strategic use of Large Language Models to assist in identifying and verifying high-value, production-hardened logic for transplantation.

papers.intro:
Software transplantation is the automated process of extracting a specific behaviour — an “organ” — from a donor system and integrating it into a host system. First formalized in an invited keynote paper for the Working Conference on Reverse Engineering (WCRE 2013)Harman et al. (2013), this field addresses the fundamental challenge of software reuse: the ability to build on existing components rather than starting from scratch (Frakes and Kang, 2005). While McIlroy at the 1968 NATO Software Engineering conference envisioned a world of mass-produced, modular components (McIlroy, 1968), the practical reality of software engineering remains divided between structured integration and ad-hoc copying. Although transplantation was not formally defined until 2013, as this survey shows, there was work on related ideas dating back to 2008.

Although transplantation was not formally defined until 2013, as this survey shows, there was work on related ideas dating back to 2008.

Today, the dominant mechanism for reuse is the software library. By leveraging pre-existing packages, developers can integrate complex functionality with minimal effort. However, libraries are not a panacea; they introduce significant supply chain vulnerabilities, where a security flaw in a single dependency can compromise thousands of downstream systems. Furthermore, libraries are often difficult to efficiently adapt to the needs of a particular codebase, may suffer from “bloat” by including unnecessary features, or a suitable library may simply not exist for niche requirements.

To manage these variations more formally, Software Product Line (SPL) engineering was introduced to facilitate reuse across sets of systems that share common features (Metzger and Pohl, 2014). By managing core assets and variations (often via conditional compilation or preprocessor directives), SPLs allow for rapid development of related products. However, SPL architecture requires substantial upfront investment and is difficult to adopt when it is not clear if a software will evolve into multiple variants (Krueger, 2001). Furthermore, a vast majority of reuse opportunities remain unsuitable for SPL engineering, as they involve “one-off” cross-project integrations or occur in domains where the lack of stability and high fragmentation make the creation of a unified platform technically and economically infeasible (Minich, 2013; Clements et al., 2005).

More recently, Large Language Models (LLMs) have introduced a transformative paradigm for reuse by distilling the vast corpus of code within their training data into a generative interface. While they have revolutionised reuse, they do not completely solve the problem for three key reasons. First, the generated output is frequently characterized by inefficient (Huang et al., 2024) and verbose code (Dou et al., 2024). Second, LLMs can produce “subtly incorrect” code — logic that appears plausible but contains edge-case bugs or security vulnerabilities that are difficult for human reviewers to detect (Tambon et al., 2025; Fakhoury et al., 2024). Third, while they outperform previous generative technologies, LLMs still struggle with the “long tail” of reuse: rare, domain-specific, or proprietary logic underrepresented in their training sets. Ultimately, LLM-powered development trades the challenge of writing code for the new, non-trivial overhead of prompt engineering and verification, a shift that is not always a net win for developer productivity (Wang et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2024).

Software transplantation seeks to bridge this gap by providing the flexibility of manual reuse with the rigour of automation, predicated on the principle that the most reliable code is that which has already survived the rigours of production. By isolating logic at the functional level, it provides a means to reuse battle-tested code without the security risks of external libraries or the architectural overhead of SPLs, or the reliability concerns inherent in probabilistic LLM-generated code. Automated transplantation offers a verifiable alternative by reusing existing, battle-tested logic from known-good donor systems.

papers.title: XQR30: ALMA Observations Reveal the Diverse Structure of Cold Gas within z>6 Quasar Host Galaxies
papers.abstract: We present 0.25(~1.5kpc) ALMA observations of the [CII] and dust continuum emission from the host galaxies of 24 luminous z~6 quasars. Together with archival data from 17 quasars, this constitutes a nearly complete sample of all quasars with J-band magnitudes of J_AB<20.0 and redshifts between 5.8 and 6.6, which are the limits defined in the VLT/XSHOOTER legacy survey, XQR-30. For the full sample of 41 quasars, we find that 39(95%) of the quasar host galaxies are detected in [CII] emission with [CII] luminosities ranging between (0.3 and 9.2)x10^9Lsun, and 39(95%) of the quasar host galaxies are detected in continuum emission with continuum flux densities ranging between 0.22 and 16.3mJy. We detect eight [CII]-emitting companion galaxies, which is consistent with the expected number of galaxies based on clustering results. We find that z~6 quasar host galaxies have a range of morphologies, and by defining a new parameter, the kinematic position angle alignment parameter, Delta_PA_{kin-CII}, we show that most quasar host galaxies deviate from a standard disk model. This suggests that [CII] emission probes structures beyond simple disk rotation, such as bars, tidally disturbed gas, etc. We show that the dust emission is more compact than the [CII] emission independent of the morphology of the galaxy. Finally, we provide rough dynamical mass estimates within twice the [CII] half-light radius for the majority of the galaxies, and show that the average dynamical mass within the inner few kpc is consistent with estimates of the average mass in stars, gas and the SMBH.

papers.intro:
Massive galaxies are expected to form in strong galaxy overdensities, where conditions are more conducive to the rapid buildup of galaxies through mergers and gas accretion [38, 107, 22]. The most massive galaxies are believed to form and grow most rapidly [19], giving rise to massive quiescent galaxies at z>4z>4 [25, e.g.,]. This makes it crucial to observe them at the earliest times z≳6z\gtrsim 6, in order to understand the environment and physical conditions within these galaxies that facilitate this rapid growth and evolution. However, the number density of massive, high-redshift galaxies is small, and only very large area surveys have the necessary volume to detect these galaxies [18, e.g.,]. An alternative approach to finding massive galaxies is to study high-redshift quasars. Quasars are luminous active galactic nuclei 11 1 In this paper, we will refer to the compact object and its immediate surrounding as a quasar or quasi-stellar object (QSO) whereas the surrounding galaxy is referred to as the quasar host galaxy.. Their emission is bright enough that optical and near-infrared surveys, such as the Sloan Digital Sky Survey (SDSS), Pan-STARRS and VIKING can detect them out to z≳7z\gtrsim 7 [41, 8, 112, e.g.,]. Since quasar luminosity is correlated to the mass of the supermassive black hole [26, 74, 42, e.g.,], which in turn is correlated with the mass of the galaxy host [45, 47, e.g.,], we can use luminous high-redshift quasars as an efficient way to pinpoint the location of massive, star-forming high-redshift galaxies.

Currently there are over 300 z≳6z\gtrsim 6 luminous quasars known [40], and this number is ever increasing as more telescopes are surveying the sky. However, studying the galaxies that host luminous quasars remains difficult, in part because the quasar outshines the host galaxy by orders of magnitude in the rest-frame optical and near-infrared [77, e.g.,]. This has recently changed. Observations with the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) have proven effective at detecting the stellar light from the host galaxies of luminous quasars at z≳6z\gtrsim 6 [34, 121, 98, 122, 35, 71, 70, 88, 99]. Complementary to these observations are those taken at millimeter wavelengths, because millimeter observations trace the dust and cold gas within the quasar host galaxy: the former through measurements of the redshifted dust continuum emission, and the latter through measurements of fine-structure line emission, particularly from ionized carbon, [C II] [15, 29, e.g.,]. Millimeter observations have several advantages: 1) the host galaxy dominates the emission at these wavelengths, 2) the emission is largely unaffected by dust obscuration, and 3) millimeter interferometry allows for improved resolutions that can resolve the interstellar medium (ISM) of these galaxies. As a result, the Atacama Large Millimeter/sub-millimeter Array (ALMA) has observed more than a hundred z≳6z\gtrsim 6 quasars [115, 31, 59, 104, 113, 13, e.g.,].

As a result, the Atacama Large Millimeter/sub-millimeter Array (ALMA) has observed more than a hundred z≳6z\gtrsim 6 quasars [115, 31, 59, 104, 113, 13, e.g.,].

There are several important results that have come from studying the host galaxies of quasars with ALMA. Spatially unresolved observations have shown that the dust continuum and [C II] emission of quasar host galaxies is bright with total far-infrared luminosities similar to the most massive galaxies in our local universe [10, 68, 115, 31, e.g.,]. This confirmed the assumption that luminous quasars reside in massive galaxies. These unresolved observations have also revealed a large number of companion galaxies [27, 118, 82], which is consistent with the picture that these galaxies reside in galaxy overdensities. Resolving the [C II] and dust emission in more extended ALMA configurations (∼\sim0.′′\farcs3) have revealed that the dust emission is more compact than the [C II] emission [104, 113, e.g.,], although both show extended emission out to ∼10\sim 10 kpc [87, 11, 12]. Using the kinematic information from the [C II] emission line, these resolved observations also revealed the diverse morphology and kinematics of the host galaxies with some galaxies exhibiting signs of rotation and/or merger activity while others showing no sign of ordered motions [84, 100, 113]. Finally, using the most extended configurations with ALMA that probe scales less than 400 pc at z∼6z\sim 6 (<<0.′′\farcs08), these observations have started to reveal detailed ISM conditions such as dust temperature gradients within the galaxy [110, 80], the origin of the [C II] emission [79], evidence for kinematics beyond simple disk rotation [123, 85], alignment of the [C II] and dust emission with the radio jet [108], and the location of the quasar within its host galaxy [78, 116].

In addition to pinpointing the position of the massive host galaxy, the rest-frame ultraviolet and optical light from the quasar can also provide detailed information on the properties of the supermassive black hole (SMBH), in particular the mass of the SMBH that is powering the quasar. These masses are derived from the strength and width of emission lines in the spectra of quasars, in particular Mg II and Hβ\beta. Local studies have shown a correlation between the mass of the bulge and the mass of the SMBH over many orders of magnitude [45, 47, 63]. By studying this correlation at high redshift, one can constrain how this correlation evolved over cosmic time [54]. Numerous observations have studied the black hole – galaxy mass correlation using z≳6z\gtrsim 6 quasars [115, 117, 105, 95, 31, 59, 89, 84, 113, e.g.,]. Generally, these observations reveal that luminous quasars fall above the local correlation, although this is partly driven by an observational bias from selecting only luminous quasars [64, 66, 96]. Nevertheless, the high quasar luminosity makes these objects ideal laboratories to study feedback and joint evolution to understand what drives the growth of these SMBHs.

Generally, these observations reveal that luminous quasars fall above the local correlation, although this is partly driven by an observational bias from selecting only luminous quasars [64, 66, 96]. Nevertheless, the high quasar luminosity makes these objects ideal laboratories to study feedback and joint evolution to understand what drives the growth of these SMBHs.

papers.title: Diverse Stellar Components Resolved by JWST in the Massive Galaxy SPT0311-58
papers.abstract: SPT0311$-$58 is comprised of two clumpy dusty star-forming galaxies inhabiting a $z=6.9$ protocluster core. Within a $16$ kpc diameter, there are 26 spectroscopically confirmed members. The 12 highly dust-obscured clumps were identified by their rest-frame [CII] emission, and the 14 less obscured clumps in the rest-frame ultraviolet (UV). We present new NIRCam and MIRI imaging from JWST of the central regions, which respectively trace the rest-frame UV and near-infrared. Combining this imaging with supplementary data from the Hubble Space Telescope and Atacama Large Millimeter Array (ALMA) provides the most complete picture of SPT0311$-$58 to date. Using 14 photometric bands and ALMA dust continuum to model the spectral energy distribution of SPT0311$-$58, we present well-informed stellar masses and star-formation rates (SFR) on local ($\sim1.5$ kpc) and global scales. We find that SPT0311$-$58 has a total stellar mass of $M_\star=3.2^{+3.2}_{-1.6}\times10^{11}\, M_\odot$ and SFR of $1.5^{+0.89}_{-0.53}\times10^3\, M_\odot\, \text{yr}^{-1}$. We compare these measurements to simulations and known, rare classes of high-redshift objects observed by JWST, namely massive $z\approx6$--$8.5$ Lyman-break galaxies, $z>6$ quasars, and other merging/clumpy $z\sim6$--$7$ systems. SPT0311$-$58 is comparable to $z>6$ quasars in both stellar mass and SFR, but is more extreme than the other reference populations for both quantities. Additionally, we compare our measurements with the star-formation histories (SFH) of five massive quiescent galaxies from the Early eXtragalactic Continuum and Emission Line Science (EXCELS) survey. We find that SPT0311$-$58 has a higher SFR than expected from the SFHs of the EXCELS galaxies at $z=6.9$, but is otherwise a plausible progenitor to massive quiescent galaxies.

Dusty star-forming galaxies (DSFGs) are among the most extreme systems in the Universe [84, 13, 21]. These galaxies can have star-formation rates (SFR) reaching up to thousands of solar masses per year [63, 69, 33], and they contribute significantly to the total SFR density out to zz ∼\sim 4–5 [103]. DSFGs are highly luminous in the submillimeter regime because dust obscures and reprocesses rest-frame optical and ultraviolet (UV) stellar radiation into far-infrared/submillimeter emission. DSFGs can exhibit incredibly high SFRs, but vary in their mass-weighted SFRs, or specific SFRs (sSFR). When compared to the star-forming main sequence (SFMS), some DSFGs are consistent with the high mass expectation of a typical star-forming galaxy [68, 28, 34, 33], while others are clear starbursts [30, 62]. These intense episodes of star formation play a crucial role in the buildup of stellar mass, and such episodes are also thought to occur in the early formation histories of massive quiescent galaxies [93, 94]. Therefore, DSFGs have long been speculated to be viable progenitors of these massive elliptical/quiescent galaxies [13, 27, 83, 94, 87, 33, 10]. The discovery of quiescent galaxies beyond z>z> 3–4 [41, 36, 20, 19, 40], however, implies rapid formation between z∼6z\sim 6 –10 [3].

Additionally, 64 presented UV/optical photometry that revealed extended UV emission associated with SPT0311−-58E. At the time, imaging UV emission directly was somewhat rare among studies of DSFGs given the high dust obscuration of these systems. The resolution, however, was insufficient to enable a more detailed characterization of the stellar component.

papers.title: Euclid DR1 Legacy Science on Ultracool Dwarfs: Halpha activity, kinematic age and rotation of M7--L1 dwarfs from DESI DR1, SPHEREx and Euclid
papers.abstract: The fraction of late-M dwarfs with detectable Halpha rises toward the stellar-substellar boundary while their emission weakens relative to the bolometric luminosity, a contrast attributed to the fading continuum. We measure how much of this rise the continuum explains and whether younger populations or longer activity lifetimes contribute. We select 8939 dwarfs of type M7 or later, all but 22 of them M7-L1, from DESI DR1. We compare active fractions at common thresholds in equivalent width and in log(L_Ha/L_bol), the Halpha-to-bolometric luminosity ratio, in spectra sensitive to each threshold. We jointly model continuum fading, emission weakening and an extra active component. Kinematics use Gaia astrometry and DESI radial velocities for dwarfs with G < 19, free of proper-motion selection. From M7 to M9 the active fraction rises by 28 points at 5 Angstrom equivalent width. At log(L_Ha/L_bol) = -4.5 it falls by 23.5 points. SPHEREx and photometric bolometric fluxes agree within 0.03 dex. Joint fits require M8 emission to be 0.12-0.15 dex weaker than at M7. The brighter M8 dwarfs require an extra active component; the larger sample at most marginally. At log(L_Ha/L_bol) = -4.7, inactive M7 and M8 dwarfs have larger velocity dispersions than active ones. The measured rotators, mostly M6-M7 dwarfs, have saturated Halpha. Euclid DR1 NISP spectra of 152 M7-L1 dwarfs (144 at S/N >= 5) test the optical type scale, and VIS images resolve three close binaries (0.22-0.53 arcsec) with common proper motion. We confirm that the rise in equivalent-width incidence comes mostly from the fading continuum acting on weakening emission. Conditional on an age-velocity relation and uniform ages, a step model gives thin-disk activity lifetimes at log(L_Ha/L_bol) = -4.7 of 5.9 (5.3-6.6) and 6.4 (5.2-8.0) Gyr at M7 and M8. Both bins contain mostly stars, so these lifetimes describe the lowest-mass stars.

papers.intro:
The fraction of M dwarfs with detectable Hα\alpha emission rises toward the stellar–substellar boundary, while their Hα\alpha luminosity falls relative to the bolometric luminosity. Hα\alpha is a widely measured tracer of M-dwarf magnetic activity (Hawley et al. 1996; Reiners & Basri 2008). Both trends were found in nearby dwarfs (Gizis et al. 2000) and in spectra from the Sloan Digital Sky Survey (SDSS) and its Baryon Oscillation Spectroscopic Survey (BOSS) (West et al. 2004; Schmidt et al. 2015). The luminosity decline extends from late-M to L and T dwarfs (Mohanty & Basri 2003; Reiners & Basri 2010; Pineda et al. 2016). At these temperatures the photospheres become neutral enough that magnetic fields couple weakly to the gas (Mohanty et al. 2002; Rodríguez-Barrera et al. 2015). The two trends are compatible because the optical continuum fades faster than the line toward later types, so a line of falling luminosity can keep or gain equivalent width; the conversions from equivalent width to luminosity were introduced for this reason (Walkowicz et al. 2004; West & Hawley 2008; Schmidt et al. 2014). What has not been measured at M7–M9 is how much of the rise the continuum accounts for, whether the distribution of emission strength itself changes with type, and whether the dwarfs stay active for longer.

The M7–L1 range spans the hydrogen-burning limit (Kirkpatrick et al. 1999; Martín et al. 1999; Cruz et al. 2007; Kirkpatrick et al. 2021). Its population could become younger toward later types, because brown dwarfs cool through these types while hydrogen-burning stars stay in them (Burrows et al. 2001; Chabrier & Baraffe 2000). Activity could last longer at lower mass: Galactic dynamics imply activity lifetimes that increase through the M sequence (West et al. 2006; West et al. 2008), and age-calibrated activity and flare samples support a connection with age (Kiman et al. 2021; Medina et al. 2022). Empirical lithium ages, calibrated on open clusters, are harder to apply to field dwarfs this cool: even for members cooler than 4300 K in clusters of 60–300 Myr, two versions of one estimator differ by 37–136 Myr (Tata et al. 2026). Studies of late-M dwarfs have related activity to motion (Gizis et al. 2000; Bochanski et al. 2007a; Reiners & Basri 2009; Kiman et al. 2019), and L-dwarf studies extend the comparison across the boundary (Schmidt et al. 2007; Faherty et al. 2009; Zapatero Osorio et al. 2007; Seifahrt et al. 2010; Burgasser et al. 2015). Rotation is a second age-sensitive observable: slow mid-M rotators have larger dispersions (Newton et al. 2016; West et al. 2015), and Hα\alpha and X-ray activity saturate at rapid rotation and decline at longer periods (Newton et al. 2017; Wright et al. 2018), with complementary spectroscopic constraints from CARMENES (Jeffers et al. 2018). DESI is a 5000-fibre spectrograph on the Mayall 4 m telescope covering 3600–9824 Å (DESI Collaboration et al. 2016; DESI Collaboration et al. 2022), a range that includes Hα\alpha and the molecular bands used for typing. We combine these spectra with Gaia DR3 astrometry (Gaia Collaboration et al. 2016; Gaia Collaboration et al. 2023) and rotation periods from the TESS All-Sky Rotation Survey (Boyle et al. 2026), with further periods that we measured from public ZTF and TESS light curves (Bellm et al. 2019; Masci et al. 2019; Ricker et al. 2015). SPHEREx, the NASA all-sky spectral survey, measures 0.75–5 μ\mum spectrophotometry across the sky (Doré et al. 2018; Crill et al. 2020; Bock et al. 2026). With Gaia parallaxes the bolometric fluxes give luminosities, which we use beside spectral type as the independent variable. Near-infrared luminosity at fixed type, from 2MASS and Gaia, picks out unresolved binaries. papers.title: Kinetic-Ballooning and Resistive X-Point Dynamics in Quasicontinuous Exhaust Tokamak Plasmas
papers.abstract: We investigate quasicoherent modes (QCMs) and their interaction with scrape-off-layer (SOL) plasma blobs (filaments) in the type-I-ELM-free quasicontinuous exhaust (QCE) regime, extending the analysis in [K. Zhang et al., Phys. Rev. Lett. 137, 055102 (2026)]. Two-fluid electromagnetic turbulence simulations are compared for two self-consistent turbulence states with different separatrix densities. In both cases, a separatrix-spanning QCM resides within the radial-electric-field well, whereas blobs are observed only in the case with higher separatrix density. The QCM exhibits similar kinetic-ballooning-mode (KBM) signatures in both cases, with modest differences in coherence and harmonic content. The primary difference is the presence of an additional resistive X-point mode (RXM), which emerges as the near-X-point collisionality increases. The coexistence of the KBM and RXM shifts the potential--density cross-phase from its KBM-like value toward the interchange value in the SOL, allowing QCM perturbations to be ejected as blobs. These intermittent blobs account for over half of the net radial $E\times B$ transport in the far SOL. Neither QCM onset nor blob ejection requires an increase in upstream collisionality. The results distinguish the KBM-dominated mechanism that regulates the pedestal from the RXM-assisted blob-launching mechanism that enables intermittent SOL exhaust.

Reconciling high energy confinement with tolerable steady-state exhaust remains a central challenge for magnetic-confinement fusion [1]. Type-I edge-localized modes (ELMs) contribute to particle and impurity exhaust, but the associated transient heat loads pose a severe threat to plasma-facing components in reactor-scale devices such as ITER and DEMO [2, 3]. Even in the absence of ELMs, the narrow scrape-off-layer (SOL) heat-flux footprint presents a major difficulty. Multi-machine regressions indicate that the SOL heat-flux decay length scales approximately as λq∝Bpol−1\lambda_{q}\propto B_{\mathrm{pol}}^{-1} [4], leading to a millimeter-scale exhaust channel when extrapolated to ITER conditions [5, 4]. An attractive reactor regime must therefore combine an H-mode pedestal and the absence of large ELMs with sufficiently strong, continuous radial transport to broaden the exhaust footprint.

The enhanced-Dα (EDA) and quasicontinuous-exhaust (QCE) regimes are prominent examples of such type-I-ELM-free operation. EDA was first identified in Alcator C-Mod [6] and is characterized by a persistent electromagnetic fluctuation known as the quasicoherent mode (QCM). The QCM is localized around the pedestal foot, where it provides continuous particle transport, limits pedestal growth, and mitigates impurity accumulation. EDA is typically accessed at moderately high plasma shaping and separatrix density nsepn_{\mathrm{sep}} [7, 8]. QCE, first observed in ASDEX Upgrade (named type-II ELMs[9] and later renamed to QCE [10]) and subsequently realized in TCV [11] and JET [12], generally requires stronger shaping and higher nsepn_{\mathrm{sep}} [13, 14]. Its pedestal remains close to marginal stability against high-nn ballooning modes localized near the separatrix [15, 16]. QCE plasmas also exhibit QCM-like fluctuations, although their frequency spectra are generally broader than those measured in EDA [17]. The experimentally observed continuous transition from EDA to QCE with increasing nsepn_{\mathrm{sep}} suggests that a common QCM-like instability contributes to pedestal regulation in both regimes [18, 17, 19].
