QCMs have been observed in both EDA and QCE regimes and studied extensively across several devices. Although the radial envelope of the QCM is generally understood to span the separatrix [17, 22], measurements of its propagation direction and density–potential cross-phase αϕ,n\alpha_{\phi,n} differ among devices, leading to different interpretations of the underlying instability. Within a simplified classification based on linear instabilities, drift-wave-like fluctuations are characterized by 0<αϕ,n<π/20<\alpha_{\phi,n}<\pi/2 and typically propagate in the electron-diamagnetic direction. Kinetic-shear-Alfvén-wave-like fluctuations are characterized by π/2<αϕ,n<π\pi/2<\alpha_{\phi,n}<\pi and are generally associated with propagation in the ion-diamagnetic direction. A cross-phase of αϕ,n=π/2\alpha_{\phi,n}=\pi/2 is characteristic of a pure interchange response, without a strong preference for either diamagnetic propagation direction. In Alcator C-Mod, the QCM was initially interpreted as a resistive X-point mode [23] and was subsequently associated with an electron drift wave with electromagnetic contributions [24, 25, 26]. These interpretations were consistent with observations of propagation in the electron-diamagnetic direction and a small cross-phase, αϕ,n∼0\alpha_{\phi,n}\sim 0 [26]. Later measurements in Alcator C-Mod by Theiler et al. [22], however, indicated propagation in the ion-diamagnetic direction near the minimum of the radial electric field ErE_{r}, where the QCM is localized. Consistent with this result, measurements in AUG showed that the QCM propagates in the ion-diamagnetic direction within the ErE_{r} well, with a plasma-frame phase velocity approximately one half of the ion diamagnetic velocity [17]. The corresponding density–potential cross-phase is close to αϕ,n∼π\alpha_{\phi,n}\sim\pi [17, 27]. These signatures are more consistent with kinetic-shear-Alfvén dynamics and a kinetic ballooning mode (KBM) than with a conventional electron drift wave. The diagnostic picture nevertheless changes outside the separatrix. In the AUG SOL, the measured cross-phase decreases toward αϕ,n∼0\alpha_{\phi,n}\sim 0 [27], resembling the phase relation reported in some earlier Alcator C-Mod observations. The apparent differences among these measurements may therefore reflect a genuine radial variation in the QCM dynamics rather than mutually exclusive mode identifications.

The mechanism by which edge turbulence generates blobs depends on the confinement regime and remains incompletely understood [28]. Candidate mechanisms include nonlinear drift-wave dynamics [29], interchange instability [30], and Kelvin–Helmholtz instability driven by shear in the E×BE\times B flow [31]. The QCM-identification and blob-launching problems are inseparable. If the same dominant instability drives QCM in both EDA-like and QCE states, what will enable QCM-scale perturbations to develop into radially propagating blobs in QCE but not under EDA conditions? The onset of blobs must result either from a qualitative change in the nonlinear dynamics of QCM or from its interaction with the mean flow or an additional mode. These possibilities remain unresolved.

papers.title: Weight-space programming for tractor guidance controller: large language models natively write neural network weights that steer a real tractor
papers.abstract: Weight-space programming is a process where a large language model reads and writes the weights of a neural network directly, guided by a natural language specification, without an optimiser or gradient descent. This study applies it to automatic tractor guidance, where a 253-parameter neural network steers along paths of lines and arcs and must be adapted when the machine changes, such as a slower steering actuator. GPT-6 Astra and Claude Fable 5.1 (also 5.2) edited the network for our research tractor using a small budget of simulated evaluations to repair a network trained for another tractor and write a controller into a network with zero weights. We compared them with an evolution strategy, gradient descent and pure pursuit in simulation and on the real tractor. Both models read the network and analysed the closed loop with control theory correctly, and Fable's repair without simulation succeeded only occasionally. With simulated feedback, both models repaired the trained network in single sessions and wrote a working controller from zero weights, whereas from zero the evolution strategy found none. The controllers written from zero were sparse and in a classical cascaded structure; one model edited the trained network while the other replaced it. Gradient descent reached higher accuracy with far more simulation, and all language model controllers steered the real tractor without intervention, with errors of the same order as pure pursuit. Language models can program the weights of a neural controller directly, much as control engineers design one. We call this Weight-Space Engineering.

papers.intro:
Weight-space programming is a process where a general-purpose large language model (LLM) reads and writes the weights of a neural network directly, guided by a natural-language specification instead of an optimiser or gradient descent (Takehi et al., 2026). The MIT Computer Science and Artificial Intelligence Laboratory (CSAIL) introduced the term weight-space programming in a research blog post on 2 November 2026 (Takehi et al., 2026). This study employed the AMX G-trac tractor as the target machine (Fig. 1). To illustrate this concept, every weight of a network may be viewed as a knob (Fig. 2).

Weight-space programming is a process where a general-purpose large language model (LLM) reads and writes the weights of a neural network directly, guided by a natural-language specification instead of an optimiser or gradient descent (Takehi et al., 2026). The MIT Computer Science and Artificial Intelligence Laboratory (CSAIL) introduced the term weight-space programming in a research blog post on 2 November 2026 (Takehi et al., 2026). This study employed the AMX G-trac tractor as the target machine (Fig. 1). To illustrate this concept, every weight of a network may be viewed as a knob (Fig. 2).

A human engineer chooses the network architecture, the data or the reward, and the loss, and a numerical optimiser then tunes every weight by gradient descent. In reinforcement learning, the gradient comes from the reward, for example with proximal policy optimisation (PPO) (Schulman et al., 2017; Andrychowicz et al., 2021). The resulting controller works but remains a black box, where every weight is used and no one can explain why a single number has its value. A trained policy is tied to its plant, as a model-free policy learned for one actuator delay does not transfer to another delay (Chen et al., 2021). Therefore, adapting a trained network to a new machine means retraining it.

GPT-6 Astra repaired a failing reinforcement-learning policy for a car in the Kinetix physics environment in one reply, which changed 3.5 % of the weights (Takehi et al., 2026). The model also wrote game-playing networks into all-zero weights, and these played better than networks trained with proximal policy optimisation for 100 million steps (Takehi et al., 2026). First follow-up studies verified discrete decision policies by model checking (Gross, 2026) and debugged a robot policy in simulation (Zhang et al., 2026). However, all these results concern games, discrete tasks or simulation. This study addresses whether the same capability can serve the engineering of a controller for a physical machine, with feedback dynamics, limits and safety.

In this paper, automatic guidance means steering a tractor along a path with satellite positioning, such as GNSS or earlier GPS. This paper sorts tractor guidance controllers into eras by who writes the controller and in what form (Table 1), where the eras overlap and do not replace each other. In Era 1, a human writes a control law with a few hand-tuned parameters. A tractor was steered automatically with centimetre-level GPS in 1997 by a state-feedback law whose gains were computed once offline from weights chosen by the engineer (O’Connor, 1997). Autosteering systems typically use PID control on the cross-track error with gains set by trial and error (Heraud and Lange, 2009), and pure pursuit has the look-ahead distance as its single parameter (Coulter, 1992; Snider, 2009). In Era 2, a human writes a model and a cost, and a numerical optimiser computes the action online from them, which includes nonlinear model predictive control of tractors and tractor-implement combinations (Backman et al., 2012; Kayacan et al., 2018; Soitinaho and Oksanen, 2023; Moll and Oksanen, 2026), although the weights of its cost function still need manual tuning (Backman et al., 2011). Era 3 involves a numerical optimiser writing the weights of a neural network from data or reward, such as deep reinforcement learning on a simulated field robot (Baby et al., 2024) and headland turns of the AMX G-trac learned with proximal policy optimisation and tested on the real tractor (Pindl et al., 2024). Mixing eras, for example nonlinear model predictive control with a neural network, is not a new era. Era 4 consists of an LLM writing the weights of a neural network from understanding, which this paper addresses.

Weight-space programming is the act of reading, explaining, repairing or writing weights directly for tasks such as games, text and images (Takehi et al., 2026). Programming is the act of writing code, whereas software engineering is the systematic, disciplined and quantifiable approach to developing, operating and maintaining software. This paper defines the term Weight-Space Engineering (WSE), which relates to weight-space programming as software engineering relates to programming and contains weight-space programming as one step. Weight-Space Engineering applies where the network acts in a technical system with physical consequences, for example a controller in a feedback loop with a plant. For a feedback controller, Weight-Space Engineering is control engineering, and this approach generalises to engineering in general. In WSE the human engineer works one level up and provides a specification of the plant, objective and limits, and gives knowledge of the field, such as control theory and intentions, but never the direction of an edit. The engineer does not explain what each number of the network means and may not know it, while the LLM grasps the network through the given theory and designs inside the network itself. Weight-Space Engineering keeps the parts of an engineering process and their costs, including evaluations, tokens, time and the engineer’s effort. This process includes verification and validation through unseen tests, analysis with the theory of the field and a test on the machine, as well as deployment and maintenance, such as adapting a network to a changed machine. Traceability is maintained where the stated reasoning is checked against the result. In classical control engineering, the engineer designs the control law, whereas in WSE the engineer specifies, gives the theory, sets the evaluation budget and verifies, while the LLM designs. Table 7 lists each element of Weight-Space Engineering and how this study followed it.

papers.title: Every Measurement, Every Direction, All at Once: Multimodal Flow Matching for Molecules and Spectra
papers.abstract: Generative modeling in science is often data-limited, where experiments are expensive. However, each experiment may yield several coupled measurements of the same physical entity. Standard generative models often train only on a single direction, discarding supervision from the rest. We argue that each experiment contains more training signal than this asymmetry allows the model to exploit: random masking enables measurements to serve as either conditioning inputs or prediction targets, yielding multiple supervised denoising tasks from a single experiment. We investigate this premise with MOSAIC, a multimodal flow matching transformer over molecular 3D structure and UV, IR, and Raman spectra. MOSAIC is a single model that is capable of any-to-any generation: generating any subset of modalities from any disjoint subset of the others. On QM9S, MOSAIC achieves 88.8% molecular graph recovery, outperforming the strongest spectra-to-structure baseline by 23.2% in structure generation, while simultaneously outperforming a structure-to-spectra specialist model in spectral generation. Ablations show that the any-to-any objective improves structure generation over structure-only training across model sizes. Furthermore, MOSAIC supports arbitrary subsets of available measurements and enables molecular identification by matching generated spectra to experimental references.
papers.intro:
In scientific domains, experiments can be costly but often provide several complementary sources of information: a molecule pairs a three-dimensional structure with simulated UV, IR, and Raman spectra (Figure 1, left) [1, 2], each offering a distinct view of the same physical entity [3]. These views are physically linked, molecular structure governs the spectral response, while UV, IR, and Raman spectra constrain the structures consistent with them. Standard conditional generative models typically learn only one direction of this relationship, such as generating molecular structures from spectra. We argue that this asymmetry arises from task setup rather than the data itself: When scientific measurements are coupled by a shared underlying system and co-occur at training time, every view carries supervision about that system [4, 5]. Generative models that impose a constraint on the direction(s) of generation potentially leave untapped supervision signal on the table.

Consequently, we propose that multimodal generative models should be trained with no such constraint as shown in Figure 2a. Every modality can act as either a target or condition. Therefore, one expensive sample yields multiple supervised denoising tasks for the same model. Our approach significantly expands the model’s inference-time capabilities (Figure 2c). It can perform inference across arbitrary observed and target modality subsets, unlocking capabilities such as matching to spectral libraries, missing-modality imputation, structure-to-spectra generation, and cross-spectra translation.

MOSAIC encodes molecular structures into per-atom latent representations using a UAE-3D autoencoder [6], while representing UV, IR, and Raman spectra as sequences of spectral tokens. Unlike the equivariant denoiser used in prior work [8], our model operates on learned structural representations. papers.title: Quality Control for the LGAD sensors of the ATLAS High Granularity Timing Detector
papers.abstract: The High Granularity Timing Detector (HGTD) currently in the production phase will mainly mitigate the pile-up effect in the ATLAS forward region and serve for bunch-by-bunch luminosity measurements in the high-luminosity (HL) phase of the Large Hadron Collider (LHC). The HGTD utilizes Low Gain Avalanche Detector (LGAD) technology, covering the pseudorapidity range between 2.4 and 4.0, and provides high-precision timing information to distinguish collisions occurring close in space but well-separated in time. A pre-production batch of 8-inch silicon wafers was fabricated and a systematic quality control test campaign was carried out. This paper describes the Quality Control (QC) required for full-size (15 $\times$ 15 array) sensors, including leakage-current and breakdown measurements performed on all sensors at the vendor sites, as well as more detailed electrical characterizations at the participating ATLAS-HGTD institutes. In addition, the electrical characterization of full-size sensors after irradiation is reported.

papers.intro:
The High Luminosity phase of the Large Hadron Collider (HL-LHC) will reach an instantaneous luminosity of 7.5 ×\times 1034 cm-2s-1 [2]. A new High Granularity Timing Detector (HGTD) will be installed in front of the end-cap and forward calorimeter at 2.4 << |η||\eta| << 4.0 to measure charged-particle trajectories in time and space, mitigating pile-up and increasing the reach of the new all-silicon Inner Tracker (ITk) [1]. The Low Gain Avalanche Detector (LGAD) [16], based on an n-in-p structure with a p-type gain layer beneath the np junction on the top side and reversely biased from the back side, was chosen as the sensing technology. The internal gain degrades after irradiation due to acceptor removal in the LGAD gain layer [10, 4]. In order to partially compensate for the loss of gain, the operating bias voltage should be increased but is limited to 550 V (corresponding to an average electric field of 11 V/µ​m11\text{\,}\mathrm{V}\mathrm{/}\mathrm{\SIUnitSymbolMicro}\mathrm{m} for an active sensor thickness of 50 µ50\text{\,}\mathrm{\SIUnitSymbolMicro}), to avoid destructive single-event burnout (SEB) from localized high ionization charges [11, 3]. A single bias voltage will be applied to the back side of the two LGAD sensors assembled in one module with two readout ASIC chips during the operation. The sensors are required to have a time resolution better than 40 ps at the start-of-life for a Minimum Ionizing Particle (MIP). After receiving an end-of-life fluence of 2.5 ×\times 1015\mathrm{10^{15}} neq/cm2\mathrm{n_{eq}/cm^{2}} (1 MeV neutron equivalent fluence), the sensors should maintain a time resolution better than 50 ps, and a most probable collected charge of at least 4 fC.

During the past decade, LGAD technology has been widely developed by many producers, including CNM [15], FBK [18], HPK [6], BNL [8], IHEP-IME [20] and USTC-IME [12]. The ATLAS-HGTD collaboration conducted a systematic evaluation of the most promising LGAD options from multiple vendors, covering both laboratory measurements and test-beam results [13]. Ultimately, two sensor designs were adopted: the IHEP-IME version (designed by IHEP and fabricated by IME) and the USTC-IME version (designed by USTC and fabricated by IME). The two designs are independent, although they share the same production facility at IME. Taking into account an estimated assembly yield of 75%\%, ATLAS-HGTD will require approximately 22000 full-size (15 ×\times 15 array) good sensors.

To validate the feasibility of final production, a pre-production batch was produced between early 2023 and the end of 2024, corresponding to at least 5% of the total quantity of sensors. The pre-production was accompanied by systematic quality control tests. One area of quality control is the electrical characterization of 15 ×\times 15 array sensors. Company Quality Control (CQC) comprises Current-Voltage (I−VI-V) characterization at the vendor sites, using a single probe needle or a 15 ×\times 1 probe card. Another aspect of quality control, called Sensor Quality Control (SQC) on a subset of sensors after Under Bump Metallization (UBM) deposition and dicing, includes per-pad I−VI-V tests at the participating ATLAS-HGTD institutes using probe needles under conditions identical to CQC and a matrix test using a 15 ×\times 15 probe card. The gain layer depletion voltage is extracted from the Capacitance-Voltage (C−VC-V) data. The results of the SQC measurements are used to validate and refine the CQC measurement setups and the CQC procedures to be performed on all sensors during the production phase. Electrical characterization of sensors after irradiation is performed, to validate the radiation hardness and complement dedicated irradiation tests on QC-TS reported previously [19]. This paper is organized as follows: Section 2 lists the acceptance criteria, Section 3 describes the samples and experimental setup, Section 4 presents the results of the CQC and Section 5 shows the results of the SQC. The results of irradiated sensors are discussed in Section 6. Section 7 gives the conclusions.

papers.title: Explicit Dual Model Predictive Path Integral Control
papers.abstract: In this work, we present a fully sampling-based explicit dual control algorithm that combines a particle filter and model predictive path integral control for partially observed nonlinear systems. The key idea is to roll out multiple sampled input sequences from all particles of the particle filter to obtain a belief-averaged control cost that induces caution. The same rollouts are used to sample imagined future measurements, which are drawn from the predictive distribution of the particle belief. This results in a Monte Carlo information term that gives a sample estimate of the expected information gain of each sampled input sequence and thereby induces probing. In contrast to existing explicit dual control schemes, the proposed scheme neither relies on gradients of the dynamics or measurement models nor requires a Gaussian belief. Furthermore, all computations can be parallelized across input sequences, particles, and imagined measurements, which makes the scheme amenable to real-time implementation on suitable hardware. We demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method in a simulation example of a planar terrain-aided navigation task.
papers.intro:
In many applications, a controller has to regulate a nonlinear system whose state or parameters cannot be measured directly and can only be inferred from noisy and possibly non-injective measurements, which makes learning about the system and controlling it inseparable tasks. In this setting, the optimal stochastic output-feedback controller acts on the belief, i.e., the conditional probability distribution of the hidden variables given all past inputs and outputs (Mesbah, 2018). Since the applied inputs determine which measurements are collected in the future, they also shape future beliefs, which is known as the dual effect (Feldbaum, 1960; Bar-Shalom and Tse, 1974). The optimal dual controller therefore exhibits two properties: it acts with caution where the hidden variables are uncertain, and it probes the system to reduce this uncertainty whenever the expected gain in future performance outweighs the resulting deviation from the control task (Bar-Shalom and Tse, 1976). In principle, the optimal policy can be computed by stochastic dynamic programming (SDP) in the belief space (Feldbaum, 1960), which, however, is tractable only for small problems, since the belief is in general infinite-dimensional. Approximations are commonly classified into implicit and explicit dual control methods (Mesbah, 2018).

In principle, the optimal policy can be computed by stochastic dynamic programming (SDP) in the belief space (Feldbaum, 1960), which, however, is tractable only for small problems, since the belief is in general infinite-dimensional. Approximations are commonly classified into implicit and explicit dual control methods (Mesbah, 2018).

Implicit dual control methods approximate the SDP problem directly such that caution and probing emerge implicitly from their optimal solution. For example, wide-sense dual control methods compute a series expansion of the cost-to-go around a nominal trajectory and propagate only the mean and variance of the belief inside the prediction (Tse et al., 1973; Klenske and Hennig, 2016). Other implicit methods use techniques from approximate dynamic programming, such as scenario-based formulations (Arcari et al., 2020a; Arcari et al., 2020b; Hanssen and Foss, 2015), iterative dynamic programming (Thompson and Cluett, 2005), or forward dynamic programming (Bayard and Schumitzky, 2010). Online POMDP solvers with particle beliefs (Silver and Veness, 2010; Somani et al., 2013; Sunberg and Kochenderfer, 2018) can also be regarded as implicit dual controllers; they are gradient-free, handle multi-modal beliefs, and can include information rewards (Araya-López et al., 2010; Fischer and Tas, 2020), but their search trees grow quickly with the horizon for continuous actions and observations. In general, the computational cost of implicit methods hinders their application to systems that require high control frequencies (Mesbah, 2018).

Explicit dual control methods circumvent the computational complexity by introducing a heuristic probing mechanism into the control formulation. This can be achieved, e.g., by imposing persistent excitation constraints on the inputs (Marafioti et al., 2014), by adding a cost term that penalizes predicted model or state uncertainty (Heirung et al., 2015; Hovd and Bitmead, 2004), by maximizing a measure of the information matrix (Rathouský and Havlena, 2013), or by rewarding an information-theoretic measure of the expected learning (Alpcan and Shames, 2015). While computationally efficient, explicit methods often require differentiable models to construct the probing mechanism and are solved by gradient-based solvers, which struggle with highly nonlinear or non-smooth models and non-convex costs (Rawlings et al., 2017).

While computationally efficient, explicit methods often require differentiable models to construct the probing mechanism and are solved by gradient-based solvers, which struggle with highly nonlinear or non-smooth models and non-convex costs (Rawlings et al., 2017).

Sampling-based approaches such as Model Predictive Path Integral (MPPI) control instead update a nominal input sequence by a cost-weighted average of sampled sequences (Williams et al., 2018). Since only forward evaluations of the dynamics are required, the rollouts can be parallelized, which has enabled real-time control of small-scale vehicles (Williams et al., 2017), agile drones (Zhai et al., 2026), and legged robots (Alvarez-Padilla et al., 2025). In output-feedback settings, MPPI is commonly combined with a filter whose point estimate is treated as exact, i.e., under certainty equivalence, while cautious MPPI variants (Abraham et al., 2020; Das and Tanaka, 2026) and particle-based output-feedback MPC (Stahl and Hauth, 2011; Sehr and Bitmead, 2017) account for the uncertainty, but only learn passively, since their open-loop input sequences cannot anticipate future measurements (Bar-Shalom and Tse, 1974).

To compute an explicit information term, a prediction of the future belief is required. Dual control schemes commonly represent the belief and its predicted evolution by a Gaussian propagated through Kalman filter recursions (Hovd and Bitmead, 2004; Arcari et al., 2020b; Messerer et al., 2023), which poorly approximates the multimodal beliefs that often arise from nonlinear dynamics and non-injective measurements. Particle filters (PFs) represent such beliefs by weighted samples and only require forward evaluations of the dynamics and the measurement likelihood (Chen, 2003), which matches the computational structure of MPPI. In dual control, PF beliefs have been combined with different mechanisms to predict the effect of future measurements on the belief: Flayac et al. (2017); Flayac et al. (2018) augment a PF-based controller with an information term derived from the Fisher information matrix, but require gradients of the measurement model; Chen et al. (2021) predict the PF posterior under hypothesized future measurements, but only for a finite set of admissible actions; Knaup et al. (2024) use a PF within MPPI to estimate unknown parameters, but predict the future belief from the expected state under the current belief, similar to the maximum-likelihood observation assumption in belief-space planning (Platt et al., 2010), which induces probing only through a bias in the predicted belief rather than through a grounded information term.

papers.title: As Student Rollouts Continue, Visual Backdoors Keep Growing
papers.abstract:
Conventional knowledge distillation can facilitate the propagation of backdoors from teacher models to student models. However, how this risk manifests in On-Policy Distillation (OPD) remains insufficiently studied. OPD has recently emerged as an important post-training paradigm for Vision-Language Models (VLMs). Unlike traditional offline distillation, OPD does not require teacher-generated responses. Instead, it uses the teacher's probability distributions to supervise response trajectories generated online by the student. Since the initial student model typically generates benign responses and receives no explicit supervision from malicious target responses, OPD appears to offer some inherent resistance to backdoor propagation.
  In this paper, we challenge this intuition and reveal a more subtle risk of visual backdoor propagation in OPD. Through experiments across multiple model families and datasets, together with theoretical analysis, we identify three main findings. First, unlike the relatively gradual propagation observed in traditional offline distillation, backdoors rarely emerge in OPD at low poisoning ratios. However, the attack success rate rapidly approaches 100% once a critical threshold is exceeded. Second, backdoor propagation does not depend on explicit malicious responses. Instead, it is driven by the continuous accumulation of anomalous probability mass assigned by the teacher. Finally, based on these findings, we propose a novel trigger design that enables visual backdoor propagation with zero explicit trigger injection. These findings further reveal an overlooked mechanism of backdoor propagation in OPD and highlight its potential security risks.

papers.intro:
In recent years, On-Policy Distillation (OPD) has become an important paradigm for the post-training of large language models (LLMs) and has been increasingly applied to Vision-Language Models (VLMs) (Agarwal et al., 2024). OPD enables effective knowledge transfer by supervising student-generated response trajectories with token-level probability distributions from a teacher model. Recent studies have further demonstrated its effectiveness in visual reasoning and fine-grained visual understanding tasks (Bousselham et al., 2025; Yoon et al., 2026). However, OPD is fundamentally a form of Knowledge Distillation (KD). Therefore, it may also transfer malicious behaviors embedded in the teacher model while transferring beneficial capabilities. Traditional KD typically uses teacher-generated responses, output distributions, or intermediate features for supervision (Kim and Rush, 2016). As a result, backdoors in the teacher model may propagate to the student through these relatively fixed supervision paths (Chen et al., 2024a). Such backdoor transfer is relatively straightforward, and its propagation conditions, attack effectiveness, and defense methods have been extensively studied (Ge et al., 2021; Chen et al., 2025; Chen et al., 2024b). In contrast, OPD introduces online student sampling and dynamic probability supervision. However, the patterns and underlying mechanisms of backdoor propagation under this different distillation paradigm remain insufficiently studied.

However, the patterns and underlying mechanisms of backdoor propagation under this different distillation paradigm remain insufficiently studied.

Unlike traditional offline distillation, OPD does not rely on fixed response trajectories generated by the teacher in advance. Instead, the student generates responses online under its current policy and aligns its probability distribution with that of the teacher through Reverse-KL divergence. Since the initial student model typically generates benign responses and receives no explicit supervision from malicious target responses, OPD appears to offer some inherent resistance to backdoor propagation. We then inject a certain proportion of triggered samples into the downstream OPD training data. This allows the student to learn the backdoor behavior without explicit malicious response labels.

papers.title: Stochastic Dynamics of Domain Walls on a Racetrack: Impact of Inhomogeneity of Magnetic Anisotropy
papers.abstract: Racetrack memory is a spintronic technology that stores information in current-driven magnetic domain walls (DW), offering a promising route toward non-volatile, high-density, and high-speed memory devices. In ultrathin magnetic films, atomic-scale interface disorder can produce spatially inhomogeneous magnetic anisotropy, creating a complex spatially varying energy landscape that strongly influences DW motion. In this work, we model anisotropy inhomogeneities using a two-dimensional fractal Weierstrass--Mandelbrot function, which provides independent control over the disorder amplitude and characteristic spatial scale. Micromagnetic simulations reveal pronounced stochasticity of current-driven domain-wall transport even in the absence of thermal fluctuations. Transport is quantified by the transmission fraction, defined as the fraction of DWs that successfully reach a detector after propagating through a disordered racetrack. We investigate its dependence on current density, disorder amplitude, and the spatial scale of the anisotropy inhomogeneity. The resulting transmission statistics are described by Gaussian error-function profiles and exhibit a universal scaling behavior upon normalization by the corresponding median values. Statistical analysis of DW trajectories further characterizes the disorder-induced fluctuations of the propagation process. The variance of the random DW positions shows a pronounced dependence on disorder amplitude and is well described by the proposed phenomenological model. These results provide a quantitative framework for describing stochastic DW transport in structurally disordered racetracks and establish disorder-induced reliability limits in racetrack-memory devices.

Owing to its non-volatility, high storage density, fast operation, and potential for three-dimensional integration, racetrack memory is considered a strong candidate for next-generation memory and logic architectures [61, 4, 25, 12]. Continued advances in materials engineering and magnetic-texture manipulation are essential for realizing reliable and scalable racetrack-memory devices [35].

One of the major challenges in racetrack memory is the stochastic nature of magnetic-texture motion [52, 47, 32]. In practical devices, densely packed spin textures must be displaced and detected with high precision [34]. Thermal fluctuations constitute an unavoidable source of stochasticity in magnetic systems, while nonequilibrium spin-current noise associated with spin-transfer and spin-orbit torque mechanisms can further influence the dynamics of magnetic textures [17, 9, 49, 30].

Such quenched disorder gives rise to pinning, depinning transitions, threshold currents, and velocity fluctuations, resulting in stochastic domain-wall propagation [57, 31, 59, 63, 22, 43, 27].

A common approach to modeling disorder-induced pinning is to represent structural inhomogeneities as discrete pinning centers. Within this framework, the dynamics of domain walls has been studied in terms of the density and spatial distribution of pinning sites, with the characteristic distance between pinning centers relative to the domain-wall width playing an important role in determining the transport properties [24, 37, 36, 19]. Other approaches account for more extended or granular forms of disorder, providing descriptions of inhomogeneities specific to particular magnetic material [8, 11]. For skyrmions, however, the discrete-pinning-center picture may not adequately describe the experimentally observed transport behavior. It was demonstrated in Ref. [62] that short-scale spatial variations of the energy landscape can strongly pin skyrmions, resulting in finite critical currents, reduced velocities, and current-induced annihilation of pinned textures. This work highlighted the importance of disorder length scales comparable to the characteristic size of a magnetic texture, motivating a multiscale description of the disorder landscape.

papers.title: Personalized Causal Low-Bitrate Coded Speech Restoration with Speaker Embeddings
papers.abstract: Legacy low-bitrate speech codecs such as AMR-NB remain widely used in telephony, where they restrict speech bandwidth and degrade listening quality. Coded speech restoration (CSR) aims to restore the speech bandwidth while improving the overall quality of coded speech, but typically without adapting to different speakers. In this paper, we systematically investigate personalization for restoration of speech coded at low bitrates, using a causal, low-complexity Universal Bandwidth Extension Generative Adversarial Network (UBGAN) model as the basis. We propose two personalization methods based on speaker embeddings, which incur little additional computational cost at inference: (i) conditioning a single CSR model on speaker embeddings, and (ii) cluster-based model selection, where multiple personalized models are trained on clusters of acoustically similar speakers. Experiments are performed on AMR-NB coded speech at 4.75 kbps. Experimental results with disjoint seen- and unseen-speaker test sets show that cluster-based model selection does not consistently outperform the non-personalized UBGAN baseline, whereas embedding conditioning significantly improves ViSQOL and WB-PESQ scores for both seen and unseen speakers.

papers.intro:
Despite recent advances in neural speech and audio coding [15], low-resource telephony networks continue to rely on legacy low-bitrate codecs such as AMR-NB [1], which restrict the coded speech bandwidth, degrade listening quality, and contribute to listener fatigue [2]. Therefore, BWE (BWE) is typically included as part of CSR (CSR) [25, 31, 12]. However, BWE can also magnify existing artifacts: distortions present in the lower band may propagate into the generated high-frequency content, potentially reducing overall quality [12]. For this reason, a target sampling rate of 16 kHz is often an appropriate compromise between increasing speech bandwidth beyond narrowband telephony and avoiding excessive amplification of codec artifacts at higher target sampling rates. Nevertheless, even at 16 kHz, residual codec artifacts and a loss of speaker-specific nuances may persist, raising the question of whether personalized CSR can help mitigate these effects.

Personalization for CSR is motivated by the success of personalization in related areas such as speech enhancement [17, 26, 27, 10, 34], BWE [32], text-to-speech synthesis [5], automatic speech recognition [6, 7], voice activity detection and diarization [9, 20], and neural speech codecs [14]. In these works, two main methods are commonly explored. One line of research conditions a single model on speaker embeddings [10, 32, 5, 34, 6, 7, 9, 20], allowing a single model to adapt to different speakers. Following another research direction, multiple models are trained for small groups (clusters) of speakers, often combined with speaker-informed model selection at test time [17, 26, 27, 14]. Such clusters are typically obtained by grouping speakers in an embedding space. Because a personalized system can, in principle, exploit characteristic voice traits such as rhythm and timbre [30], it is worth investigating whether personalization can also improve CSR. Despite this potential, to the best of our knowledge, personalization has not yet been systematically investigated for CSR.

This paper investigates personalization for causal low-bitrate CSR using the Universal Bandwidth Extension Generative Adversarial Network (UBGAN) [12] as a non-personalized CSR basis, aiming to restore 8 kHz AMR-NB coded speech at 4.75 kbps to 16 kHz wideband speech. At test time, we assume that a short clean enrollment utterance from the same speaker is available, from which a speaker embedding is computed. We consider and compare two alternative personalization methods for CSR: (i) embedding conditioning, which conditions a single CSR model on speaker embeddings; and (ii) cluster-based model selection, which trains a separate CSR model per cluster. Both methods are designed to introduce only minimal additional computational cost to the CSR model at test time. Whereas [24] explored these personalization methods with a non-causal HiFi-GAN+ [28] basis, in this paper we investigate whether they also benefit a causal, low-delay, and low-complexity UBGAN CSR model, and additionally evaluate a hybrid combining both methods. An experimental comparison is provided on the VCTK dataset [33] for both seen speakers included in the training set and held-out unseen speakers.

papers.title: Sub-electron noise with a buried-channel DePFET: characterisation of novel DePFET concepts
papers.abstract: Depleted P-channel Field Effect Transistor (DePFET) pixel sensors combine Fano-limited energy resolution with fast, low-noise readout and are used in instruments ranging from particle tracking to X-ray astronomy. In this work, two novel DePFET technologies that address the two factors of the signal-to-noise ratio through fundamental changes to the intrinsic design are characterised: a buried-channel design aimed at reducing the limiting low-frequency noise by weakening the coupling between the channel and Si/SiO$_2$ interface traps, and a super-$g_q$ design intended to increase the charge gain by reducing the effective internal-gate capacitance. Their noise and energy resolution were mapped across the transistor bias space, over a wide temperature range (100-260 K) and for integration times of 0.4-9 $\mu$s (readout times of 2-19.2 $\mu$s per row), and compared with standard DePFETs as developed for the NewAthena Wide Field Imager (WFI). All three variants reach their lowest noise at about 155 K. The buried-channel device achieves an excellent equivalent noise charge (ENC) of 0.96 e$^-$ (at most 0.83 e$^-$ after subtracting the readout-electronics noise), demonstrating sub-electron noise over a complete 64$\times$64 DePFET matrix in a single readout, alongside a power consumption reduction of more than 50%. The super-$g_q$ DePFET shows a 2.6-fold increase in charge gain (about 1100 pA/e$^-$) but exhibits higher total noise due to an excess noise contribution. The results highlight the potential of the novel DePFETs, with the buried-channel technology offering immediate benefits for low-noise applications such as the WFI.
papers.intro:
Driven by the aspiration to answer new scientific questions, the requirements placed on silicon detectors for spectroscopy and imaging continue to grow. In this context, low noise is essential for precise charge measurement, since it sets the smallest signal that can be reliably distinguished from the noise floor and thus the achievable signal-to-noise ratio (SNR). In spectroscopy, low noise sharpens the energy resolution of spectral lines and lowers the minimum detectable energy, whereas in imaging it preserves faint sources and low-contrast features that would otherwise be lost. Beyond these direct benefits, a low noise floor also relaxes system-level design trade-offs. Smaller pixel pitches become feasible despite increased charge sharing, whereas shorter readout times support higher frame rates, mitigate pile-up, and decrease the accumulation of leakage charge, thereby facilitating operation at elevated temperatures. Applications that require thin sensors or have a limited material budget, and therefore exhibit lower charge deposition, also benefit.

It is within this tension between competing detector parameters that further development of the DePFET (Depleted P-channel Field Effect Transistor) sensor becomes especially valuable. Owing to their adaptability to high frame rates, high spatial resolution, Fano-limited energy resolution, and wide dynamic range, DePFETs have been selected for a broad range of current and planned instruments [2]. These are the PXD in the Belle II experiment for particle tracking [1], the DePFET-based MIXS sensor onboard the planetary science mission BepiColombo for X-ray spectroscopy [32], the development of ultrafast real-time imagers for direct electron detection (EDET) for transmission electron microscopes (TEMs) [25] or the development of the Wide Field Imager (WFI) of the next generation X-ray imaging spectroscopy onboard the NewAthena satellite [30].

Alongside implementations in various gate dimensions, optimised Infinipix and Quadropix layouts, RNDR devices with an improved transfer channel, on-pixel frame store structures, and MOS-CCD test devices with DePFETs at the readout node were fabricated.

The basic layout of a standard DePFET technology is shown in figure 1 in top view (left) and in 3D with cuts along the p-channel and through the clear-structure (right). It consists of a p-channel MOSFET on a high-resistivity, n-doped silicon substrate. A shallow channel implant adjusts the threshold voltage and improves its pixel-to-pixel uniformity, while a deep n-implant beneath the transistor channel forms a potential minimum for electrons. By applying a sufficiently high reverse bias to a thin p+ doped layer on the backside, which also serves as the entrance window, the substrate is completely depleted by means of sidewards depletion, rendering the entire volume sensitive. Absorbed ionising radiation generates electron-hole pairs that separate in the depletion field: holes drift to the back contact, while electrons drift to the potential minimum, where they accumulate. The collected electrons induce mirror charges in the p-channel, modulating its conductivity. In analogy to an external gate voltage, the deep n-implant is commonly referred to as the internal gate (IG), because of this steering effect on the channel current. The intrinsic, or internal, amplification is quantified by the charge gain, defined as the change in drain current per collected electron and is denoted as gqg_{q}. The internal gate can be reset on demand by applying adequate voltage pulses to the adjacent Clear and Clear-Gate contacts. This creates a potential gradient to the Clear that drains the accumulated electrons.

The presented work investigates the noise and spectral performance of two novel DePFET technologies, the buried-channel DePFET and the super-gqg_{q} DePFET, each addressing one of the two factors of the SNR, and compares them with the standard technology. Their design differences are described in section 2 and the measurement system and the analysis in section 3. A bias configuration for the lowest noise is established in section 4, covering the depletion and clear-process voltages and the optimum intrinsic DePFET transistor settings. Their noise behaviour is further explored with respect to temperature and integration time (sections 5 and 6). Common measurement limitations are discussed in section 7, together with the advantages and drawbacks of the novel technologies. The main findings are summarised in section 8.

papers.title: Temporal polarization properties of accretion flows into supermassive black holes: INSANE as an alternative
papers.abstract: Temporal variability and polarization provide unique diagnostics of the magnetic field structure and plasma dynamics in accretion flows around supermassive black holes. We investigate the temporal polarization properties of horizon-scale emission using general relativistic magnetohydrodynamic (GRMHD) simulations coupled with polarized general relativistic radiative transfer (GRRT) for three accretion states: Standard and Normal Evolution (SANE), Magnetically Arrested Disk (MAD), and an intermediate regime (INSANE). Fourier polarization-mode decomposition, through the ratio $|\beta_m|/|\beta_2|$, shows that MAD produces the most rotationally symmetric EVPA patterns, SANE the most asymmetric, and INSANE lies in between. The multi-scale temporal behaviour of the intensity is investigated using the Continuous Wavelet Transform and Hilbert-Huang Transform. Both methods identify localized oscillatory features associated with magnetic-flux eruption events in the MAD simulations. In the shorter interval examined, INSANE distributes its variability more evenly among several time-scales, while the SANE behaviour depends more strongly on the electron-temperature prescription. To quantify the spectral distribution, we define a fast power fraction $F_{\mathrm{fast},I}$ for periods of 80-200 $M$ within a broad band of 80-1500 $M$. Both methods give the smallest fractions for MAD; the ordering of state medians, INSANE > SANE > MAD, persists when the upper fast-band boundary is varied from 200 to 500 $M$. Our analysis demonstrates that combining polarization morphology with multi-scale temporal analysis provides a useful means of distinguishing magnetization states, supporting INSANE as a distinct observational alternative to conventional MAD/SANE for interpreting horizon-scale observations of M87$^{*}$ and related systems.

papers.intro:
Black holes accreting at low Eddington ratios power some of the most energetic relativistic jets in the Universe, yet the physical state of the plasma in the immediate vicinity of the event horizon remains uncertain (Yuan & Narayan, 2014). A key unresolved question concerns the magnetic flux threading the black hole and inner accretion flow properties, which determine whether the system operates in a Standard And Normal Evolution (SANE) configuration, a Magnetically Arrested Disk (MAD) state, or an intermediate regime with partial magnetic flux accumulation (Narayan et al., 2012b). This distinction has profound implications for jet launching, particle acceleration, and the temporal variability of the emitted radiation.

A key unresolved question concerns the magnetic flux threading the black hole and inner accretion flow properties, which determine whether the system operates in a Standard And Normal Evolution (SANE) configuration, a Magnetically Arrested Disk (MAD) state, or an intermediate regime with partial magnetic flux accumulation (Narayan et al., 2012b). This distinction has profound implications for jet launching, particle acceleration, and the temporal variability of the emitted radiation.

The nearby galaxy M87 provides an exceptional laboratory for studying these processes. With horizon-scale imaging achieved by the Event Horizon Telescope (EHT) (Event Horizon Telescope Collaboration et al., 2019a; Event Horizon Telescope Collaboration et al., 2022a), combined with multi-wavelength monitoring and polarization measurements, M87 offers direct observational access to plasma dynamics occurring on horizon-scale variability (Event Horizon Telescope Collaboration et al., 2021a; Event Horizon Telescope Collaboration et al., 2021b). A complementary perspective is provided by observations of Sgr A*, the supermassive black hole at the centre of the Milky Way, where rapid intrinsic variability and lower jet power suggest a different accretion environment and potentially a lower net magnetic flux state (Event Horizon Telescope Collaboration et al., 2022b; Event Horizon Telescope Collaboration et al., 2022c). While several EHT modelling efforts for M87 indicate that MAD configurations reproduce many observed features, particularly jet energetics and polarized structure, current observational constraints do not uniquely exclude SANE or intermediate-magnetization (“weak-MAD”) flows (Event Horizon Telescope Collaboration et al., 2021a; Event Horizon Telescope Collaboration et al., 2021b; Event Horizon Telescope Collaboration et al., 2025a; Event Horizon Telescope Collaboration et al., 2025b). In contrast, for Sgr A*, present observational and modelling studies generally favour SANE or moderately magnetized configurations, with strongly arrested MAD states appearing less consistent with the observed variability and polarization properties (Event Horizon Telescope Collaboration et al., 2022b; Event Horizon Telescope Collaboration et al., 2022c; Event Horizon Telescope Collaboration et al., 2024a). Together, these systems highlight the importance of variability diagnostics for distinguishing among different magnetic flux regimes in low-luminosity accreting black holes.

General Relativistic Magnetohydrodynamic (GRMHD) simulations predict distinct variability signatures associated with different magnetization states. SANE disks typically exhibit turbulence-dominated, small-scale stochastic fluctuations, whereas MAD systems display more coherent large-scale magnetic structures that can modulate emission on longer and often correlated timescales (Narayan et al., 2003; Igumenshchev et al., 2003; Igumenshchev, 2008; Begelman et al., 2022). Intermediate or partially arrested disks, sometimes referred to as INSANE or semi-MAD states, may produce variability characteristics that lie between these two extremes, complicating the interpretation of observational data (Raha et al., 2025). Consequently, systematic comparisons between variability predictions of SANE, intermediate, and MAD simulations are essential for constraining the magnetic state of the M87 accretion flow.

Accretion flows forming the horizon-scale environments of black holes are intrinsically time-dependent, driven by magnetohydrodynamic turbulence, magnetic reconnection, and dynamical plasma instabilities. At millimeter wavelengths, particularly near 1.3 mm, the observed emission is dominated by synchrotron radiation produced by relativistic electrons energized within these turbulent magnetized flows (Event Horizon Telescope Collaboration et al., 2019c). Because the emitting plasma evolves on orbital and inflow timescales close to the innermost stable circular orbit (ISCO), the brightness distribution of the source is expected to vary on characteristic dynamical timescales that depend strongly on the black hole mass and spin (Bardeen et al., 1972).

At millimeter wavelengths, particularly near 1.3 mm, the observed emission is dominated by synchrotron radiation produced by relativistic electrons energized within these turbulent magnetized flows (Event Horizon Telescope Collaboration et al., 2019c). Because the emitting plasma evolves on orbital and inflow timescales close to the innermost stable circular orbit (ISCO), the brightness distribution of the source is expected to vary on characteristic dynamical timescales that depend strongly on the black hole mass and spin (Bardeen et al., 1972).

For the Galactic center black hole Sgr A*, these characteristic timescales are on the order of minutes to tens of minutes, implying that appreciable structural variability can occur even during a single observing night, complicating the interpretation of time-averaged images. In contrast, the substantially larger mass of the M87 black hole shifts the relevant dynamical timescales to days or weeks, suggesting that short-duration observing campaigns should capture comparatively modest structural evolution, while longer baselines may reveal measurable changes in the morphology and azimuthal brightness distribution of the emission ring (Wielgus et al., 2020). Indeed, multi-epoch very-long-baseline interferometry (VLBI) observations spanning several years have already indicated the presence of long-term structural variability in M87, consistent with expectations from turbulent accretion dynamics.

The 2017 EHT observing campaign of M87, which covered multiple nights separated by several days, sampled only a few characteristic dynamical times near the ISCO. Consequently, only moderate day-to-day variations in ring thickness and brightness asymmetry were inferred, highlighting the importance of time-dependent modeling for interpreting interferometric observables. Because the EHT measures complex visibilities corresponding to the Fourier components of the sky brightness distribution, temporal evolution in the accretion flow is encoded directly in the variability of visibility amplitudes, phases, and polarization quantities rather than solely in reconstructed images (Event Horizon Telescope Collaboration et al., 2019b).

papers.title: Guarded Swarms in the Loop: A ROS 2/PX4 Digital Twin for Hybrid Digital-Analog Coordination of UAV/UGV Swarms
papers.abstract: Swarms of unmanned aerial and ground vehicles (UAV/UGV) operating in contested environments cannot rely on software alone for physical safety, since the software stack and its networks are part of the attack surface. The Guarded Swarms architecture addresses this by pairing a digital coordination layer, built on Topic-Based Communication Space Petri Nets (TB-CSPN), with an independent analog safety layer that can veto unsafe actuation commands. So far, the architecture has been specified and argued for, but not executed. We present the first executable instantiation of Guarded Swarms as a digital twin built on ROS 2, the PX4 autopilot in software-in-the-loop mode, and Gazebo, with two UAVs and one UGV in a coastal counter-UAS scenario. The TB-CSPN transition chain, from multi-modal sensing through human authorization to vehicle tasking, is mapped one-to-one onto ROS 2 nodes, and the analog layer is modeled as a per-vehicle Virtual Safety Board that gates every command. Eight groups of experiments show that the three negative guarantees of the architecture (no mission from conflicting, temporally incoherent, or unauthorized evidence) hold at three distinct stages of the chain in all 60 counterfactual runs; that threat confirmation is bounded by the narrowest sensing modality; that the safety layer exercises its full modeled envelope independently of the coordination layer; and, under fault injection, that it prevents every collision caused by a forged mission or a compromised worker once its veto is enforced by an independent gate, whereas a veto left to the compromised worker prevents none. The twin also exposes implementation-level hazards that the architectural specification does not address, and it draws an explicit line between the properties that simulation can validate and those that only hardware can.

papers.intro:
Swarms of unmanned vehicles have moved from single teleoperated platforms to coordinated groups that share a mission, with clear benefits in coverage, redundancy and resilience [1, 2]. Coordination in such swarms is almost entirely a software matter: planners, middleware and distributed controllers decide who does what and when. In contested environments this is also a weakness. An adversary can spoof navigation or sensing signals [3], inject commands into a compromised stack, or deny communications; and even without an adversary, a software defect or a perception error can drive a vehicle into a physically dangerous state. If the software layer is the only safeguard, nothing downstream prevents an unsafe command from reaching the motors.

Coordination in such swarms is almost entirely a software matter: planners, middleware and distributed controllers decide who does what and when. In contested environments this is also a weakness. An adversary can spoof navigation or sensing signals [3], inject commands into a compromised stack, or deny communications; and even without an adversary, a software defect or a perception error can drive a vehicle into a physically dangerous state. If the software layer is the only safeguard, nothing downstream prevents an unsafe command from reaching the motors.

The Guarded Swarms architecture [4, 5, 6] answers this problem by splitting responsibility between two layers that do not trust each other. A digital coordination layer, formalized in the TB-CSPN framework [7], turns heterogeneous sensor evidence into authorized missions through explicit, auditable Petri-net transitions. An analog safety layer, present on each vehicle and independent of software, validates or vetoes actuation commands at the last moment before they reach the actuators. The two layers share no state and meet only at the actuation command, where the safety layer has the last word.

papers.title: Euclid: Quick Data Release (Q1) -- The evolution of the radio-loud AGN fraction-stellar mass relation to $z\sim3$ in the Euclid Deep Field North
papers.abstract: The incidence of radio-loud active galactic nuclei (RLAGN) and their energetic output via AGN feedback are crucial in understanding the evolution of galaxies and the large-scale structure of the Universe. In the local Universe, the incidence of RLAGN has been shown to correlate strongly with host galaxy properties, particularly stellar mass. Using the large-area survey capabilities provided by Euclid and the LOw Frequency ARray (LOFAR), we present the first study of the RLAGN incidence--stellar mass relation to $z=3.0$. We perform a stringent analysis accounting for cross-matching reliability and stellar-mass incompleteness. In addition, we test the robustness of our results against AGN and host galaxy classification. This yields a sample of $3\,154$ RLAGN in the Euclid Deep Field North, comprising $2\,803$ low-excitation radio galaxies (LERGs). We find that the LERG incidence as a function of stellar mass and radio luminosity follows a tight correlation over more than two orders of magnitude in stellar mass to $z=3.0$. The slope of the power-law relation decreases from $\gamma\approx2.5$ in the local Universe to $\gamma\approx1.0$ at $z=3.0$, indicating a relative increase in low-mass LERGs at earlier epochs. Separating the LERG population into actively star-forming and quiescent galaxies reveals that quiescent LERGs show a much steeper relation between incidence and stellar mass, with $\gamma\approx2.5$ compared to star-forming LERGs that show $\gamma\approx1.5$. However, the relation seems to be independent of whether galaxies are star-forming or quiescent at $z\geq2$, where both populations show relatively flat relations with $\gamma\approx1.0$. Our results suggest an evolutionary picture in which the LERG population transitions from cold-mode, merger-dominated accretion at earlier epochs to a scenario in which systems require a massive hot halo to fuel the AGN in the local Universe.

It is now well accepted that most massive galaxies host a smbh (smbh) at their centre (Kormendy and Richstone 1995; Volonteri 2012), and that there is a tight correlation between the mass of the smbh M∙M_{\bullet} and the bulge of galaxies in the local Universe. For example, M∙M_{\bullet} correlates with the bulge stellar velocity dispersion (Ferrarese and Merritt 2000; Gebhardt et al. 2000; Tremaine et al. 2002), and similarly, bulge mass or bulge luminosity shows a tight correlation with M∙M_{\bullet} (see Kormendy and Ho 2013 for a review). These correlations between smbh and their host galaxies suggest co-evolution, often attributed to phases of agn (agn) activity.

These correlations between smbh and their host galaxies suggest co-evolution, often attributed to phases of agn (agn) activity.

During the agn phase, the smbh actively accretes material from its host galaxy and can release vast amounts of energy through radiation and matter outflows. Some agn additionally launch relativistic, magnetically driven jets of hot plasma, which can deposit substantial amounts of kinetic energy into the surrounding medium (Fabian 2012). agn activity can couple its released energy to the ambient medium and regulate subsequent galaxy growth. This process, commonly referred to as agn feedback, may suppress star formation in the host galaxy or cooling flows in galaxy groups and clusters, resulting in negative feedback. In some circumstances, however, agn activity may instead enhance star formation, leading to positive feedback. These processes are therefore thought to play an important role in regulating galaxy evolution (Fabian 2012; Somerville and Davé 2015; Harrison and Ramos Almeida 2024).

Observations of rlagn in the local Universe (z≲0.3z\lesssim 0.3) have shown that they broadly separate into two accretion modes associated with different Eddington-ratio regimes: radiatively efficient (‘radiative mode’) and radiatively inefficient (‘jet mode’) agn (e.g., Heckman and Best 2014; Tadhunter 2016; Hardcastle and Croston 2020). The latter are thought to host a radiatively inefficient adaf (adaf; Narayan and Yi 1994), with most of their energy released through two-sided collimated jets, whereas radiative-mode AGN emit predominantly electromagnetic radiation from a geometrically thin, optically thick accretion disc (Shakura and Sunyaev 1973). Radiative mode agn are also observed to drive outflows, but the coupling of these outflows to the surrounding medium is poorly understood (e.g., Harrison and Ramos Almeida 2024).

The general interpretation is that herg tend to accrete efficiently from cold gas by either external (e.g., galaxy mergers) or internal (e.g., bars or instabilities) processes, where a plentiful gas supply can lead to the formation of a standard accretion disc (Allen et al. 2006; Hardcastle et al. 2007; Heckman and Best 2014, e.g.,). papers.title: FastSpecFit: Spectrophotometric Modeling of 38 Million Extragalactic Targets from the Dark Energy Spectroscopic Instrument Second Data Release
papers.abstract: Optical spectrophotometry provides a direct window into the physical conditions, kinematics, and formation histories of galaxies and quasars. FastSpecFit is an open-source Python software package that forward-models each Dark Energy Spectroscopic Instrument (DESI) spectrum jointly with its broadband photometry, convolving stellar-population synthesis and emission-line templates with each fiber's native spectral resolution. This forward-modeling approach preserves DESI's uncorrelated pixel statistics, fits a typical spectrum in ~0.1 s of single-core time, and scales to tens of millions of objects, with uncertainties estimated via Monte Carlo resampling. FastSpecFit measures stellar velocity dispersions, non-parametric star-formation histories, stellar masses, star-formation rates, dust attenuation, K-corrections, rest-frame magnitudes, and fluxes and equivalent widths for 46 emission lines, including separate narrow and broad components for the Balmer lines. We describe these algorithms in detail, validate the measurements against independent codes, and present the resulting value-added catalog for DESI Data Release 2, which provides spectrophotometric and physical properties for 38 million extragalactic targets at 0<z<4. We also release a companion photometry-only catalog and document the catalogs previously released for the DESI Early Data Release and Data Release 1.

papers.intro:
The Dark Energy Spectroscopic Instrument [85, 35, 38, DESI;] is conducting an eight-year survey (2021–2029) which will ultimately yield spectroscopic redshifts for more than 60 million galaxies and quasars over 17,000 deg2. These data are being made public in a series of staged releases. The Early Data Release [39, EDR;], comprising 1.7 million unique spectra from the survey validation (SV) campaign (2020 December–2021 May), was released in 2023 June. Data Release 1 [40, DR1;], released in 2025 March, uniformly reprocessed the SV data and added the first 13 months of the main-survey sample, for a total of 20.4 million unique spectra. Data Release 2 (DR2), the subject of this paper, extends the main-survey data through 2024 April, its first three years, includes an unprecedented 38 million unique redshifts, and is scheduled for public release in the first part of 2027. Each successive release has sharpened DESI’s baryon acoustic oscillation distance measurements to sub-percent precision and currently shows a 2.8–4.2σ\sigma preference for an evolving dark energy equation of state over the standard Λ\LambdaCDM concordance cosmological model [3, 4, 5, 1, 2].

Each spectrum DESI acquires encodes a wealth of astrophysical information beyond its redshift. The shape and absorption-line content of the stellar continuum trace the underlying stellar populations, dust content, and kinematics of a galaxy, while its emission-line spectrum constrains the star-formation rate, chemical abundances, ionization state, and gas kinematics, as well as the presence and strength of an active galactic nucleus (AGN) [28, and references therein]. Extracting these physical properties at DESI scale—and combining them with broadband photometry to normalize the overall spectral energy distribution (SED)—requires a fitting code that is fast, robust, and automated across an enormous range of signal-to-noise ratios (S/N), redshifts, and galaxy types.

Various publicly available codes already perform this kind of spectrophotometric modeling. Full-spectrum fitting codes—among them pPXF [21, 20], GandALF [115, 116], STARLIGHT [27], FIREFLY [139], FIT3D/pyPipe3D [112, 113], ULySS [73], alf [32], and others—extract the kinematics and properties of the stellar populations and line-emitting gas; SED-fitting codes such as CIGALE [16], Bagpipes [22], Prospector [67], and MAGPHYS [33] combine photometry (and, in some cases, spectroscopy) with physically motivated stellar population synthesis (SPS) models to infer star-formation histories, stellar masses, and dust properties; and codes like PyQSOFit [52] are tailored to fitting the ultraviolet (UV) and optical spectra of quasars.

Each of these codes makes different trade-offs among flexibility, physical realism, and computational speed, but none were designed to be run efficiently on the tens of millions of spectra acquired by DESI. Existing codes also do not take advantage of the DESI resolution matrix, which compactly encodes the instrumental resolution and guarantees uncorrelated uncertainties from pixel to pixel [15, 54].

FastSpecFit11 1 https://fastspecfit.readthedocs.io/en/latest has been developed to meet both these challenges, scaling efficiently to tens of millions of spectra while fully exploiting DESI’s native spectral resolution. Using a forward-modeling fitting approach, FastSpecFit convolves physically motivated stellar continuum and emission-line templates with each fiber’s resolution matrix and compares the result directly to the observed spectra, preserving the uncorrelated pixel statistics that resampling would otherwise destroy (§III). In addition, FastSpecFit is engineered for speed; it fits a typical DESI spectrum in ≈0.1\approx 0.1 s on a single CPU core (≈5\approx 5 s including the default 50 Monte Carlo realizations; §V.3), making it possible to process the full DESI dataset—and to refit it as the data-reduction pipeline and SPS models evolve—with modest computing resources. This speed also makes it practical to estimate parameter uncertainties from repeated fits to Monte Carlo-resampled data rather than from computationally expensive posterior sampling (§III.7), and, via a hybrid message passing interface (MPI) plus multiprocessing design, to scale from a single serial process on a laptop to thousands of cores on a supercomputer (§V.3).

FastSpecFit11 1 https://fastspecfit.readthedocs.io/en/latest has been developed to meet both these challenges, scaling efficiently to tens of millions of spectra while fully exploiting DESI’s native spectral resolution. Using a forward-modeling fitting approach, FastSpecFit convolves physically motivated stellar continuum and emission-line templates with each fiber’s resolution matrix and compares the result directly to the observed spectra, preserving the uncorrelated pixel statistics that resampling would otherwise destroy (§III). In addition, FastSpecFit is engineered for speed; it fits a typical DESI spectrum in ≈0.1\approx 0.1 s on a single CPU core (≈5\approx 5 s including the default 50 Monte Carlo realizations; §V.3), making it possible to process the full DESI dataset—and to refit it as the data-reduction pipeline and SPS models evolve—with modest computing resources. This speed also makes it practical to estimate parameter uncertainties from repeated fits to Monte Carlo-resampled data rather than from computationally expensive posterior sampling (§III.7), and, via a hybrid message passing interface (MPI) plus multiprocessing design, to scale from a single serial process on a laptop to thousands of cores on a supercomputer (§V.3).

Beyond speed, FastSpecFit is designed to be flexible, applying only the physical constraints the data strictly require and otherwise letting the data determine the best-fitting model. The continuum model imposes only minimal priors: non-negative stellar population coefficients, an energy-conserving dust model, and a freely fitted stellar velocity dispersion bounded widely enough to accommodate the full spectral diversity of DESI targets. In exchange for speed and robustness at low S/N, the default configuration we adopt deliberately fixes other ingredients, including the stellar metallicity, the slope of the attenuation curve, and the infrared (IR) dust-emission parameters (§III.1, §III.4.3), although users can relax most of these choices with custom templates and fitting options (§III.8). The emission-line model is similarly flexible, supporting independent narrow and broad kinematic components and capturing the broad Balmer-line emission that distinguishes type 1 AGN whenever the data require it. Unlike codes that target a specific class or spectral type, FastSpecFit applies this same machinery uniformly to every spectrum, without assuming in advance whether the target is quiescent, star-forming, post-starburst, or hosts an AGN. This flexibility minimizes classification-driven selection effects and maximizes the discovery potential of a dataset as large and diverse as DESI, where unusual or physically ambiguous objects emerge naturally from the fit rather than requiring special-case handling.

papers.title: When Do Typed Decision Models Work in Transportation? Evidence from Travel Choice and Traffic Signal Control
papers.abstract: Typed decision models combine natural-language understanding with a structured interface that returns a selected action and an option-level probability distribution without generating lengthy textual responses. Their low inference cost and response latency make them attractive for transportation problems with predefined alternatives. This paper investigates their effectiveness, robustness, and efficiency in two representative transportation tasks: individual travel-mode choice prediction and sequential traffic signal control. We systematically evaluate TypeSafe Jev and GPT-6 Luna Decisions against conventional transportation methods, reinforcement learning algorithms, and four chat-based large language models. Experiments on the Swissmetro dataset show that typed decision models achieve lower prediction accuracy than traditional discrete choice models and the strongest chat-based baseline, while their performance varies substantially with input representation and question framing. In closed-loop traffic signal control experiments, typed decision models demonstrate competitive performance against established controllers in several scenarios, but exhibit performance degradation under more challenging network conditions. Furthermore, the typed models achieve lower inference latency and computational cost than the evaluated chat-based large language models, highlighting their potential for efficient, zero-shot transportation decision-making. Overall, these findings demonstrate both the potential and limitations of typed decision models, emphasizing the importance of input design, task characteristics, and robustness evaluation for their effective application in transportation systems.

papers.title: 3D-VASE: Volumetric-Aware Scalable and Efficient Multi-Layer Design Synthesis for 3D-Printed Microfluidics
papers.abstract: Additive manufacturing (3D printing) enables complex multi-layer microfluidic devices, but the physical synthesis of passive-flow designs remains a key bottleneck. In such systems, designers must encode timing synchronization and target dosing directly into channel geometry, even though the available routing space across multiple 3D layers is often highly congested, which makes scaling to complex designs difficult. Existing approaches formulate placement, routing, and fluidic constraints as a single monolithic optimization, leading to combinatorial explosion and poor performance on complex designs. This paper presents a volumetric-aware two-stage synthesis framework that decouples global structure from routing detail. A Mixed-Integer Programming (MIP) model first computes a compact multi-layer placement, followed by a dynamic 3D routing engine that enforces timing and volumetric constraints during path construction. To further improve routability in dense layouts, we introduce a hierarchical conflict resolution strategy combining local rip-up-and-reroute with controlled global expansion. Experimental results show that, under timing and volumetric constraints, 3D-VASE consistently improves synthesis speed and, in most test cases, also improves layout quality. Notably, for difficult large-scale cases where prior methods often failed to return any solution within the time limit, 3D-VASE produces feasible high-quality layouts within practical runtimes. These advances enable fast, iterative design-space exploration for complex 3D-printed microfluidic systems.

Microfluidic devices enable miniaturized and automated laboratory processes in applications ranging from diagnostics and drug delivery to cell biology and chemical synthesis (Whitesides, 2006; Dittrich and Manz, 2006; Sackmann et al., 2014). Conventional fabrication techniques such as photolithography and polydimethylsiloxane (PDMS) glass bonding have enabled many advances, but they rely on complex cleanroom workflows and are largely limited to planar layouts (Halldorsson et al., 2015; Sia and Whitesides, 2003). Three-dimensional printing (3D printing), especially stereolithography (SLA), offers rapid prototyping, reduced fabrication barriers, and vertically stacked flow layers with internal channels and vias (Au et al., 2016; Nielsen et al., 2020; Bhattacharjee et al., 2016; Waheed et al., 2016; Shallan et al., 2014; Comina et al., 2014). In multi-layer 3D-printed microfluidic chips, fluid control is fundamentally a geometric design problem. Many assays require strict synchronization so that multiple streams arrive at a reaction chamber simultaneously and with prescribed mixing ratios (Song et al., 2003; Ward and Fan, 2015). Compared with valve-rich platforms, such as conventional PDMS chips that rely on active on-chip actuation for timing and dosing, many 3D-printed systems primarily use passive flow layers, meaning that fluid behavior must be programmed directly into channel geometry (Halldorsson et al., 2015). In this setting, geometry is not merely a packaging concern; it becomes the mechanism for achieving functional correctness.

In passive-flow systems, the arrival time TT is fundamentally determined by channel hold-up volume VV and inlet flow rate QQ: when QQ is fixed by the pump, a larger VV leads to later arrival. Consequently, channel length, cross-sectional area, layer transitions, and routing detours directly influence both arrival timing and delivered volume. This dependence makes the design space extremely sensitive to geometric changes in the routing layout. A modification that appears minor from a geometric perspective, such as shifting a path to avoid congestion or inserting a detour around an obstacle, can change VV enough to disturb synchronization or dosage targets. As a result, manual design refinement becomes slow and error-prone, especially in dense multi-layer layouts where spatial constraints and fluidic constraints interact continuously.
