Translating the above fluidic mechanism into a design automation problem is highly challenging. Prior microfluidic design automation has largely focused on electrode-array-driven digital microfluidics (Fair, 2007; Su and Chakrabarty, 2008; Xu and Chakrabarty, 2008; Cho et al., 2003), planar or interactive continuous-flow CAD support (Sanka et al., 2019), control-layer-based large-scale integration (Tseng et al., 2019), or manual multi-layer modeling for 3D-printed devices (Zhang et al., 2024). These tools improve design productivity, but they do not provide an end-to-end automatic placement-and-routing flow for passive-flow 3D-printed chips under timing and volumetric constraints. papers.title: Check Your Blind Spots: Decision-Guided Perception by Probing the Planner with Hypothetical Objects
papers.abstract: Not every perception error changes the planner's action. Yet adaptive-resolution perception chooses where to spend high-resolution computation from image cues, which can neither reliably point to an object that low resolution missed nor tell which objects matter to the planner. We observe that the planner can say where an object would matter before anything is seen: inserting a hypothetical object at a location tests whether its action would change. Decision-Guided Speculative Perception (DGSP) treats the low-resolution scene and its action as a draft and probes the planner in this way to obtain a decision-sensitivity field, the locations where an unseen object would change the action. Only this field and the support, the detections on which the current action rests, are verified at high resolution, repeatedly until the action is stable. For two planner classes, we prove that DGSP returns exactly the action of whole-frame high-resolution perception if crop detections match whole-frame ones and the crops cover the field, conditions that real images meet approximately. On three driving datasets, it reproduces this action on about 98% of frames with about a quarter of the pixels. At the pixel cost of uniform downscaling, it repairs more of the draft's disagreements with this action, brakes falsely less often, and recovers many more of the decision-relevant objects that the draft misses.

papers.intro:
An autonomous vehicle perceives its surroundings in order to act on them. Megapixel cameras let it detect small and distant objects [3, 44], but running a detector on every frame at native resolution strains the compute budget of onboard hardware. Adaptive-resolution methods therefore spend high resolution selectively: on image regions chosen by object priors [37, 38], learned saliency [30, 42], or coarse detections [9, 19], or on whole frames, by adapting the input scale [4], the detector configuration [13], or the choice of model [12]. Their signals come from the image or the system state, not from the planner, which limits them in two ways. They cannot reliably point to what low resolution failed to show: a missed object leaves no detection to refine, and locating it would require the very inference we try to avoid. Nor do they know what matters: an object far from the vehicle’s path can receive as much computation as one forcing it to brake. In Figure 1(a), detected-object refinement sharpens the vehicles it already sees and leaves a nearer cut-in vehicle unseen, retaining decelerate where hard-brake is required; whole-frame inference in Figure 1(b) removes this blind spot only at full cost.

A human driver resolves this differently. Before changing lanes, a driver checks the blind spot, not because a car is likely to be there, but because a car there would change what the driver does; when driving straight ahead, the same spot goes unchecked. The intended action thus decides where to look, before anything is seen. Our key observation is that a planner can make this decision explicitly: whether an object at a given location would change the action is a question about the planner, not about the image, and the planner can answer it for a hypothetical object placed there. The choice of where to perceive thereby moves from the image to the planner, and an unseen object need not be found in order to know where it would matter.

papers.title: oMEGACat-JWST I.: Project description and photometric data release
papers.abstract: Omega Centauri (NGC 5139, $\omega$ Cen) is the most massive globular cluster in the Milky Way and the likely stripped nucleus of an accreted dwarf galaxy. Extensive HST observations have uncovered many of its peculiar features, including complex subpopulations and kinematic evidence for an intermediate-mass black hole via central fast-moving stars. High-precision astrometric follow-up is essential to constrain the orbits of these stars. We present oMEGACat-JWST, a deep photometric and astrometric catalog of $\omega$ Cen's core and surroundings that extends our previous oMEGACat efforts to near-infrared wavelengths. The superior sensitivity and angular resolution of the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) provide significant astrometric and photometric improvements, particularly for faint stars. Our catalog is based on a custom reduction of NIRCam and NIRISS imaging across three JWST programs extending out to two half-light radii (10'). In total, our catalog contains approximately 677 000 sources. In the region overlapping with oMEGACat, we achieve high relative completeness (> 90% of HST sources recovered) while detecting over 86 000 new sources below HST's detection limit. Astrometric tests demonstrate a single-image precision as good as 0.5% of a NIRCam pixel (0.15 mas) at mF115W=18; at mF115W=23 the precision is still 1 mas. Color-magnitude diagrams based on our data show the well-known split between the primordial Helium and the Helium enriched populations and are particularly sensitive to light-element (CNO) variations of faint stars. oMEGACat-JWST provides the most complete photometric catalog of $\omega$ Cen's core to date. Combined with HST data, it enables multi-wavelength subpopulation analyses. Together with future monitoring observations, its high astrometric precision will improve our understanding of the kinematics of the central fast-moving stars in $\omega$ Cen.

papers.title: FastFrames: Video Generation at Interactive Latency
papers.abstract: Autoregressive video diffusion models generate frames based on new observations and inputs, making them a promising medium for interactive visual experiences. However, existing models are orders of magnitude too slow for fluid interaction. This paper introduces FastFrames, a family of fast autoregressive video diffusion models that achieves interactive latency without compromising quality. We profile the inference pipeline of state-of-the-art models and find that operations often treated as fixed implementation details, such as VAE decoding and KV cache updates, in fact account for over half of end-to-end inference latency. We challenge the assumption that these components are indispensable and replace them with lightweight alternatives. Our 1.3B variant runs at 36 ms per frame, or 28 responses per second (RPS), on a single B200 GPU while matching the generation quality of a state-of-the-art model that is nearly 8x slower. Our 14B variant runs at 45 ms per frame, or 22 RPS, on an 8x B200 GPU node and yields significantly better visual quality and realism. We show that FastFrames enables real-time interaction in applications such as camera-conditioned and physics-conditioned video generation.

Video diffusion models (Ho et al., 2022b; Ho et al., 2022a; Singer et al., 2023; Blattmann et al., 2023) synthesize realistic videos (Wang et al., 2025; Seedance Team et al., 2026; Black Forest Labs, 2026; MiniMax, 2026), compose diverse scenes and visual concepts (Deng et al., 2026; Chou et al., 2025; Pan et al., 2026), and respond to camera and action controls (Wang et al., 2024; He et al., 2025). In particular, autoregressive (AR) models (Jin et al., 2025; Deng et al., 2025; Chen et al., 2025; Teng et al., 2025) generate videos incrementally, allowing them to incorporate new controls or observations. They are a promising medium for interactive visual applications, such as world simulation (Chou et al., 2026; Seo et al., 2026), games (Yu et al., 2025; Robbyant Team et al., 2026), and predictive models for robotics (Ye et al., 2026; NVIDIA, 2026).

Recent works have significantly accelerated AR video diffusion models, primarily through distillation and few-step sampling (Yin et al., 2024a; Yin et al., 2025). Some now report real-time generation speeds based on frames per second (FPS) (Huang et al., 2025; Zhu et al., 2026). However, FPS alone does not establish whether a model can respond to user inputs in real time. For instance, a model that generates a 30-frame clip as a single batch in one second achieves 30 FPS, but the user must still wait one second to see a response. Seamless real-time interactivity demands low input-to-response latency, as established in interactive systems research (Miller, 1968). Human-computer interaction studies have reported delay-detection thresholds of approximately 50 to 60 ms (Annett et al., 2014; Deber et al., 2015; Forch et al., 2017).

However, FPS alone does not establish whether a model can respond to user inputs in real time. For instance, a model that generates a 30-frame clip as a single batch in one second achieves 30 FPS, but the user must still wait one second to see a response. Seamless real-time interactivity demands low input-to-response latency, as established in interactive systems research (Miller, 1968). We define this latency as the delay between the arrival of a new input signal (e.g., a steering command) and the presentation of the first RGB frame that depicts its effects. papers.title: Collisionality scaling of the tokamak density limit
papers.abstract: The threshold at which density-limiting plasma instabilities occur in tokamak fusion reactors is not well understood. Here, we present the first large-scale empirical evidence of a common collisionality threshold present across multiple devices and confinement regimes. Machine-learning-guided analysis of a diverse experimental database identifies a scaling in edge effective collisionality ($\nu_*$) that bears resemblance to the widely utilized Greenwald limit but yields a substantially lower false positive rate. This threshold decreases with dimensionless pressure ($\beta$), consistent with theoretical expectations for enhanced transport from electromagnetic effects on resistive ballooning mode turbulence. These results suggest that future burning plasma devices such as ITER and ARC could potentially achieve higher density, and thus fusion power, than previously expected.

papers.title: Coordinating integration of multidisciplinary design analysis and optimisation codes with design structure matrices
papers.abstract: The integrated analysis and optimisation codes used to design nuclear fusion reactors need to become increasingly large scale, multidisciplinary and complex to computationally verify design requirements more thoroughly and earlier in the design process. Though the manner in which the integrated models are coupled can have significant implications for computational efficiency, the structure of couplings typically remains hidden in the implementation of a design framework. As this problem is not unique to fusion, we frame integrated design problems as applications of the broader field of Multidisciplinary Design Analysis and Optimisation (MDAO). Originally developed for complex system design problems in e.g. aerospace, the MDAO field uses (extended) Design Structure Matrices (DSMs) to display the architecture of integrated analysis and optimisation codes. The aim of this work is to introduce these DSM methods and demonstrate how they can be used to improve the transparency and efficiency of design codes in fusion. As a proof of concept, DSM methods are applied to two case studies: stellarator optimisation with SIMSOPT and the PROCESS systems code. With these cases, we illustrate how a DSM can help identify structural assumptions in the code, and how architectural insight can be used to improve computational efficiency. In particular, we demonstrate the computational impact by modifying the PROCESS solver architecture based on the feedback loops revealed in an automatically generated DSM, yielding a significant reduction in model evaluations. Such architectural changes are considered especially impactful for future design frameworks that combine higher fidelity models with large numbers of inexpensive models.

papers.intro:
Optimisation is commonly used in the conceptual design of fusion reactors to explore the design space and find suitable candidate concepts. Systems codes optimise a complete fusion reactor using simple models to represent all physics and engineering disciplines [1, 2]. This yields self-consistent and optimal concepts to be used as a starting point for detailed analysis of the specific disciplines. Such integrated analysis and optimisation codes inform decision making in the early design phase, and in turn have a significant impact on the success of the design project [3].

Such integrated analysis and optimisation codes inform decision making in the early design phase, and in turn have a significant impact on the success of the design project [3].

Enabled by the increasing availability of computational power, this model-based engineering approach is expanding to verify the feasibility of requirements more thoroughly in earlier design phases. This is expected to reduce development cost, time and risk as fewer prototypes and experiments are required, and more alternative designs can be considered in more detail [4, 5]. Moreover, key requirements (e.g. regarding nuclear safety and fusion performance) may necessitate high fidelity verification in silico, as physical experiments are expensive or even impossible [6]. Eventually, such approaches are envisioned to develop into digital twins which support not only reactor design but also operation with multi-fidelity integrated models [7, 8].

A key aspect of such approaches is the modularity of analysis models in an overarching framework, which enables the codes to keep the software structured when integrating more disciplines. Various modular frameworks have been developed for integrated design analysis (e.g. JINTRAC [9], OMFIT [10], FERMI [11]), often focusing on specific parts of a fusion reactor [12]. Reactor design optimisation codes such as PROCESS [13, 14], SYCOMORE [15] and FUSE [16] also feature various degrees of modularity, but are limited to lower fidelity models. Initial approaches to integrate higher fidelity models include the CFETR Integration Design Platform [17, 18] and BLUEMIRA [19], which combines the BLUEPRINT [20] and MIRA [21] codes. Such approaches are particularly important for stellarator design, as 3D shape optimisation (with e.g. SIMSOPT [22], DESC [23]) lies at the heart of a stellarator concept [24]. Enabling integration of systems codes and stellarator optimisation approaches is the direct motivation for this work [25].

Even with a modular approach, the increasing scale and multidisciplinarity of design codes come at the cost of transparency, as it becomes difficult to keep an overview of the complex dependencies between analysis models. This challenges validation of the integrated model, as it is hard to assess if all relevant interfaces are captured, and if not, what assumptions have been made. Especially for cross-disciplinary dependencies this is critical, as they may contain interface assumptions that are not easily caught by disciplinary experts. This opacity subsequently affects the interpretability of the results, as it is difficult to determine what models and assumptions have led to the produced results.

Optimisation problems concerning large-scale, complex, multidisciplinary systems are not unique to fusion. Originating in aerospace, the field of Multidisciplinary Design Analysis and Optimisation (MDAO) has emerged to address such problems [26, 27, 28]. Here multidisciplinary refers to the modularity of the disciplinary codes that are integrated: large-scale codes typically remain modular and are coupled via strictly defined interfaces. For complex systems, the resulting couplings tend to create feedback between models that cannot be decoupled without sacrificing accuracy of results. This approach is not limited to design optimisation codes; it generally applies to integrated modelling approaches as well, in which case it is referred to as Multidisciplinary Analysis (MDA). Though the choice of disciplinary models and algorithms is important, the MDAO field focuses in particular on the arrangement of models, solvers and optimisers: the MDAO architecture. Many MDAO architectures can be defined to solve the same mathematical optimisation problem, structuring the couplings between models and drivers in different ways [29, 30].

The MDAO architecture can have significant impact on optimisation performance, in terms of achieved optimality, computational efficiency and robustness [31, 32, 33, 34]. In particular, usage of an (in)appropriate optimisation architecture for the problem at hand can lead to significant differences in computational efficiency, because the architecture determines the structure of iteration loops in the code, which drive computational cost. As the integration of more disciplines rapidly increases the possibilities for different arrangements, architectural considerations become more important. Any such considerations first of all require insight into the applied architectures, further motivating the need for increased transparency of MDAO codes.

papers.title: The Impact of Seeding Threshold on Wandering Black Hole Populations and Merger Rates
papers.abstract: Cosmological simulations following massive black holes (MBHs) with dynamical friction subgrid models predict hundreds to thousands of off-centre, wandering MBHs in massive galaxies. We investigate how the wandering MBH population changes with halo mass seeding threshold. We present cosmological zoom-in simulations of a $(15\,\mathrm{cMpc})^3$ volume to $z=2$, using the halo mass seeding thresholds of ASTRID, EAGLE and Illustris-TNG $(5\times10^{9}-5\times10^{10}\,\mathrm{M}_{\odot}/h)$, with a fixed MBH seed mass of $m_\mathrm{seed}=2\times10^{6}\,\mathrm{M}_{\odot}/h$. The subgrid dynamical friction model for MBHs switches to accurate integration around MBHs using the \textsc{ketju} module above $m_{\bullet} \geq 2\times10^{7}\,\mathrm{M}_{\odot}/h$. We find that the seeding threshold greatly affects the MBH population: the number of seeded MBHs varies by a factor of ten and the number of wandering MBHs in the most massive galaxy ($M_\star=4.4\times10^{11}\,\mathrm{M}_\odot$) varies from 2 to 115. An MBH can become a wanderer in two ways. Interactions with other galaxies can offset a central MBH in low-mass galaxies ($M_\star\sim10^{8}\,\mathrm{M}_\odot$) if seeded in low mass halos $(\lesssim10^{10}\,\mathrm{M}_\odot/h)$. Alternatively, wandering MBHs can be added through mergers. The growth of the most massive MBHs is insensitive to the seeding threshold. While the total number of MBH mergers varies by an order of magnitude, the number of massive dynamically resolved MBH mergers differs by most a factor of $\sim3$ between seeding thresholds. The dynamically resolved binaries coalesce typically on timescales of $\sim10-250\,\mathrm{Myr}$ after becoming bound.

papers.intro:
Massive black holes (MBHs) are ubiquitous in centres of massive galaxies (e.g. Kormendy and Ho 2013), however, the masses and environments where the seeds of such MBHs form are still uncertain (see e.g. Regan and Volonteri 2024). Possible MBH seeding mechanisms include light seeds from the remnants of Population III stars (Madau and Rees, 2001), runaway collisions in dense stellar clusters (Portegies Zwart et al., 2004) and direct collapse from atomic cooling halos (e.g. Inayoshi et al. 2020 and the references therein). All three formation channels are extensively studied in numerical simulations (see e.g. Rantala et al. 2024; Mehta et al. 2026; Chon et al. 2026 for recent studies). The revolutionary observations made with the James Webb Space Telescope (J​W​S​TJWST) indicate that MBHs grow to reach very high masses of m∙∼108​M⊙m_{\bullet}\sim 10^{8}\,\mathrm{M}_{\odot} already during the first billion years of the Universe (Übler et al., 2023; Harikane et al., 2023; Maiolino et al., 2024; Übler, 2026), indicating that MBHs must efficiently grow in mass in the early Universe.

In the Lambda cold dark matter (Λ​CDM)(\Lambda\rm CDM) cosmological model, galaxies grow hierarchically through gas accretion and galaxy mergers, which invariably lead to MBH mergers. The evolution of MBH binaries is generally divided into three phases (Begelman et al., 1980). First, an unbound pair of MBHs with a separation of the order of multiple kpc begins to sink to the centre of the galaxy merger remnant. The sinking is caused by dynamical friction (Chandrasekhar, 1943; Ostriker, 1999). As the separation decreases to pc scales, the binary first becomes bound and then hardened. At this stage, the orbital evolution is dominated by interactions with nearby stars, said to be a part of the loss-cone (e.g. Milosavljević and Merritt 2003). The binary transfers both energy and angular momentum to the stars, ejecting them from the centre of the galaxy (Quinlan, 1996; Sesana et al., 2006). If the binary exists in a gas-rich system, viscous torques from a circumbinary disk can also affect the orbital evolution (e.g. Tiede et al. 2020). Finally, gravitational wave emission dominates the binary evolution at separation of ≲10−3​pc\lesssim 10^{-3}\,\mathrm{pc} and results in coalescence after rapid orbital inspiral (Peters and Mathews, 1963; Peters, 1964).

In cosmological simulations targeting large volumes, resolving either the seeding of MBHs or the evolution of binaries is challenging due to limited mass resolution. The MBH dynamics are traditionally not accounted for in cosmological simulations. Instead, a method called ‘repositioning’ is often used, which fixes each MBH to remain at the local minimum of the gravitational potential (e.g. Springel et al. 2005a; Johansson et al. 2009b; Booth and Schaye 2009; Vogelsberger et al. 2013; Schaye et al. 2015; Bahé et al. 2022). With repositioning, MBHs are artificially merged from large separations, which results in premature mergers (e.g. Buttigieg et al. 2025). An improvement was made in the ROMULUS and ASTRID simulations, which employed dynamical friction subgrid models (Tremmel et al., 2015; Chen et al., 2022) instead of repositioning (see also Pfister et al. 2019; Genina et al. 2024). However, such a treatment still requires the MBH binaries to be artificially merged from large separations (Tremmel et al., 2017; Ni et al., 2022), missing the phases of stellar-driven hardening and gravitational wave emission. These phases can be resolved in simulations with ketju (Rantala et al., 2017; Mannerkoski et al., 2023), which resolves the interactions between MBHs and stellar particles with algorithmic regularisation, and includes post-Newtonian corrections for MBH binaries. The code has been used in both isolated galaxy merger (Liao et al., 2023; Liao et al., 2024a; Liao et al., 2024b; Wright et al., 2026) and cosmological zoom-in simulations (Mannerkoski et al., 2021; Mannerkoski et al., 2022; Keitaanranta et al., 2026). Another approach to including small-scale effects is the RAMCOAL model (Li et al., 2025), which also includes viscous drag from a circumbinary disk through a subgrid model but, in contrast to ketju, uses a subgrid approach also for the stellar hardening.

The MBH dynamics are traditionally not accounted for in cosmological simulations. Instead, a method called ‘repositioning’ is often used, which fixes each MBH to remain at the local minimum of the gravitational potential (e.g. Springel et al. 2005a; Johansson et al. 2009b; Booth and Schaye 2009; Vogelsberger et al. 2013; Schaye et al. 2015; Bahé et al. 2022). With repositioning, MBHs are artificially merged from large separations, which results in premature mergers (e.g. Buttigieg et al. 2025). An improvement was made in the ROMULUS and ASTRID simulations, which employed dynamical friction subgrid models (Tremmel et al., 2015; Chen et al., 2022) instead of repositioning (see also Pfister et al. 2019; Genina et al. 2024). However, such a treatment still requires the MBH binaries to be artificially merged from large separations (Tremmel et al., 2017; Ni et al., 2022), missing the phases of stellar-driven hardening and gravitational wave emission. These phases can be resolved in simulations with ketju (Rantala et al., 2017; Mannerkoski et al., 2023), which resolves the interactions between MBHs and stellar particles with algorithmic regularisation, and includes post-Newtonian corrections for MBH binaries. The code has been used in both isolated galaxy merger (Liao et al., 2023; Liao et al., 2024a; Liao et al., 2024b; Wright et al., 2026) and cosmological zoom-in simulations (Mannerkoski et al., 2021; Mannerkoski et al., 2022; Keitaanranta et al., 2026). Another approach to including small-scale effects is the RAMCOAL model (Li et al., 2025), which also includes viscous drag from a circumbinary disk through a subgrid model but, in contrast to ketju, uses a subgrid approach also for the stellar hardening.

papers.title: Dual and Binary AGN at Cosmic Dawn: The need for a JWST Program to resolve the merger channel of Early Black Hole Growth
papers.abstract: The discovery with JWST of accreting black holes (BHs) at z=4-9 in numbers far exceeding pre-JWST expectations, many of them overmassive relative to their hosts and linked to the enigmatic Little Red Dots (LRDs), raises the question of how early BHs form and grow. Hierarchical assembly predicts that galaxy mergers drive gas to galactic nuclei and bring BHs together, leaving a direct observational signature: dual AGN at tens of kpc separations and sub-kpc to few-kpc "duets" in post-merger galaxies, which are the progenitors of the low-frequency GW sources targeted by pulsar timing arrays and LISA. JWST has opened the window to study these systems at z>3. However, these early discoveries are very limited number and come from heterogeneous, largely serendipitous samples, so these systems can hardly be used for robust statistical studies. Within the Genesis initiative We propose a uniformly selected census of dual AGN and their hosts from cosmic noon to cosmic dawn, as a science case for the Genesis initiative. Our tiered strategy uses the survey imaging and spectroscopy for candidate selection at no extra cost, followed by NIRSpec IFU confirmation, multi-band NIRCam (and MIRI/ALMA) host characterisation, and multi-epoch revisits. Confirming and characterising about 100 pairs requires of order 1000 hr, well beyond the ceiling of standard TAC programs, and demands multi-cycle continuity. The census will deliver pair fractions as functions of redshift, separation and luminosity, BH masses and mass ratios, host properties and environments, and the empirical anchor needed to turn merger models into realistic LISA rate forecasts.

papers.title: The long-period central star of planetary nebula MPAJ1508-6455
papers.abstract: A significant fraction of planetary nebulae have been shown to host short-period binary central stars, but longer period central stars are scarcer. We aim to characterise the central star of the planetary nebula MPAJ1508-6455 which has previously been claimed to be an intermediate-period binary with a period of approximately 12 days. We study archival and catalogue photometry to probe the previously reported photometric variability and binary spectral energy distribution. We use long-term high-resolution spectroscopic monitoring to measure the radial velocity curves of the two components of the central binary, as well as derive their atmospheric parameters. We also undertook kinematical and chemical abundance analyses of the nebula itself. We find that the central binary of MPAJ1508-6455 has an orbital period of more than five years with a large eccentricity. The binary comprises a relatively low temperature sdO-type central star and a spun-up K-type giant companion. The Kiel mass of the central star is approximately half the dynamical mass derived from the radial velocities. While the nebular systemic velocity and inclination are consistent with the radial velocities of the binary, the nebular abundance pattern adds support for a lower mass progenitor which did not experience hot bottom burning (and is thus more consistent with the Kiel mass than the mass derived from the radial velocities). To the best of our knowledge, the central star of MPAJ1508-6455 is only the fourth planetary nebula central star to have a spectroscopically confirmed orbital period longer than one year.

papers.intro:
Common-envelope (CE) evolution naturally acts to shrink the orbital periods of close binaries as orbital energy and angular momentum is transferred to the envelope (Paczynski, 1976). However, binary population synthesis models often fail to reproduce the observed distribution of orbital periods, predicting a significant population of “intermediate” period (orbital period, Porb, of 10 days or more) binaries which are generally not observed (Toonen and Nelemans, 2013). Instead, the post-interaction orbital period distribution is bi-modal, comprising short-period, clearly post-CE, systems peaking at around an orbital period of Porb=10 hrs, and longer period systems with orbital periods of Porb≳{}_{\mathrm{orb}}\gtrsim100 days, which are thought to form via wind mass transfer (Boffin, 2015). What is abundantly clear is that there is a dearth of systems found with orbital periods between ∼\sim10–100 days.

Several “intermediate” period binaries, with periods in the aforementioned ∼\sim10–40 day range, have been reported inside planetary nebulae (PNe), but most have not stood up to further scrutiny. Sowicka et al. (2017) reported radial velocity (RV) variability of the central star of PN IC4776, consistent with a tentative 9 day orbital period, but higher resolution observations obtained by Miszalski et al. (2019) revealed the true orbital period to be 3.1 days. RV measurements of the central star of NGC 2346 by Mendez and Niemela (1981) were found to be consistent with an orbital period of Porb=16 days, although a 1 day period could not be ruled out. Subsequent high-resolution spectroscopy by Brown et al. (2019) confirmed that the purported A-type companion had an orbital period of Porb=16 days – seemingly cementing it as an intermediate period post-CE binary. However, it has been recently claimed that the companion to the A-type star is not the central star, and instead the central star is part of a higher-order multiple in a much wider orbit (Zijlstra, 2025). Similarly, the central star of K 1-6 shows a 21.3 day photometric period (Frew et al., 2011), but further study has demonstrated that the orbital period must be significantly longer and, furthermore, that the nebula is unlikely to be a PN at all (Merc et al., 2026).

The central star of MPAJ1508−-6455 was reported to be a 12.5 day period binary based on survey photometry and the presence of emission lines that are frequently associated with the irradiation of a cool companion (Miszalski, 2009; Miszalski et al., 2011). papers.title: Inference after coding agents
papers.abstract: Empirical research is changing rapidly as AI coding agents are becoming increasingly proficient in every step of it, from writing code to manipulating data. We argue that while the potential of coding agents for science is vast, their use in hypothesis testing poses a substantial threat to classical inference, as these agents enable a supercharged form of selective inference. In particular, we argue that coding agents carrying out empirical research introduce a new type of post-selection inference that combines human-like, open-ended search over an implicit space of estimators with programmatic replayability of both the selection and the estimation process. Indeed, we find that on simulated data with zero effects, four frontier agents report significant p-values between 54% and 98% of the time when asked to produce a compelling finding. We propose a simple procedure for detecting and correcting these distortions. After an agent has completed its analysis, we reset and replay it on subsamples of the data to estimate the agent's relative probability of selecting that analysis when it looks statistically favorable. For agents with stable selection behavior, the resulting corrected test is asymptotically valid and consistent conditional on selection. Importantly, the correction is learned from the black-box agent's actual choices rather than a model of how it searches, so it remains valid even as AI technology continues to evolve rapidly. In simulations, the correction robustly lowers the high false rejection rates to near the nominal 5%. We illustrate the method on applications from two published papers.

papers.intro:
Coding agents, large language model (LLM)-based systems that can interact with a computing environment by reading files, writing and executing code, and invoking command-line tools, first emerged around 2023 (Lucas and Open Interpreter Contributors, 2023) before gaining widespread use in early 2025 (Anthropic, 2025) with the introduction of Claude Code. Since then, “agentic” AI has rapidly gained a foothold in the market, with estimated annualized spending on AI coding applications reaching $34 billion by September 2026, up from approximately $4.4 billion in 2025 (Menlo Ventures, 2026). While their initial user base was mostly concentrated among software engineers and so-called “vibe coders”, programmers who delegate all their coding to AI agents, their applicability to tasks ranging from data analysis and scientific simulations to literature reviews and paper editing has contributed to their growing adoption in empirical science.

While their initial user base was mostly concentrated among software engineers and so-called “vibe coders”, programmers who delegate all their coding to AI agents, their applicability to tasks ranging from data analysis and scientific simulations to literature reviews and paper editing has contributed to their growing adoption in empirical science.

Indeed, empirical researchers are increasingly delegating large parts of data analysis and scientific modeling to coding agents (Codreanu et al., 2026; Hermle et al., 2026; Johnston et al., 2026). In a survey of social scientists in Feb–Mar 2026, Lyttelton et al. (2026) found that 20% of quantitative social scientists, including 39% of economists, regularly used coding agents. A researcher typically provides a coding agent with data and a description of the question they want to test or the design they want to implement. Like a human analyst, the agent can then inspect the data, choose variables, estimate a few models, and inspect their results before deciding what implementation is worth reporting. While this recent development has the potential to drastically speed up empirical science, it also poses a threat to valid statistical inference. Unless the precise hypothesis and method to test it are fully specified in a type of agentic pre-registration design, the fact that coding agents typically pull a rich information set into their context window before formulating their hypothesis means that classic statistical inferential guarantees, which assume the hypothesis is specified before looking at the data, will typically fail to hold.

We develop a method that detects when a coding agent chooses its analysis based on the results it sees and corrects the reported pp-value for such data-driven selection. In particular, because coding agents are programs, we can reset and replay them on resampled versions of the data. This offers a way around the black-box nature of agent-driven selection by empirically estimating how often agents reselect a given analysis when it looks statistically favorable on a dataset. We can estimate this frequency by exploiting the fact that coding agents emit executable analysis code. After an agent has selected and coded up its analysis, our replay method executes that code on subsamples of the data, sorting these subsamples by how favorable their pp-values look compared to the agent’s original pp-value. If the agent is more likely to reselect its analysis on favorable subsamples, this offers evidence of data-driven selection by the agent. The ratio of the frequency with which the agent selects the analysis on favorable subsamples to its overall selection frequency, which we refer to as the selection multiplier λ\lambda, measures how strongly the agent’s selection depends on the results. The idea is visualized in Figure 1: the coding agent, by selecting an analysis q∗q^{*} from the space of potential analyses, distorts the uniformity characteristic of a calibrated pp-value, leading to the pp-values reported by the agent piling up near zero. Our method estimates this distortion by replaying the agent and corrects for it, restoring the uniformity and hence validity of the corrected pp-values.

papers.title: The topology of the mean action spectrum
papers.abstract: We prove that if an area-preserving diffeomorphism of the closed two-disk is neither a pseudo-rotation nor a periodic map, then the closure of its mean action spectrum contains an interval of positive length. This partially answers a question of Hutchings. We do not require any additional assumptions on the area-preserving map, such as non-degeneracy or specific behavior near the boundary.

papers.title: CaFe: Causally Faithful Conditional Traffic Scenario Generation
papers.abstract: Language-conditioned traffic simulation enables scalable test scenarios steered by natural language. The goal is to control selected agents while surrounding traffic reacts to their observed behaviour. For example, a vehicle instructed to cut in late should cause the following vehicle to brake only when the manoeuvre becomes observable. Yet simulators can leak private instructions across agents, causing surrounding vehicles to react before the instructed behaviour becomes observable. Such premature reactions defuse desired events and alter the ensuing closed-loop scenario. Existing benchmarks measure what agents do, not what they could have known, leaving this failure unmeasured. We formalise it as intent leakage and address it through evaluation, data and modelling. Our paired intervention test holds an instructed agent's executed trajectory fixed while varying its private instruction, isolating leakage-induced changes in surrounding agents. We also construct WOMD-PACT, an automatically generated, verifiable dataset of 531,099 WOMD scenes with timed behaviour tags with reaction episodes identified through a counterfactual ghost test and grounded private instructions. Finally, we introduce CaFe, a dual-stream diffusion-forcing simulator fine-tuned in closed loop that restricts inter-agent interactions to public beliefs, preserving legitimate anticipation without leaking private intent. Our evaluation reveals that existing conditioning designs displace 23-83% of nearby uninstructed agents through private-intent leakage, even when the instructed agent's executed motion is held fixed. CaFe eliminates measurable leakage while maintaining comparable WOSAC realism (0.763), demonstrating that causal faithfulness can be enforced without sacrificing measured simulation realism.

papers.intro:
The validation of autonomous vehicles (AVs) requires, among many other aspects, exposing the system to safety-critical interactions, such as aggressive cut-ins or failures to yield, which occur rarely in logged driving data. Traffic simulation addresses this scarcity by reproducing such interactions on demand. Rule-based simulators and scenario description languages [2, 10, 13] offer precise control but require scenarios to be authored by hand, whereas data-driven simulators [36, 45, 42, 17] learn realistic behaviour from logged driving yet provide little control over which interactions arise. Conditional generation reconciles the two by steering a learned behaviour model with goal positions [48, 49], behaviour tags [37] or natural language [38, 47, 37, 43, 4]. Instructions are typically given to a subset of agents, while the others respond based on what they observe. For instance, one vehicle may be instructed to cut in ahead of another, leaving the response of surrounding traffic to the simulator.

This extends interventional evaluation of interactive prediction to private instructions held by any agent. We therefore compare paired closed-loop rollouts with shared random seeds, replaying the instructed agents’ generated trajectories with and without their instructions. The uninstructed agents observe identical instructed-agent motion in both runs, so any difference in their responses reveals leakage, while a simulator without leakage yields exactly zero.

papers.title: A Model-Driven Automation Pipeline for Building Operation
papers.abstract: Building Control Systems (BCS) engineering in the Architecture, Engineering, Construction & Operations (AECO) domain remains a complex, manual, and error-prone process, with fractured tools and manual commissioning causing design and built reality to diverge into a performance gap. We argue that a fully integrated and automated, tool-supported workflow spanning design, programming, and operation is feasible and can improve efficiency while reducing manual effort and configuration errors. Building on model-driven engineering, we present an automated process pipeline for modeling, programming, and auto-commissioning BCS. It uses two domain-specific modeling languages with tooling support to synthesize and deploy executable artifacts from platform-independent models, replacing a fractured, multi-stakeholder handoff process with a defined four-step workflow and improving consistency across the engineering lifecycle. Our evaluation reports notable efficiency gains, improved adaptability, moderate-to-high user acceptance, and good performance with solid scalability.
papers.intro:
Over the last decades, Software Engineering (SE) has played a central role in enabling automation in a wide variety of application domains [1]. In turn, SE has also tremendously benefited from advances in automation [27]. Model-Driven Engineering (MDE) is a prime example of this relationship, capitalizing on software tools and formal models to provide higher-level abstraction and manage complexity, while simultaneously enabling automation of various process activities along the software development lifecycle (SDLC) [38, 17, 23]. To date, despite the application for many engineering activities, MDE however remains largely confined to SE, and parts of systems engineering and the domain of Cyber-Physical Systems (CPS) [29].

To date, despite the application for many engineering activities, MDE however remains largely confined to SE, and parts of systems engineering and the domain of Cyber-Physical Systems (CPS) [29].

However, even in the area of CPS engineering, MDE has not yet touched on all aspects, and significant gaps remain in the end-to-end automation of development workflows and processes. For example, in building engineering [31], the engineering of Building Control Systems (BCS) remains a fractured, largely manual, barely automated, and often error-prone task [16, 15]. While Building Information Modeling (BIM) already provides a model-based approach for virtually integrated design, construction, and operation (ViDCO) that comprises object-based modeling, model-based collaboration, and network-based integration [36], BCS engineering still remains barely automated. This is further exacerbated by the lack of proper tool support and by existing media breaks at the modeling level [15]. These issues become evident during information exchange between both stakeholders and their tools and systems, respectively [15, 16, 42].

Such a workflow facilitates control logic development by elevating automation programming from low-level, vendor-specific code to high-level, domain-specific models, thereby systematically reducing the complexity of managing heterogeneous devices and languages while increasing automation throughout the development lifecycle. We hypothesize that such a workflow can yield benefits consistent with MDE in software and system engineering, including improved efficiency, ease of use, and consistency [8, 20, 4, 30].

To address these challenges, in this paper, we introduce a novel model-driven tool environment that realizes an end-to-end automation pipeline for integrated BCS modeling, programming, and commissioning. Our approach is based on two Domain-specific Modeling Languages (DSMLs) [37] that enable the specification of device configurations and control logic. Using model-to-text (M2T) generation [21], the pipeline emits runtime artifacts (device configurations and control logic) which are automatically deployed to a physical BCS installation, thereby exploiting model-based tool integration (MBTI) [22] to connect development tools and system hardware. Our evaluation reports notable efficiency gains and improved system adaptability, moderate-to-high user acceptance, and good performance with solid scalability due to the framework’s end-to-end automation and high-level, platform-independent modeling capabilities. As part of this, we claim the following major contributions: – Two DSMLs for platform-independent specification of BCS hardware installations and control logic for clear separation of concerns between physical device topology and behavioral logic. – An integrated model-driven development and deployment pipeline that combines DSML-based modeling, automated validation, code generation, and deployment to provide an end-to-end automated workflow from high-level (vendor-independent) models to operational (vendor-specific) BCS installations. – A systematic modeling methodology comprising four steps that supports both initial system commissioning and rapid post-commissioning adaptations. – A defined four-step engineering process with explicit role assignments that replaces the incumbent fractured handoff chain, supporting both initial commissioning and incremental post-commissioning adaptations without re-engaging an executing company. – An evaluation demonstrating notable efficiency gains regarding commissioning, improved system adaptability, moderate-to-high user acceptance, and good performance with solid scalability in a mobile demo setting with sensors and LED lights using Beckhoff automation hardware (CX5140 controller). – A fully implemented and publicly available artifact including language definitions, code generators, and deployment tools for the Beckhoff TwinCAT 3 platform [26]. papers.title: Estimation and Model Selection in Factor Models with Long Memory
papers.abstract: Panels in economics, finance and climate science are often driven by common components that differ in memory, such as common trends, cycles, or joint shocks. We study approximate factor models whose common factors are fractionally integrated with heterogeneous and unknown memory and develop the asymptotic theory of principal components for the panel in levels. Our theory builds on the eigenvalues of the sample covariance matrix being ordered by memory asymptotically: a nonstationary factor group with memory $d>1/2$ generates eigenvalues of order $NT^{2d-1}$, whereas stationary factors generate eigenvalues of order $N$. Principal components estimate the factors consistently up to rotation, while adjacent factor groups are separated at a rate given by their memory gap. The information criteria of Bai and Ng remain consistent for the total number of factors, with their penalties acting as thresholds on eigenvalues that are asymptotically ordered by factor memory. When the nonstationary factors lose their variance advantage, estimation in levels remains consistent, whereas after differencing the factors can become undetectable. A Monte Carlo study shows that factor-number selection in levels tolerates more idiosyncratic noise than selection after first differencing. For monthly temperatures at $308$ European weather stations, our methods select two factors. The first is a persistent common warming factor. The estimated common component implies that 2021-2025 was $2.15^\circ\mathrm{C}$ warmer than 1960-1990, with the strongest warming in Eastern Europe. After first differencing, the criterion selects one factor, and loses regional heterogeneity as compared to the model in levels.

Applied time series analysis often assumes observables to be driven by components that differ in memory: While macroeconomic variables follow their potential growth path in the long-term, they are driven by the business cycle, season, and noise in the short-run (Harvey, 1989; Morana, 2014). Financial volatility is smooth at low- and rough at high-frequencies (Ray and Tsay, 2000; Asai and McAleer, 2015; Gatheral et al., 2018). Climate is subject to warming trends, but also driven by persistent cycles, season, and noise. When a panel of NN series shares its trends, cycles, and noise, the decomposition implies a factor structure in which some common factors differ in memory.

papers.title: Sub-Meter Canopy Height Synthesis from Sentinel-2 via Anchored Residual Flow
papers.abstract: Canopy height models (CHMs) - per-pixel maps of vegetation top height - are essential for forest carbon accounting, wildfire fuel mapping, and tree-level ecology, yet sub-meter CHMs require airborne LiDAR refreshed on multi-year national cycles. We produce 0.5 m CHMs from free 10 m Sentinel-2 imagery, a 20$\times$ cross-modal super-resolution task where optical reflectance must predict geometric height it does not directly observe. Motivated by the perception-distortion trade-off, we derive two operating points with shared conditioning. A deterministic regressor (Anchor) targets low distortion; a conditional flow matching model, trained on the Anchor's residual in a learned CHM latent space (AR-flow), targets perceptual fidelity. Trained on 197k LiDAR-paired tiles spanning 69 ecoregions across the contiguous United States and evaluated on 2,530 held-out tiles against eight baselines, the Anchor achieves 2.83 m MAE using only free satellite input. The AR-flow reduces sliced Wasserstein distance from the Anchor's 1.13 to 0.208, at a higher MAE of 3.68 m. Crown-scale statistics improve, but strict individual-tree detection remains weak: generated sub-pixel detail represents plausible structure rather than measured individual trees. Quarterly continental refresh becomes tractable, letting satellite monitoring inform timing and extent for more expensive data acquisitions.

Canopy Height Models (CHMs) – per-pixel vegetation-top height – are essential for carbon accounting, wildfire fuel mapping, and tree-level ecology. Sub-meter CHMs require airborne LiDAR at ~$100–300/km2; USGS 3DEP set out to complete national 3D elevation collection in eight years [40]. Satellite-derived CHM products include Meta CHMv2 [5], Planet Forest Carbon Monitoring [33], and CTrees [9]. Meta CHMv2, the strongest baseline in our evaluation, uses commercial Maxar imagery. Sentinel-2 acquires globally every 5 days at 10 m, at zero marginal cost.

Mapping S2 imagery to a sub-meter CHM requires predicting geometric height from optical reflectance. The target is a scalar height field, but accurate average heights and plausible crown structure impose different demands on the prediction. This is an instance of the distortion-perception trade-off [3]: carbon inventory requires calibrated mean height, whereas crown delineation requires fine-scale structure. We provide two operating points and outperform the commercial-input baseline on the reported perception metrics using free input.

This regressor, the Anchor, targets the minimum mean squared error (MMSE) estimate. Stage 2 learns a flow on the residual between the frozen Anchor and the ground-truth latent. This anchored residual flow (AR-flow) supplies the structural variation lost through regression. The two outputs emphasize height accuracy and perceptual fidelity, respectively. Section 3 describes both stages. We evaluate encoder and flow choices at matched compute (Sections 5.2–5.3), compare ten products (Sections 5.6–5.7), and assess crown structure and seasonal cadence (Sections 5.8–5.9).

papers.title: Finite time blow-up for the Willmore flow of symmetric figure-eight tori
papers.abstract: We show that the Willmore flow of symmetric figure-eight tori of revolution produces a finite time singularity, provided the initial energy is below $12\pi$. Our approach relies on the connection with elastic curves in the hyperbolic plane and a fine analysis of Palais--Smale sequences in the relevant energy regime.

papers.title: CueClash: Frontier Vision-Language Models Judge 3-D Relations Close to the Picture Plane
papers.abstract: A vision-language model (VLM) can judge 3-D relations from the picture or from the ground layout. In photographs the two usually agree. We separate them with CueClash, rendered scenes in which the 2-D cue for each of five relations is right on exactly half the statements. The shortcut gap is accuracy when the cue is right minus accuracy when it is wrong. For Claude Opus 5.5, GPT-5.5 and Gemini 3.6 Flash at low reasoning effort it is +18 to +37 percentage points. It is +7 to +29 without two relations whose cue-wrong items are confounded with borderline cases or occlusion. Given ground coordinates and each relation's definition, they answer 99 to 100% correctly. Pixel measurements with camera depths remove most of the gap for objects fitting through openings. The failure lies in the step from the picture to the layout. The maps that the models draw of the scene from above mostly keep the depth order but, like the picture, shorten depth. GPT-5.5's maps stay close to a copy of the picture. Opus 5.5's and Gemini's maps undo about 0.6 of this shortening. Gemini's then shrink all depths by a further uniform factor. Opus 5.5 follows the picture mainly on fits, and its maps correct depth about as much as human observers of real scenes do. The three models also lose accuracy on CV-Bench photographs where a reliable 2-D cue misleads. In two open models the layout information reaches the language model, but their maps lose much of it.
papers.intro:
Is the pink cube in Figure 1 narrow enough to pass between the purple cylinder and the orange sphere? In the picture it looks too wide, because the cube spans 132 pixels and the gap only 60. On the ground the gap is 1.85 units and the cube 1.12, so the cube fits with room to spare. The picture is wrong about the widths only because the cube stands nearer the camera than the gap does. Claude Opus 5.5, GPT-5.5 and Gemini 3.6 Flash, which we call the frontier models, all say that it does not fit. Shown a to-scale map of the same scene from above, all three say that it does.

In natural photographs the two rarely come apart. The taller silhouette usually belongs to the taller object, just as silhouettes that overlap usually belong to objects that touch. A model that reads relations straight off the image can then score about as well as one that recovers the layout (Geirhos et al., 2020). The usual remedy, giving the model a depth map, coordinates or a bird’s-eye view, adds a second confound, because it changes what the model is told and the form in which it is told at the same time.

We study the question with CueClash, a benchmark built on a controlled cue conflict. The five relations are closer, taller, touching, between and fits (Table 1). For each relation we name the 2-D cue that a reader of the picture would use, such as comparing pixel widths for fits. We balance the statements so that this cue is right on exactly half of them. Items on which the cue gives the right answer are cue-right items, and the others are cue-wrong items (Figure 2). A model that only reads the cue then scores 50%, the same as a coin. A model’s shortcut gap is its accuracy on cue-right items minus its accuracy on cue-wrong items, in percentage points. The gap measures how far the answers follow the picture. The items come in three difficulty tiers, easy, medium and hard.

papers.title: DGF-Asym: Adaptive Peer Weighting for Collective Estimation under Noisy and Faulty Sensing
papers.abstract: Collective estimation under unreliable sensing requires robots to adaptively balance personal observations and social information from peers. We propose DGF-Asym, a decentralized collective estimation method extending the DeGroot-Friedkin model with asymmetric peer weighting based on retrospective predictive performance. The method supports consensus formation without prior sensor-noise statistics or explicit fault models while keeping inter-robot communication asynchronous. We evaluate DGF-Asym in simulated collective navigation under noisy observations and time-varying sensor faults. Compared with three baselines, it produces more stable estimates and more reliably sustains the decision criterion, at the cost of longer decision times. However, overall performance depends on fault ratio, group size, and influence-threshold selection. Our results demonstrate the potential of adaptive peer weighting for stable model-free collective estimation under unreliable sensing.

papers.intro:
Multi-robot systems can accomplish tasks that are difficult or impossible for a single robot by collectively making decisions, acting, and exchanging information about their environment. Their effectiveness, however, depends critically on the reliability of the information shared among team members. In open or adversarial settings, robots may receive false or misleading information from external intruders or from compromised or defecting members of the team. Previous work has shown that even small numbers of disruptive robots can substantially impair the performance of an entire multi-robot system [1].

Multi-robot systems can accomplish tasks that are difficult or impossible for a single robot by collectively making decisions, acting, and exchanging information about their environment. Their effectiveness, however, depends critically on the reliability of the information shared among team members. In open or adversarial settings, robots may receive false or misleading information from external intruders or from compromised or defecting members of the team. Previous work has shown that even small numbers of disruptive robots can substantially impair the performance of an entire multi-robot system [1].

This raises a fundamental challenge for robust collective estimation: how should robots combine information received from others with evidence obtained through their own sensors? While communication can increase the amount of available information and thus compensate for limited individual observations, blindly trusting communicated information makes the system vulnerable to misinformation [1]. Conversely, relying on local observations discards potentially valuable knowledge held by other robots. Effective information fusion, therefore, requires mechanisms that balance these two sources of information while accounting for their uncertainty and reliability. In this work, we study information fusion in multi-robot systems in the presence of potentially unreliable information, with the goal of enabling individual robots to form accurate beliefs while remaining robust to faulty observations communicated by other agents. We propose a fully decentralized collective estimation method for multi-robot systems based on the DeGroot-Friedkin model [2] that we extend with dynamic peer-specific social-information weighting. DeGroot-Friedkin’s self-appraisal mechanism enables robots to continuously update the weight they put on their personal information based on the perceived influence on the collective estimate. Our dynamic peer-specific social-information-weighting mechanism further enables robots to assign different importance levels to information received from individual neighbors, rather than treating all neighbors with the same importance as in the original formulation. We evaluate the method under increasing sensor noise, varying proportions of robots with defective sensors producing random observations, and different group sizes in a realistic robot simulator. In a collective navigation task, we demonstrate that our proposed dynamic peer-specific social weighting extension of the DeGroot-Friedkin model results in improved estimation stability, while being sensitive to fault ratio and group size.

papers.title: Quantum differential interference contrast microscope
papers.abstract: Optical sensing and imaging of transparent unstained biological and material specimen makes use of optical interference to translate phase shifts into intensity measurements, that are readily available in the optical domain. This is the case of Differential Interference Contrast (DIC) microscopes. However, environmental disturbances such as acoustic vibrations, air currents, temperature shifts, and mechanical drifts cause random phase noise that degrades the precision attainable in the estimation of the unknown phase shift. Although there are tools to compensate for these random phase drifts, such using common path interference techniques or phase stabilization systems, these are not always an option and its introduction is generally at the expense of device simplicity and robustness. Here we introduce a quantum version of Differential Interference Contrast microscopy (qDIC), that makes use of quantum interference for polarization analysis. When compared with standard schemes that make use of coherent light, our approach shows that the transfer of classical DIC microscopy into the quantum domain offers a route towards quantum-enhanced resilience to environmental disturbances, allowing the enhancement of phase sensitivity without sacrificing the simplicity and robustness of the optical setup.

papers.title: Magnon-Phonon-Polariton Optomechanics in a van der Waals Magnet
papers.abstract: The layered anti-ferromagnet CrSBr hosts self-hybridized exciton-polaritons that couple parametrically to coherent magnons and phonons. In this work, we explore the tripartite optomechanical interaction between these quasiparticles in suspended CrSBr membranes supporting high-$Q$ breathing-type acoustic phonon modes. Using resonant pump-probe spectroscopy on the polariton state, we resolve the coupled dynamics in the $\simeq 20$ GHz range while sweeping the magnon mode across the phonon resonance with an external magnetic field. We observe an attractive magnon-phonon interaction of strength $V/2\pi = -43$ MHz, which primarily leads to phonon amplification. At the magnon-phonon resonance, we find predominantly unidirectional energy flow from magnons to phonons while the possible back-action is limited by kinetic losses of coherent magnons. Our study enables direct interfacing of collective magnetic excitations with sound and light in layered van der Waals materials, paving the way for quantum-coherent transduction in the GHz range with optical readout.

papers.intro:
Hybrid optomechanical quantum systems combine the spectral selectivity and geometric tunability of sharp mechanical resonances with the sensitive, non-contact excitation and readout provided by optics [10, 13, 11]. Another class of hybrid quantum systems leverages the coupling of mechanical resonances to collective spin excitations. Magnons, the quanta of spin waves, can transport information without charge flow. Coupling them to mechanical motion may be used to extend coherent magnon propagation length [1, 38]. Coupling magnons to mechanical excitations has been investigated in nanomagnets, low-dimensional devices [48, 3, 25, 26], and established platforms such as yttrium iron garnet (YIG) [56, 57]. In YIG-based cavity magnomechanics, magnons couple to phonons via magnetostriction and to microwave photons via the magnetic-dipole interaction [56, 58], while optomagnonics extends this coupling to optical photons through magneto-optical effects [49]. For such tripartite systems, theory predicts magnon–photon–phonon entanglement [30], mechanically mediated magnon-to-optics quantum state transfer [18], microwave–optics entanglement [19], and broadband magnomechanical frequency conversion [16], and magnon-mediated microwave-to-optical conversion [23]. However, in these platforms, the magnetic, mechanical, and optical degrees of freedom reside in separate components or couple only weakly, which limits conversion efficiencies [23, 58]. This motivates the search for materials and hybrid quantum architectures in which coupled optical, mechanical, and magnetic degrees of freedom coexist within strongly coupled light–matter states, such as polaritons, enabling quantum coherent GHz\mathrm{GHz} transduction with optical readout.

papers.title: Zernike-efficient phase contrast with a scanned electron probe
papers.abstract: For weak-phase objects, scanning transmission electron microscopy (STEM) with a far-field detector transfers at most half of the phase information per electron that Zernike phase-contrast (ZPC) conventional transmission electron microscopy (CTEM) achieves. We propose APEX (Apex Phase-plate EXit-wave imaging), a scanned-probe mode that combines a defocused probe, a $\pi/2$ phase element in a magnified image of the probe crossover, and in-focus image-plane detection at each scan position. It applies the generalized Zernike framework of Dwyer and Paganin to a scanned probe. In a linear model of a thin weak-phase object with an ideal phase dot, APEX transfers nearly the full Zernike Fisher information over a wide band, substantially more than diffraction-plane four-dimensional STEM (4D-STEM). In idealized simulations of myoglobin in vitreous ice at a cryo-EM dose (elastic scattering only, no chromatic aberration, full coherence), ideal-dot APEX at a probe defocus of 1 $\mu$m reconstructs the phase more accurately than defocused 4D-STEM ptychography with one untuned probe setting. At a defocus of about 25 $\mu$m, a crossed laser phase plate (XLPP) acts as the $\pi/2$ element, and APEX of a periodic specimen cell comes close to CTEM with the same plate. In two dimensions, this mode is equivalent to laser phase-plate CTEM of a small, scanned area. A single simulated APEX scan with the XLPP also separates two myoglobin phase screens 150 nm apart in vacuum, at known depths, which is not possible with one ZPC CTEM exposure.

papers.title: Lost in the Funnel: Selection-Induced Miscalibration in Ranking and Decision Systems
papers.abstract: Modern ranking and decision systems combine components with divergent objectives, and scores calibrated at the model boundary are used as calibrated probabilities throughout the funnel, across filtering, reranking, business-rule enforcement, and auctions. Yet calibration is typically validated only where the score is produced, so its breakdown where the score is used is routinely overlooked. We ask when calibration survives this selection, how inherited error differs from selection effects, and what can fail for a perfectly calibrated score at a component boundary. We study these questions through a boundary-wise diagnostic framework of residual identities. We target rubric-judged relevance rather than presentation-dependent metrics such as CTR, so calibration is measurable at every funnel layer of interest. We first present an industry-wide case study that applies our diagnosis to settings where calibration deteriorates at decision time, tracing the degradation to selection rather than model error. This diagnosis motivates Funnel-Aware Recalibration (FAR): post-hoc, selection-policy-aware recalibration at the boundary where scores drive decisions. In a live two-region production A/B test, FAR cuts decision-time expected calibration error (ECE) by 60-80% and improves auction efficiency. We further adapt two public datasets to simulate industry settings, providing additional evidence for the mechanism. We plan to release the adapted datasets and their generation pipeline to support further research. Finally, we distill these findings into practical operating principles for calibrating multi-stage scoring systems.

papers.title: Balancing Exploration and Exploitation in Constrained Combinatorial Optimization with U(1)-Symmetric Tensor Trains
papers.abstract: Tensor Train (TT) decomposition has emerged as a powerful tool for mitigating the curse of dimensionality in a variety of machine learning and combinatorial optimization tasks. Recent advances show that TT-based generative models can efficiently represent and explore high-dimensional discrete spaces, even when the cost function structure is unknown. However, incorporating hard linear constraints into TT-based optimization remains challenging, as existing interpolation and sampling approaches often fail when feasible points are rare. In this work, we develop a general TT-based framework for constrained combinatorial optimization built upon U(1)-symmetric tensor networks. Our method introduces an expressibility-enhancement mechanism for constructing sparse symmetric tensors and a graph-based diversity measure that guides sample selection during training. On assignment benchmarks, expressibility enhancement and diversity-aware selection improve mean solution quality over their respective baselines. The assignment-selected diversifying strategy also extends to nonpolynomial Set Partitioning, with larger relative gains observed in the higher-tensor-rank data families. Separate runtime benchmarks show substantial speedups over ConstrainTNet and PROTES on non-degenerate assignment workloads; comparisons with simulated annealing depend on constraint information and computational budget, but, overall, support the practicality of the current implementation.

papers.intro:
Tensor Train (TT) decomposition has become a powerful tool in the domains of Artificial Intelligence and Combinatorial Optimization in recent years. The idea of squeezing high-dimensional data via tensor train decomposition originated in the field of quantum mechanics (Affleck et al., 1987; White, 1992), where many-dimensional systems naturally arise from particle interactions. In 2011, Oseledets formalized the approach and brought these ideas into computational mathematics (Oseledets, 2011). To date, TT decomposition was applied to low-rank network layer approximation (Novikov et al., 2015), LLM fine-tuning (Yang et al., 2024), optimization (Antil et al., 2023; Mugel et al., 2022), options pricing (Arenstein & Kastoryano, 2025), and some others (Dolgov & Savostyanov, 2020; Iudin et al., 2026; Sulimov et al., 2017; Sozykin et al., 2026)

This paper focuses on applications of TT in combinatorial optimization. In comparison to classical mixed-integer linear programming (MILP) TT is not limited to linear cost functions and does not use any integrality relaxation. In comparison to Constraint Programming (CP) solvers (Biere et al., 2009) and QAOA (Farhi et al., 2014), the cost function structure may be unknown. Compared with Bayesian optimization (Jones et al., 1998), TT can offer favorable scaling when the required ranks remain moderate .

Compared with Bayesian optimization (Jones et al., 1998), TT can offer favorable scaling when the required ranks remain moderate .

We know two paradigms for TT-based optimization. First, we may request cost function values at specific grid points, then interpolate the entire landscape using a low TT-rank assumption (Zheltkov & Osinsky, 2019; Sozykin et al., 2022). Second, we may apply a generative approach (Batsheva et al., 2023): based on some data, learn a probability distribution that encourages low-cost values, and store it as TT. Then we may sample new data from it and use the data for further training until a stopping criterion is reached. TT-format speeds up both the training and sampling phases, making high-dimensional distribution tractable.

The challenge of applying TT to combinatorial optimization appears when variables are constrained to a feasible region (e.g., by linear equalities). In such a case, building a TT surrogate for the cost function is difficult due to a large fraction of infeasible grid points. The probability of finding any feasible point is small, and interpolation based on infeasible points is not informative. On the contrary, even a straightforward generative approach may be pre-trained on feasible data, and in a sampling phase, all infeasible samples may be eliminated. However, if the constraints are hard to satisfy, the algorithm’s efficiency may decrease significantly. To address the challenge of constraint embedding, the authors in (Nakada et al., 2025) used the method of nilpotent matrices. While effective for some practical cases, it is not generalizable to arbitrary linear equations because of exponential scaling with the number of constraints. In (Ryzhakov & Oseledets, 2023), the authors represent the method of exact constraints encoding, but only for constraints that have a particular structure, which is consistent with the tensor train linear topology and locality of interactions. The paper (Lopez-Piqueres et al., 2023) suggests using U⁡(1)U(1)- symmetric tensor networks for problems with linear constraints. The available feasible dataset was used to build a sparse probability distribution tensor, assigning zero probability to all infeasible vectors. Later, an exact framework for incorporating any linear inequalities into a symmetric TT structure was developed (Lopez-Piqueres & Chen, 2025), with a code available on git (Lopez-Piqueres, 2024).

Main contributions. We developed a library for constrained optimization, using tensor trains. Our approach is based on a generative U⁡(1)U(1)-symmetric paradigm, which accommodates arbitrary integer linear equalities, although computational cost depends on the resulting charge structure. Two major contributions expand the paradigm: i) We suggested the expressibility enhancement step, increasing feasible dataset exploitation. Thus, instead of only two strategies of building a sparse U⁡(1)U(1)-symmetric tensor from the feasible data, as in the pioneer paper, we suggest a family of such strategies, controlled by a parameter (exploitation power). The tested enhancement improves mean assignment solution quality over the original construction. ii) We represented a sparse symmetric tensor train as a graph of U⁡(1)U(1) charges, and suggested a graph diversity measure, which helps to choose which samples to use for training on the next algorithm iteration (increasing exploration). The assignment-selected diversifying strategy also improves mean quality on entropic Set Partitioning, with benefits concentrated in higher-tensor-rank data families. Our Julia implementation achieves 7777–448×448\times speedups over ConstrainTNet (Lopez-Piqueres, 2024) on the specified non-degenerate assignment kernel benchmark, depending on size and sampling backend.

The tested enhancement improves mean assignment solution quality over the original construction. ii) We represented a sparse symmetric tensor train as a graph of U⁡(1)U(1) charges, and suggested a graph diversity measure, which helps to choose which samples to use for training on the next algorithm iteration (increasing exploration). The assignment-selected diversifying strategy also improves mean quality on entropic Set Partitioning, with benefits concentrated in higher-tensor-rank data families. Our Julia implementation achieves 7777–448×448\times speedups over ConstrainTNet (Lopez-Piqueres, 2024) on the specified non-degenerate assignment kernel benchmark, depending on size and sampling backend.

papers.title: Do LLM Agents Still Need to Be Told How to Self-Improve?
papers.abstract: LLM agents increasingly drive their own learning. Self-improvement methods delegate various components of model optimization to the models themselves. As models become more capable, this motivates a basic question: do these increasingly capable models still need us to specify how they should self-improve? In this paper we study an autonomous paradigm in which, given basic primitives, resources, and a general goal for self-improvement, agents construct their own self-learning algorithm for context-based optimization. Using the setting of gameplay as a testbed, a frozen LLM agent is given a compute budget and tools for collecting experience and updating text documents, and allowed to freely experiment without an externally imposed loop or access to real-world data. We find that sufficiently capable models do self-improve under these conditions, demonstrating strategies that align with classic cognitive frameworks for self-regulated learning and constructs from machine learning literature on self-generated curricula. Furthermore, we study the extent to which the learned text artifacts transfer to external benchmarks, observing improvement across different game horizons, mechanics, and 3D navigation.

papers.title: A Survey of Modeling Languages for Automotive Digital Twins
papers.abstract: The demand for digital twins and suitable modeling techniques in the automotive industry is increasing rapidly. Yet, there is no common understanding of digital twins in automotive, nor are there modeling techniques established to create automotive digital twins. Recent studies on digital twins focus on the analysis of the literature on digital twins for automotive or in general and, thus, neglect the industrial perspective of automotive practitioners. To mitigate this gap between scientific literature and the industrial perspective, we conducted a questionnaire survey among experts in the German automotive industry to identify (i) the desired purposes for and capabilities of digital twins, (ii) the modeling techniques related to engineering and operating digital twins across the phases of automotive development, and (iii) the role informal models play during automotive development. To this end, we contacted 189 members of the Software-Defined Car research project and received 96 responses. The results show that digital twins are considered most useful in the usage and support phase of automotive development, representing vehicles as-operated. Moreover, simulation models, source code, and business process models are currently considered the most important models to be integrated into a digital twin alongside the associated, established tools. Furthermore, informal models are frequently created digitally, e.g., using PowerPoint, mainly employed for communication and documentation during the conception and development phase.
