papers.intro:
Digital Twins (DTs) (Kritzinger et al., 2018; Tao et al., 2018) are complex software systems that connect to an actual system, e.g., a (simulated) vehicle, obtain data from it, represent it based on this data, and use this data to optimize its behavior (ISO/DIS, 2020; Digital Twin Consortium, 2022; Eramo et al., 2021). They are used in a variety of domains, including agriculture (Alves et al., 2019), manufacturing (Bolender et al., 2021), medicine (Lauzeral et al., 2019), and many more (Dalibor et al., 2022b). Typical purposes of digital twins include monitoring (Magargle et al., 2017), validating (Hua et al., 2022), predicting (Rajesh et al., 2019), and optimizing the behavior of the actual system. For this, DTs require different properties (Digital Twin Consortium, 2022), such as, collecting data, model processing, simulation, bi-directional communication. Related studies collected various definitions of DTs across domains from the literature (Dalibor et al., 2022b) and investigated how DTs can be engineered for the production of automotive and what their added-value could be (Biesinger et al., 2019). While other related studies focusing on modeling languages (Wortmann et al., 2020; Amrani et al., 2021) and model-based engineering (Liebel et al., 2018) exist, they either only query existing literature or are tailored to a certain domain within the automotive development life cycle, e.g., to embedded systems (Liebel et al., 2018; Akdur et al., 2018). Concerning informal models, different studies have examined the use of informal models (Störrle, 2017b), sketches (Baltes and Diehl, 2014; Walny et al., 2011), and diagrams (Cherubini et al., 2007) in software development. However, no study focusing on the utilization of informal model in the automotive development exists.

papers.title: stable-envs-v1: Fast and Reproducible Environments with Controllable Variations
papers.abstract: Training World Models (WMs) relies on processing large amounts of high-dimensional data, which typically needs to be stored, read into memory, and moved from memory to compute units. In principle, GPU-native rendering avoids this movement of large image tensors from memory to compute cores, allowing for better GPU utilization, and training speed-ups. Rendering on-demand also allows to control perceptual appearance through the application of visual variations on-the-fly, allowing for higher diversity in training. To this end, we introduce stable-envs, an open-source library for fast, GPU-native rendering allowing to apply controllable variations on multiple simulation environments. By rendering image observations directly on GPU, stable-envs allows end-to-end training speed-ups of up to 1.33x, with no loss of performance. Besides faster training runs, stable-envs also enables reproducible, large-scale evaluations through batched physics while maintaining full determinism. stable-envs currently supports 80 simulation environments across multiple CPU- and GPU-backends, and is openly available at: https://github.com/galilai-group/stable-envs

papers.intro:
Pixel-based World Models (WMs) learn environmental dynamics solely from visual observations. In practice, training WMs from image frames requires efficiently processing large amounts of high-dimensional image data, collected (1) online, interacting with an environment (Ha and Schmidhuber, 2018; Hafner et al., 2019; Hafner et al., 2025), (2) offline, via a behavior policy used to collect trajectories (Zhou et al., 2024; Sobal et al., 2026; Maes et al., 2026b), or (3) both. Regardless of its source, image data can be challenging to process: even compact WMs trained on medium-sized, task-specific datasets such as Maes et al. (2026b, LeWM), can require processing ∼\sim200GB of image data.11 1 1 byte per pixel @uint8, 224x224 frames, 20k trajectories of 200 steps each on average.. Storing and processing such volumes for simple environments (e.g., maze navigation) can be challenging in practice, and potentially prohibitive for complex environments, e.g. high-fidelity robotics simulators, e.g. Mittal et al. (2025).

To mitigate these storage requirements, open-source libraries built for training models from pixel-space trajectories often store visual observations as compressed videos, which are then decoded into individual frames before or during training, e.g., Cadene et al. (2026). While effective for storage, video decoding introduces additional overhead: loading, decoding, and storing individual frames ahead of training can take several hours for large datasets. Streaming decoded frames concurrently with model updates can avoid this time-consuming pre-processing step, but requires carefully balancing frame production and consumption to prevent GPU under-utilization. Crucially, both approaches typically still require transferring decoded frames from CPU to GPU, introducing additional data-movement overhead.

For WMs trained in simulation, rendering observations (1) on-the-fly and (2) directly on the GPU avoids storing large image datasets and transferring image tensors between CPU and GPU. However, rendering can itself become a training bottleneck, making frame throughput critical for efficient training. Existing libraries typically achieve high throughput through CPU-based environment vectorization and parallelization (Raffin et al., 2021; Towers et al., 2026; Weng et al., 2022). While effective at scaling environment execution, these approaches do not necessarily accelerate individual environments and can incur substantial overhead when generating and transferring large image tensors to the GPU. Other frameworks, such as Isaac Lab (Mittal et al., 2025), ManiSkill3 (Tao et al., 2025), and MuJoCo Playground (Zakka et al., 2025), leverage GPU-accelerated simulation and rendering to achieve high throughput across many environments on the GPU. However, these frameworks often rely on specialized simulation backends and hardware requirements, limiting portability across research workflows—e.g., Isaac Lab’s GPU renderer is not supported by Hopper-class NVIDIA GPUs (e.g., H100) nor macOS.

To mitigate these scalability and accessibility issues, we introduce stable-envs, a lightweight, research-friendly library, designed for fast and reproducible GPU-native rendering across multiple simulation environments. For each supported environment, we port or re-implement the original physics simulation and expose its complete internal state, enabling (1) fast rendering (2) exact state saving and restoration for reproducibility and (3) controllable visual variations behind a single, shared API. In summary, our contributions are: • Fast, reproducible, and controllable environment rendering. Through optimizations such as batched rendering and custom GPU kernels, stable-envs achieves up to 8.5x higher environment throughput than CPU-native baselines. By exposing the full simulator state, stable-envs also enables exact state restoration and independent sampling of visual factors of variation, allowing fully-reproducible experiments under controlled visual changes. • A comprehensive, GPU-native simulation library. stable-envs currently supporting 80 simulation environments used for world-model research. All environments support batched physics stepping and rendering on the GPU, allowing for efficient training and evaluation of pixel-based WMs. • Accelerated end-to-end world-model training. Thanks to on-the-fly and on-GPU rendering, stable-envs enables up to 1.33x faster training of WMs through stable-worldmodel (Maes et al., 2026a), with no degradation in downstream planning performance. papers.title: Auditors Struggle to Catch Sabotage In End-to-End Transcripts of AI Safety Research
papers.abstract: As AI systems are increasingly used to automate AI R&D, misaligned systems could sabotage research intended to improve model safety and alignment. To stress-test defenses against such sabotage, we use a human expert as a proxy saboteur on AI safety research. We conduct a red-team/blue-team game where a human researcher runs AI safety experiments from scratch and auditors try to tell which were sabotaged and how. Given access to the full research transcript and the ability to run experiments, human auditors mostly fail to distinguish sabotaged from benign research: they achieve an AUROC of 0.59, not significantly better than chance, and fully identify the specific sabotage in only 17% of cases. Despite not being allowed to run experiments, the best frontier models outperform human auditors (Fable 5.1: AUROC 0.73, 32% full identification) within noise and weaker models perform comparably. When the saboteur chooses which experiments are attacked, rather than being required to sabotage every question given, sabotage identification drops further. Our results suggest that research sabotage by expert-level agents is difficult to detect with current auditing methods and provide a new setting for studying research sabotage.

papers.title: Stable recurrences of the super-transition array formalism from marked generating functions
papers.abstract: The conventional evaluation of super-transition-array (STA) mean energies and variances uses partition recurrences with alternating terms that can lose numerical accuracy. Here we apply a marked-generating-function approach to derive coupled coefficient recurrence relations that avoid these sums and directly accumulate fixed-occupation partition functions and arbitrary-order moments of the configuration-average (centroid) transition energies. Unlike explicit expansions into products of subshell occupations, the resulting recurrences require only one coefficient numerator per moment order. The same approach provides recurrences for polynomial occupation-number averages, which can be contracted to obtain the contributions of individual configurations to the STA variance and the Boltzmann energy correction entering the partition function. These contractions avoid the explicit evaluation of individual occupation-product averages and reduce the number of auxiliary quantities required. Numerical examples demonstrate agreement with direct configuration enumeration, including regimes where the alternating Bar--Shalom recurrences lose accuracy. Complementary hole-counting recurrences are also derived for all quantities, starting from a full supershell.

papers.intro:
Super-transition arrays (STAs) were introduced by Bar-Shalom, Oreg, and Goldstein in 1989 [1] as a statistical framework for replacing transition arrays from an impractically large number of configurations in hot dense plasmas. The original formulation provided expressions for the first three STA moments: the total strength, mean transition energy, and variance. Their evaluation relied on recurrence relations involving alternating sums, both in the construction of the supershell partition functions and in the subsequent evaluation of the moments. The cancellation of large positive and negative contributions can lead to severe numerical instabilities, particularly at low temperatures and for large supershell occupations. Importantly, accurate partition functions alone do not eliminate these instabilities, since catastrophic cancellation can also occur in the expressions for the STA moments themselves.

papers.title: Right Diagnosis, Unsafe Route: Auditing Clinical AI Decision Trajectories and Corrective Oversight for Validity and Potential Harm
papers.abstract: A clinical AI system can reach a correct final diagnosis through intermediate decisions that could have harmed the patient, and can repair an error while introducing new risks. Most evaluations score final diagnoses; even stepwise benchmarks, which release a case's evidence over time, score whether systems reach the right diagnosis or gather the right information, not whether the decisions a patient passes through are safe. We make patient safety the target of stepwise evaluation. A trajectory audit replays real admissions checkpoint by checkpoint, lets each system decide with only the evidence released so far, and rates every test, treatment and disposition for its potential harm to the patient and, separately, for clinical validity, against the documented final diagnosis and physician-written disease rubrics yet on the evidence available when the decision was made. An LLM judge scores every decision, and a physician reference standard (triple annotation and senior adjudication of a stratified sample) calibrates the rates. An oversight audit branches each trajectory at its first actionable error and measures, on the same branches, whether corrective feedback repairs the error and whether it introduces new harm. Across 300 cases from a hospital cardiology cohort, MIMIC-IV and the public ASCENT benchmark, with up to seven AI systems per source, 55.2% of hospital trajectories reaching an acceptable final diagnosis passed through a decision with moderate or severe potential harm and 24.8% through a clinically unacceptable one; the harm rates were 76.2% on MIMIC-IV and 39.6% on ASCENT. Structured corrections resolved 73.6% of first errors versus 24.8% after bare rejection, yet new potentially unsafe decisions followed 30.2% of corrections versus 19.7% of rejections. A correct final diagnosis does not certify a safe trajectory, and a successful correction does not certify a safe recovery.

papers.intro:
Claims about clinical AI systems are often claims about final diagnoses reached after reading a complete case vignette or chart (Singhal et al., 2023; McDuff et al., 2025). A growing body of work has moved evaluation into the stepwise setting in which care actually unfolds: benchmarks release a case’s evidence over time and ask systems to gather information, order examinations and commit to diagnoses and treatments as it arrives (Hager et al., 2024; Schmidgall et al., 2026; Liu et al., 2024; Li et al., 2024; Johri et al., 2025; Fan et al., 2024; Nori et al., 2025; Choi et al., 2026), and they show that performance differs sharply between the stages of a case (Rao et al., 2026; Qiu et al., 2025). These evaluations score whether a system reaches the right diagnosis, gathers the right information or keeps the cost of testing down. None asks the question a patient would ask first: could the decisions made along the way have harmed me? Safety evaluations, in turn, rate single responses or recommendations (Han et al., 2024; Arora et al., 2025; Wu et al., 2025), not the sequence of decisions a patient passes through as the evidence changes. Between admission and discharge, a clinical decision-support system would recommend or omit tests, start or withhold treatments, and argue for escalation or discharge; a correct discharge diagnosis can coexist with an omitted antiplatelet on day one or a premature plan to send a high-risk patient home. This paper puts patient safety at the centre of stepwise evaluation: it asks how often clinical AI passes through potentially harmful decisions on its way to a correct final diagnosis, and whether corrective oversight can make those clinical decision trajectories safer.

papers.title: Cataclysmic Variables from XMM-Newton and eROSITA
papers.abstract: Cataclysmic variables (CVs) are interacting binaries where a white dwarf accretes material from a late-type donor. The most evolved systems, referred to as period-bouncers, host degenerate donors. We present XMM-Newton and eROSITA, which provide complementary views of the CV population. We summarize the capabilities of XMM-Newton for timing and spectroscopic studies, and its ability to characterize accretion geometries, magnetic field strengths, and short-term variability across magnetic/non-magnetic CVs. These data allow studies of individual systems, including magnetic period-bouncers with soft X-ray spectra and faint luminosities that offer insights into the late stages of CV evolution. We then present an overview of eROSITA as the first X-ray all-sky survey in the soft band since ROSAT, and its impact on population studies. The eRASS:4 catalog expands the known X-ray sky and will enable volume-limited samples of CVs, complete up to 500pc for standard CVs and up to 250 pc for period-bouncers. Cross-matching eROSITA detections with optical catalogs produced the largest sample of X-ray-selected CV candidates to date, that will refine X-ray diagnostic diagrams, reassess the demographics of magnetic/non-magnetic systems, and identify new highly evolved CVs. Finally, we describe ongoing searches for unknown systems, including CVs selected through probabilistic cross-matching with Gaia, and period-bouncers identified through a multi-wavelength scorecard. These efforts led to the discovery of new period-bouncers and a promising detached period-bouncer candidate, that could validate alternative models for the evolution of CVs. Together, XMM-Newton and eROSITA provide an unprecedented view into the structure, evolution, and demographics of CVs, with eROSITA laying the groundwork for future studies of compact binary evolution, the Galactic Ridge X-ray emission, and related phenomena.

papers.title: Low-state X-ray spectra of magnetized neutron stars: Probing accretion regimes in SFXTs
papers.abstract: Supergiant fast X-ray transients (SFXTs) are a subclass of high-mass X-ray binaries characterized by prolonged quiescent states, making them ideal sources for studying accretion onto highly magnetized neutron stars (NSs) at low rates. In this work, we present a broadband spectral analysis of three SFXTs: IGR J16418$-$4532, IGR J17544$-$2619, and IGR J11215$-$5952, using archival $XMM-Newton$, NICER, and $ NuSTAR$ observations. Joint spectral fitting of the NICER and $NuSTAR$ data for IGR J16418$-$4532 confirms the presence of a cyclotron resonant scattering feature (CRSF) at $\sim 50$ keV, implying a NS magnetic field strength of $\sim 6\times10^{12}$ G. We detect a cyclotron line at $\sim27$ keV in IGR J17544$-$2619, significantly higher than the previously reported energy of $\sim17$ keV, a difference that may reflect luminosity-dependent changes in the accretion flow. Using a double-Comptonization model, we identify the characteristic two-hump spectral shape in IGR J16418$-$4532 and IGR J17544$-$2619 at luminosities $\lesssim10^{35}$ $\rm erg\,s^{-1}$, indicating that this spectral transition is a universal feature of accreting magnetized NSs independent of the source type. Furthermore, the ratio between the cyclotron line energy and the intersection energy of the two humps in both sources is consistent with the empirical relation established in Be/X-ray binaries, suggesting that the overheated polar cap atmosphere model used to explain X-ray pulsars in low-luminosity states is also applicable to SFXTs. In contrast, IGR J11215$-$5952 shows a smooth single-component spectrum at all flux levels, which indicates a relatively weak magnetic field of the NS.

papers.intro:
High-mass X-ray binaries (HMXBs) are binary systems typically hosting a neutron star (NS), emitting X-rays powered by accreting matter via stellar wind and/or Roche-lobe overflow from an early-type O or B companion star (for recent reviews, see, e.g., Martínez-Núñez et al. 2017; Fornasini et al. 2024). HMXBs can be classified as supergiant X-ray binaries (sgXBs) and Be/X-ray binaries (BeXBs) based on the spectral type of the companion star. In BeXBs, the NS orbits a Be-type companion surrounded by a circumstellar disk. These systems exhibit characteristic Type I outbursts and rare Type II outbursts, resulting in a wide range of X-ray luminosities. Supergiant fast X-ray transients (SFXTs), a subclass of wind-fed sgXBs, also exhibit extreme X-ray variability, with luminosities of ∼1032\sim 10^{32} erg s-1 (in’t Zand, 2005; Bozzo et al., 2010, e.g.,) during prolonged quiescent states and peak luminosities up to 103810^{38} erg s-1 (Romano et al., 2015) during short (typically lasting a few hours) X-ray flares. High-mass X-ray binaries (HMXBs) are binary systems typically hosting a neutron star (NS), emitting X-rays powered by accreting matter via stellar wind and/or Roche-lobe overflow from an early-type O or B companion star (for recent reviews, see, e.g., Martínez-Núñez et al. 2017; Fornasini et al. 2024). HMXBs can be classified as supergiant X-ray binaries (sgXBs) and Be/X-ray binaries (BeXBs) based on the spectral type of the companion star. In BeXBs, the NS orbits a Be-type companion surrounded by a circumstellar disk. These systems exhibit characteristic Type I outbursts and rare Type II outbursts, resulting in a wide range of X-ray luminosities. Supergiant fast X-ray transients (SFXTs), a subclass of wind-fed sgXBs, also exhibit extreme X-ray variability, with luminosities of ∼1032\sim 10^{32} erg s-1 (in’t Zand, 2005; Bozzo et al., 2010, e.g.,) during prolonged quiescent states and peak luminosities up to 103810^{38} erg s-1 (Romano et al., 2015) during short (typically lasting a few hours) X-ray flares. Such pronounced luminosity variations in both BeXBs and SFXTs indicate substantial changes in the accretion process onto the NS, although the mechanisms responsible for their transient X-ray emission are not yet fully understood.

Recent observational studies show that the spectra of accreting X-ray pulsars (XRPs) differ significantly at low and high mass accretion rates (see, e.g., Mushtukov and Tsygankov 2024 for a review). At high luminosities (LX≳1036L_{\rm X}\gtrsim 10^{36} erg s-1), the spectra of XRPs are generally described by an absorbed power law with an exponential cutoff at high energies (Nagase, 1989; Filippova et al., 2005). However, at lower luminosities (LX≲1035L_{\rm X}\lesssim 10^{35} erg s-1), the spectra of some XRPs exhibit a characteristic “two-hump” shape (Tsygankov et al., 2019a; Tsygankov et al., 2019b, e.g.,). In such systems, where the NS is highly magnetized (B∼1012B\sim 10^{12}–101310^{13}\penalty\ G), the accreted matter near the magnetosphere couples to magnetic field lines and is channeled onto the polar caps of the NS, forming hot spots. The characteristic two-hump spectral shape can be explained by radiation emerging from an accretion-heated atmosphere of a strongly magnetized NS (Mushtukov et al., 2021; Sokolova-Lapa et al., 2021). The soft component is associated with thermal radiation reprocessed in the atmosphere, while the hard component is shaped by cyclotron emission and resonant Compton scattering. Cyclotron photons produced by collisional excitation of electrons undergo resonant scattering during their propagation through the atmosphere, which broadens the high-energy spectral component. Both theoretical studies mentioned above explore this general physical picture using different approximations and numerical approaches to radiative transfer.

papers.title: The low-luminosity state of the Be/X-ray pulsar IGR J06074+2205
papers.abstract:
Context. At low accretion rates, X-ray pulsars can develop a two-hump spectrum through the thermalization and Comptonization of cyclotron photons in an accretion-heated, strongly magnetized atmosphere. Sources with independently measured cyclotron-line energies, $E_{\rm cyc}$, are particularly important because they provide a direct estimate of magnetic field strength and allow the continuum shape to be tested against spectral formation models.
  Aims. We investigate the luminosity-dependent spectral evolution of the Be/X-ray pulsar IGR J06074+2205 and constrain the accretion regime in its newly observed low-luminosity state.
  Methods. We analyzed three NuSTAR observations obtained during the 2023 and 2025 outbursts, corresponding to the high-, intermediate-, and low-luminosity states at $L_{3-79}\simeq5\times10^{36}$, $4\times10^{35}$, and $6\times10^{34}$ erg s$^{-1}$, respectively. We supplemented these data with Swift/XRT observations and performed broadband spectral analysis of all three states.
  Results. The high-luminosity spectrum follows a classical cutoff power law, whereas the intermediate- and low-luminosity spectra require two thermal Comptonization components to reproduce their two-hump shape. In the intermediate state, the cyclotron line, first reported at $\sim50$ keV in the high-luminosity state, lies on top of the high-energy hump. We interpret the low-luminosity state as representing stable accretion from a cold disk. IGR J06074+2205 thus joins the very limited sample of X-ray pulsars with cyclotron-line energies that have been observed with a double-humped spectral shape.

papers.intro:
At low accretion rates, the broadband spectra of several X-ray pulsars (Mushtukov and Tsygankov, 2024, XRPs;) depart from the canonical cutoff power-law continuum and develop two broad humps at a few keV and at several tens of keV (Tsygankov et al., 2019b). The double-hump spectral shape can be explained by radiation emerging from an accretion-heated, strongly magnetized neutron star (NS) atmosphere. Mushtukov et al. (2021) considered a scenario in which a substantial fraction of the accretion energy is released through cyclotron photons generated by collisional excitation of atmospheric electrons. These photons are subsequently reprocessed in the overheated atmosphere. Sokolova-Lapa et al. (2021) showed that a similar spectral shape can also arise without this additional source of cyclotron photons through Comptonization of thermal radiation. Both of the models rely on similar radiative processes while differing in their assumptions about atmospheric structure and the relative contribution of collisionally generated cyclotron photons.

papers.title: Circular Vector Tomography with Partial Radial Data
papers.abstract: In this article, we introduce and study several generalized circular Radon transforms acting on smooth vector fields compactly supported in a planar annulus, with centers restricted to the outer acquisition circle and truncated measurement radii. The operators of interest are the longitudinal and transverse circular Radon transforms and their weighted analogues. We characterize the kernels of the individual unweighted transforms. Then we establish the reconstruction of a vector field from the combined longitudinal and transverse circular Radon transform data. We further show that the pairs formed by each transform and its weighted analogue is not sufficient for the complete recovery of a vector field. However, we demonstrate that full reconstruction is possible with suitable additional data. Finally, we numerically implement and validate the derived inversion formulas.

The circular Radon transform maps a function to its integrals over circles. Circular and spherical mean transforms arise in sonar and radar imaging, thermoacoustic tomography, and photoacoustic tomography; see, for example, [9, 10, 18] and the references therein. These applications have motivated extensive research on injectivity, inversion formulas, range characterization, and reconstruction from incomplete data; see [9, 10, 17, 21].

The reconstruction of scalar functions from circular or spherical means has been studied using several analytical methods. Early results include Norton’s Fourier–Bessel inversion for a circular acquisition geometry [24], Fawcett’s inversion of higher-dimensional spherical averages [15], and Andersson’s work on the determination of functions from spherical averages [12]. In the planar case, Agranovsky and Quinto [3] characterized the possible sets of non-injectivity for compactly supported functions, using microlocal methods and properties of harmonic polynomials. Ambartsoumian and Kuchment [9] subsequently studied injectivity by techniques related to finite propagation speed and the domain of dependence for the wave equation.

When the centers lie on the boundary of a domain surrounding the unknown, a variety of inversion procedures are available. Finch, and Patch [17] investigated reconstruction from spherical means with centers on a surrounding surface, while Finch, Haltmeier, and Rakesh [16] obtained inversion formulas in even spatial dimensions. Alongside inversion, the characterization of data that can arise as circular or spherical means is a fundamental question. Ambartsoumian and Kuchment [10] established a complete range description for the planar circular transform with centers on a circle, involving moment-type conditions and restrictions associated with zeros of Bessel functions. Agranovsky, Kuchment, and Quinto [2] developed range descriptions for spherical mean transforms in higher dimensions, while Agranovsky, Finch, and Kuchment [1] investigated the role of moment conditions in such characterizations. More recent range characterizations for the spherical mean transform were obtained in [4, 5, 14].

Vector-field tomography is motivated by imaging problems in which directional or weighted measurements are available. Kunyansky, McDugald, and Shearer [22] studied weighted Radon transforms of vector fields in connection with magnetoacoustoelectric tomography, demonstrating the importance of combining unweighted and linearly weighted observations. The extension of circular Radon transforms to vector fields is motivated by inverse problems involving directional measurements. In geometries where measurements are collected over circles, the tangential and normal components of a vector field give rise to circulation and flux measurements, respectively. Their reconstruction properties are therefore of interest in problems involving fluid flow and current-density imaging. Recent developments in photoacoustic vector tomography, such as the reconstruction of blood-flow velocity fields by Zhang et al. [26], further demonstrate the importance of vector-field imaging. Although these imaging methods do not directly yield circular vector integrals, they provide motivation for investigating such measurements in circular acquisition geometries.

Building on scalar annular inversion, we first establish constructive recovery from the joint unweighted measurements. We then examine the additional information carried by first-order weighted measurements. The longitudinal weighted pair determines the field up to an arbitrary rotationally invariant radial component, whereas the transverse weighted pair leaves an arbitrary rotationally invariant tangential component undetermined. We further show that the undetermined component can be recovered from an angular average of the complementary unweighted data. Complete reconstruction is also possible using two pointwise independent linear weights together with the unweighted longitudinal data. Finally, we numerically implement and validate these formulas for smooth vector fields compactly supported in the annulus using MATLAB.

papers.title: Layerwise Learning-Rate Scaling in Vision Networks: Effective-Rate Identification, Power-Mean Aggregation, and Budget Dependence
papers.abstract: Layerwise learning-rate scaling assigns different learning rates to different parts of a network. Although established in fine-tuning pretrained models, its effects in vision networks trained from scratch are commonly assessed by training each candidate recipe. We show that, in this setting, the rate-related component of a layerwise strategy is well summarized by an effective learning rate computable directly from its multiplier profile. Across matched-control comparisons, changes in test accuracy closely track changes in training loss (r = -0.996), which supports an optimization-progress explanation of the short-budget rate effect. Increasing the untuned base learning rate tenfold shifts the rate-matched contrast upward in all six tested architectures (p = 0.016) and increases the number of architectures in which a published discriminative schedule, excluded from model fitting, outperforms the uniform control from two to five of six (p = 0.031). Within the evaluated strategy space, a parameter-weighted power mean with exponent 0.35 (95% confidence interval [0.20, 0.50]) accounts for 42.6% of within-architecture variance, compared with 36.4% for the arithmetic mean. Ranking candidates by this scalar without training improves the selected candidate's mean percentile rank from the 26th to the 10th and reduces its mean accuracy shortfall relative to the best candidate from 3.70 to 1.12 points. The rate-related effect decays as the training budget increases; relative to tuned baselines, the overall strategy effect falls within the prespecified practical-equivalence margin in two of three architectures. A separate grouping-related contrast can persist at long budgets, although its direction and magnitude depend on the architecture.

papers.intro:
Neural architecture search (NAS) [1, 2] automates what the network is. A complementary design choice is how it is trained, including layerwise learning-rate (LLR) scaling, which assigns different rates to different depths. Discriminative fine-tuning is established for pretrained models [3, 4, 5, 6], and layerwise adaptive-rate methods such as LARS [7] and LAMB [8] are used in large-batch training. For vision networks trained from scratch, however, the effects of a layerwise schedule and the way they depend on its multiplier profile remain less well characterized.

We address this question using matched controls, an intervention on the base rate, an out-of-sample comparison with a published schedule, and longer-budget experiments that distinguish rate-related effects from architecture-dependent grouping effects.

papers.title: From active nests to fast wind gusts: Nested flux emergence as a precursor of persistent non-axisymmetric coronal holes
papers.abstract: Recurring flux emergence within active nests reshapes the Sun's large-scale magnetic field and creates unipolar magnetic regions that can support coronal holes. The fast solar wind emerging from coronal holes drives space weather across the heliosphere. We investigated how the emergence of active nests at the peak of solar cycle 25 drove changes in global magnetic topology, coronal hole formation, and solar wind speed. Coronal holes were identified from composite SDO/AIA maps and their magnetic field properties were extracted from SDO/HMI magnetograms. Spherical harmonic decomposition quantified how magnetic flux was distributed at different spatial scales and was used to extrapolate the coronal field. We compared coronal structure with SOHO/LASCO-C2 observations and the solar wind measured at 1 au. Emerging magnetic flux within active nests rapidly surpassed the pre-existing magnetic flux in 2024, strengthening the non-axisymmetric field and shifting the corona into a tilted-dipole state. This dipolarisation stabilised the large-scale magnetic field, with the heliospheric current sheet anchored above active nests. Unipolar magnetic regions from the edges of active nests sustained non-axisymmetric coronal holes covering 6 to 14% of the solar surface in 2025, comparable to the 12% covered by polar coronal holes at solar minimum. Flux emergence near the tilted-dipole's negative pole returned the corona to a quadrupole-dominated state in 2026. Active nests helped stabilise the coronal magnetic field, while the decay and transport of unipolar magnetic flux sustained persistent, non-axisymmetric coronal holes. Differential rotation between unipolar regions triggered episodic expansion and contraction of the largest coronal holes. Early identification of specific active nest configurations, combined with the solar cycle phase, could improve the forecasting of coronal holes and fast solar wind.

papers.intro:
Dynamo-action within the convection zone drives the evolution of the Sun’s magnetic field over an 11-year cycle (Brun and Browning, 2017, for a review, see). Magnetic flux emerges at the photosphere, forming active regions that produce flares and coronal mass ejections (van Driel-Gesztelyi and Green, 2015), whilst modifying the large-scale magnetic field topology (Réville and Brun, 2017). As the solar cycle progresses, active regions shift the distribution of photospheric magnetic field from low-degree, axisymmetric (aligned with the rotation axis) spherical harmonics toward more complex, non-axisymmetric components (DeRosa et al., 2012; Finley and Brun, 2023). Eventually, the transport and cancellation of emerged magnetic flux reverses the Sun’s polar magnetic fields (Hathaway, 2015). The evolution of the Sun’s magnetic field shapes the heliosphere, organising both the fast and slow solar wind streams (Wang et al., 2010). The fast solar wind presents a major space weather hazard, driving co-rotating interaction regions and preconditioning interplanetary space for the propagation of coronal mass ejections and energetic particle events (Richardson, 2018, for a review, see).

Coronal holes, dark regions of the Sun’s surface at extreme-ultraviolet (EUV) and soft x-ray wavelengths (Timothy et al., 1975; Bohlin, 1977; Zirker, 1977), are the source of the fastest solar wind streams at 1 au (600 to 800 km/s). Coronal holes have lower temperatures and densities than their surroundings, and contain relatively weak magnetic field with a net magnetic polarity (Cranmer, 2009, for a review, see). The unipolar magnetic regions within coronal holes are comprised of small-scale funnels (at granular and super-granular scales) that open into the large-scale magnetic field and solar wind above (Wedemeyer-Böhm et al., 2009; Finley et al., 2022). Polar coronal holes appear when meridional transport of magnetic flux from the previous cycle accumulates unipolar magnetic field at the Sun’s poles (Sun et al., 2015). During the solar cycle, the emergence and decay of active regions creates locally imbalanced magnetic flux that allows non-axisymmetric coronal holes to develop (Karachik et al., 2010; van Driel-Gesztelyi et al., 2012; van Driel-Gesztelyi and Green, 2015). The rotation of non-axisymmetric coronal holes is enforced by the large-scale magnetic field, with interchange reconnection allowing their boundaries to slip relative to the surface differential rotation (Wang et al., 1988; Wang and Sheeley Jr, 1993). The longitudinal drift of coronal holes over several months reflects their connection to flux emergence and solar cycle phase (Krista et al., 2018; Heinemann et al., 2020; Harris et al., 2022). Nearly 50% of all active regions are formed by nested flux emergence, appearing in close proximity to previously emerged flux (Castenmiller et al., 1986; Harvey and Zwaan, 1993; Schrijver and Zwaan, 2008; Norton et al., 2025). Active nests tend to anchor the heliospheric current sheet (HCS) directly above them (Balthasar and Schüssler, 1983; Neugebauer et al., 2000; Benevolenskaya, 2005; Obridko et al., 2011; Yang et al., 2024; Tähtinen et al., 2024). They influence the Sun’s large-scale magnetic field by amplifying non-axisymmetric magnetic field components (Tähtinen et al., 2026; Tähtinen, 2026) and stalling the reversal of the coronal magnetic field (Finley, 2024). This study investigates the formation of persistent non-axisymmetric coronal holes, linked to flux emergence in active nests and the stability of the coronal magnetic field. Section 2 describes the data products and identification method for coronal holes. Section 3 provides an overview of solar activity, flux emergence, large-scale magnetic field evolution, and coronal hole growth over solar cycle 25. We then highlight the largest continuous non-axisymmetric coronal hole, that persisted for almost two years. In Sect. 4, we discuss how nested flux emergence shaped the coronal magnetic field and produced the unipolar magnetic regions that allowed coronal holes to develop. We conclude that certain patterns of active nests in Carrington coordinates serve as precursors to coronal holes and fast solar wind streams, providing a pathway to improve space weather predictions.

papers.title: Improved accuracy of the reference photon calibration standards in the network of gravitational-wave observatories during the O4 observing run
papers.abstract: The global network of gravitational wave observatories uses systems known as Photon Calibrators to provide absolute calibration via laser radiation pressure. Successive detector improvements are increasing sensitivity, enabling not only increase the detection rate but also detections with high signal to noise ratios. To optimally extract information from these detected signals, continual effort is directed at pushing the state of the art of the interferometer calibration accuracy. To improve the accuracy of the locally-maintained laser power standards for photon calibration, a new global calibration scheme was implemented by using transfer standards calibrated at both the National Institute of Standards and Tech- nology (NIST) in the US and the Physikalisch-Technische Bundesanstalt (PTB) in Germany during the recently completed fourth observing run. We report the results of a long-duration NIST-PTB bilateral comparison conducted over almost three years and the results of propagation of transfer standard calibrations to the reference power sensors maintained at each observatory.

Current gravitational-wave interferometers use systems that are referred to as Photon Calibrators (Pcals) to provide absolute calibration. The Pcals produce periodic fiducial displacements of suspended interferometer mirrors at discrete frequencies across the 20 Hz to 2 kHz detection band via photon radiation pressure [14, 12, 11]. Since these periodic displacements of the mirrors are proportional to the incident Pcal laser power, accurate and precise calibration of the displacement fiducials depends on accurate estimation of the power impinging on the mirrors.

To date, LIGO Pcal power sensor calibrations have been based on transfer standards (TS) calibrated by the US national metrology institute (NMI), the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) [14, 8]. papers.title: Physics-informed neural networks for spacecraft trajectory optimization with exact boundary conditions
papers.abstract: We use neural networks to optimize trajectories by modeling the position as a function of time and minimizing the thrust with respect to the network parameters. This corresponds to an unsupervised training procedure in which physical laws are incorporated directly into the optimization objective. In standard physics-informed neural networks, initial and terminal states are enforced through additional weighted loss terms, resulting in a multi-objective optimization problem that is highly sensitive to the choice of loss weights and can lead to poor convergence and reduced accuracy. To address this challenge, we construct a simple transformation, exploiting the mathematical structure of trajectory optimization problems, to enforce boundary conditions exactly a-priori. This transformation can be interpreted as a reparameterization of the solution space that embeds the boundary conditions directly into the function. This converts the original constrained optimization problem into an unconstrained one over admissible trajectories. I.e. the transformation eliminates the boundary condition penalty terms and reduces the problem to a single-objective optimization. Crucially, trajectory optimization comes with a low-dimensional boundary, which allows particularly simple and stable constructions of distance functions compared to general domains in partial differential equations. Numerical experiments demonstrate that the proposed approach meaningfully improves convergence behavior and solution accuracy.

Machine learning has gained recent interest as a tool in astronautics and aerospace engineering (AAE), e.g. for data-driven modeling, control [49, 64], or design of complex systems [9]. Applications range from aerodynamic shape optimization [58] and turbulence modeling [45] to design [36] and satellite fault diagnosis [31]. Data-driven surrogates have been particularly effective in reducing the computational burden of high-fidelity numerical simulations, e.g. for model optimization, parameter estimation or uncertainty quantification [47].

Data-driven surrogates have been particularly effective in reducing the computational burden of high-fidelity numerical simulations, e.g. for model optimization, parameter estimation or uncertainty quantification [47].

Machine learning has also gained interest for trajectory optimization specifically. Already Ampatzis and Izzo [2] demonstrated the use of machine learning for surrogate modeling of objective functions in interplanetary trajectory design. Deep learning and/or reinforcement learning has gained particular interest recently and has been used for interplanetary missions under uncertainty [67], low-thrust orbital transfer [57, 8], intercept guidance [23], planetary landing [24], uncontrolled re-entry prediction [51] and autonomous spacecraft guidance during proximity operations [21]. Beyond deep or reinforcement learning, many other models and algorithms have been proposed, e.g. hybrid models for collision avoidance [27] or Gaussian mixture models (GMMs) [22] to equip the trajectory optimization with a notion of uncertainty. Data-driven optimization has also expanded to the aviation domain, where machine learning techniques assist in designing fuel-efficient aircraft trajectories subject to operational constraints [65]. In proximity operations, learning-based trajectory planning has been used through deep neural networks [5, 66], incl. e.g. transformers for rendezvous scenarios [28].

We demonstrate that the imposition of exact boundary conditions via this transformation can improve both convergence behavior and solution accuracy for trajectory optimization problems.

For this, we identify and exploit a structural property of trajectory optimization problems that allows boundary conditions to be embedded directly into the function class, thereby converting a multi-objective learning problem into a better-conditioned single-objective optimization problem. This eliminates the need for boundary condition penalty terms altogether. In contrast to more general settings, we exploit the typically relatively simple geometric structure of boundary conditions in trajectory optimization specifically. We demonstrate that the imposition of exact boundary conditions via this transformation can improve both convergence behavior and solution accuracy for trajectory optimization problems.

papers.title: Structural Response to the Hidden Charge Order in Sr$_3$Fe$_2$O$_7$
papers.abstract: We previously reported `hidden' charge order below $\sim$330 K in the centrosymmetric skyrmion host Sr$_3$Fe$_2$O$_7$ [J.-H. Kim et al., Phys. Rev. Lett. 127, 097203 (2021)], finally identifying the charge disproportionation and localization transition that had been first seen in the 1960s. We detected this through resonant x-ray scattering, which directly probes electron density, but is only indirectly sensitive to the lattice structure. This left open the question of whether the charge-ordering transition has a true structural component or consists merely of the reorganization of electrons. Neutrons probe the lattice directly, and we now show, based on neutron data, that the charge order is accompanied by a clear structural modification.

papers.title: Pareto-Informed Smart "Predict, then Optimize" for Multi-Objective Combinatorial Problems
papers.abstract: Many real-world planning applications, from logistics, routing to resource allocation, give rise to optimization problems that need to balance multiple, conflicting objectives. While machine learning is often used to predict the unknown parameters or costs of these problems, standard models trained on prediction accuracy can lead to suboptimal plans. Decision-Focused Learning (DFL) addresses this by integrating the downstream optimization task into the training objective. However, existing DFL methods for multi-objective problems rely on simple scalarization, which fails to capture the rich trade-offs of the Pareto Frontier. To address this gap, we propose a Pareto-aware extension to single-objective Smart "Predict, then Optimize" (SPO+) for multi-objective combinatorial optimization problems. Our loss function leverages the true Pareto Frontier, forming a target decision that aligns with a sampled preference vector, and minimizes regret against this target. Experiments on multi-objective shortest path and multi-objective knapsack problems show that our approach outperforms traditional two-stage Mean Squared Error (MSE) baselines. It also surpasses scalarization-based SPO+ approaches.

papers.intro:
Decision making in complex operational domains, such as logistics, infrastructure management, or resource allocation, frequently involves navigating complex trade-offs between multiple conflicting objectives (Hauer, 2009; Kuhlemann et al., 2024; Mandell, 1991). For example, a logistics provider must constantly balance the speed of delivery against fuel consumption and monetary cost, where the optimal choice is rarely the same for all three objectives. For problems with a discrete solution space, Multi-Objective Combinatorial Optimization (MOCO) (Ahmed and Deb, 2012; Jia et al., 2024) provides a formal framework for finding optimal trade-offs; however, this requires the objective coefficients (i.e. costs) to be known in advance.

A fundamental difficulty in applying automated planning to real-world domains is that these crucial parameters are often uncertain and dynamic. In a transportation network, the cost to traverse a segment of a road is not a static value, but a function of time-varying characteristics such as current weather patterns, traffic congestion, time of day or whether it is a holiday (Ruß and Gust, 2023). This uncertainty has led to the widespread adoption of ”predict, then optimize” approach (Mišić and Perakis, 2020; Vanderschueren et al., 2022). In this two-stage approach, a machine learning (ML) model first predicts the unknown cost vector, c^\hat{c}, based on observable features, xx. Subsequently, these predictions are treated as fixed parameters which are fed into a deterministic combinatorial solver to compute a supposedly optimal plan or decision, w⁡(c^)w(\hat{c}).

While modular and intuitive, this sequential approach suffers from a critical weakness known as the “prediction-decision gap”(Elmachtoub and Grigas, 2022; Elmachtoub et al., 2023; Shah et al., 2024). Standard ML approaches are typically trained to maximize predictive accuracy by minimizing a loss function like Mean Squared Error (MSE) between the predicted costs, c^\hat{c} and the true costs, cc. The underlying assumption is that more accurate predictions will invariably lead to better decisions. However, a substantial body of research has demonstrated that this assumption can be false (Elmachtoub and Grigas, 2022; Mandi et al., 2024). The reason is that not all prediction errors are equal; a model with a low overall error may make small mistakes on costs critical to the solver, leading to highly suboptimal decisions, while a model with higher error on irrelevant costs may yield a near-optimal decision. This misalignment between the learning objective and the ultimate decision-making goal can lead to demonstrably poor outcomes in practice.

To bridge this gap, Decision-Focused Learning (DFL) has emerged as an alternative (Mandi et al., 2024; Schutte et al., 2024). Recent works, such as “Smart Predict, then Optimize” (SPO+), directly incorporate the structure of the downstream optimization problem into the ML model’s training objective (Elmachtoub and Grigas, 2022). Instead of minimizing prediction error, they aim to minimize decision regret i.e. the quality loss incurred by making a decision based on predicted costs compared to the optimal decision that would have been made with true costs. This allows the ML model to focus on parts of the prediction that have impact on the actual solutions.

While the DFL framework has demonstrated considerable efficacy for single-objective problems its extension to multi-objective optimization contexts remains unexplored. In such problems, there is typically no single solution that is optimal across all objectives simultaneously. The concept of a single “best” solution is replaced by the concept of Pareto optimality. A solution is Pareto optimal if it is impossible to improve its performance on any single objective without degrading its performance on at least one other (Khouadjia et al., 2013). The set of all such solutions constitutes the Pareto set, and their corresponding values in the objective space form the Pareto Front.

A common strategy for adapting single-objective DFL to a multi-objective setting is to use linear scalarization, which combines multiple objectives into one using a preference vector. This approach is fundamentally limited, as it is only capable of finding solutions on the convex hull of the Pareto Front and fails for many combinatorial problems where the front is non-convex. This leaves a significant research gap: the need for a DFL method that is both computationally tractable and can effectively handle the non-convex trade-offs inherent in multi-objective problems.

In this paper, we introduce an extension to SPO+ specifically designed for multi-objective combinatorial optimization problems. While there have been previous works that extend SPO+ to Multi-Task settings (Tang and Khalil, 2023) with multiple independent objectives, our work extends SPO+ to problems with true conflicting objectives that necessitate trade-offs. We introduce a loss function that overcomes the limitations of naive scalarization in the multi objective setting, whilst maintaining its advantages. In our approach, we inform the learning process with knowledge of the true Pareto Front. An ideal target solution from the Pareto Front is selected based on cosine similarity (Ruchte and Grabocka, 2021b) with a sampled Preference, whilst still solving the problem via scalarization. This provides an accurate and geometrically sound learning signal to the model, guiding it to learn cost predictions that lead to high-quality decisions even in non-convex regions of the solution space.

Our Pareto-informed approach significantly outperforms standard baselines in minimizing decision regret. We demonstrate the efficacy and generality of our approach across multiple domains, with strong performance on both the Multi-Objective Shortest Path and Multi-Objective Knapsack problems (Bazgan et al., 2017). Our implementation utilizes the popular PyEPO framework (Tang and Khalil, 2024), and extends it to generate multi-objective costs, providing a valuable baseline for future research in this area.

papers.title: Improving Early Detection of Scientifically Interesting Radio Sources Using Enhanced Isolation Forest
papers.abstract: The rapid growth of radio astronomical surveys has created a major challenge in identifying scientifically interesting sources from large populations of observed objects. This study investigates whether enhanced Isolation Forest (iForest) methods can improve the early detection and ranking of scientifically interesting radio sources. Four iForest variants, Standard Enhanced, Pooled Gain, Kurtosis-based, and Hypervolume, are evaluated using 1,031 extended radio sources from the MeerKAT Galaxy Cluster Legacy Survey (MGCLS). Each source is represented by a 52-dimensional feature set derived using Bootstrap Your Own Latent (BYOL) self-supervised learning and principal component analysis (PCA), while expert scientific-interest ratings are used to define the ground-truth labels. The methods are evaluated using Average Precision (AP), receiver operating characteristic area under the curve (ROC AUC), Precision@10, Precision@50, and cumulative anomaly detection. Pooled Gain achieves the highest Average Precision (AP = 0.201) and the strongest early-stage ranking performance (P@10 = 0.600), identifying six expert-validated anomalies among the ten highest-ranked sources. Standard Enhanced and Kurtosis-based achieve the highest ROC AUC (0.677), while the AUC values of the four variants range from 0.653 to 0.677. These results indicate that feature-aware isolation strategies can improve the prioritization of scientifically interesting sources at the top of the ranked list, although overall discrimination remains comparable across the evaluated variants. The findings support the use of enhanced Isolation Forest methods as an initial ranking mechanism within human-in-the-loop systems for large-scale radio astronomical surveys.

papers.intro:
The Square Kilometre Array (SKA) and its precursors represent a paradigm shift in observational astronomy [1]. MeerKAT, the SKA precursor in South Africa, generates approximately 2 terabytes of data per hour during typical observations [2]. The MeerKAT Galaxy Cluster Legacy Survey (MGCLS) alone has cataloged over 1 million radio sources, each requiring classification and analysis [2]. At a conservative estimate of 30 seconds per source for human inspection, complete manual review would require over 8,300 person-hours, an impossibility for any research team [3]. This data avalanche requires automated methods to identify the approximately 1% of sources that exhibit scientifically interesting properties while filtering out the remaining 99% that display standard morphologies [3, 4]. Previous work by Lochner and Bassett [3] demonstrated that machine-learning approaches, particularly anomaly-detection algorithms, can effectively address this challenge when combined with human expertise.

Astrophysical anomalies are sources with unusual morphological, spectral, or temporal characteristics that may be of scientific interest [3, 4]. Morphological examples include X-shaped radio galaxies, whose unusual wings may be associated with backflow or a reorientation of the jet axis following a merger [5]; one-sided radio sources, for which relativistic beaming is a possible explanation [6]; giant radio galaxies that extend to megaparsec scales and can be used to probe the intergalactic medium [7]; and the recently identified Odd Radio Circles (ORCs) [8].

papers.title: ResoLUT: Distilling Residual Networks into Lookup-Table Networks
papers.abstract: Logic networks built from Boolean gates or lookup tables (LUTs) promise efficient hardware inference, but training them at depth and learning their connectivity remain difficult. We do not train logic as logic. Instead, ResoLUT distills a trained residual network (ResNet) layer by layer into LUT trees, preserving its multi-bit residual stream and BatchNorm while extracting connectivity from the teacher rather than learning it. To our knowledge, ResoLUT is the first convolutional logic network in computer vision to retain a ResNet-style multi-bit residual stream. Hard LUT decisions are used throughout training and inference, avoiding a discretization gap in the logic. ResoLUT-20 reaches 95.66% on CIFAR-10 with twice the trees, and ResoLUT-56 reaches 78.87% on CIFAR-100 and 53.69% on ImageNet at 64px, the best results of logic and lookup-table networks on CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100, showing that LUT networks can scale in depth. We explore and quantify the role of the residuals and the tree budget and shape. The most optimized model, a ResoLUT-8 with one eighth of the trees and further optimizations, fits on an FPGA and reaches 90.04% at 189k images per second, the highest throughput among the compared models above 85% on CIFAR-10.

Digital hardware computes with logic gates and lookup tables (LUTs). A machine learning model that is made of such primitives needs no multipliers, no weight memory traffic and no floating point operations, and it can be unrolled into a single pipelined circuit. Logic gate networks (LGNs) pursue this idea: Petersen et al. [35] relax each two-input gate to a distribution over the 16 Boolean functions, train with gradient descent and discretize afterwards. Convolutional logic trees [36], learnable wiring [4, 13] and better relaxations [50] have since made LGNs more accurate and cheaper to train. LUT networks generalize the node from a two-input gate to a KK-input lookup table [46, 45, 4] (K=2 for LGN).

Convolutional logic trees [36], learnable wiring [4, 13] and better relaxations [50] have since made LGNs more accurate and cheaper to train. LUT networks generalize the node from a two-input gate to a KK-input lookup table [46, 45, 4] (K=2 for LGN).

The accuracy of logic networks, however, has not followed the progress of conventional networks, and the obstacle is depth. A logic layer maps bits to bits, and every gate that is not a pass-through discards part of its input: the image is represented by progressively fewer independent bits, and the gradient that reaches the early layers, a product of many relaxed gates, vanishes. In line with this, the discretization gap of the relaxation grows with depth [50], LILogic Net stops improving after two to four layers [13, 14], stacked LUT layers lose accuracy rapidly in the pilot runs of BitLogic [8], and even with dedicated initializations the standard gate parametrization loses accuracy with depth, while a reparametrization that avoids this gains little from further depth [40]. The existing remedies keep the residual path at a single bit: residual initializations start every gate as a pass-through so that a deep network is initially an identity [36], logical skip connections combine the input and the output of a block with a Boolean gate [25], and explicit skip paths of fixed pass-through gates do not improve on the initialization [40]. Residual initialization does not guarantee a persistent pass-through, since training may discard it. None of these remedies enables a block to add a graded correction. A separate difficulty is connectivity: every gate chooses its inputs from a combinatorial space, and learnable connectomes were found to scale poorly beyond flat networks [13, 14].

In conventional networks the corresponding problem was solved by BatchNorm [22] and the residual stream [20]. We ask whether the numerical originals can be kept in a logic network: a multi-bit residual stream and BatchNorm. Our answer, ResoLUT, rethinks a residual network as a network of four-input lookup tables (Fig. 2). Instead of training logic as logic, it follows the teacher–student idea [21, 38]: a trained ResNet is converted layer by layer, and each LUT layer learns to reproduce the output of the layer it replaces. The residual stream runs next to the LUT layers as a low-precision integer per channel and position; each LUT layer ends in a counter whose count, rescaled by a per-channel affine map that absorbs BatchNorm, is added to the stream; the next layer reads the stream through fixed comparators. Every learned operation remains a lookup table, while the stream keeps a graded value instead of a single bit, so a block can apply a small correction without re-encoding its input. Connectivity is extracted from the teacher’s weights, which turns a combinatorial search into a sequence of small regressions, and only truth tables are trained, with a forward pass that is the exact hard network.

papers.title: A Science Traceability Matrix for Micro-arcsecond Resolution X-ray Imaging
papers.abstract: Our ability to understand the highest energy processes and environments in astronomy is directly tied to our ability to probe their physical processes at the smallest scales. Despite transformative progress in high-angular resolution instruments across the radio through optical, angular resolution within the X-rays has plateaued around $\sim0.1-1''$, and therefore our window into the innermost regions of the high energy Universe lies primarily within spectral, timing, and/or polarimetric studies rather than direct imaging. This represents a significant barrier to gaining a robust understanding of key science questions, including the mechanisms of accretion and jet launching, the accretion activity and angular momentum losses of binary active galactic nuclei (AGN) leading to gravitational wave events, and the space weather events that may influence atmospheric evolution and prebiotic chemistry on potentially habitable exoplanets. The Accretion Explorer Interferometer (AEI) is a mission concept for X-ray imaging that could achieve up to $\mu$as resolution, $\sim5-6$ orders of magnitude better than current instrumentation. Here we present the scientific discovery space enabled by such an advance, and highlight areas of uncertainty and open questions that are critical to investigate for future development of this concept.

papers.intro:
Despite significant technological advancement across multi-wavelength observatories, our only window into the X-ray universe lies within unresolved images. In fact, Chandra, the highest resolution X-ray imager currently flying, can attain angular resolutions of only ∼0.5−1′′\sim 0.5-1^{\prime\prime}, lagging significant behind its multi-wavelength counterparts that regularly achieve angular resolutions in the milli-arcsecond (mas; HST, JWST, VLA, ALMA) and even micro-arcsecond (μ\muas; EHT) range. Even next generation X-ray mission concepts such as the Advanced X-ray Imaging Satellite [66, AXIS;] and the Lynx X-ray Observatory [40, Lynx;] propose limited advancements in angular resolution, either maintaining the status quo at ∼1.5′′\sim 1.5^{\prime\prime} or modest improvements to ∼0.1′′\sim 0.1^{\prime\prime}, respectively. While these missions can enable dramatic new scientific studies and goals [66, e.g.,], they build off of an architecture that inherently limits our capabilities with X-ray imaging to observing larger scales, and resigning our window into the smallest scale processes to indirect spectral or polarimetric studies [64, 114, 140, e.g.,].

This technological gap represents a significant barrier towards truly understanding the most energetic processes in the Universe. For example, one of the most fundamental questions in extragalactic astrophysics is how supermassive black holes (SMBHs) grow to such immense sizes, up to billions of times the mass of our Sun. The primary method by which SMBHs grow is by accumulating material from its host galaxy into an accretion disk that “feeds” the central black hole. This process requires the gas to lose significant amounts of angular momentum in order to reach the SMBH, however the mechanisms by which this happens remains largely unclear as the accretion disk size for even the most nearby X-ray active SMBHs is just ∼50​μ\sim 50~\muas in diameter [33, 78], far below the resolution capabilities of current or proposed X-ray facilities. Studying the high energy emission from the accretion disk will give us a window into how this angular momentum is transferred from the disk, and therefore how the SMBH feeds.

Closer to home, extreme stellar flares can significantly affect planetary atmospheres and environments relevant to habitability on a planet, either by promoting prebiotic chemical processes or by eroding planetary atmospheres that are important for maintaining habitable surface conditions [see 3, 117, for reviews]. To date, the only resolved images we have of these flares are for our own Sun, with resolutions as fine as tens of km [124, e.g.,]. A resolved picture of the spatial distribution of flares across a larger sample of stars would offer critical insight into active region dynamics and their effects on planetary atmospheres, with implications for habitability.

AEI is designed to resolve black hole accretion and image stellar coronal structures and flaring activity. A detailed discussion of the AEI architecture can be found in the NIAC report [136]. In Section 2, we briefly describe the concept and key technical specifications. This dramatic increase in spatial resolution opens up a fundamentally new discovery space, enabling science cases to directly peer into the innermost regions of an accreting SMBH, from the fundamental mechanics of accretion to the launching of powerful jets that drive energy into the larger galaxy [see 137, for a more complete review]. Our team examined four science pillars to assess the most transformative science cases for an X-ray interferometer reaching μ\muas resolution. The high-level science traceability matrix (STM) is published in our NIAC report [136]. Here we report additional details for the science cases investigated in the NIAC study, and expand to include other science priorities for an ultra-high resolution X-ray imager. Finally, in Section 7, we identify open questions regarding the new scientific discovery space within reach with a μ\muas-scale X-ray interferometer and highlight places where precursor science could provide further insight into these future science goals.

papers.title: Formal Analysis of a Fault-Tolerant Extension of the ROSACE Flight Controller
papers.abstract:
Autonomous avionics controllers must satisfy stringent real-time functional and performance require- ments even in the presence of run-time faults. In this paper, we analyze ROSACE, an open-source control engineering benchmark for flight control systems, focusing on its run-time resilience against faults such as sensor noise and sensor failures. We extend the benchmark with an FDIR (Fault Detection, Identification and Recovery) component based on Triple Modular Redundancy.
  Our approach builds upon COMPASTA, a tool for Model-Based Design developed on top of the TASTE tool by ESA. COMPASTA enables the modeling and injection of faults into a system's design. Moreover, it implements a simulation-based verification and validation workflow, automating the generation and execution of a set of test cases, based on a user-defined notion of coverage. Using COMPASTA, we construct a set of formal models, with faults and with FDIR, and we formally analyze their impact on the system properties. The analysis is based on the coupling of the formal models with the Simulink models used for the simulations.

papers.title: Electrical addressing of compensated magnetic order in artificial spin ice
papers.abstract: Compensated magnetic systems, such as antiferromagnets, hold immense potential for spintronic devices thanks to vanishing stray fields, robustness to perturbations, and ultrafast dynamics. Yet, electrical writing and reading of their order remains a major challenge. Here we use artificial spin ice as a mesoscale platform in which compensated order can be engineered, directly imaged, and electrically controlled. Specifically, we demonstrate combined electrical writing and reading of a compensated state in a triangular artificial spin ice. Exploiting the orientation dependence of the spin-orbit torque switching current, we independently switch three nanomagnet sublattices through a single current channel, with the planar Hall effect providing sublattice-resolved readout. This grants access to all eight magnetization states of the triangular plaquette, including its fully compensated state, yielding a nonlinear, history-dependent electrical response. Our results establish an approach to electrically programmable compensated magnetic systems and provide an important foundation for reconfigurable magnetic devices and unconventional computing.

papers.title: Ethics Suppression in AI Development: A Comparative Case Study of Responsible AI Under Competitive Pressure
papers.abstract: This study explores the governance tensions among Google, OpenAI, Meta, and Microsoft, focusing on how competitive AI development can lead to the ethics suppression. The study aims to examine how ethical oversight loses practical influence even when responsible AI structures are formally in place, especially during rapid technological competition. Despite the rapid growth of responsible AI frameworks and ethical principles in the tech sector, there has been less focus on how these concerns are actually applied when pressure to deploy increases. This paper introduces the concept of ethics suppression in AI development, highlighting that while ethical oversight may exist on paper, its practical authority can diminish during decision-making. Using a comparative qualitative case study examining corporate governance documents, public statements, and reports on governance issues, we identify common issues such as reduced authority, a weakened ability to escalate concerns, urgency in deployment, and fragmented governance. Our findings indicate that heightened competition can weaken the influence of ethical oversight, even in organisations with established responsible AI practices. By differentiating ethics suppression from ethics washing, it offers a framework for organisations and policymakers to evaluate the effectiveness of ethical oversight in competitive AI development.

papers.title: Polylogarithmic Regret via Certainty Equivalence in Degenerate LQR
papers.abstract: Singular input penalties, as in minimum variance control, can reduce what must be identified to control an unknown linear system. In online linear quadratic control, certainty equivalence can achieve polylogarithmic regret when the optimal controller is identifiable from data collected under optimal feedback. With a positive definite input penalty, however, this condition is restrictive, since for an invertible state matrix it requires all unknown parameters to be identifiable under optimal feedback. We show that singular input penalties relax this requirement, expanding the class of problems in which certainty equivalence achieves polylogarithmic regret. Specifically, we prove that a certainty-equivalence algorithm with a short initial exploration phase achieves $O(\log^2 T)$ expected regret over $T$ interactions whenever controller identifiability holds. We complement this guarantee with an $\Omega(\sqrt{T})$ minimax lower bound for a family containing a system where controller identifiability fails. For minimum variance control, knowing the range of the input matrix suffices for controller identifiability, a weaker requirement than knowing the full input matrix, as assumed in prior work with positive definite input penalties. This condition also covers underactuated systems, as we illustrate with a cart-pole example.
papers.intro:
Learning to control an unknown system during operation requires balancing exploration, which collects informative data to reduce uncertainty about the dynamics, with exploitation, which uses the available knowledge to achieve good control performance. The linear–quadratic regulator (LQR) with unknown dynamics has become a standard benchmark for studying this trade-off in online control and in reinforcement learning with continuous state and action spaces. In LQR, under a fixed feedback ut=K​xtu_{t}=Kx_{t}, the next state xt+1=A​xt+B​ut+wtx_{t+1}=Ax_{t}+Bu_{t}+w_{t} depends on (A,B)(A,B) only through the closed loop A+B​KA+BK, so models that share this closed loop cannot be distinguished from the collected data. A certainty-equivalence (CE) learner, which always plays the controller that is optimal for a nominal system estimate, may therefore keep collecting data that cannot reveal such model errors. Moreover, classical results show that convergence of self-tuning LQ controllers to the optimal controller generally requires identification of the true parameter (Polderman, 1986). This motivated a variety of exploration strategies (Abbasi-Yadkori and Szepesvári, 2011; Mania et al., 2019; Bartos et al., 2026), which attain the worst-case optimal 𝒪~​(T)\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}(\sqrt{T}) regret rate over TT interactions with the unknown system (Simchowitz and Foster, 2020). CE can achieve faster, polylogarithmic rates when additional structure, such as prior knowledge of the dynamics, makes the data generated under optimal feedback sufficiently informative to identify all unknown parameters. In this work, we show that singular input penalties (degenerate LQR) can allow CE to achieve finite-time polylogarithmic expected regret even when the dynamics are not fully identifiable under optimal feedback.

Shirani Faradonbeh et al. (2020) showed that an episodic CE scheme attains O⁡(log2⁡T)O(\log^{2}T) asymptotic regret almost surely, assuming that the parameters lie in a known set over which the closed-loop prediction error uniformly bounds the error of the optimal gain. Lee et al. (2024) established finite-time polylogarithmic expected-regret bounds for CE with a known linear representation of the dynamics when the optimal controller persistently excites the unknown parameters.

The extent to which singular input penalties relax this requirement remains unaddressed.

In this setting, CI requires all unknown parameters to be identifiable under optimal feedback whenever A⋆A_{\star} is nonsingular (Liu, 2026, Corollary 2). The extent to which singular input penalties relax this requirement remains unaddressed.

A separate line of work studies minimum variance control (MVC). In a related multivariate stochastic regression setting, Lai (1986) obtained asymptotically logarithmic regret by combining CE with sparse probing inputs. Lai and Wei (1987) extended this approach to MVC of finite-order scalar autoregressive models with exogenous inputs (ARX models). More recently, Singh et al. (2024) established finite-time polylogarithmic regret for self-tuning regulation of ARX models, of order log⁡T\log T for bounded noise and log3⁡T\log^{3}T for sub-Gaussian noise. Lin et al. (1985) further argued that CE can fail to converge to the optimal controller for cost criteria other than minimum output variance. Together, these results suggest that degenerate input costs can also contribute to making full parameter identification unnecessary. However, the MVC guarantees for ARX models concern scalar-output regulation without an input penalty. They do not provide guarantees for general quadratic state costs in underactuated systems, or for costs that penalize only some input directions.

papers.title: Non-Intrusive Rubin Substructuring for Geometrically Nonlinear Structures via Nonlinear Manifolds
papers.abstract: Component mode synthesis enables modular reduction of large structural models, but its extension to geometrically nonlinear systems remains challenging. This work generalizes the Rubin method by introducing a cubic displacement manifold that statically condenses high-frequency free-interface modes onto the retained low-frequency modes and residual attachment modes. The reduced equations of motion, with cubic polynomial restoring forces, are derived by Galerkin projection onto the manifold tangent subspace. The consistency of the reduced forces is guaranteed by the cubic expansion of the component-level reduced manifold. We further present a non-intrusive procedure that combines elastic-force identification with finite-difference estimates of tangent-stiffness derivatives, which allows the reduced model to be constructed from the linear Rubin model and tangent-stiffness evaluations. In the proposed numerical tests, the reduced assembled models accurately reproduce the nonlinear responses of the full finite-element models, including internal resonance and modal coupling. Scalability and significant computational gains are demonstrated with an industrial scale model of a wing-box tip tank assembly, for which an online speed-up of about 24,666 was obtained.
