papers.intro: With the steady exponential growth in computational power that occurred in the last decades, numerical simulations have become the norm in early design stage of mechanical and aerospace components. Such analyzes enable optimized designs, thus improving functionality, structural integrity, and reliability of the end product. To this end, the Finite Element method (FE) has been successfully employed to derive finite-dimensional systems of ordinary differential equations that are numerically solved to predict structural vibrations under in-service loads. For a broad set of applications, such as aerospace panels, wind turbines, solar arrays, and MEMS, large displacement formulations must be considered for accurate predictions. These formulations are based on nonlinear strain-displacement kinematic relations, such as the Green-Lagrange strain tensor or the von Kármán strain law [4]. This type of nonlinearity, which goes by the name of Geometric Nonlinearity, is inherited by the elastic forces in the Equations of Motion (EoMs), which are a nonlinear function of the nodal variables. Moreover, fine meshes, usually needed to capture sharp stress gradients in bodies with complex geometries, lead to high dimensional EoMs. The combination of high dimensionality with geometric nonlinearity severely increases the computational cost for time integration of the EoMs, as the numerical solution schemes are based on iterative Newton solvers that repeatedly entail the assembly and factorization of large matrices. Over the past two decades, the need for faster simulations has sparked research on Reduced Order Models (ROMs), which are low dimensional equivalents of the corresponding large high fidelity models. For the analysis of structures modeled with geometric nonlinearities and linear-elastic material constitutive law, simulation-free ROMs can be efficiently constructed by leveraging the physics encoded in the EoMs, without the need of expensive runs of the full order model [34, 30, 31, 42, 13, 20, 19, 46]. Consequently, these methods arguably represent the most efficient alternatives to Data-Driven approaches, whereby the ROM is constructed from time-histories of nodal variables, using, for instance, Proper Orthogonal Decomposition. Among the most established data-free approaches we list the Implicit Condensation and Expansion (ICE) [13, 32], the method of Modal Derivatives [16, 30], the method of Dual Modes [21], the Quadratic Manifold [20], and Spectral Submanifolds [10, 19, 45]. Although extremely effective, these reduction procedures do not reflect the modularity of industrial workflows, whereby the design of different components of a given structure is performed independently by different teams. Component Mode Synthesis techniques (CMS) [1] were developed to alleviate the computational burden for dynamic analysis by resorting to a primitive form of parallel computing, consequently preserving modularity. In fact, the reduction philosophy behind CMS consists of constructing a ROM for each component of a structure —referred to as substructure —and subsequently assembling the different ROMs to predict the response of the structure as a whole. In pioneering work, substructure ROMs were constructed using static solutions to imposed displacements at the interface with connected substructures [9, 17]. These modes, known as Static Modes (SMs), were collected in a Reduction Basis (RB) that was used to approximate the solution using Galerkin projection. To improve accuracy, Hurty [15] and Craig & Bampton [3] complemented the RB with Fixed Interface Modes i.e. Vibration Modes (VMs) obtained by restraining all interface DoFs.This reduction method is known as the Hurty-Craig-Bampton (HCB) method. However, Fixed Interface Modes are, in some cases, not well representative of the substructure internal dynamics, as the fixed boundary conditions used to obtainsuch modes significantly differ from the actual boundary conditions that the interface experiences when the whole structure is vibrating.[28]. Moreover, Fixed Interface Modes are not easily identifiable from standard testing procedures, as free boundary conditions are practically more convenient to implement. These shortcomings led McNeal [28] and Rubin [40] to present a reduction method dual to the HCB method, using Free-Interface Modes (FIMs) instead of Fixed Interface Modes in the RB. Differently from Fixed-Interface-Modes, FIMs are computed as the VMs of the structures when the boundary nodes are not restrained. More recently, FIMs were also used in the Dual-Craig-Bampton method [38], a reduction technique which uses the same reduction space used in Rubin but constructs the ROM EoMs by also projecting the compatibility conditions. While mature for linear problems, CMS remains challenging for geometrically nonlinear problems. In [24, 25], the authors investigated the response of beams and panels vibrating in the large displacements regime using a modified version of the HCB model, which is constructed by adding quadratic and cubic nonlinear components to the linear restoring force. The nonlinear restoring force was identified using ICE from a set of static solutions to applied loads computed from the linear HCB RB. A similar approach was used in [29], though the nonlinear ROM was constructed from the Rubin RB. Although ICE-based procedures proved to be effective, they require a careful choice of the load cases used for model training, especially to avoid buckling [11]. Additionally, the ROM computation can easily become intractable, as the number of static load cases required by ICE grows with the third power of the number of vectors in the linear RB [25]. Another line of research investigated the possibility of tackling geometric nonlinearities by extending the HCB RB, or Rubin RB, with companion vectors aimed at capturing the nonlinear coupling between modes. In [49], the authors complemented the HCB RB using the Static Modal Derivatives (SMDs) corresponding to the Fixed Interface Modes, while in [48] they complemented the Rubin RB using the SMDs corresponding to FIMs and second order perturbation vectors of Static Modes. The pitfall of such procedures lies however in the quadratic growth of the number of additional companion vectors with the number of columns in the linear RB, which can severely undermine reduction efficiency. To overcome this limitation, we recently proposed in [43] to extend the HCB method by enslaving the amplitudes of companion vectors to the amplitudes of the modes in the HCB RB, through a quadratic manifold. In this way, accurate nonlinear predictions were possible without increasing the dimensionality of the linear HCB model. In this work, we build on [43] to extend the Rubin reduction method to systems with geometric nonlinearities. The reduction space is defined from the substructure ROM EoMs in FIMs coordinates, after neglecting inertia, damping and forcing of high frequency FIMs, as done in [43]. This allows us to implicitly define a reduction manifold that is explicitly computed using Taylor series perturbation theory. Unlike [43], the reduction manifold is truncated at third order instead of second order, to be consistent with the use of cubic forces in the reduced EoM. Interestingly, we show that increasing the manifold expansion order incurs almost no additional computational cost compared to the second order manifold, as we reuse quantities computed for the cubic restoring forces. The computed ROM is in polynomial form, thus it enables great speed-ups compared to full order simulations. Unlike [43], the computational procedure for ROM construction presented herein is fully non-intrusive, as the ROM can potentially be computed from standard outputs of commercial FE programs. In fact, the nonlinear ROM is fully identified from a set of tangent stiffness matrix evaluations. We organize the manuscript as follows. In Section 2 we set the full order model equations, introduce notation, and briefly outline the linear Rubin method; in Section 3 we derive the ROM manifold equations and the ROM EoMs; in Section 4 we detail the numerical procedure for ROM computation; eventually, in Section 5, we apply the presented reduction procedure to three different test cases, two academic and one large scale industrial benchmark.

papers.title: Stress Testing a Multimodal Large Language Model Grading Assistant on Kinematics Graph Reading
papers.abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) can recognize graph features yet award credit without sufficient graphical support. This exploratory study examines selected grading outputs for synthetic responses to four kinematics exercises, generated through visual distortion and progressive transformation toward reference graphs. Different model and prompt configurations were used. Some judgments correctly distinguished instantaneous zero velocity from rest over a finite interval and recognized positive curvature. Yet a severely distorted velocity--time graph received full credit despite disconnected and branching traces and an unclear zero-velocity reference. Other submissions graded under the same configuration lost substantial credit. Numerical cutoffs intended to distinguish meaningful features from drawing irregularities were supplied without a coordinate convention for unnumbered graphs, leaving the basis of exact partial-credit awards unresolved. Stress testing can expose unsupported awards before classroom use. For the configurations examined, we do not recommend accepting scores as final grades without instructor review, including review of full-credit responses.

papers.title: Probing Phase Fluctuations in Cuprates by Multidimensional Josephson Spectroscopy
papers.abstract: The normal state of cuprate superconductors is believed to host precursor electron pairing above the superconducting transition temperature. These pre-formed pairs, which extend over an unknown temperature range, are expected to lack long-range phase coherence. Because spectroscopic evidence for this hypothesis is only indirect, new methods to probe these physics are needed. Nonlinear terahertz spectroscopy allows one to probe high-order time correlation functions and is therefore sensitive to fluctuations. Measurements of third-harmonic generation along the superconducting planes have revealed responses persisting above Tc, but a clear relation between these optical responses and specific properties of the fluctuating state has not yet been established. Here, we apply angle-resolved multidimensional terahertz spectroscopy to probe the optical nonlinearity of the Josephson tunneling resonance in La1.83Sr0.17CuO4 across the superconducting to normal state transition. We find that among all third-order nonlinear responses, the non-rephasing multidimensional signal is especially sensitive to non-mean field fluctuations of the order parameter. We measure a crossover occurring at T ~ Tc between a mean-field optical nonlinearity that dominates at low temperatures and one that is mediated by short-range superconducting fluctuations. We present a theoretical framework that connects the out-of-plane optical response in both regimes to the fluctuating in-plane superconducting state, and contrast the sensitivity of different types of terahertz nonlinearities to fluctuating order.

papers.title: Baryonification V: Thermal Sunyaev-Zel'dovich maps from dark-matter-only lightcones
papers.abstract: Baryonic feedback is a major theoretical uncertainty for Stage-IV weak lensing (WL) surveys. The thermal Sunyaev-Zel'dovich (tSZ) effect traces the hot gas redistributed by feedback, so combining it with WL can calibrate feedback and improve cosmological constraints. Doing so with simulation-based inference requires correlated lensing and Compton-$y$ maps across many cosmologies and feedback scenarios. We present two methods to generate Compton-$y$ maps from dark-matter-only $N$-body light cones using the component-wise baryonification (BFC) model, which produces separate gas and stellar fields and computes the gas pressure from hydrostatic equilibrium. The two methods, painting pressure profiles onto halos or redistributing the signal along the baryonified gas, agree to within a few per cent. We calibrate the model to the fiducial and strongest AGN feedback FLAMINGO simulations by jointly fitting gas mass fractions and thermal pressure profiles, measuring the non-thermal pressure from the simulated gas velocities rather than treating it as a free parameter. The predicted Compton-$y$ profiles match FLAMINGO within halo-to-halo scatter, and when painted onto the FLAMINGO halos we reproduce the tSZ power spectrum of both feedback models to $\sim5\%$ for $500\lesssim\ell\lesssim3000$. Applied to a \emph{CosmoGridV1-like} $N$-body simulation, our maps agree with FLAMINGO within $\sim10\%$ for $300\lesssim\ell\lesssim8000$; the remaining differences come from the few hundred most massive clusters, and removing them from both halo catalogs brings the two into agreement. Our method thus enables accurate and efficient tSZ forward models from $N$-body simulation suites such as CosmoGridV1, an important step towards joint WL and tSZ simulation-based inference for Euclid, LSST, and the Simons Observatory.

Energetic feedback from active galactic nuclei (AGN) and supernovae redistributes gas within and around halos and suppresses the matter power spectrum on non-linear scales (van Daalen et al., 2011; Chisari et al., 2019b; van Daalen et al., 2020; Schaye et al., 2023). Since these scales carry much of the lensing signal, the strength of baryonic feedback is one of the leading theoretical uncertainties (Semboloni et al., 2011; Schneider et al., 2020) for Stage-IV weak-lensing (WL) surveys such as Euclid11 1 https://www.esa.int/Science_Exploration/Space_Science/Euclid, the Rubin Observatory Legacy Survey of Space and Time (LSST)22 2 https://www.lsst.org/, and the Roman Space Telescope33 3 https://roman.gsfc.nasa.gov/.. Observables that trace the baryons directly, in particular the hot, ionized gas, probe this redistribution and can therefore constrain the feedback that WL analyses would otherwise have to marginalize over.

The thermal Sunyaev-Zel’dovich (tSZ) effect is especially well suited to constrain feedback. It arises from inverse Compton scattering of Cosmic Microwave Background photons off hot electrons, and its amplitude, the Compton-yy parameter, is the line-of-sight integral of the thermal electron pressure Pe∝ne​TeP_{\rm e}\propto n_{\rm e}T_{\rm e}. The signal therefore depends both on where the gas is located and on how much thermal energy has been injected by feedback. Compton-yy maps have been produced by Planck, the Atacama Cosmology Telescope (ACT), and the South Pole Telescope (SPT), with deeper maps expected from the Simons Observatory (SO), and the angular power spectrum Cℓy​yC_{\ell}^{yy} has been measured over a wide range of scales (Planck Collaboration et al., 2016; Choi et al., 2020; Reichardt et al., 2021; Efstathiou and McCarthy, 2025). Its amplitude scales steeply with the matter fluctuations, Cℓy​y∝σ87C_{\ell}^{yy}\propto\sigma_{8}^{7} (Komatsu and Seljak, 2002), while its shape at ℓ≳1000\ell\gtrsim 1000 traces the same feedback that suppresses the matter power spectrum (Battaglia et al., 2012). Hydrodynamical simulations generally overpredict the measured Cℓy​yC_{\ell}^{yy} unless a low-S8S_{8} cosmology is adopted (McCarthy et al., 2014; McCarthy et al., 2018; McCarthy et al., 2025), illustrating how closely cosmology and feedback are intertwined in this observable. Moreover, since the integrated Compton-yy signal of a halo scales roughly as M5/3M^{5/3}, Cℓy​yC_{\ell}^{yy} at ℓ≲1000\ell\lesssim 1000 is dominated by a few massive, low-redshift clusters, making the field strongly non-Gaussian and subject to large sample variance. Some analyses therefore treat the brightest clusters separately (Rotti et al., 2021).

SBI also provides a natural framework for combining probes. A joint SBI analysis of tSZ, WL, and their cross-correlations with upcoming data from SO and Stage-IV lensing surveys therefore requires thousands of mocks of all probes, generated consistently from the same underlying large-scale structure while varying both cosmology and feedback.

Baryonification (BFC), first introduced in Ref. (Schneider and Teyssier, 2015), provides an efficient alternative to hydrodynamical simulations. BFC models displace particles in a dark-matter-only (DMO) NN-body simulation according to physically motivated parametric gas, stellar, and dark matter density profiles, with several variants that share this principle but differ in their profiles and parametrisation (Schneider et al., 2019; Aricò et al., 2021b; Aricò et al., 2021a; Anbajagane et al., 2024; Schneider et al., 2025). Because BFC only post-processes a DMO simulation, it adds little to the cost of the NN-body run and can be used with existing simulation suites. The model parameters control the radial shapes of the gas and matter profiles, which in turn set physically meaningful quantities such as the halo gas fraction. This allows for retuning the model to different feedback scenarios and to sample its parameters alongside the cosmological parameters, rather than fixing them to a single subgrid model. BFC reproduces the suppression of the matter power spectrum found in a wide variety of hydrodynamical simulations to within a 1–2% (Giri and Schneider, 2021; Schneider et al., 2025; Zhou et al., 2025) and has been applied in various combinations to cosmological and astrophysical inference using WL, X-ray gas fractions, and kinetic SZ data (Schneider et al., 2022; Grandis et al., 2024; Bigwood et al., 2024; Kovač et al., 2025; Siegel et al., 2026; Bucko et al., 2026).

papers.title: Symmetry-reduced k-point sampling and Wannier analysis with localized Gaussian orbitals
papers.abstract: Brillouin-zone sampling with localized orbitals requires consistent transformations between sparse real-space matrices and complex Bloch states. Symmetry reduces the number of reciprocal-space problems, but scalar integration weights alone cannot reconstruct the matrices and wavefunctions needed for densities and orbital analysis. We develop a unified formulation of these transformations for nonorthogonal Gaussian bases and describe its implementation in CP2K. Atom permutations, local orbital rotations, and lattice phases connect irreducible-point solutions to full symmetry orbits while preserving the overlap metric. Direct and fast lattice transforms couple this construction to self-consistent calculations, including complex orbital optimization and finite-temperature occupations. Gauge-consistent full-mesh orbitals and directed inter-point overlaps support Wannier90 export, Wannier construction, and Hamiltonian interpolation. In silicon and aluminium tests, symmetry reduces a 64-point mesh to four representatives while retaining cell energies or electronic free energies within $1.5\times10^{-12}$ hartree of the unreduced calculation. Hybrid exchange and many-body applications illustrate the additional role of auxiliary bases and transfer momenta. The resulting framework connects symmetry-reduced integration to gauge-consistent analysis of periodic electronic states within a localized-orbital representation.

papers.intro:
Periodic electronic-structure calculations replace an extended material by a finite cell with Bloch boundary conditions [1]. The remaining integration over the Brillouin zone determines how reliably that cell represents the bulk. Large insulating supercells often require only the zone center, whereas compact cells and metallic occupations demand explicit sampling. Converging the self-consistent-field (SCF) equations at a single k-point does not remove this quadrature error. Conversely, reducing a mesh by symmetry should preserve its physical content, not change the approximation being solved.

Localized atomic orbitals offer an efficient representation for density-functional theory (DFT) in the Kohn–Sham (KS) formulation [2, 3]. Periodic localized-basis methods are well established, including Gaussian-orbital and numerical atom-centered implementations [4, 5]. Their locality makes real-space matrices sparse, but their nonorthogonality introduces a k-dependent overlap metric. The present work addresses the transformations needed to preserve both properties when exploiting crystal symmetry and evaluating quantities that connect different k-points.

We use CP2K as the implementation platform. Its Quickstep module combines the Gaussian and plane wave (GPW) method with the Gaussian augmented plane wave (GAPW) all-electron extension [6, 7, 8, 9, 10]. Orbitals are expanded in localized Gaussian atomic orbitals (AOs), while charge densities and electrostatic potentials use multigrids and plane waves. Atom-pair blocks are stored in the distributed block-compressed sparse row (DBCSR) representation [11]. Each block carries an image-cell index as well as basis-function indices. Bloch matrices are assembled from these blocks by phase-weighted lattice sums, and the density matrix is returned to the same image-cell representation after solving the reciprocal-space problem. The use of these methods in ab initio molecular dynamics is reviewed by Hutter, Iannuzzi, and Kühne [12].

papers.title: D/H and 12C/13C ratios of benzonitrile and indene in TMC-1 support bottom-up formation of polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbon-like molecules
papers.abstract: Polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons (PAHs) have recently been detected in cold dark clouds through their rotational spectra, but it is currently a matter of debate whether they form through a bottom-up process from small hydrocarbons or through a top-down scenario involving the fragmentation of large PAHs inherited from a previous evolutionary stage of diffuse cloud. Isotopic ratios can shed light on the origin of PAHs in cold dark clouds. Large aromatic molecules observed in the infrared are enriched in deuterium and may also be enriched in 13C because they likely formed in the ejecta of evolved stars. We synthesized indene deuterated at the aliphatic position in the laboratory and measured its rotational spectrum, together with those of the nine 13C singly substituted isotopomers of indene. We used the measured spectra of the D and 13C isotopic species of indene, together with previously measured spectra of D and 13C isotopic benzonitrile, to search for these species in the cold dark cloud TMC-1 using QUIJOTE data obtained with the Yebes 40m telescope. We used a line stack method to tentatively detect deuterated benzonitrile and detect 13C-substituted benzonitrile, but find no evidence of either the D or 13C isotopic species of indene. We derive an aromatic D/H ratio of 0.53 % from benzonitrile, an aliphatic D/H ratio <3.3 % from indene, and 12C/13C ratios of 126 and >55 for benzonitrile and indene, respectively. These values are consistent with isotopic ratios derived for other molecules in TMC-1 and show no enrichment in either D or 13C that could be ascribed to inheritance from large PAHs in a top-down scenario; a bottom-up scenario is therefore the most likely.

papers.intro:
Polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons (PAHs) have long been suspected to be ubiquitous and abundant in the interstellar medium as carriers of aromatic infrared bands (AIBs); these bands are observed in almost every astronomical environment exposed to ultraviolet (UV) radiation (Leger & Puget, 1984; Allamandola et al., 1985; Tielens, 2008). Due to the nonspecific nature of the infrared bands, there is still a debate about whether PAHs or other large organic molecules are carriers of AIBs (Kwok, 2022; Tielens, 2026). Unambiguous identification of PAHs in the interstellar medium was achieved only a few years ago, with the detection through rotational spectroscopy of individual molecules in, paradoxically, the UV-shielded environment of cold dark clouds. The current inventory of PAH-like molecules detected in the emblematic starless core TMC-1 comprises single rings (cyclopentadiene and benzene), two-fused rings (indene and naphthalene), three-fused rings (acenaphthylene, cyclopentindene, and phenalene), the four-ring species pyrene, and the seven-ringed molecule coronene (Cernicharo et al., 2021a; Cernicharo et al., 2021b; Cernicharo et al., 2024a; Cernicharo et al., 2026; McGuire et al., 2018; McGuire et al., 2021; McCarthy et al., 2021; Lee et al., 2021; Burkhardt et al., 2021a; Wenzel et al., 2024; Wenzel et al., 2025a; Wenzel et al., 2025b; Cabezas et al., 2025; Fuentetaja et al., 2026). For most of these cycles, observations have detected the polar cyano derivative rather than the pure hydrocarbon. In addition to TMC-1, some of these cycles have also been observed in other cold dark clouds (Burkhardt et al., 2021b; Agúndez et al., 2023a; Wenzel et al., 2026) and in warm molecular clouds in the Galactic center (Rivilla et al., 2026). Polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons have also been unequivocally identified in Solar System bodies such as the Murchison meteorite (Basile et al., 1984) and the Ryugu asteroid (Zeichner et al., 2023).

Polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbon-like molecules are clearly present in cold dark clouds with large abundances (10-9-10-8 relative to H2; Agúndez & Cernicharo 2026), but it is not clear how they form in this particular kind of environment. Evidence based on the spatial similarity of carbon chains and cycles (Cernicharo et al., 2023) and the correlation in the abundance of these two types of molecules (Agúndez et al., 2023a) points to a bottom-up scenario in which PAH-like species form from small hydrocarbon molecules in situ in the cold dark cloud. However, there is a debate on which chemical pathways are sufficiently efficient to account for the large abundances observed (Yang et al., 2024; Mallo et al., 2025; Jacovella et al., 2026; Loison et al., 2026; Agúndez & Cernicharo, 2026). In addition, the abundances of PAH-like species in TMC-1 are rather uniform and independent of size (Wenzel et al., 2025a; Wenzel et al., 2025b; Agúndez & Cernicharo, 2026), which is difficult to explain within the framework of a bottom-up scenario. An alternative is a top-down scenario in which the observed PAH-like molecules form through the fragmentation of large PAHs (those responsible for the AIBs) inherited from the previous evolutionary stage of diffuse cloud (Pety et al., 2005; Zhen et al., 2014; Burkhardt et al., 2021b; Goicoechea et al., 2025; García-Bernete et al., 2026).

Infrared observations do not provide constraints on the 12C/13C ratio of AIB carriers, but the origin of these large aromatic molecules is commonly ascribed to the ejecta of evolved stars (Kwok, 2004; Tielens, 2008), which are enriched in 13C compared with the interstellar medium (Milam et al., 2009; Ramstedt et al., 2014; Ziurys et al., 2020). Therefore, if the PAHs unambiguously identified in cold dark clouds form through fragmentation of large PAHs inherited from the previous diffuse cloud stage in a top-down scenario, we would expect them to be enriched in deuterium and 13C.

(2025) for deuterated benzonitrile, from archive data for 13C benzonitrile, and from measurements carried out in this work for deuterated and 13C indene, for which the deuterated form was synthesized in the laboratory. papers.title: When Does Discrete Ricci Curvature Help? An Edge-Level Analysis of Curvature-Enhanced GCNs for PPI Prediction
papers.abstract: Curvature-enhanced graph convolutional networks (CGCN) incorporate Ollivier-Ricci curvature (ORC), grounded in optimal transport theory, into message passing, motivated by the claim that curvature-weighted edges alleviate "over-squashing" at structural bottlenecks. But does CGCN's improvement actually come from mitigating over-squashing? We investigate this on four real-world protein-protein interaction (PPI) datasets, comparing CGCN against a standard GCN at the level of individual edges rather than aggregate metrics alone. While CGCN improves aggregate AUC, AUPR, and F1 across all four datasets, this gain is concentrated almost entirely on low-degree edges, while performance on low-curvature (bottleneck) edges systematically degrades in three of four datasets, the opposite of what the over-squashing motivation predicts. Examining the learned edge-weight function directly, together with clustering-validity metrics, edge-distance ratios, and a layer-depth ablation across four depths, we find evidence for an alternative account: curvature-weighting sharpens the separation between clusters, which improves intra-cluster predictions at the cost of inter-cluster (bottleneck) ones. We test this account against topologically defined communities rather than the classification labels used elsewhere. Additionally, we offer practical guidance on when to prefer CGCN over standard GCN, depending on whether intra- or inter-cluster predictions matter most.

Interactions between biomolecules–proteins, drugs, genes, and microbes–often involve multiple binding partners acting cooperatively, and understanding these interactions remains a central problem in computational biology Moll et al. (2006). Many such systems, along with larger-scale networks like social, citation, and transportation networks, can naturally be represented as graphs, making Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) a natural tool for modeling them. Standard architectures such as GCN Kipf and Welling (2016), GAT Veličković et al. (2017), and GIN Xu et al. (2019) rely on neighborhood aggregation over directly connected nodes.

Geometric deep learning embeds structural priors of this kind directly into network architectures rather than treating them as post-hoc descriptors Bronstein et al. (2021); Atz et al. (2021). One such prior is discrete Ricci curvature, most commonly formalized for graphs via Ollivier–Ricci curvature (ORC) Ollivier (2009) (grounded in optimal transport theory) or Forman–Ricci curvature (FRC) Sreejith et al. (2016). ORC characterizes each edge according to its neighborhood’s connectivity: edges in densely connected, highly clustered regions tend to have positive curvature, reflecting redundant alternative paths, while edges spanning sparsely connected regions have negative curvature, reflecting a lack of such alternatives — these are structural bottlenecks Topping et al. (2022).

One way to leverage discrete Ricci curvature on graphs is via discrete Ricci flow Ni et al. (2019), which iteratively adjusts edge weights or lengths based on local curvature differences to reshape the network’s internal geometry. This technique finds applications in geometric embeddings Ni et al. (2018), community detection Ni et al. (2019), or graph rewiring methods Topping et al. (2022).

Alternatively, discrete Ricci curvature can be incorporated into GNNs directly to mitigate structural failure modes. Over-squashing occurs when information from distant nodes must repeatedly traverse such bottleneck edges across multiple rounds of message passing, causing it to be increasingly compressed and distorted as it propagates Topping et al. (2022). A related failure mode, over-smoothing, arises in densely connected regions, where repeated averaging across redundant paths causes node representations to become increasingly similar and less discriminative Chen et al. (2020). Because negatively curved edges coincide with the regions where over-squashing is expected to concentrate Topping et al. (2022), curvature has been proposed as a signal for identifying and correcting for these bottlenecks via graph rewiring (e.g., SDRF Topping et al. (2022), FoSR Karhadkar et al. (2023)), curvature-based positional encodings, or curvature-weighted message passing Yadav and Xia (2025) (e.g., CGCN Shen et al. (2024), CurvGN Ye et al. (2020), CGNN Li et al. (2022)). Here, we focus on the curvature-weighted message passing paradigm, instantiated by CGCN Shen et al. (2024), which incorporates ORC directly into the message-passing operator to weight edges by local geometry.

Our contribution is threefold: (1) we confirm that CGCN improves aggregate metrics (AUC, AUPR, F1) across all four datasets, consistent with Shen et al. (2024); (2) we show this improvement is not uniform — it concentrates almost entirely on low-degree edges, while performance on low-curvature (bottleneck) edges systematically degrades under CGCN in three of four datasets, the opposite of what the over-squashing motivation would predict; and (3) by examining the learned edge-weight function directly and testing it against clustering-validity metrics, inter/intra-cluster distance ratios, and a layer-depth ablation, we provide empirical support for the following explanation: curvature-weighting sharpens cluster separation in the learned embeddings, improving prediction of intra-cluster edges at the cost of the inter-cluster (low-curvature) edges themselves.

papers.title: Structural balance in complex networks: from measurement to dynamics, emergence and implications
papers.abstract: Structural balance theory, introduced in social psychology to describe how friendly and hostile ties organize into consistent patterns, has been reinterpreted through statistical physics and complex networks. In the classical formulation, a triad with positive or negative links, representing friendship and hostility, is balanced when the product of its signs is positive; a balanced network splits into at most two internally friendly, mutually hostile groups. This review synthesizes how the triadic formulation has been extended to a statistical-ensemble perspective in which balance is encoded by immanent three-body interactions described by a proper Hamiltonian, balanced configurations correspond to low-energy states, and balance measures serve as order parameters for transitions between consensus, polarization, and disorder. We organize the field into three sections: Measurement, Dynamics and Emergence, and Implications. In Measurement, we compare measures of structural balance and null models, and show that conclusions for a given system depend on the chosen measure and null model. In Dynamics and Emergence, we review deterministic and stochastic systems, including the gradient, Hamiltonian, and local triad models, and examine how noise, topology, and competing mechanisms determine whether balance emerges. In Implications, we survey consequences for belief formation, opinion contagion dynamics, polarization, international relations, and markets. Across domains, the evidence is strongest for local triadic stability and weakest for system-wide balance. Balance is not synonymous with harmony: balanced structures can reflect cohesion, polarization, or persistent conflict. Its empirical relevance is well supported in some reciprocal social systems, but remains less settled in biological and other complex networks.

The concept was first formulated by Fritz Heider in 1946, who hypothesized that a person forms a positive tie (e.g., a friendship) with a second person when they share the same attitude toward a third entity. When their attitudes differ, they instead form a negative tie (e.g., an enmity). Heider described these attitude configurations as balanced [171].

papers.title: More lower bounds for Hales--Jewett and van der Waerden numbers
papers.abstract: We give explicit colourings improving the comparison lower bounds assembled here for several Hales--Jewett and van der Waerden numbers. The main algebraic tool generalises Rabung's power-residue colouring from arithmetic progressions to arbitrary sets. If every translate of a t-element set S in F_p meets at least two classes of the r-th power character, and the integer weights have both parities, then a period-2p one-weight colouring of [t]^p has no monochromatic combinatorial line. The 19 displayed algebraic certificates comprise 18 improvements and one closed-form reproduction; they include HJ(4,3)>=164, HJ(5,4)>=7418, and HJ(5,6)>=34034. The underlying period-p construction also proves kappa_ow(t,r)>=p-1 for the one-weight bracket ceiling, in particular kappa_ow(5,4)>=7416 and kappa_ow(5,6)>=34032. Warm breakout-weighted tabu search on the type simplex gives HJ(3,4)>=51. Whole-colouring local search gives W(8,3)>522, W(11,3)>1193, and W(17,3)>3620. All accepted certificates are available separately and are checked by direct enumeration; unresolved searches are reported as UNKNOWN, not UNSAT.

papers.title: Deal With It: On Better Schedules for Listwise Reranking
papers.abstract: Listwise LLM rerankers cannot reliably rank hundreds of documents in a single call, and rely on schedules to orchestrate their calls. Parallel schedules split candidates into groups and advance a fixed quota from each. When a group holds more of the top passages than its quota, some are cut, and expensive repair calls become required. We show that the way candidates are split matters where such a quota can bind, and that, in expected cuts, the best split there deals them round-robin by retriever rank, like cards. Although not conceptually new, dealing has remained unanalyzed. We prove that, under a simple retriever model, no split with equal quotas cuts fewer of the true top ten on average, and that contiguous chunks cut more as the retriever improves. DealRank, the simplest schedule our analysis allows, is on average within 0.1 nDCG@10 points of the best schedules over six LLMs, in two rounds. It is consistently 1.1 to 1.4 times faster than BlitzRank with concurrent first calls up to a thousand candidates. There, it needs three rounds and is eleven times faster than the sliding window. In existing schedules such as BlitzRank, dealing reduces repair calls from 59% of queries to 14%, improving latency with no significant change in quality. Random partitioning appears equivalent at a quota of four, as predicted, but ties results to the seed and trails by 1.3 nDCG@10 points at a quota of one over a dense retriever.

papers.title: Towards Data-Efficient, Real-Time World Models
papers.abstract: State-of-the-art world models have been used to produce sequences of gameplay that accord with provided user-input actions. However, high quality, consistent gameplay generation often comes at the cost of inference speed, making real-time interactive play and ideation challenging. The substantial quantities of data used to train state-of-the-art models have also made custom training of these models appear impractical, limiting many of their potential uses in creative fields. In this work we demonstrate a major step towards efficient world models: achieving both fast high-quality inference, and improved data efficiency. This is done by replacing the next-token prediction paradigm with a two-stage discrete diffusion-based approach, introducing a lightweight refinement transformer which carries out iterative masked predictions. Building on an autoregressive world model capable of generating highly consistent and complex sequences over minutes (Kanervisto et al., 2025), we achieve substantial model speed-up (79x) with a modest quality trade-off. Additionally, we demonstrate that this model can be trained to reproduce high-quality, consistent gameplay using a dataset containing approximately one day (28 hours) of gameplay data. Our results demonstrate progress towards removing barriers to the use of world models in settings where real-time inference and data efficiency are essential.

papers.intro:
In recent years, impressive progress has been achieved towards high quality video generation. Large scale models (Brooks et al., 2024; Google DeepMind, 2025b) trained on real-world footage, video games, and interactive 3D environments have showcased a potential to learn rich and complex environments and interactions. While text remains the main mode of interaction with video generation models, there is growing interest in action-controlled models (e.g. using navigation keys, game controller actions), often referred to as interactive video models or world models (Google DeepMind, 2025a; Decart and Etched, 2024; He et al., 2025). Potential applications for such world models include self-driving simulation (Russell et al., 2025), robotics (NVIDIA et al., 2025), and supporting creative ideation and game development (Kanervisto et al., 2025). In the context of video gaming, models trained on large scale single game environments have demonstrated an ability to learn and faithfully reproduce game maps and physics, complex interactions and character abilities in a responsive environment (Che et al., 2025; Alonso et al., 2024).

This is due to the inherently sequential nature of next-token prediction in a high-dimensional discrete space: generating a single frame requires hundreds of sequential forward passes through a large transformer. A model capable of real-time, high-fidelity, consistent gameplay generation would greatly expand the potential of world models in practical settings, providing instant responses to user inputs.

However, discrete diffusion alone is not enough to achieve real-time interactivity (see Figure 5) as iterative feed-forward passes remain costly. Instead, we propose to decompose world modelling in two components: 1) a large backbone transformer modelling temporal dependencies which predicts the first image draft in a single forward pass, and 2) a lightweight discrete diffusion transformer which iteratively refines this prediction. This formulation, combined with a register-based context compression that compresses long context histories into compact representations, preserves the expressivity of a large transformer with much better scaling to diffusion steps. papers.title: Randomization-Based Nonparanormal Adjusted Marginal Inference
papers.abstract: Adjusting for prognostic baseline covariates in the analysis of randomized controlled trials is recommended to increase the precision of treatment effect estimates. Such adjustment, however, introduces a complication known as noncollapsibility: for effect measures such as the log-odds or log-hazard ratio, the estimated treatment effect becomes conditional instead of marginal. Methods that target a marginal estimand even after covariate adjustment have been developed, but typically rely on population-based inference, which assumes patients are randomly sampled from some larger population, rarely true in practice. Such methods have been shown to inflate type I error, particularly in small samples or when many covariates are adjusted for. Inference based on randomization requires no such assumption, as it relies on the randomization scheme, which is known exactly, yielding a test that is exact even in finite samples. We present a randomization-based test for covariate-adjusted marginal treatment effects, built on nonparanormal adjusted marginal inference, applicable to continuous, binary, ordinal, and time-to-event outcomes. In simulation studies, this test controls type I error where the standard Wald test does not. Applied to 20 historical phase III time-to-event randomized trials, the covariate-adjusted estimator achieves precision gains comparable to an existing competitor method.

papers.intro:
Adjusting for prognostic baseline covariates in the primary analysis of randomized controlled trials (RCTs) is recommended because it can increase the precision of treatment effect estimates (Food and Drug Administration, 2023; Van Lancker et al., 2024). However, directly including covariates in the linear predictor of a regression model introduces a complication: the treatment effect becomes conditional rather than marginal. For many widely used effect measures, such as the log-odds ratio and the log-hazard ratio, the two do not coincide, even in the absence of confounding, a phenomenon known as noncollapsibility (Greenland et al., 1999; Daniel et al., 2021). Because the estimand of interest in RCTs is often the marginal effect, several methods have been developed to obtain marginal treatment effect estimates while still benefiting from covariate adjustment (Tsiatis et al., 2008; Zhang et al., 2008; Lu and Tsiatis, 2008; Ye et al., 2024; Dandl and Hothorn, 2026).

Yet, the inference procedures accompanying these methods typically rely on population-based asymptotic theory (Rosenberger et al., 2019). Standard errors and hypothesis tests are derived from the sampling distribution of an estimator across hypothetical repeated samples. Such approximations can become unreliable when the number of estimated parameters is large relative to the sample size, even if the assumed model is correctly specified (Portnoy, 1988; MacKinnon and White, 1985). This is particularly relevant for covariate adjustment, where additional covariates typically introduce additional parameters. Indeed, simulation studies have reported type I error rates above the nominal level when many covariates are adjusted for relative to the available sample size (Tackney et al., 2023; Zhang et al., 2025; Dandl and Hothorn, 2026).

Randomization itself offers a different basis for inference (Cox, 2009; Rosenberger et al., 2019; Guo and Basse, 2023). Unlike population-based inference, which treats the patients’ outcomes as random according to some assumed data-generating process, randomization-based inference conditions on the enrolled patients and takes the treatment assignment as the source of randomness. This distinction is important because the mechanism governing treatment assignment is specified by the trial design and is therefore exactly known. Under the sharp null hypothesis of no treatment effect, each patient’s outcome would have been the same regardless of which treatment they received. The observed outcomes could therefore equally well have arisen under any other assignment permitted by the randomization design. Comparing the observed test statistic with its distribution over these possible assignments provides an exact reference distribution for testing the null hypothesis (Fisher, 1935; Kempthorne, 1955; Edgington and Onghena, 2007). When this distribution is computed from the randomization scheme itself, the resulting randomization test controls the type I error rate under the sharp null without requiring a model for the outcome distribution. The choice of test statistic, even if motivated by a parametric model, can therefore affect power without compromising the validity of the test, provided the randomization distribution is constructed correctly (Rosenberger et al., 2019).

We show how randomization-based inference can be incorporated into NAMI by using its score residuals to construct a test statistic within a general permutation-testing framework (Hothorn et al., 2006). The idea is to fit NAMI under the null hypothesis and use the resulting score residuals, which target the marginal rather than the conditional effect, to measure the association between the outcome and the randomized treatment assignment. In this way, the model determines the test statistic, while the randomization scheme determines the reference distribution against which it is assessed. This reference distribution, defined by the treatment assignments permitted by the trial’s design, can be obtained by enumerating all permitted assignments, approximated through Monte Carlo resampling, or approximated using the asymptotic distribution of the permutation statistic (Strasser and Weber, 1999). Evaluating the exact randomization distribution provides finite-sample type I error control under the sharp null.

papers.title: Byzantine Resilience of Robot Gathering under Round-Robin Scheduling
papers.abstract: We study deterministic gathering of $n$ anonymous, oblivious mobile robots in the plane under round-robin scheduling with rigid movement, in the presence of $f$ Byzantine robots. Robots observe all robot positions with their multiplicities, while their local coordinate systems may change adversarially between activations. The goal is for all correct robots to gather at a single point in finite time and remain there forever. We analyze ToMax, a simple algorithm that moves to a point of maximum multiplicity and stays still if and only if its current position is the unique maximum. We prove that ToMax achieves gathering whenever $f\le\lfloor\sqrt{n}/2\rfloor$, establishing an $\Omega(\sqrt{n})$ lower bound on the achievable Byzantine resilience.

We study the Byzantine resilience of deterministic gathering by Look–Compute–Move (LCM) robots [20] under round-robin scheduling. The gathering problem requires all correct (non-Byzantine) robots to reach a common point in finite time and remain there forever, regardless of the adversarial behavior of the Byzantine robots. Our focus is on how many Byzantine robots can be tolerated as the number of robots grows.

Our result provides a starting point for determining how Byzantine resilience scales with the number of robots beyond fully synchronous activation.

The LCM model, introduced by Suzuki and Yamashita [20], provides a formal framework for studying distributed algorithms for mobile robots. The model has since been extensively studied, particularly in the context of fundamental coordination problems such as gathering and pattern formation. In each LCM cycle, a robot observes its surroundings (Look), computes a destination (Compute), and moves toward it (Move). Variants of the model differ in the robots’ capabilities and the assumptions on their environment. Oblivious robots retain no information between cycles, whereas non-oblivious robots can retain internal state. In the luminous model [8, 9], each robot has a persistent light whose color is drawn from a finite set and is visible to itself and other robots.

The solvability of various problems, including gathering, depends on the scheduling model, which dictates the timing and order of robot activations. Under fully synchronous (FSYNCH) and semi-synchronous (SSYNCH) scheduling, execution proceeds in rounds: FSYNCH activates every robot in each round, whereas SSYNCH activates an arbitrary nonempty subset, whose members execute their cycle phases synchronously. Under asynchronous scheduling (ASYNCH), phases may overlap across robots, and observations may become outdated before they are acted upon. Centralized (or sequential) schedulers allow only one robot to execute a complete cycle at a time; RR further fixes a cyclic activation order. A kk-bounded scheduler allows each other robot at most kk activations between consecutive activations of any given robot.

With rigid movement, a robot always reaches its computed destination; with non-rigid movement, a move may be interrupted, subject to a fixed positive minimum progress guarantee, with closer destinations reached. For sensing, robots may or may not have the ability to detect multiplicity at a location. Without multiplicity detection, a snapshot reveals only occupied locations. Weak multiplicity detection distinguishes one robot from multiple robots at each occupied location, while strong multiplicity detection reveals the exact number.

papers.title: Sharp Gaussian Brunn-Minkowski inequalities
papers.abstract: We prove Gaussian Brunn-Minkowski inequalities for multiple sets. These are of the type: $$\prod_{i=1}^I \gamma_{\Sigma_i}(K_i)^{\tilde \lambda_i} \le C_{\text{sharp}}\gamma_\Gamma\Big(\sum_{i=1}^I \lambda_i K_i\Big),$$ with convex sets $K_i \subset \mathbb{R}^n$, whose barycenter $b_{K_i,\Sigma_i}$ with respect to the Gaussian measure $\gamma_{\Sigma_i}$ is zero, where $\lambda_i, \tilde \lambda_i \in (0;1)$ such that $\sum_{i=1}^I \lambda_i=\sum_{i=1}^I \tilde \lambda_i=1.$ In addition, we provide natural conditions on the matrices $\Gamma, \Sigma_1,\cdots,\Sigma_I \in \mathrm{Sym}_{>0}(n)$, which are given through a pointwise inequality involving the Karcher mean. Furthermore, we study equality cases of the corresponding functional forms in such situations. We also investigate the role of centering in the (B)-property by giving a counterexample for convex bodies with zero Lebesgue barycenters in dimensions at least three and thereby answering negatively a question of Faifman-Polterovich in \cite{Faifman_Polt}. Finally, a new slicing approach is introduced, which allows us to pass from centered convex sets to sets with arbitrary barycenters such that their weighted sum is convex. Based on this idea, we show a new Gaussian Brunn-Minkowski inequality $$e^{|\sum_{i=1}^I \lambda_i b_{K_i,I_n}|^2/2n} \gamma_n \Big(\sum_{i=1}^I \lambda_i K_i \Big)^{1/n} \ge \sum_{i=1}^I \lambda_i e^{|b_{K_i,I_n}|^2/2n} \gamma_n(K_i)^{1/n},$$ and consider a further application in the direction of the Gaussian correlation inequality, together with the rigidity for both inequalities.

papers.title: Universal scaling of brine migration in ice
papers.abstract: Sea ice hosts mobile brine inclusions whose migration influences salt redistribution, microstructure and transport within the ice. Although their motion under temperature gradient is commonly described as a diffusion-limited process, experimental evidence has remained rare and insufficient because migration is slow and controlled inclusion seeding is challenging. Here we introduce an experimental method to trap and monitor hundreds of inclusions in ice under controlled temperature gradients. Using four solutes, three imposed gradients and two order of magnitude in initial concentration, we quantify migration dynamics over a broad range of conditions. We find that, except close to the ice front, inclusion migration is consistent with a regime limited by solute diffusion. After applying a universal scaling, both our data and previous measurements collapse onto a master curve, providing a general framework for describing solute transport in ice.

papers.title: PAISF: A Partially Adaptive In-Order Selection Function for Routing in On-Chip, Inter-Chiplet, and Wafer-Scale Networks
papers.abstract: The growing number of compute elements per chip, along with advances such as chiplet systems and wafer-scale integration, drives the need for scalable and efficient routing algorithms for irregular topologies. A routing algorithm consists of a routing function (RF) that ensures deadlock freedom and a selection function (SF) that avoids congestion and, in some cases, guarantees in-order packet delivery. We propose two novel SFs for irregular topologies, ISF and PAISF, which ensure in-order delivery by hashing a packet's entropy value to determine its path. Packets with the same entropy follow the same path and arrive in order. Compared to a deterministic RF, a deterministic SF, and Multi, three alternative in-order delivery strategies, (PA)ISF improves throughput by 15.2% and reduces energy per packet and latency under load by 12.1% and 11.3%, at the cost of a zero-load latency increase by 3.3% on average across workloads and topologies.
papers.intro:
The rising demand for compute power from ever larger machine learning (ML) models drives growth in the number of compute elements per chip. Since many ML workloads are limited by data movement [1], scalable and efficient network-on-chips (NoCs) are critical. Although the 2D mesh (M) topology has long been the de facto standard, more scalable topologies [2, 3, 4] have recently emerged. Furthermore, to sustain performance improvements despite the slowdown of Moore’s law and the end of Dennard scaling, chiplet systems and wafer-scale integration (WSI) have been adopted, giving rise to specialized topologies tailored for inter-chip interconnects (ICIs) [5, 6, 7, 8, 9] and wafer-scale systems [10].

A key component of any network is the routing algorithm, which determines how packets are forwarded from source to destination. The routing algorithm is invoked whenever a packet arrives at a router and consists of two subroutines: the routing function (RF), which identifies a set of next hops that guarantee deadlock and livelock freedom, and the selection function (SF), which selects one of these hops to optimize performance by avoiding congestion. While there is extensive work on RFs [11, 12, 13, 14] and SFs [15, 16, 17, 18, 19] for mesh topologies, routing in recently proposed irregular NoC, ICI, and WSI topologies remains less explored.

While there is extensive work on RFs [11, 12, 13, 14] and SFs [15, 16, 17, 18, 19] for mesh topologies, routing in recently proposed irregular NoC, ICI, and WSI topologies remains less explored.

In this paper, we present two new SFs for irregular topologies: in-order selection function (ISF) and partially adaptive in-order selection function (PAISF), which adapts to current network congestion. The key feature of both SFs is that the sender can decide whether the packets of a given message need to be delivered in-order (io) or if delivering them out-of-order (ooo) is sufficient. (PA)ISF ensures correct ordering independently of the underlying RF by selecting the next hop through hashing an entropy value assigned to each packet, similar to the approach used in Ultra Ethernet [20]. Assigning the same entropy value to all packets of a message ensures they follow the same path and remain in order, while assigning random entropy values allows packets to take different paths, exploiting path diversity and improving performance. Ensuring in-order delivery is critical for many applications; if the network does not handle this, each endpoint requires a reorder buffer (ROB), adding significant complexity and cost. Moreover, if a ROB is full, packets must be dropped and retransmitted, potentially causing substantial performance degradation.

Ensuring in-order delivery is critical for many applications; if the network does not handle this, each endpoint requires a reorder buffer (ROB), adding significant complexity and cost. Moreover, if a ROB is full, packets must be dropped and retransmitted, potentially causing substantial performance degradation.

We compare our proposed SFs against three approaches for ensuring in-order delivery. First, a deterministic RF that routes all packets of a source-destination pair along a single path, making an SF unnecessary. Second, a deterministic selection function (DET) that always selects the same next hop, even when the RF offers multiple alternatives. Third, the Multi [21, 22] middle layer, which operates between RF and SF, identifies disjoint source-destination paths, and reorders packets at the destination router’s input buffer, avoiding a ROB at the endpoint while exploiting path diversity. Compared to these baselines, our SFs increase saturation throughput by 15.2% and reduce energy per packet and latency under load by 12.1% and 11.3% on average, at the cost of a 3.3% increase in zero-load latency. papers.title: Interfacial electrostatics: From polar insulators to charged-layer metals
papers.abstract: Polar discontinuities are typically described as arising from charged atomic planes, a spontaneous polarization, or a combination, in insulating films interfaced with vacuum, nonpolar insulators or metals. The resulting electrostatics are well established for systems such as LaAlO$_3$/SrTiO$_3$, BaTiO$_3$/SrRuO$_3$, and BiFeO$_3$/SrRuO$_3$. However, recent observations of "polar-discontinuity-like" behavior at interfaces in which the metal contains formally charged layers (e.g., rare-earth nickelates) challenge this picture. In this work, we summarize the theoretical framework used to define and quantify interface charge, layer polarization, and screening in the three reference systems above, and then discuss signatures attributed to the formal-charge polar discontinuity arising when SmNiO$_3$, a metal with formally charged (001) layers, is interfaced with ferroelectric BaTiO$_3$. We show how concepts developed for polar discontinuities between two insulators and for screening at metallic interfaces can rationalize the reported effects and identify where our understanding of these systems leaves open questions.

papers.intro:
Interfacial phenomena have repeatedly attracted considerable attention from the perovskite oxide community, both to develop next-generation electronic devices, and because they can lead to non-trivial and intriguing physics. Notably, uncompensated interface charges can cause a variety of effects at the interface or in the interfacing materials. Such charges lead to the formation of a two-dimensional electron gas (2DEG) in LaAlO3/SrTiO3 heterostructures [1, 2, 3, 4], the presence of a critical thickness for the spontaneous polarization in ferroelectric thin films [5, 6, 7], or unusual ferroelectric topological textures [8, 9, 10].

Interface charges can arise when there is a change in the value of the polarization perpendicular to the interface – a so-called polar discontinuity – and their origin and screening have been extensively studied in theory and experiments [3, 4, 11, 5, 12]. Within the modern theory of polarization, a polar discontinuity occurs at an interface between materials with different bulk polarizations [13, 14, 15, 11]. For a (001) interface, the spontaneous polarization of ferroelectrics such as BaTiO3 contributes to the bulk polarization and hence to the bound interface charge. In centrosymmetric materials such as LaAlO3, formally charged atomic (001) planes can likewise produce a polar discontinuity at the interface with vacuum or a material with uncharged layers. The screening of these interface charges can be modeled via an effective screening length at metal interfaces [16, 12, 6] or by accounting for the energetic cost of generating screening charges via other compensation mechanisms [1, 17].

papers.title: Kolibri: Color Finds the Place, Refinement Sets the Pose for RGB-D Localization in Colored Point Clouds
papers.abstract: An agent or robot in a scanned building must locate its camera in rooms that no model saw during training. Point cloud registration methods can align each RGB-D frame with the building's colored point cloud, accurately but at a high cost. We observe that geometric refinement brings nearby initial poses to the same final pose, so the learned component only needs to find the place. Kolibri does this with a graph network of 55,712 parameters that describes 10 cm cubes of points, called cells, by their color, local shape and neighbors. With the same refinement, it matches GeDi on 96 unseen ScanNet rooms (81.4% against 80.3% within 5 cm and 5{\deg}) and on a held-out test of 10 further rooms, in 82 ms per frame on an RTX 2080 Ti. The saved time allows for search without a room label. In one point cloud of 100 rooms, Kolibri loses 1.3 points against knowing the room, while retrieving the room first loses 56.0. In a hospital emergency department scene from a real scan, it localizes 86.5% of the frames rendered from the scan in 384 ms each, where GeDi needs 91 minutes per frame on cubes of the scan for a similar recall. The method needs colors that agree between the frame and the point cloud. On gray frames and across cameras with different color responses, point cloud registration methods keep the lead.
papers.intro:
We scanned the emergency department of a university hospital on foot with a handheld laser scanner (BLK2GO) and obtained a colored point cloud of it. Robots and simulated pedestrian agents need to locate their cameras anywhere in it, without a room label or an initial position. Each view forms a RGB-D frame, with paired color with depth, so point cloud registration methods can align it with the point cloud. The difficulty is cost. On views rendered from the scan with simulated depth noise, GeDi [33] needs 91 minutes per frame to search overlapping cubes of the scan, while Kolibri, the method we present here, reaches a similar recall on the whole scan in 384 ms. The rendered colors agree with the point cloud by construction, and the baseline comparison uses 30 frames, one per walk (Sec. 4.5). The hospital scan motivated the method but remained untouched while we developed it on public benchmarks.

Point-to-plane refinement adjusts a pose by pulling frame points onto nearby surfaces of the point cloud. It is a variant of iterative closest point (ICP) [3, 8]. Nearby initial poses often converge to the same result, within a region we call the refinement basin. On real ScanNet frames, Kolibri and BUFFER-X both start in this region for 62% of frames. papers.title: Verifying Agents in Rubric-Graded Environments
papers.abstract: As AI agents take on increasingly open-ended and complex tasks, verifying their outputs has proven to be difficult. Rubric-graded agent environments, where a verifier judges multiple natural-language criteria against the deliverables and environment state changes produced by the agent, have emerged as a popular paradigm. We conduct the first systematic study of verifiers for rubric-graded agent environments. First, we create BankerVerifierBench (BVB), a meta-evaluation dataset of 2,464 human-judged rubric criteria across 24 investment-banking tasks. Next, we develop a methodology that derives from any rubric corpus the capabilities a verifier should possess, yielding a nine-capability taxonomy that we distill into three general design principles---reactive verification, environment alignment, and domain guidance---which we implement in Gandalf, an open-source verifier. Finally, we evaluate Gandalf against three existing verifiers on BVB. Gandalf matches or exceeds every baseline's F1 at lower cost: with Gemini 3 Flash it matches the strongest baseline's F1 (0.864 vs. 0.852) at one-fifth of its cost, and with GPT-5.4 models it improves F1 by over 0.12 at lower cost. Gandalf also generalizes to OpenClaw, a structurally different personal-productivity environment, where it again achieves the highest F1 (0.955 vs. 0.934 for the best baseline). We release BVB, Gandalf, and the code and data to reproduce our experiments.

papers.title: WATERFALL: Workflow for Adaptive Training with Evolutionary Reward Formulation and Automated Learning Loops
papers.abstract: Reward design remains a central bottleneck in reinforcement learning (RL), particularly in sparse-reward, long-horizon and partially observable settings requiring dependency chaining, memory, and deceptive affordance disambiguation. While recent foundation-model approaches reduce manual reward engineering, most assume goal-conditioning, task descriptions, expert demonstrations, or ground-truth metrics. These assumptions are problematic in partially observable environments, where task-relevant objectives, affordances, and dynamics must be discovered through interaction rather than disclosed a priori. We formalise this problem setting by introducing WATERFALL, an iterative population-based workflow for automated reward discovery under the strict observability constraints inherent in POMDP environments. WATERFALL achieves this by (i) synthesising diverse programmatic reward candidates via persona-conditioned generation, (ii) evaluating candidate behaviour from raw visual rollouts utilising a Swiss-system evolutionary tournament judged by vision-language models to identify elites, and (iii) leveraging longitudinal assessment histories to iteratively mutate, escalate, or prune candidates. We evaluate WATERFALL across fully observable and reveal-gated partially observable environments ranging from discrete to continuous, comparing against sparse-reward RL, intrinsic-motivation and foundation-model reward-synthesis baselines. Our results indicate that WATERFALL discovers and refines reward programs without access to privileged information, outperforming baselines that retain their native information advantages, most clearly in the POMDP regime. Extensive ablations substantiate that visual evidence, tournament-based selection, and iterative refinement are jointly important. Enforcing this contract is what separates autonomous reward discovery from benchmark-privileged reward shaping.
papers.intro:
Designing reward functions remains one of the most persistent bottlenecks in Reinforcement Learning (RL). For tasks with sparse or delayed supervision, the reward is often the difference between efficient learning and complete failure, yet hand-engineering a robust dense reward requires substantial domain expertise and repeated trial-and-error, and notably limits cross-task generalisation (Sutton and Barto, 2018; Ng et al., 1999; Triantafyllidis et al., 2023). Intrinsic-motivation methods, such as Count-Based Exploration (CBE), the Intrinsic Curiosity Module (ICM) and Random Network Distillation (RND), ease this sparsity by rewarding novelty or prediction error (Tang et al., 2017; Pathak et al., 2017; Burda et al., 2019), yet cannot infer the valuable task semantics that challenging RL problems require.

Consider robotic exploration before a downstream task is assigned: A drawer conceals an object whose existence, and any interaction it affords, becomes known only once the drawer is opened. This exposes a fallacy: How can an external reward interface specify reward logic over structure whose existence is established after the interaction that reveals it? That is our research question. Supporting learning without repeatedly supplying task-specific knowledge is valuable in real-world exploration, where privileged supervision may be unavailable. Parity tests reward construction without asymmetric task-information channels. It is deliberately stricter than deployability, but allows a shared high-level goal. Our goal-free experiments additionally withhold task specifications, testing how far interaction and pretrained priors can ground executable rewards for behaviours discovered through exploration. What matters is whether reward discovery proceeds from the agent’s evidence or “hand-holding” by an external, artificial source. Both are useful, but only the former applies where task structure is initially unknown and must be discovered through interaction.

papers.title: LASH-PAT: Deadlock-Free Adaptive Shortest-Path Routing for Inter-Chiplet Interconnects
papers.abstract: With the slowdown of transistor scaling, chipletbased systems, and in particular chiplet-based wafer-scale integration, have emerged as a promising approach to sustain growth in computing capability per cost for modern processors and accelerators. In recent years, many specialized inter-chiplet interconnect topologies have been proposed. In these topologies, the simple, well-established, and deadlock-free dimension-order routing scheme is not applicable due to its reliance on regular mesh structures. In this work, we study routing in these recently proposed inter-chiplet interconnect topologies by categorizing and evaluating nine deadlock-free routing functions for irregular topologies known from data center networking in this new context. This reveals a trade-off between turn-based routing, which enables path diversity, and layered routing, which ensures shortest-path delivery. To resolve this trade-off, we propose LASH-PAT, a routing function that extends layered shortestpath routing with adaptive path diversity. LASH-PAT supports multiple shortest paths and dynamically selects among them based on local congestion while preserving deadlock freedom. When compared to the best-performing baseline routing function for each combination of topology, traffic pattern, and evaluated metric, LASH-PAT improves throughput by 21.15% and reduces energy per packet by 12.77%, while providing latency comparable to the lowest-latency baseline routing function.
papers.intro:
The growing compute demands of increasingly large machine learning (ML) models require continuous improvements in the computing capability per cost of high-performance processors and accelerators. For multiple decades, the computer architecture community was able to meet this demand by scaling up the number of transistors per chip, enabled by Moore’s law and Dennard scaling. However, due to the slowdown of Moore’s law and the end of Dennard scaling, new approaches are required to sustain performance improvements. The two most promising directions are 2.5D chiplet integration [99, 57, 82] and wafer-scale integration [104, 77, 106, 71, 43]. The former reduces design and manufacturing cost by enabling system modularity, chiplet reuse, heterogeneous integration, frequency and power binning, and improved yield [62, 66], while the latter enables packing more compute power into the high-bandwidth on-chip communication domain [39]. When combined, these two approaches are referred to as chiplet-based wafer-scale integration [70].

Since data movement is a major bottleneck for many ML workloads [44], the design of scalable and efficient inter-chiplet interconnect (ICI) is critical to overall system performance. While the 2D mesh topology has long been the de facto standard for network-on-chips (NoCs), recent work has proposed specialized ICI topologies [41, 42, 25, 48, 6, 88, 85] for both 2.5D chiplet systems on passive substrates [98, 51, 97] and active interposers [100, 14]. These topologies exploit the unique characteristics of 2.5D chiplet systems to improve performance, but they no longer support the established deadlock-free dimension-order routing algorithm, which relies on a mesh structure.

In this work, we investigate the performance of nine different routing functions (RFs) for irregular topologies [92, 83, 101, 52, 54, 20, 91, 60], primarily known from data center networking, when applied to chiplet-based wafer-scale systems. These methods can be broadly divided into two categories based on their deadlock-avoidance mechanism. Turn-based routing is similar to turn models for 2D mesh topologies [30, 13] and achieves deadlock freedom by prohibiting specific “turns” in the network. Layered routing achieves deadlock freedom by using virtual layers to break cyclic channel dependencies. Turn-based RFs typically provide path diversity but do not necessarily provide shortest paths, while layered RFs often guarantee shortest-path routing but may not provide path diversity. Exploiting path diversity is important to mitigate local congestion and achieve high throughput, while shortest-path routing is important to minimize latency.

papers.title: Sobolev theory for the inverse problem of time-dependent density functional theory on the torus
papers.abstract: We show that, given a sufficiently regular time-dependent density, there exists a unique potential such that the Schr\"odinger equation with this external potential has the prescribed one-particle density. We treat densities that are twice differentiable in time and of finite Sobolev regularity in space; the resulting potentials are continuous in time and of finite Sobolev regularity in space. Our method of proof is to rewrite the problem as a nonlinear Schr\"odinger equation with a loss of derivatives, which we in turn handle with a completion-of-the-square argument. This is a refinement of our recent work [Lauritsen, Lewin, and Oldenburg, arXiv:2609.08984], which handled this loss of derivatives using the Cauchy-Kovalevskaya theorem and treated analytic-in-space densities and potentials.

papers.title: Finding Patient Zero in Temporal Contact Networks: A Comparative Study
papers.abstract: Identifying the source of an epidemic, i.e., the patient zero, in a temporal contact network is important for effective outbreak containment and resource allocation. While several methods have been proposed for this task, they have rarely been evaluated under comparable conditions, and no systematic comparison exists for temporal contact networks. We address this gap with a comparative study of seven major methods, namely Steiner Tree (ST), Individual-Based Approximation (IBA), Dynamic Message Passing (DMP), Monte Carlo Mean-Field (MCMF), Soft Margin Estimator (SME), Backtracking Network (BN, a graph neural network), and Belief Propagation (BP). We unify all methods under a single problem formulation and evaluate them on eight diverse temporal networks. In the main experiment, we compare source detection performance for varying basic reproduction numbers. Three complementary experiments on a subset of networks study (i) learning curves, (ii) partial observability, and (iii) parameter misspecification. We find that BP and BN are the strongest source detectors overall. SME is strong under partial observation but mediocre otherwise. IBA, DMP, and MCMF share a common weakness rooted in their factorized-likelihood assumption, leading to overconfident predictions. We identify scaling these methods to larger networks as the most pressing direction for future work.

papers.title: Governance Risks in Decentralized Autonomous Organizations (DAOs): Implications for Traditional Financial Institutions
papers.abstract: As financial institutions increasingly interact with blockchain ecosystems through decentralized finance, stablecoins, tokenized assets, and distributed ledger infrastructure, they come to depend on systems governed wholly or partly by decentralized autonomous organizations (DAOs). This paper examines how DAO governance differs from traditional corporate governance and what this implies for risk management in regulated financial institutions. Using a qualitative comparative framework grounded in OECD governance principles, Basel Committee guidance, and FINMA circulars, the study maps DAO deliberation, voting, and accountability mechanisms against established governance and risk-management principles and illustrates associated risks through selected real-world cases. The analysis shows that DAOs preserve core governance functions but redistribute them across token holders, delegates, community forums, smart contracts, and legal wrapper entities. This creates distinct risks, including voting-power concentration, weak proposal controls, legal uncertainty, and unclear accountability, which established frameworks do not fully capture, while also offering two transferable strengths: a transparent, traceable decision record and a direct link between approval and execution. The paper contributes a structured assessment framework linking DAO governance characteristics to existing governance, outsourcing, technology-risk, and operational-resilience processes, enabling institutions to address DAO-governed dependencies through targeted extensions of current practices rather than a separate risk framework.

Blockchain technology has evolved from supporting cryptocurrencies to enabling organizational structures that coordinate economic activity without centralized management [8]. Among the most prominent examples are Decentralized Autonomous Organizations (DAOs), which govern collective decisions through blockchain-based mechanisms rather than conventional corporate hierarchies [13]. Instead of relying primarily on boards, executive management and legally defined fiduciary duties, DAOs commonly use governance tokens, community proposals, off-chain discussion forums, voting processes and smart contracts that can automatically execute approved outcomes.
