Instead of relying primarily on boards, executive management and legally defined fiduciary duties, DAOs commonly use governance tokens, community proposals, off-chain discussion forums, voting processes and smart contracts that can automatically execute approved outcomes.

This governance model matters beyond decentralized finance. Financial institutions increasingly interact with blockchain-based ecosystems through stablecoins, tokenized assets, decentralized liquidity protocols, settlement infrastructure and cryptoasset service providers. Exposure may be direct—holding or providing custody for governance tokens, offering products that reference DAO-governed protocols, using DAO-governed stablecoins, or integrating DAO-controlled protocols into treasury, collateral, settlement or liquidity-management processes—or indirect, through vendors, fintech partners, tokenization platforms, oracle providers, bridges, wallet infrastructure or custody solutions whose operations depend on DAO-governed protocols or smart-contract upgrades. Even where an institution remains legally and organizationally conventional, protocol changes, access conditions, collateral rules or upgrade decisions shaped by DAO governance can therefore affect its operational resilience, legal enforceability, client protection and third-party risk management.

This paper addresses the following research question: How do governance mechanisms in Decentralized Autonomous Organizations differ from traditional corporate governance structures, and what risk implications arise for regulated financial institutions as a result of these differences? To answer this question, the paper compares the Governance dimension of a contemporary DAO taxonomy [15]—Deliberation, Voting and Accountability—with traditional corporate governance mechanisms derived from the OECD Principles of Corporate Governance [16], Basel governance principles for banks [4] and selected FINMA supervisory requirements. The objective is not to evaluate individual DAOs empirically, but to identify governance differences and risk implications at the framework level.

This paper addresses the following research question: How do governance mechanisms in Decentralized Autonomous Organizations differ from traditional corporate governance structures, and what risk implications arise for regulated financial institutions as a result of these differences? To answer this question, the paper compares the Governance dimension of a contemporary DAO taxonomy [15]—Deliberation, Voting and Accountability—with traditional corporate governance mechanisms derived from the OECD Principles of Corporate Governance [16], Basel governance principles for banks [4] and selected FINMA supervisory requirements. The objective is not to evaluate individual DAOs empirically, but to identify governance differences and risk implications at the framework level.

This paper makes three contributions. First, it systematically connects DAO governance taxonomy research with established corporate and banking governance principles through a functional comparison of deliberation, voting and accountability. Second, it develops an institution-oriented assessment framework that links DAO governance characteristics to existing governance oversight, third-party risk, technology-risk, compliance and operational-resilience processes. Third, it shows that DAO-governed dependencies do not require new institutional risk categories: existing risk-management structures can be extended to account for distributed decision-making, concentrated effective control and potentially limited legal accountability. The analysis addresses regulated financial institutions broadly, including banks, asset managers and market infrastructure providers, but uses banking governance as its prudential benchmark.

papers.title: Trusting Trust in AI Software Engineering Agents: The Why, What, and How?
papers.abstract: AI software engineering agents are increasingly integrated into development workflows, from autocomplete assistants to autonomous repair agents and multi-agent software development pipelines. Trust matters because these agents can produce, revise, and pass on artifacts that developers, other agents, or organisations may later rely on under uncertainty and risk. Yet trust in such systems is often treated as a single measurable property of an AI system. This is insufficient for software engineering, where trust depends on who relies on the agent, how that reliance is structured, and which properties must hold in that deployment. We propose a structural framework for reasoning about trust in AI software engineering agents. Inspired by the recursive nature of trust in software systems, we decompose trust into three analytical questions: Why trust?, identifying the trust scenario; What trust?, identifying the trust configuration; and How much trust?, identifying the trust properties. From these questions, we derive three scenarios, four configurations, and five trust-relevant properties, state which of these are closed by construction and which remain open to revision, and instantiate the resulting profile on a ChatDev-style multi-agent workflow. The framework is conceptual, and is offered as a foundation for the empirical work that would validate it, rather than as a numerical trust metric.

papers.title: Stokes flow in a wedge with a moving contact point: well-posedness with a fixed contact angle and Navier slip
papers.abstract: We study 2D Stokes flow in a wedge-like region bounded by a solid substrate with Navier slip and by a free surface driven by surface tension. The two meet at a moving contact point with a fixed contact angle. This is the model of a moving contact line at scales below the slip length, in its simplest setting. The slip length is the only length scale, and nothing is prescribed at the contact point beyond the angle: no relaxation law for the angle, and no contact-point dissipation. Slip removes the paradox found by Huh and Scriven, the infinite dissipation at a contact line that moves without slip, but in this model a weaker singularity remains. We give, to our knowledge, the first rigorous characterisation of this singularity for solutions of the free-boundary problem near the stationary state. For small contact angles and small initial data satisfying two compatibility conditions, we prove local existence, uniqueness and Lipschitz dependence on the data. The compatibility conditions are the price of the fixed angle for solutions regular in time up to the initial time. Rather than hiding the singularity, the solution class carries it explicitly in corner expansions. The velocity is continuous up to the contact point. The pressure has a logarithmic singularity, the slip-regularised version of that of Huh and Scriven. Its coefficient is proportional to the contact-point velocity. The slope of the free boundary has a corresponding logarithmic correction, the slip-scale counterpart of the Cox-Voinov relation. The linearised problem combines terms of different scaling, which prevents a direct treatment by the Mellin transform. We solve it by a Lax-Milgram argument, and an auxiliary test function problem shows that the variational solution satisfies the equations. Explicit Mellin representations then yield the corner expansions, and the nonlinear problem is solved by a contraction argument.

papers.intro:
A viscous fluid resting on a solid substrate and bounded by a free surface meets the substrate along a contact line. At rest the configuration has been understood since Young [67]: the interface meets the substrate at the angle at which the surface tensions balance. In motion — a drop spreading, a plate drawn out of a bath, a meniscus advancing along a capillary — the neighbourhood of the contact line resists the classical description, and the difficulty is old and well documented. Huh and Scriven [33] computed the local flow under the no-slip condition, a similarity solution of the kind introduced for viscous corner flows by Dean and Montagnon [8], Moffatt [50] and Taylor [63]. Huh and Scriven found a stress of the order μ​U/r\mu U/r at distance rr from a contact line moving with speed UU, the Huh–Scriven singularity. The rate of dissipation and the force on the substrate therefore diverge logarithmically; in their phrase, “not even Herakles could sink a solid if the physical model were entirely valid, which it is not”. Dussan and Davis [12] traced the difficulty to the kinematics rather than to any constitutive assumption: no slip and a moving contact line force the interface to roll onto the substrate and the velocity field to be multivalued at the contact line. This is the paradox of Huh and Scriven — the classical model admits no moving contact line with finite dissipation — and it has to be resolved below some small scale.

With slip the force on the substrate is finite [31], and the flow organises itself into two regions, which carry two different notions of contact angle. In the inner region, at scales comparable with the slip length, the full free-boundary Stokes problem has to be solved, and the interface meets the substrate at the microscopic angle. This angle is a property of the materials in contact: it is either held at its equilibrium value or relaxed towards it by a constitutive law imposed at the contact line. In the outer region, at scales large compared with the slip length, the slope read off the interface is the apparent, or macroscopic, angle, which is not prescribed but produced by the flow. It is the one that experiments see. For small angles its cube differs from the cube of the microscopic angle by a multiple of the speed of the contact line, with a factor that depends logarithmically on the distance to the contact line divided by the slip length. This is the Cox–Voinov relation, derived by matched asymptotics in the works of Voinov [65], Hocking [31] and Cox [7]; see also [32]. For a completely wetting fluid it leads to Tanner’s law [62] for the rate at which a drop spreads.

papers.title: SandBAR: A Band-Asymmetric Architecture for Underwater Image Restoration with Removable Frequency Scaffolding
papers.abstract: Light scattering, absorption and turbidity degrade underwater imagery through complementary frequency tendencies: large-scale, channel-dependent appearance distortions and local high-frequency detail loss. This band asymmetry motivates different forms of restoration for global colour and local structure. Our primary contribution is SandBAR, a novel unified band-asymmetric architecture for underwater image restoration. Rather than treating frequency processing as an isolated module, SandBAR organises the restoration pipeline around band asymmetry at the block, encoder and objective levels. Within this architecture, we introduce a novel band-asymmetric sandwich block with a reserved post-attention repair slot and the Split-band Parallel Asymmetric Repair Kernel (SPARK), a novel module that applies channel-aware large-support correction to the low band, which predominantly carries large-scale appearance distortions, and lightweight local refinement to the detail-bearing high band, thereby restoring global colour while preserving fine structure. To deliver the global cast to the depth at which the network represents global structure, a learnable low-frequency guidance path injects a low-pass view of the input into the deep encoder, and a three-scale spatial-frequency objective supervises the same axis throughout the decoder. Building on the reserved post-attention slot, we further introduce Post-attention Scaffold Training (PaST), a novel removable nonlinear scaffolding scheme that trains the permanent SandBAR graph under band-specific capacity and runs it at inference without that capacity. SandBAR reaches 29.89 / 28.92 / 22.77 dB on EUVP / LSUI / UIEB and establishes a new three-domain mean state of the art on the benchmark family, exceeding the strongest published result by approximately 1.0 dB. PaST adds no parameters or FLOPs at inference and preserves matched latency.

Underwater image degradation is not a single uniform loss of visual quality. Light scattering, absorption and turbidity jointly reduce visibility, distort colour and blur fine structure. Their effects are physically interwoven: attenuation and backscatter vary with water conditions, scene range and content, so no single mechanism belongs exclusively to one spatial-frequency band [1, 2]. In the image domain, however, the resulting degradation often exhibits complementary frequency tendencies. Large-scale, channel-dependent distortions dominate background colour and smooth appearance, whereas edges, textures and small objects concentrate high-frequency structure and lose contrast first. We refer to this empirical tendency as band asymmetry. It motivates smooth, channel-structured correction for the low-frequency component and local detail refinement for the high-frequency component. Figure 1 illustrates this behaviour: SandBAR corrects the large-scale colour cast while preserving fine object texture and boundaries.

Deep underwater restoration has advanced rapidly, from physics-guided CNNs [17, 16] through transformers [24, 28] to recent spatial–spectral state-space models [23]. Band asymmetry nevertheless enters these architectures in one of two ways. Uniform backbones leave it implicit and rely on a homogeneous stack to discover the distinction during training. Frequency-aware designs [6, 14] model it explicitly through decomposition and specialised per-band processing. These approaches generally treat band asymmetry either implicitly or within an individual component, rather than organising block topology, encoder guidance and supervision around it as one underwater restoration architecture. Moreover, explicit frequency operations remain active at inference, so their additional branches and band-specific transformations must be executed for every restored image. This creates both an architectural gap and a practical tension between explicit frequency modelling and efficient inference.

papers.title: Think Once, Act Fast: Cost-Effective Recursive Self-Improvement for Decision Model Harness
papers.abstract: Fast System-1 models enable responsive actions but struggle with complex or unfamiliar tasks. Large language model (LLM)-based System-2 provides strong reasoning capabilities, yet repeated invocation incurs substantial latency and computational costs. To bridge this gap, we propose JevRSI, a System-1/System-2 collaboration framework that transforms LLM reasoning into transferable decision support through recursive harness improvement. A Jev-style System-1 model enables low-latency action selection, while an asynchronous System-2 LLM develops a modular harness. The harness integrates procedures, state memory, and world models to provide decision contexts spanning the past, present, and future. Utility-driven retrieval selects modules based on both contextual relevance and their utility on previous tasks. Environmental feedback guides targeted revisions and enables recursive self-improvement. Experiments across three datasets show that JevRSI consistently improves decision quality, matching or surpassing LLM agents in several settings. It preserves low-latency execution with favorable performance-cost trade-offs. Moreover, System-2 development interventions decrease as the harness evolves, amortizing System-2 costs through continuous improvement. Our project is available at https://github.com/usail-hkust/JevRSI.

papers.intro:
Developing agents that act efficiently and accurately across diverse environments remains a fundamental challenge in artificial intelligence. Large language models (LLMs) offer broad knowledge and powerful reasoning capabilities, but their computational overhead and latency hinder time-sensitive applications and tasks (e.g.embodied agents, autonomous driving). Existing approaches follow three paradigms. System-1 agents employ lightweight models, including rule-based systems, small LLMs, and vision-language-action (VLA) models (Kim et al., 2024). They successfully enable fast decision-making but often struggle with complex or unfamiliar tasks. System-2 agents leverage larger LLMs for deliberate reasoning, offering great flexibility with extensive inference cost (Yao et al., 2022; Prasad et al., 2023). System-1/System-2 cooperative methods combine these strengths by selectively invoking sophisticated reasoning while delegating routine decisions to fast executors, aiming to balance decision quality and execution efficiency (Lin et al., 2023; NVIDIA et al., 2025).

System-1/System-2 cooperative methods combine these strengths by selectively invoking sophisticated reasoning while delegating routine decisions to fast executors, aiming to balance decision quality and execution efficiency (Lin et al., 2023; NVIDIA et al., 2025).

However, existing System-1/System-2 collaboration methods primarily focus on allocating computation by selecting when to invoke System-1 or System-2 (Lin et al., 2023). Each System-2 invocation still incurs substantially greater latency. This motivates distilling LLM reasoning into reusable support for System-1 while preserving its responsiveness. Jev-style (Almeida, 2026) decision models offer a promising paradigm for this goal. Its structured probabilistic decision interface supports fast, high-quality decision-making and strong generalization, making it well suited to System-1 execution. To equip decision models with LLM reasoning capabilities, we propose recursively improving its harness, constructing informative decision context and guide action selection. LLM-based System-2 leverages interaction feedback to revise the harness, allowing recursive self-improvement to support subsequent decisions. Through this cycle, we aim to continually improve decision quality while preserving the responsiveness of System-1 execution.

papers.title: TRAIL-IRL: Crossed Reward-Temperature Mixtures for Unlabeled Trajectory Clustering
papers.abstract: Different paths need not imply different preferences, trajectories also differ in how randomly actions are chosen. Many multi-reward inverse reinforcement learning (IRL) methods assume common action randomness and can confound it with preference heterogeneity. We introduce TRAIL-IRL, which clusters unlabeled trajectories using rewards for preferences and temperatures for action randomness. Its crossed mixture pairs each reward with a shared set of temperature levels, allowing action regularity to vary within preference groups. With centered and normalized rewards in a known finite-state environment, we establish the identifiability conditions under which the distribution of sufficiently long trajectories determines rewards, temperatures, mixing weights, and class counts up to relabeling. Under the same conditions and reward constraints, common-temperature reward mixtures with the same component count cannot reproduce a crossed mixture with multiple temperatures. We develop a generalized expectation-maximization algorithm and select class counts using the Bayesian information criterion (BIC). Simulations show improved predictive fit, reward recovery, and trajectory classification over common-temperature mixtures with the same component count. For 140 bird-year trajectories from 79 white storks, BIC favors four reward classes and three temperature levels over common-temperature candidates. Younger birds have higher posterior membership probabilities for a southwestward migration class, whereas older birds have higher probabilities for a northern retention class. Within reward classes, higher temperatures are associated with more variable movement directions and positions farther ahead along the migration route, consistent with social information use and collective sensing.

Advances in GPS tracking, biologging, and automated sensing have expanded the availability of trajectory data in animal ecology (Kays et al., 2015; Nathan et al., 2022), pedestrian mobility (Brščić et al., 2013; Rudenko et al., 2020), and urban transportation (Barmpounakis and Geroliminis, 2020). A trajectory records an individual’s successive locations and their observation times (Zheng, 2015). These records provide information on movement routes, speeds, changes in direction, and stopping patterns.

Movement behavior varies across individuals, and group labels are often unavailable. Clustering methods recover recurring patterns from the trajectories themselves. Geometric methods define similarity through path shape and distance (Lee et al., 2007; Morris and Trivedi, 2009; Zheng, 2015). Regression mixtures and functional models identify groups by modeling trajectory curves and their variation over time (Gaffney and Smyth, 1999; James and Sugar, 2003; Gaffney et al., 2007; Jacques and Preda, 2014). Neural methods learn representations for trajectory clustering and similarity comparison (Yao et al., 2018; Li et al., 2018; Chang et al., 2023). These methods describe observed movement patterns, but do not explicitly infer the behavioral objectives that may underlie them.

Inverse reinforcement learning (IRL) infers such behavioral objectives by estimating a reward function from observed trajectories under a decision model (Ng and Russell, 2000; Abbeel and Ng, 2004). The reward function represents preferences over states and actions, and the decision model relates action choices to immediate and expected future rewards. Single-reward methods, including linear programming IRL (LP-IRL) (Ng and Russell, 2000) and maximum-entropy IRL (Ziebart et al., 2008), estimate a common reward function without inferring latent trajectory groups. When objectives differ across individuals, reward-mixture models jointly infer group-specific reward functions and latent group memberships (Babeş-Vroman et al., 2011; Ramponi et al., 2020; Bighashdel et al., 2023). For example, DPM-BIRL (Choi and Kim, 2012) uses a Dirichlet process mixture to group trajectories according to the reward functions that explain their observed behavior.

Individuals pursuing the same objective can also differ in how they plan and choose actions. Existing IRL formulations model such differences through variation in strategy preferences (Chen et al., 2020), planning horizons (Yao et al., 2024), or computational budgets (Jacob et al., 2024). In this paper, we focus on action regularity, the consistency with which individuals favor actions that advance a given objective. In entropy-regularized decision models, this consistency is controlled by a temperature parameter, which governs the concentration of action choices under a given reward (Ziebart et al., 2008; Geist et al., 2019). DPM-BIRL (Choi and Kim, 2012) uses a fixed decision-precision parameter shared across individuals to describe this regularity. We allow temperature to vary among individuals who share a reward and infer action-regularity groups from unlabeled trajectories.

We propose TRAIL-IRL (Inverse Reinforcement Learning for Temperature–Reward Association and Inference of Latent Groups) to infer reward and action-regularity groups from unlabeled trajectories. The crossed reward–temperature mixture, denoted by RT⁡(K,H)\mathrm{RT}(K,H), combines KK reward classes and HH temperature classes into K×HK\times H latent components, with each trajectory generated from one reward–temperature pair. Reward parameters are shared across temperature classes, and temperature parameters are shared across reward classes as well. This structure allows trajectories with the same objective to differ in action regularity, and trajectories with different objectives to share the same level of regularity. To characterize these two sources of variation, we develop an algorithm that jointly estimates the reward and temperature parameters and infers each trajectory’s reward and temperature class labels. The number of reward classes KK and the number of temperature classes HH are also selected from the observed trajectories.

papers.title: Pluggable Subband-Decoupled Fusion and Unlabeled Capture Prototype Calibration: Bridging High-SNR Null-Subcarrier Regrowth and Low-SNR Coherent Preambles for Cross-Domain IoT RF Fingerprinting
papers.abstract: Zero-overhead physical-layer authentication at edge wireless access points (APs) is vital for securing resource-constrained Internet of Things (IoT) transceivers against credential cloning, yet cross-domain IEEE 802.11a/g radio frequency fingerprint identification (RFFI) faces an acute signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) crossover. Power-amplifier spectral regrowth on unpopulated null subcarriers resists indoor multipath at high SNR but decays quadratically below the thermal noise floor, whereas populated active in-band preambles survive low SNR yet degrade under severe multipath, causing static fusion to lose up to 44.7 percentage points (pp). To our knowledge, we propose the first RFFI framework that dynamically modulates active in-band waveforms and unpopulated null-subcarrier regrowth via a blind physical SNR gate: Pluggable Gated Subband-Decoupled Fusion with Unlabeled Capture-Aware Prototype Calibration (GSDF-CAPC). Avoiding the 20-35 dB subband gradient imbalance of joint training, GSDF pairs any frozen pretrained host backbone with a 46.3K null-subcarrier plug-in encoder (NS-Branch), fusing scale-standardized logits and gate-warped spherical embeddings under a source-calibrated lag-64 thermal-SNR gate with exact low-SNR fallback. Over unlabeled target AP captures, forward-only unbalanced optimal-transport calibration (UOT-CAPC) aligns shifted prototypes under packet-arrival skew and recovers parameter-free balanced Sinkhorn (U-CAPC) at equipartition. Across DataPort-WiFi, WiSig, and ORBIT MobRFFI, zero-retrain GSDF wins all 72/72 paired runs across eight backbones with 0.00 pp low-SNR loss, while edge IB-Host + GSDF (92.6K-93.3K active parameters, 1.82 ms single-core CPU latency) and timing-synchronized GSDF-STO / GSDF-Tri reach 57.50%-65.05% three-benchmark Macro-F1 (89.04%-100.00% over 5-10-packet IoT bursts).

Physical-layer radio frequency fingerprint identification (RFFI) authenticates wireless Internet of Things (IoT) transceivers directly from analog front-end hardware impairments—including power-amplifier (PA) amplitude-to-amplitude (AM/AM) and amplitude-to-phase (AM/PM) nonlinearities, quadrature I/Q mixer imbalance, and baseband filter tolerances—imprinted onto standard synchronization preambles [1, 2, 3, 4]. Because MAC identifiers and pre-shared cryptographic keys can be cloned or extracted across low-cost smart-building sensors, industrial actuators, and consumer Wi-Fi IoT nodes, passive waveform-level verification at edge access points (APs) provides an essential zero-overhead defense [5, 6, 7]. Practical indoor Wi-Fi IoT deployments, however, violate the stationary-channel premise of single-room laboratory evaluations: an edge gateway classifier enrolled on one source AP must survive unseen room impulse responses, multi-week hardware drift, uncalibrated replacement APs, co-channel interference, single-core gateway CPU budgets without discrete GPUs, and wide thermal signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) variations spanning >30>30 dB near the AP down to 0–5 dB for cell-edge or through-wall IoT devices [8, 9, 10].

papers.title: Testing the Pareto law through a Stein-Laplace characterization
papers.abstract: A Stein--Laplace characterization yields two closed-form goodness-of-fit statistics for the Pareto type-I family with unknown shape and known lower endpoint. The signed integral statistic $T_n$ has a standard normal limit after studentization, but explicit non-Pareto alternatives show that it is not omnibus consistent. The integrated squared discrepancy $S_n$ yields a consistent test against every fixed non-Pareto alternative on the specified support with a finite, positive logarithmic moment. We derive the weighted chi-square null limit of $nS_n$ and give conditions for an asymptotically valid parametric-bootstrap and plug-in covariance-operator method. The latter uses Nystr\"om eigenvalue approximation to avoid repeated sample generation and parameter estimation. A large Monte Carlo comparison study shows competitive performance relative to existing procedures in the literature. In the paired study, the two calibrations have similar empirical power, with slightly higher small-sample rejection rates for the bootstrap in some settings. In the timing experiment, covariance-operator calibration is approximately $28$--$37$ times faster at $n=200$. An exploratory threshold-sensitivity analysis of Danish fire-insurance losses illustrates the dependence of Pareto goodness-of-fit conclusions on the specified tail region.

papers.title: Inverse Boundary Value Problems for a Coupled Semilinear Klein-Gordon System
papers.abstract:
This article addresses the coefficient identification inverse problem for a coupled nonlinear Klein-Gordon equation with cubic nonlinearity. More precisely, we consider a coupled nonlinear Klein-Gordon equation in a bounded cylinder contained in $\mathbb{R}^{1+\ell}$, where $ \ell\geq 2$, and establish the unique recovery of the time-independent coefficients appearing in both the zeroth-order perturbation and nonlinearity term from both full and partial boundary measurements of the solution. The unique recovery of zeroth-order coefficients is obtained via first-order linearization; however, the nonlinearity coefficients are recovered using the higher-order linearization.
  Finally using the unique continuation principle, we establish the unique identification of the coefficients from the partial boundary measurements of the solution.

papers.title: Bounded functions on the character variety for quadratic extensions of $\mathbb{Q}_p$
papers.abstract: For any finite extension $L$ of $\mathbb{Q}_p$, Schneider--Teitelbaum defined and studied the character variety in $p$-adic Fourier theory. It is a rigid analytic curve over $L$ that parameterizes the set of locally $L$-analytic characters of $o_L$. It is conjectured that all bounded functions on the character variety of Schneider--Teitelbaum come from $p$-adic measures. We prove this conjecture for all quadratic extensions $L/\mathbb{Q}_p$.

papers.title: Brown dwarfs and stars are dynamically indistinguishable as companions in AU-separation binaries
papers.abstract: Brown dwarfs occupy the mass range between stars and planets, populations whose dominant formation channels differ, which leave measurable differences in the orbital eccentricity and host-star metallicity distributions. We assemble a sample of astrometric binaries with main sequence primaries and brown dwarf companions at $\mathcal{O}$(AU) separations from $\textit{Gaia}$ DR3. The observable photocenter motions for such binaries are degenerate between a genuinely low-mass companion and a near-equal-mass binary. We break this degeneracy using $\textit{Gaia}$ XP spectrophotometry and follow-up FEROS spectroscopy, which removes removes ${\sim}70\%$ of initial low-mass-function candidates as likely near-twin binaries and leaves residual contamination of only a few percent. The resulting 368 systems, with masses and metallicities determined from the XP spectra and a selection function forward-modelled with $\texttt{Gaiamock}$, form the largest homogeneous sample of brown dwarf companions with astrometric orbits. We find the eccentricity distribution to be well described by a normal distribution. This is comparable to eccentricities of stellar companions at the same periods and higher than those of giant planets, with no significant dependence on companion mass ($\alpha=-0.13\pm0.09$) or period ($\beta=0.10\pm0.05$). The host-star metallicity distribution is likewise stellar-like, extending to [M/H]$=-0.5$, in contrast to the predominantly super-solar metallicity hosts of giant planets. After accounting for selection, the companion-mass distribution over all brown dwarf masses is consistent with an extension of stellar-binary demographics. Brown dwarf companions at AU separations down to at least $20\,M_J$ therefore appear to form predominantly through a binary-star-like channel. A possible transition to planet-like formation at lower masses cannot be located with the present sample.

papers.intro:
Binary star formation appears to have two dominating modes: direct fragmentation of a collapsing cloud with 𝒪⁡(1000​AU)\mathcal{O}(1000\mathrm{AU}) separations (Adams et al., 1989; Kratter and Lodato, 2016) and circumstellar disk instability with 𝒪⁡(100​AU)\mathcal{O}(100\mathrm{AU}) separations (Fisher, 2004; Kratter and Lodato, 2016). The latter process appears to dominate as stellar multiplicity is most common at this scale (Moe and Di Stefano, 2017, corresponding to ∼105{\sim}10^{5} days,). Meanwhile, planets appear to form through core-accretion in a protoplanetary disk (Pollack et al., 1996), or perhaps through the binary-star like disk instability (Kratter and Lodato, 2016). To create close binaries, the companion must then migrate inwards through interactions with the remaining debris, companions, or passing systems (Tohline, 2002; Moe and Kratter, 2018; Offner et al., 2023). We generally observe binaries after dynamical processing has ceased, where systems have become decoupled from their birth environments and their orbit distributions reflect both the formation process and dynamical processing.

This makes the overlapping mass regime between planets and stars – brown dwarfs – both challenging to probe and rich in physics. Brown dwarfs are conventionally defined as too small to be called stars, not able to sustain core-hydrogen burning (Hayashi and Nakano, 1963; Kumar, 1963; Kirkpatrick, 2005, ≲80​MJup{\lesssim}80\,M_{\text{Jup}},), but massive enough for deuterium burning, which does not happen below ∼13​MJup{\sim}13\,M_{\text{Jup}} (Spiegel et al., 2011; Burrows et al., 1997; Boss et al., 2007). Somewhere in or below the brown dwarf mass range is where formation changes between forming “bottom-up” from core accretion within protoplanetary discs (forming “like a planet”) or through the fragmentation and direct collapse of a star forming cloud or disk (forming “like a star”), and it has been proposed to separate brown dwarfs from planets based on formation mechanism rather than mass (Black, 1997, e.g.). Previously, dearths of intermediate mass brown dwarfs in binaries (∼30−50​MJup{\sim}30-50\,M_{\text{Jup}}) have been reported as a “brown dwarf desert“ (Grether and Lineweaver, 2006; Ma and Ge, 2014; Stevenson et al., 2023) representing such a turnover in formation mechanism, but this remains unclear as others have found no such dearth (Gaia Collaboration et al., 2023a; Wallace and Casey, 2026). It is worth creating a large, well understood sample of brown dwarfs in binaries to address where this turnover may exist.

Different formation histories may be hard to discern in individual objects, but should be reflected in population properties. For example, at AU-separations, the distribution of orbital eccentricities is typically smaller in giant planets e¯∼0.2\bar{e}{\sim}0.2 (Bowler et al., 2020; Bitsch et al., 2020) than stellar companions e¯∼0.4\bar{e}{\sim}0.4 (Duquennoy and Mayor, 1991; Wu et al., 2025). Additionally, giant planets appear to form predominantly in systems of super-solar metallicity (Gan et al., 2025), while the distribution of metallicities in stellar binaries is anti-correlated with metallicity at these separations (Raghavan et al., 2010; Moe et al., 2019; El-Badry et al., 2019). Astrometric binaries with main sequence stars and brown dwarf companions allow for the identification of the orbital parameters of the orbit (period, eccentricity), while spectroscopic measurements of the system determines the properties of the primary (mass, metallicity). The Gaia mission (Gaia Collaboration et al., 2016) and its third data release (Gaia Collaboration et al., 2023b, DR3,) provides an unprecedented opportunity to construct such a sample with its 34 month baseline and multiple yearly precise astrometric, photometric, and spectroscopic measurements. 168 000 objects with AU-scale orbits passing stringent cuts have a full orbit solution published in Gaia’s non single star (NSS) catalogue (Halbwachs et al., 2023). For main sequence stars, their mass and metallicity can be readily obtained through Gaia’s low-resolution BP-RP “XP” spectra (Li et al., 2025), which is available homogeneously for every object brighter than G<17.65G{<}17.65 in Gaia’s G-band (De Angeli et al., 2023). Determining the mass of the brown dwarf requires handling the degeneracy where low-mass dark companions and near-twins may lead to identical photocentre motions, which can be resolved spectroscopically (Li et al., 2025). Our sample constructed this way contains 368 main sequence-brown dwarf (MS-BD) systems, the largest sample of astrometric binaries with brown dwarf companions. Finally, such a catalogue has a known selection function which can be forward modelled (El-Badry et al., 2024), providing unprecedented access to the underlying physics.

The distributions of eccentricities and metallicities are compared to planetary and stellar companions in Sect. 4 and 5 respectively. papers.title: Inertial Video World Models
papers.abstract: The physical world has inertia: it evolves from what already exists rather than being recreated at every instant. However, many existing video world models lack an explicit mechanism for inertial state evolution, leaving the continuity of motion and structure implicit in video prediction. During autoregressive rollouts, repeated reconstruction can accumulate errors and destabilize the predicted dynamics. To address this limitation, we introduce InertialWorld, an Inertial Video World Model that makes inertia a structural prior for autoregressive prediction: existing scene evidence is carried across time rather than reconstructed at every step. Central to this formulation is Inertial Memory, which turns memory from passive predictive context into an evolving video state with two complementary views: a dense Eulerian grid preserves scene-aligned evidence, while persistent Lagrangian carriers bind local content to learned canonical coordinates. At each step, the model transports the carrier content according to action-conditioned motion, predicts the complete next video state from the transported carriers and dense grid, and uses a learned gate to combine transported and newly predicted content into the memory for the next step. Extensive experiments across multiple domains, including robot manipulation, 3D game simulation, and open-world navigation, demonstrate that InertialWorld achieves competitive autoregressive prediction performance against strong video world model baselines. papers.intro:
Learned world models provide predictive environments for planning and control by modeling action-conditioned dynamics (Ha and Schmidhuber, 2018; Hafner et al., 2019; Hafner et al., 2025). Within this broader family, video world models instantiate learned dynamics through action-conditioned video prediction, enabling interactive simulation in games, robotic manipulation, and embodied navigation (Micheli et al., 2022; Bruce et al., 2024; Yang et al., 2023; Bar et al., 2025). Autoregressive and diffusion-based formulations have substantially improved generation fidelity and controllability (Wu et al., 2024; Alonso et al., 2024; Huang et al., 2025; Zhu et al., 2026), while post-training further refines predicted rollouts (Wu et al., 2026b; Wu et al., 2026a). Despite these advances, physical evolution is inertial: the world evolves from what already exists rather than being recreated at every instant. Most video world models, however, still formulate temporal evolution as repeated conditional generation, predicting persistent scene content again at every step rather than explicitly carrying it forward. Since each generated state conditions the next transition, small reconstruction errors can repeatedly re-enter the rollout and destabilize predicted motion and structure (Wang et al., 2017; Babaeizadeh et al., 2021).

Within this broader family, video world models instantiate learned dynamics through action-conditioned video prediction, enabling interactive simulation in games, robotic manipulation, and embodied navigation (Micheli et al., 2022; Bruce et al., 2024; Yang et al., 2023; Bar et al., 2025). Despite these advances, physical evolution is inertial: the world evolves from what already exists rather than being recreated at every instant. Most video world models, however, still formulate temporal evolution as repeated conditional generation, predicting persistent scene content again at every step rather than explicitly carrying it forward. Since each generated state conditions the next transition, small reconstruction errors can repeatedly re-enter the rollout and destabilize predicted motion and structure (Wang et al., 2017; Babaeizadeh et al., 2021).

A prominent line of research mitigates this limitation by augmenting video prediction with memory. Recurrent video predictors retain temporal features across prediction steps (Wang et al., 2017; Wang et al., 2018), while transformer world models expose longer histories to the transition function (Chen et al., 2022; Wu et al., 2024). This additional context is particularly valuable when occlusion or accumulated generation noise makes the current frame ambiguous. Earlier features can retain identity and layout cues that are no longer directly visible but remain relevant to the next transition. Spatial and persistent memories preserve scene-aligned evidence across recurrent prediction steps (Wu et al., 2026c; Zhou et al., 2026). Object-centric representations provide a complementary form of persistence by binding content to structured entities (Locatello et al., 2020; Kipf et al., 2021), and their video extensions model the dynamics of these entities through time (Wu et al., 2022). Collectively, these mechanisms expose historical evidence to subsequent state transitions and improve temporal consistency, but retention alone does not specify how the retained content should evolve. When memory serves as context for a generic transition, the transition remains free to synthesize the next state without explicitly advancing the stored content. Transformation-based predictors demonstrate the value of warping observations or features (Jaderberg et al., 2015; Finn et al., 2016), yet warping does not by itself make transport the recurrent evolution rule of persistent memory across model-predicted steps. Thus, memory determines which past evidence remains available, whereas inertia additionally specifies what persists and where it moves. This distinction motivates the central question of this work: How can a video world model evolve the world it already remembers, rather than repeatedly reconstructing its persistent content?

To address this question, we introduce InertialWorld, an Inertial Video World Model that makes inertia a structural prior for autoregressive prediction: existing scene evidence is carried across time rather than reconstructed at every step. As illustrated in Figure 1, its central component, Inertial Memory, turns retained predictive context into an evolving video state with two complementary views: a dense Eulerian grid preserves scene-aligned evidence, while persistent Lagrangian carriers bind local content to learned canonical coordinates. At each step, the model transports the carrier content according to action-conditioned motion, predicts the complete next video state from the transported carriers and dense grid, and uses a learned gate to combine transported and newly predicted content into the memory for the next step. This carry-before-write transition establishes persistence as the default path of state evolution while preserving the capacity to model changes that transport alone cannot explain, without requiring object annotations or calibrated physical parameters. We evaluate InertialWorld on RT-1 robot manipulation (Brohan et al., 2022), Counter-Strike 3D game simulation (Huang et al., 2025), and RECON open-world navigation (Shah et al., 2021). papers.title: Accounts on Synthetic Cells
papers.abstract: Frontiers of Life is a research network of the University of Bordeaux focused on the re-engineering of living systems, starting from the construction of a synthetic cell. In this article, we present our motivation to build a cell from scratch and the elementary building blocks we worked on over the past four years. While the final objective regarding the construction of a synthetic cell remains a long-term target, the reconstruction of living cells provides both a methodology and experimental approaches to improve our understanding of living systems with potential to become the next generation of biotechnologies.

papers.title: Where Do Highly Cited Scientists Stand? A Multi-Dimensional Analysis of Positional Distribution in the Top 2% Ranking
papers.abstract: The Top 2% Scientists list is widely used. Yet current applications either only count the number of scientists in different units or criticize the list's validity as a measure of individual impact. We introduce positional enrichment, a scale-free framework that compares observed to expected counts across percentile bins on the list, revealing where a unit's scientists tend to sit along the list rather than how many it contributes. Applying positional enrichment to the 2026 single-year list, we show that countries, institutions, and research subfields each fall into a consistent pattern of three groups with Head-, Middle-, and Tail-enriched profiles. Subfield profiles are globally stable, whereas countries and institutions are heterogeneous across subfields. National and institutional differences are therefore compositional. Therefore, the reason of a country or institution sitting near the head of the list is unlikely its scientists performing better within the same subfields, while it holding more of the subfields that sit near the head. Academic age adds an independent dimension, with stronger enrichment toward the head after 25 years and exceptions in fast-moving subfields such as artificial intelligence. We show the ranking is not a flat ordering of individual influence but a subfield-organized stratification.

papers.title: Optimising Recruitment and Sample Allocation in Multi-Site Rare Disease Studies
papers.abstract: Clinical research in rare diseases is challenged by the limited availability and broad geographical distribution of eligible patients. This necessitates multi-centre collaboration and strategic selection of analytical laboratories based on capacity, cost, and capability. We present a mathematical framework based on cardinality optimisation to support key operational decisions in study design, balancing clinical relevance, feasibility, budgetary constraints, and logistical factors. The framework was implemented in the Reconstruction and Computational Modelling for Inherited Metabolic Diseases (Recon4IMD) project, aiming to recruit 1,900 diagnosed patients across 24 healthcare centres and eight metabolomic laboratories. Compared to both proportional heuristic and greedy marginal allocation baselines, the proposed optimisation model consistently achieved higher recruitment yields in simulated multi-centre scenarios and reduced metabolomic analysis costs by approximately 30% under unconstrained conditions. Notably, both the heuristic and greedy allocation baselines became infeasible under progressively tighter laboratory capacity constraints, whereas the optimised model maintained feasibility and cost control. These findings highlight the value of integrated optimisation strategies for improving recruitment, platform selection, and sample allocation in complex, resource-limited research settings.

Inherited metabolic disorders (IMDs) are rare genetic diseases that pose significant recruitment challenges due to their geographic dispersion and the need for specialised laboratories for diagnosis and monitoring. Multi-centre clinical studies have become indispensable in medical research, enabling faster recruitment and more generalisable results than single-site studies [15]. In rare diseases, no single hospital can enrol a sufficiently large cohort for meaningful results, making collaboration across multiple sites essential for achieving adequate sample sizes [35]. However, these advantages come with operational challenges, particularly in patient recruitment and sample allocation.

However, these advantages come with operational challenges, particularly in patient recruitment and sample allocation.

Recruitment in rare disease studies often remains slow, with each site typically contributing only a few patients. Ensuring consistent patient selection and diagnostic criteria across sites adds complexity, especially when expert consensus is required. Designing a multi-centre study thus involves balancing the inclusion of many centres against slow, diffuse recruitment [19]. Laboratory selection also matters: inter-site assay variability is common [23], prompting many studies to centralise testing or harmonise protocols to improve data quality. Previous research has produced piecemeal solutions for these issues, including better sample size formulas and calls for centralised laboratories [3].

Mathematical optimisation offers a powerful framework for addressing such complexity, formulating problems as the minimisation or maximisation of objectives under constraints. Within this, cardinality optimisation focuses on selecting an optimal subset of elements, minimising or maximising the number of sites, labs, or allocations. This approach, which enforces parsimony in solutions, has been effective in computational biology, such as in metabolic modelling [13], and shows promise for high-dimensional decision spaces.

Despite these advances, cardinality optimisation has not yet been integrated into operational decision-making for clinical research. While computational frameworks exist for simulating studies [22], there is a lack of applications addressing practical multi-centre questions, such as site selection, lab allocation, or logistical minimisation in a unified way. Clinical study planning still relies on heuristics, isolated analyses, and scenario iteration, rather than a comprehensive algorithmic framework. This gap presents an opportunity to improve multi-centre study design by integrating cardinality optimisation.

Traditional planning approaches often decompose study design into sequential decisions, such as defining sample-size targets, estimating recruitment capacity, and then addressing operational or logistical requirements separately [15, 33, 25]. This separation is practical but limited when decisions are interdependent. In multi-site rare disease studies, recruitment at one healthcare provider changes disease-specific cohort totals, downstream biomarker demand, analytical platform use, laboratory capacity, cost, and sample shipment patterns across the network. Laboratory allocation problems also introduce cost and capacity constraints that are difficult to address through recruitment planning alone [5]. Greedy strategies tend to prioritise local availability or immediate marginal gain, without jointly accounting for cross-disease dependencies, shared capacity constraints, clinical interest, and logistical trade-offs [4, 26]. These limitations motivate an integrated optimisation framework in which recruitment, biomarker demand, platform allocation, cost, and logistics are represented within a single constrained model.

The optimisation framework integrates recruitment planning and sample allocation within a single mathematical model. Disease-specific patient availability across healthcare providers is combined with recruitment capacity, cohort-size targets, biomarker requirements, analytical platform capabilities, laboratory throughput, analysis costs, logistical constraints, and hospital-specific clinical interests. Recruitment decisions define disease-specific cohort sizes and determine biomarker measurement demand, which is then linked to allocation across targeted and global metabolomic platforms. The unified objective combines cardinality terms, recruitment yield, logistical deviation, cost, and clinical-interest alignment to identify feasible and efficient multi-site recruitment and sample allocation strategies. Using the Reconstruction and Computational Modelling for Inherited Metabolic Diseases (Recon4IMD) project as a case study, we show how this strategy supports cost-efficient, logistically feasible, and clinically robust decision-making in complex multi-centre studies. The full mathematical formulation is provided in the Methods section.

papers.title: Hypersurfaces that are far from ruled
papers.abstract: We show that a very general complex hypersurface of degree $d$ in $\mathbb P^{n+1}$ is not ruled whenever $n\geq3$ and $d\geq2\lceil(n+2)/3\rceil$. This improves Koll\'ar's original degree bound to the bound subsequently obtained by Totaro for stable irrationality and, in particular, includes very general quartic fourfolds. More precisely, we find new bounds for the minimal degree of a dominant rational map from a very general hypersurface to a ruled variety or a conic bundle, improving on previous bounds of Chen--Stapleton. The proofs combine Koll\'ar's reduction to positive characteristic with the Jacobson correspondence for inseparable extensions.

papers.title: Orbital differentiation in a rare earth ion near half filling
papers.abstract: In the electronic structure of rare earth ions, details can be crucial for understanding the origin of correlated states. Currently, state-of-the-art wavefunction-based methods (e.g. CASSCF) can capture single-ion properties of molecular magnets and some band insulating systems, but are expensive to perform, and cannot be applied to metallic systems. Here, we carry out full multiplet calculations for SmN with the cubic rock-salt structure using the crystal field software Quanty. The calculated experimental observables from our model agree precisely with magnetic susceptibility and inelastic neutron scattering experiments, and the spatially resolved spin density also agrees with DFT predictions. By tuning the crystal field parameters, our full multiplet-derived wavefunctions reveal the presence of orbital differentiation of the ground $J=\frac{5}{2}$ manifold into two groups, which are distinct subspaces with different orbital stiffness. This violation of Hund's rule, observed with a fast and inexpensive calculation tool, represents a step forward for microscopic models of rare earth materials, and may provide support for the claim of unconventional triplet superconductivity in SmN.

papers.title: Koopmans spectral functionals for excitons in materials
papers.abstract: Accurate first-principles characterization of excitons typically relies on the Bethe-Salpeter equation (BSE) combined with quasiparticle energies from computationally demanding GW calculations. Here, we replace the GW step with quasiparticle energies from Koopmans-compliant spectral functionals, an approach we call BSE@qKI, and implement it in an automated, reproducible AiiDA workflow. For a set of benchmark semiconductors, BSE@qKI reproduces experimental band gaps and first exciton energies with mean absolute relative errors of 13% and 4%, respectively, comparable to BSE@G0W0 for the gaps and markedly better for the excitation energies. We also apply the method to the layered magnetic semiconductor CrI3, obtaining an absorption spectrum that reproduces the main experimental features. These results establish BSE@qKI as a GW-free alternative to BSE@G0W0 for systematic studies of excitonic properties in complex materials.

papers.intro:
Excitons — bound states formed by electron-hole pairs — are the quasiparticles that govern the optical response of materials [54]. They play a central role in several applications including photocatalysis [6, 93, 46], photovoltaics [80, 77, 47], plasmonics [98, 97], and chemical sensing [96]. Describing excitonic effects is therefore essential both for understanding the optical properties of materials and for designing of devices with tailored functionalities. From a first-principles perspective, many-body perturbation theory (MBPT), and in particular the Bethe-Salpeter equation (BSE) [86, 63], provides a state-of-the-art framework for describing neutral excitations. Conventionally, the BSE is solved using quasiparticle (QP) energies from the G​WGW approximation [63], often within the single-shot G0​W0G_{0}W_{0} scheme [36] (the well-known BSE@G0​W0G_{0}W_{0} approach). This route yields highly accurate optical spectra and excitonic properties, but its computational cost can quickly become prohibitive with material size (the scaling is typically ≥𝒪⁡(N3)\geq\mathcal{O}(N^{3}), where NN is the number of particles) or for systematic studies over many materials [92, 71, 9, 34, 35]. The computational burden of the G0​W0G_{0}W_{0} calculation is compounded by the subsequent construction and diagonalization of the BSE Hamiltonian. As such, it is desirable to decrease the cost of these calculations, without compromising the accuracy of the resulting excitonic description.

Koopmans spectral functionals [20, 13, 60, 49] are designed to provide accurate spectral properties at a computational cost closer to that of standard density-functional theory (DFT) [49], which makes them a promising source of QP energies. By feeding their eigenvalues directly to the BSE Hamiltonian, one can bypass the G0​W0G_{0}W_{0} calculations altogether. We call this approach BSE@qKI. It aims to retain the predictive power of the BSE while substantially reducing the computational cost of the standard BSE@G0​W0G_{0}W_{0} workflow. In this work, we assess the accuracy of the BSE@qKI approach. We first benchmark it against BSE@G0​W0G_{0}W_{0} and against experiment for five well-characterized bulk semiconductors, and we then apply it to the layered magnetic semiconductor CrI3 [56], a system in which non-collinear magnetism and spin-orbit coupling are both important. The optical spectra and excitonic properties agree well with those of BSE@G0​W0G_{0}W_{0}; for the energy of the first excitonic peak, BSE@qKI agrees better with experiment than BSE@G0​W0G_{0}W_{0} does for every benchmark material considerated. This provides a practical framework for applying the method across different classes of materials, and for carrying out high-throughput or large-scale studies of excitonic properties.

papers.title: AfriNORM: An Evaluation Benchmark for Normative Reasoning of LLMs Across African Cultures
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed across various sectors. However, current evaluation benchmarks are insufficient to assess the applicability of these models in local African contexts, as most focus on linguistic fluency (grammar/translation) rather than cultural competence. The few existing benchmarks that measure general knowledge or social conventions do not capture the African deontic modality, i.e., the strict norms and taboos that govern diverse social interactions. In this paper, we introduce AfriNORM, a scenario-based, multiple-choice question dataset designed to measure and diagnose the normative reasoning limitations of LLMs when applied to African sociocultural contexts. We introduce two metrics: a Universal Commonsense Bias Score (UCBS) to quantify commonsense bias in LLM and a Distractor Bias Score (DBS) to quantify an LLM's limited understanding of African cultural norms. We also conduct a case study on the Yor\`ub\'a language, identifying confusion gaps in two closed-source LLMs, "Gemini 2.0 Flash" and "GPT-5", and one open-source LLM, "Llama 3.1 8B Instruct" when prompted in English versus Yor\`ub\'a. While their accuracy in English is high, their performance in Yor\`ub\'a is much lower, attributable to cultural confusion rather than simple bias, indicating that the models exhibit semantic confusion when reasoning about norms in Yor\`ub\'a.

Language serves as a carrier of culture and a vehicle for transmitting a society’s values, beliefs, history, and social norms Wa Thiong’o (1998). As the adoption of large language models (LLMs) accelerates across Africa in sectors such as health, education, and finance (CIPIT, 2025; Nimo et al., 2025a), this link between language and culture raises concerns about African cultural alignment (Tao et al., 2024).

As the adoption of large language models (LLMs) accelerates across Africa in sectors such as health, education, and finance (CIPIT, 2025; Nimo et al., 2025a), this link between language and culture raises concerns about African cultural alignment (Tao et al., 2024).

While large language models are capable of producing fluent and contextually appropriate text in many languages, they struggle with complex reasoning tasks, especially when multi-step logic or nuanced cultural understanding is required, particularly in multilingual and low-resource settings (Ghosh et al., 2025). This limitation is especially significant in African contexts, where social and cultural norms often constitute a form of "lived epistemology", a knowledge system in which communal practices, spiritual traditions, and environmental relations are deeply interwoven with everyday life (Pawar et al., 2025). Therefore, the integration of LLMs into African contexts may yield incorrect, incomplete, or nonsensical responses to everyday questions in underrepresented cultures or offer social or normative guidance that, while generally correct, constitutes normative taboos for a particular culture. Existing benchmarks that address the cultural context, such as BLEND (Myung et al., 2024), mainly target social conventions, which reflect what people typically do but make no provision for social norms and taboos; what people should or must not do. This distinction is important because, while a failure to conform to convention may cause social awkwardness, a failure to observe a norm or taboo poses risks of ethical harm, deep offence, or social exclusion (Pawar et al., 2025; Ferrara et al., 2025; Hershcovich et al., 2022).

In this work, we introduce AfriNORM , a benchmark for measuring the normative reasoning gap observed in large language models (LLMs) with respect to African cultural contexts. Our methodology relies on generating complex, scenario-based questions and crafting adversarial distractor options to probe the reliability of LLM judgment. We also introduce two new metrics: the Universal Commonsense Bias Score (UCBS), which quantifies the model’s bias toward universal commonsense answers, and the Distractor Bias Score (DBS), which quantifies the degree to which the model confuses cultural norms.

papers.title: Spectropolarimetric diagnostics of the lower solar atmosphere: a review of inversion techniques
papers.abstract: The Sun, our host star, plays a fundamental role in astrophysics due to its vicinity. To understand the processes taking place in the outermost layers of the Sun, but also, indirectly, in its interior, we conduct high spectral and spatial resolution, high cadence observations of diagnostically important spectral lines. The intensity and the polarization of the electromagnetic radiation in the observed spectral lines are a result of the joint action of absorption, emission, and scattering processes, further altered by the Zeeman and Hanle effects. Spectropolarimetric inversions are the techniques devised for the inference of the physical parameters in the solar atmosphere through the interpretation of spectral line shapes and line polarization. This review aims to provide a pedagogical overview of the necessary radiative transfer formalism and cutting-edge techniques, and to help interested readers enter the field and use some of the concepts in their own research. The secondary aim is a critical assessment of the emerging directions for the development of spectropolarimetric inversions, namely, to discuss the friction between physical realism, numerical efficiency, and modeling of the instrumental effects.

The focus of this review is the solar atmosphere, that is, the Sun’s outermost layers that can be directly observed. While the atmosphere does take up a minuscule amount of solar mass (and, if we focus on the solar photosphere and chromosphere, of its radius), it is of primary interest because it hosts a plethora of interesting physical phenomena (Fletcher et al. 2011, Carlsson et al. 2019, Temmer 2021, e.g., sunspots, flares, CMEs, various other energetic events, see e.g.) but also because it is the only, albeit indirect, diagnostics of the events taking place in the solar interior, via the techniques of helioseismology (Christensen-Dalsgaard 2002, for a classical review of the topic, see). From the author’s point of view, the solar atmosphere is also extremely interesting and valuable as a natural laboratory for testing radiative transfer models and developing comprehensive techniques for radiative diagnostics (de la Cruz Rodríguez and van Noort 2017, see e.g.).

The last few decades witnessed a series of successful solar missions and ground-based telescopes focused on observing visible, ultraviolet (UV), and infrared (IR) parts of the spectrum, which continuously advanced our understanding of the Sun and its atmosphere. In space, Hinode Solar Optical Telescope (Tsuneta et al. 2008, Hinode/SOT,), Solar Dynamics Observatory (Pesnell et al. 2012, SDO,), Interface Region Imaging Spectrograph (De Pontieu et al. 2014, IRIS,), and Solar Orbiter (Müller et al. 2020, SO,) provide an uninterrupted insight into the Sun’s ever-changing atmosphere, while the large ground-based and balloon-borne telescopes provide exceptional spatial resolution and versatility in terms of instruments for analyzing the light. Telescopes like the Dunn Solar Telescope (Dunn 1969, DST,), Swedish Solar Telescope (Scharmer et al. 2003, SST,), SUNRISE (Solanki et al. 2010), GREGOR (Schmidt et al. 2012), and Goode Solar Telescope (Cao et al. 2010) have continuously increased the resolving power, eventually culminating with the Daniel K. Inouye Solar Telescope (Rimmele et al. 2020, DKIST,), which is expected to further unveil specifics of energy transport and release in the atmosphere of the Sun. This excellent spatial resolution is complemented by the targeted experiments like the CLASP sounding rocket (Narukage et al. 2016). The fundamental role in these observational developments is played by the wide range of imaging spectrographs and spectropolarimeters described in an excellent review by Iglesias and Feller (2019).

This review article aims to showcase the theoretical and numerical formalism needed to interpret these magnificent spectropolarimetric observations. The formalism that we use to model the radiation emerging from the solar atmosphere is known as the theory of polarized radiative transfer. Particular focus is on the spectral lines, regions of the spectrum that correspond to bound-bound transitions in atoms, ions, and molecules. The stark differences in the strengths of different lines, as well as the strong dependence of line opacity on wavelength, allow us to probe the solar atmosphere in depth (see the next section). At the same time, the spectral lines are sensitive to the magnetic field and plasma velocity, opening additional diagnostic approaches. Both of these advantages are naturally accounted for in the numerical methods known as spectropolarimetric inversions.

papers.title: From Preference Data to Personalization: Tracing Sycophancy in Large Language Models
papers.abstract: Sycophancy in large language models is often measured as agreement with the user, yet agreement can be appropriate when the user's claim is valid, their preference is genuine, or their experience warrants acknowledgment. We study sycophancy as inappropriate agreement: validating a claim, preference, or self-assessment when the context calls for correction, qualification, or resistance. We introduce a validity-aware sycophancy grader and SycoDrift, a persona-targeted evaluation set of 3,298 validity-annotated probes with controlled annotations for user openness and stakes. We use this framework to analyze three sources of agreement pressure: human preference data, automated judge specification, and in-context personalization. First, preference for validating responses in human datasets (Chatbot Arena, HH-RLHF, Community Alignment) is weak and concentrated where agreement is often appropriate. Second, in a selected-value, single-model experiment, emphasized judge rubrics produce consistent but modest increases relative to paired suppressed rubrics, demonstrating a plausible mechanism for training-time amplification. Third, in off-policy evaluations across 14 models, inference-time personalization increases inappropriate agreement, with the largest effect from matched user profiles placed directly before the query.
papers.intro:
Large language models (LLMs) often exhibit sycophancy: a tendency to align with the user’s stated views or preferences. They agree with incorrect claims, change correct answers under social pressure, and flatter the user (Per+, 23; Sha+24a, ; Moo+, 26). This behavior can erode trust in models and reinforce false or harmful user beliefs (Ope, 25; Che+, 26).

Large language models (LLMs) often exhibit sycophancy: a tendency to align with the user’s stated views or preferences. They agree with incorrect claims, change correct answers under social pressure, and flatter the user (Per+, 23; Sha+24a, ; Moo+, 26). This behavior can erode trust in models and reinforce false or harmful user beliefs (Ope, 25; Che+, 26).

Prior work establishes that LLMs can be sycophantic, but the source of the behavior remains unresolved. Different studies trace sycophancy to different parts of the alignment and deployment pipeline: human preference data may reward responses that validate the user (Sha+24a, ; Che+26a, ); post-training objectives may amplify misspecified social goals (Den+, 24; IHR, 26); and personalization or memory context may push models toward the user’s apparent views (Jai+, 26). Because these studies use different evaluation settings, definitions of sycophancy, and judges, their results are difficult to compare directly.

Because these studies use different evaluation settings, definitions of sycophancy, and judges, their results are difficult to compare directly.

We revisit these three sources under a shared validity-aware evaluation framework. The measurement distinction is central: agreement is not always sycophantic. A model should affirm valid claims, respect genuine preferences, and acknowledge user experiences when appropriate. The relevant failure is inappropriate agreement: validating a claim, preference, or self-assessment when the context calls for correction, qualification, or resistance.

papers.title: Maximal defect $2$-blocks with dihedral defect groups up to splendid Morita equivalence
papers.abstract: We classify, up to splendid Morita equivalence, all maximal defect blocks whose defect groups are dihedral \(2\)-groups of order at least \(8\). The classification holds for blocks over an algebraically closed field as well as for those over a suitable discrete valuation ring of characteristic zero. As a consequence, Puig's conjecture holds for this infinite family of blocks. Beyond the classification result itself, a central feature of the present work is the variety of methods required in its proof. Our arguments combine classical techniques of block theory with a broad range of tools and techniques that have emerged over the past twenty-five years. Amongst others these include in a crucial manner the Gorenstein-Walter classification of finite groups with dihedral Sylow \(2\)-subgroups, Linckelmann's glueing of local Morita equivalences to obtain a stable equivalence of Morita type, the modern versions of Fong's 1st and 2nd reduction theorems in terms of splendid and endo-permutation source Morita equivalences, the structure of the Dade group of endo-permutation modules, Boltje-Perepelitsky's extended theory of Brauer pairs for \(p\)-permutation modules, the fusion systems of the blocks involved, or the concrete knowledge of their decomposition matrices.

papers.title: Training-Free Building Change Detection with Example-Induced Discriminants
papers.abstract: Building change detection (BCD) relies on dense annotations that are costly to collect across regions. A few annotated examples offer a more economical way to specify the target, but change maps provide incomplete building supervision: they label only changed buildings and leave the building-containing date unspecified. Our key observation is that these annotations nevertheless reveal features that recognize buildings in other images, including unchanged ones. We present Linear INduced Discriminants (LIND), a training-free framework that turns regional feature contrasts into a reusable linear building classifier. Using a single frozen vision transformer, it unifies building recognition and temporal comparison in the same feature space. This approach requires neither text prompts nor an auxiliary segmentation model. Only one parameter is tuned on a single validation dataset and then kept fixed across datasets and shot settings. Extensive experiments demonstrate strong detection accuracy, cross-dataset transfer, and efficient inference, with extensions to other semantic classes and broader land-cover changes. Change annotations thus provide a compact visual specification for detection in new scenes. Code: https://github.com/lzcn/lind

papers.intro:
Building change detection (BCD) identifies construction and demolition from images acquired at different times, supporting urban monitoring, infrastructure management, and disaster assessment [8, 25]. Supervised detectors achieve strong performance [7, 14, 3, 15], but obtaining their labels requires comparing both dates and delineating genuine changes amid appearance variation. Extending monitoring to new regions also introduces differences in building appearance and seasonal conditions that challenge generalization [40, 19]. An effective detector should therefore make economical use of annotations while remaining applicable beyond the scenes from which they were collected.

Supervised detectors achieve strong performance [7, 14, 3, 15], but obtaining their labels requires comparing both dates and delineating genuine changes amid appearance variation. Extending monitoring to new regions also introduces differences in building appearance and seasonal conditions that challenge generalization [40, 19]. An effective detector should therefore make economical use of annotations while remaining applicable beyond the scenes from which they were collected.

Foundation models offer an opportunity to meet these requirements by reusing representations learned through large-scale pretraining [36, 34, 27, 23]. Adapting the Segment Anything Model (SAM) to change detection enables training-free change localization [56, 42]. Category-specific detection additionally requires relating temporal differences to the target concept. Open-vocabulary change detection (OVCD) addresses this by using language to specify the target category [26, 12, 57]. This flexibility depends on grounding a category description in the image. For buildings, a description can convey the object category while leaving roof appearance and spatial extent underspecified. Prompt and refinement settings suited to one region may also transfer poorly to another. Many systems additionally combine recognition, segmentation, and temporal comparison through intermediate masks or category assignments, allowing errors to propagate between stages [12, 17]. These limitations motivate a more direct connection between specifying the target and detecting its changes.

Annotated examples provide a concrete visual specification through the target’s appearance and extent. Visual prompting and example-conditioned segmentation demonstrate the value of this interface [45, 11, 28]. Few-shot change detection also uses annotated example pairs, but trains a task-specific network to interpret them [4]. We study how these examples can define a detector directly in frozen features, without task-specific training. Our starting observation is that features pooled from an annotated change region respond to buildings in other images, including unchanged ones, as shown in Fig. 1. A change annotation therefore exposes reusable building information beyond the particular transition it labels. This motivates constructing a building classifier from change examples and applying it to new scenes.

Extracting this information requires resolving the ambiguity of change annotations. A change map marks where a building appeared or disappeared but does not identify which date contains the building. The same pixels may be a building in one date and its surroundings in the other, and unchanged buildings outside the mask remain mixed with the background. The marked region and its complement therefore cannot serve as complete foreground and background labels. The central challenge is to recover a building-separating direction from these incomplete temporal annotations.

We present Linear INduced Discriminants (LIND), a training-free BCD framework conditioned on change-annotated example pairs. Our key idea is to turn the contrast between an annotated region and its surroundings into a reusable building discriminant. Regional contrasts provide both a cue to the building-containing date and a direction that separates buildings from their context. This construction uses incomplete change annotations to specify a linear decision rule directly, without learning a prediction head or requiring complete building masks. The resulting classifier can recognize both changed and unchanged buildings, allowing temporal comparison to focus on the target category.

Recognizable building responses must also support consistent change decisions across scenes. Response levels can vary with the example and query, while small registration errors can compare different structures across dates. We formulate change scoring as a comparison of building responses and feature dissimilarity, accounting for response variation and local misalignment within each query pair [31, 29]. Building recognition and change scoring thus operate within the same frozen feature space.
