papers.title: Multimodal Masked Diffusion Autoencoder for Modeling Impaired Driving
papers.abstract: Human cognitive state (e.g., distraction, stress), gaze, and behavior interact with the driving environment in subtle ways that AI could use to assist drivers, but ground-truth labels for human cognitive state levels are costly to obtain at scale. We propose a multimodal masked-diffusion autoencoder, ID-MAE, that adds a self-supervised objective to impairment prediction: alongside predicting the impairment label as a masked token, it reconstructs masked gaze and trajectory. To probe the effects of different modalities and types of impairments on model inference, we introduce DIVERT, a driving-simulator dataset containing 103 hours of driving data (n = 109) with ten impairment inductions spanning cognitive, visual, and emotional states, recorded with gaze, vehicle state, and scene video. We demonstrate how ID-MAE affords significant improvements in impairment inference results on both the DIVERT dataset and existing datasets, and enables strong results in additional tasks, such as trajectory and gaze prediction. For location-matched pairs, our model achieves a paired AUC of 0.706 for impairment detection on DIVERT, compared to 0.590 without reconstruction loss, improving over existing baselines. We probe the design space in terms of input modalities, masking scheme, positional encoding, attention mechanism, and decoding. We also investigate the interaction between various impairments in training and inference, demonstrating that visually demanding distractions are separable from cognitive distractions. Code and data will be available upon acceptance.

papers.intro:
The interaction of human cognitive state, gaze, and behavior lies at the core of human safety approaches [73, 106]. Reasoning about driver safety require us to understand the interplay between these over prolonged periods of time and across several modalities. For instance, consider reasoning about a driver ignoring a stopped vehicle in front of them – their fixations on the dashboard or nearby objects may be signs of whether they are distracted, tasked, or tired. However, the space of all multimodal behavior and attention sequences is prohibitively large. Within the distribution of these sequences, risk-critical factors may not be strongly observed; for example, cognitive distraction may surface only as a slight narrowing of visual scanning and marginally delayed responses to peripheral events. Self-supervised approaches for temporal signal analysis have proven invaluable [66, 26], especially where labels are scarce [99] or noisy [33]. In inherently multimodal inference tasks, such as those connecting gaze, behaviors, and latent cognitive factors, leveraging self-supervision becomes a challenging yet crucial aspect of the solution. A limited amount of data for risk-relevant, rare events [30, 23], as well as the high-dimensional nature of the behavior observation sequences, thus requires us to draw supervision from the behavior itself rather than from labels alone.

papers.title: Sample-Aligned Decoders for Latent Generative Models
papers.abstract: Latent generative models synthesize images by decoding generated latents, yet their decoder is trained only to reconstruct encoder latents and never sees the latents it decodes at test time, so the residual errors of the generator are rendered directly into the final image. Existing remedies retrain the generator, add cost at every sampling step, or make the decoder robust to perturbed real latents, assuming that generator errors resemble such perturbations. We find that they do not. Generated latents lie on the encoder latent manifold as closely as real ones, yet follow a different distribution. The decoder should therefore be adapted to the distribution of generated latents, which raises two challenges: (1) unpaired supervision, since a generated latent has no ground-truth image, and (2) latent-space drift, since a decoder freed from paired targets forgets the latent space it must decode. We propose Sample-Aligned Decoders (SAD), a post-training framework that fine-tunes only the decoder of a frozen generator at no inference cost. Generated-Sample Distribution Alignment matches decoded generated latents to unpaired real images in a frozen foundation-model feature space, and Encoder Anchor Preservation keeps the decoder close to the original one on encoder latents. Our analysis shows that the alignment is effective only on generated latents, where it corrects each sample in proportion to how much more often the generator produces such latents than the encoder; on encoder latents it can only work against the anchor. SAD improves four state-of-the-art ImageNet generators across three tokenizers, e.g., FID-50K from 1.15 to 0.98 for REPA-E, complements discriminator guidance, and extends to text-to-image generation. Our code and models are available at https://torpedo2003.github.io/SAD/.

papers.title: Shifted Hankel determinants via Hankel continued fractions
papers.abstract: The Hankel determinants $H_n(F)$ of a power series $F(x)$, as well as the shifted ones $H_n^{(1)}(F)$ and $H_n^{(2)}(F)$, can be read off from its Jacobi continued fraction, provided that all $H_n(F)$ are nonzero. Without any condition on $F$, the Hankel continued fraction ($H$-fraction) still yields all $H_n(F)$. We show that the $H$-fraction of $F$ also determines the shifted Hankel determinants $H_n^{(1)}(F)$, $H_n^{(2)}(F)$ and the backward shifted ones $H_n^{(-1)}(F)$, and we give explicit formulas for them. As applications, we provide simple proofs of Hankel determinant evaluations that were previously established by means of complicated explicit $H$-fractions.

papers.title: The interplay between ionized and warm molecular gas in the turbulent intragroup medium of Stephan's Quintet
papers.abstract: Using JWST MIRI spectroscopy, we explore the multi-phase intergalactic gas in the hot halo of the Stephan's Quintet compact group. Unlike the coolest H2 emission, which commonly shows double- peaked profiles corresponding to the velocity of the intruder and the intragroup gas, the ionized Neon emission-lines are often systematically shifted redwards in radial velocity away from the lowest H2 peak, and into the region corresponding to gas decelerated by the collision of the intruder galaxy with intragroup gas. The majority of the brightest clumps of ionized gas are spatially correlated with the brightest H2 clumps, suggesting they are coherent structures caught up in the opposing gas flows. Gas that is progressively heated, is shifted in velocity further from the velocity of the coldest H2 peaks. Larger and larger shifts in velocity are seen as one progresses from cool to warm molecular hydrogen, to lower-excitation (Neon lines) ionized and strongly shocked heated ionized gas (gas-phase Iron). The majority of the ionized Neon in the intergalactic medium is consistent with excitation in low-velocity shocks. We suggest that this behavior is the result of gas of progressively lower densities being shocked and accelerated by the interaction of pre-existing clouds with a hot flow created by the blast-wave from the collision between the intruder and the intragroup gas. One exception is the extragalactic star forming region, SQ-A, which shows higher-excitation ionized emission lines consistent with heating from a young starburst, consistent with previous photometry of young star clusters in the region.

papers.intro:
The Stephan’s Quintet (hereafter SQ) compact group represents a remarkable laboratory for studying the way in which different gas phases can survive and interact with one another in a group-wide hot halo heated by violent collisions between the component galaxies. In this system, an intruder galaxy NGC 7318b is believed to be colliding with an old tidal filament in the main group at 850-900 km s−1s^{-1}, resulting in the generation of X-ray emission along an intergalactic filament and creating enhanced emission in the wider X-ray emitting halo of the group [48, 63, 54]. This high-speed collision has created, in the intragroup medium, highly turbulent material comprising of a wide range of gas and plasma phases. This includes radio emitting plasma [3, 68], neutral [CII] emitting gas [5], cold and warm molecular hydrogen [30, 4, 14, 6, 19, 46, 70], H2O [5], as well as diffuse ionized atomic gas [68, 32, 42, 16, 18]. A remarkable result from the molecular studies is the strength and ubiquity of pure rotational lines of warm molecular hydrogen emission in the group [29, 7], defying the simplistic expectation that molecular gas would be easily destroyed in such a high speed collision.

In addition to the warm (>> 100K ) H2, the long-term survival of cold dense CO-emitting clouds seen in the Stephan’s Quintet IGM, (e. g. Emonts et al. 19) is interesting because they would be expected to be destroyed rapidly by a wide variety of processes, including Rayleigh-Taylor and Kelvin-Helmholtz instabilities [41, 71], and mechanisms such as cloud shattering [26, 27]. Nevertheless, cold molecular gas has been seen in other hot environments, for example in filaments in the Persius Cluster [60, 59, 45], or in the tails of “Jellyfish” galaxies: cluster-member galaxies which are being stripped of gas by their interaction with the hot intercluster medium [34, 35, 49, 36, 50, 51]. In these cases, somehow the clouds survive or are reformed in the turbulent flows surround the galaxies. Our study of the multi-phase mix of gas in SQ is therefore relevant in the understand the survival of gas in other halo environments.

Unlike previous ground based studies of ionized gas in SQ which have been typically limited to large (>>kpc) spatial scales, the JWST observations presented here provide an excellent opportunity to explore correlations and connections, at sub-arcsec scales, between the ionized and molecular gas phases particularly the low-order pure rotational transitions of H2 which fall in the JWST MIRI observing window. Given the highly clumpy distribution of dust and gas seen in previous work [56, 7] multi-phase structure and correlated kinematics between gas phases on these scales seems highly likely. More widespread, and much more extended ionized gas is also possible through the collision of very diffuse, low-density regions in the pre-shocked gas of both the intruder, and any preexisting group-wide gas. This gas is less likely to show sub-arsec-scale correlations between the warm H2 and the ionized gas.

That paper, which uses the same datasets as those described here, concentrates specifically on the properties and kinematics of the warm molecular gas in SQ, and showed that the warm molecular gas has mainly survived the collision, and that some of it becomes much warmer and turbulent as it is decelerated in the reference frame of joint intruder/group system.

In this section we present integrated maps over both the full ranges of H2 and [Ne II] emission, but also of selected velocity ranges, to emphasize the depth and diversity of the emission. This section also discusses how cold molecular gas may survive in such a harsh collisional environment, and compares our results with that of ram-pressure stripped tails in Jellyfish galaxies. §7 presents the conclusions. The Appendix describes how we use a comparison of the observed emission lines of Neon and Sulphur, with both shock and starburst models, to attempt to understand the excitation of the ionized gas throughout the group.

papers.title: Theoretical Instability Models of Quasi-Periodic Eruptions
papers.abstract: The nature of the Quasi-Periodic Eruptions (QPE) is still not firmly established while the phenomenon probes the innermost part of the accretion flow undergoing dramatic changes. In this chapter we review the possibility that the observed rapid variability is caused by the accretion disk instability. We summarise the defining observational properties of QPE sources: time scales of recurrence, the amplitudes of soft X-ray flares, high coherence over many cycles, and comparatively modest time-averaged luminosities. We then translate these into constraints on the characteristic radius, accretion rate, and energy reservoir of the inner disk. We review the main classes of disk instabilities relevant to supermassive black holes: radiation pressure induced thermal/viscous limit cycles, magnetically mediated inner disk transitions, and coupling to disk winds that can produce the oscillatory behavior. For each scenario we discuss the required parameter space (black hole mass, Eddington ratio, viscosity prescription, and truncation radius), the predicted spectral and timing signatures, and the degree of fine tuning needed to reproduce the observed duty cycles and flare morphologies. We highlight key tensions, including the extremely soft spectra, short recurrence times compared with standard viscous times at tens of gravitational radii, and the weak or absent contemporaneous optical/UV variability in several systems. Finally, we outline observational tests that may help distinguish between instability driven and geometrical or orbital models: phase resolved spectroscopy to track the temperature evolution, searches for hysteresis in hardness-intensity diagrams, reverberation and absorption variability tied to winds, and long baseline monitoring to measure drift in period and energy output.

papers.title: Device-Centric Cooperative Floor-Level Estimation under Sparse Anchor Deployment for Construction-Site Applications
papers.abstract: For construction-site applications in multi-story buildings, accurate floor-level estimation is important for tracking workers, equipment, and Internet of Things (IoT) devices. In buildings under construction, communication infrastructure and power-supply facilities are often limited and the indoor environment changes as construction progresses, making localization systems that rely on dense wireless infrastructure or fingerprint databases difficult to deploy and maintain. Low-power wide-area (LPWA) communication can provide wide-area coverage with a small number of temporarily deployed access points (APs), but under sparse AP deployment, AP-to-terminal observations alone may provide insufficient floor-related information for reliable floor-level estimation. To address this problem, this paper develops a device-centric cooperative floor-level estimation method that exploits inter-terminal observations as relative floor-difference information to complement AP-side information. For practical application with limited measurement data, AP-to-terminal observations are represented by an upper/lower-AP RSS contrast, while inter-terminal observations are statistically modeled according to floor-difference classes. The resulting AP-side and pairwise scores are combined in a weighted floor-label objective and approximately optimized using dual-order sequential iterated conditional modes (ICM). Ray-tracing simulations and LoRa measurement experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method under different AP deployments and terminal-selection limits.
papers.intro:
For construction-site applications in multi-story buildings, accurate floor-level estimation is an important localization function for tracking workers, construction equipment, and Internet of Things (IoT) devices [1, 2, 3]. In buildings under construction, existing communication infrastructure and power-supply facilities are often insufficient, while the indoor environment continuously changes as construction progresses. Accordingly, localization systems that rely on densely deployed wireless infrastructure or fingerprint databases are difficult to deploy and maintain. Such environments require localization techniques that can cover an entire building using only a small number of temporarily deployed wireless devices. This requirement is also consistent with the growing role of localization and sensing in future wireless systems [4, 5].

Such environments require localization techniques that can cover an entire building using only a small number of temporarily deployed wireless devices. This requirement is also consistent with the growing role of localization and sensing in future wireless systems [4, 5].

Low-power wide-area (LPWA) technologies, especially LoRa, are attractive for such environments because of their long communication range and low power consumption [6, 7]. They can provide wide-area coverage with a small number of temporarily deployed access points (APs), which serve as anchors, while received signal strength (RSS) can be obtained from ordinary packet reception without dedicated ranging hardware or strict synchronization. Previous studies have investigated LoRa-based localization in both indoor and outdoor environments [8, 9, 10, 11]. Floor-level estimation using unlicensed-band LPWA signals was experimentally investigated in [12], showing that observations from sparsely deployed APs contain useful vertical information. However, when the number of APs is limited, AP-to-terminal observations alone may not provide sufficient information to reliably distinguish all floors.

They can provide wide-area coverage with a small number of temporarily deployed access points (APs), which serve as anchors, while received signal strength (RSS) can be obtained from ordinary packet reception without dedicated ranging hardware or strict synchronization. Previous studies have investigated LoRa-based localization in both indoor and outdoor environments [8, 9, 10, 11]. Floor-level estimation using unlicensed-band LPWA signals was experimentally investigated in [12], showing that observations from sparsely deployed APs contain useful vertical information. However, when the number of APs is limited, AP-to-terminal observations alone may not provide sufficient information to reliably distinguish all floors.

One reason is the propagation behavior in multi-story buildings. RSS does not necessarily provide a simple monotonic indication of floor separation because indoor propagation is affected by floor penetration, exterior walls, and surrounding structures [13, 14, 15]. Ray-tracing studies have also shown that these effects can considerably change floor-wise propagation characteristics [16]. In [17], this propagation behavior was investigated through both ray-tracing simulations and measurement experiments and explained using floor-transmitted (FT) and wall-transmitted reflected (WT) components. The FT component decreases rapidly as the floor separation increases because of cumulative penetration loss, whereas the WT component can reach a receiver through reflected paths with less floor penetration. Consequently, AP-side floor information becomes increasingly ambiguous as the floor separation between an AP and a terminal increases, whereas observations over smaller floor separations can remain more informative.

Our preliminary study in [21] established a device-centric cooperative floor-level estimation framework that combines AP-to-terminal and inter-terminal observations. Although our preliminary study [21] demonstrated the benefit of terminal cooperation under sparse AP deployment, practical deployment requires reliable floor-related observation models constructed from limited site measurements. In real multi-story environments, observations corresponding to different floors or floor differences can overlap considerably, and parameter estimation errors under limited measurements may affect the overall floor-estimation performance.

In this paper, we propose a device-centric cooperative floor-level estimation method for construction-site applications under sparse AP deployment. Building on the cooperative floor-level estimation framework developed in [21], the proposed method extends the framework toward practical measured environments by constructing the required floor-related observation models from a limited number of site measurements and introducing lower-complexity ICM-based inference. The proposed method is evaluated through ray-tracing simulations and LoRa measurements under different AP deployments and terminal-selection limits. papers.title: Social Signal Bench: Evidence-Weighted Evaluation of Co-occurring Social Signals in Video and Audio
papers.abstract: Recognizing social signals such as interest and hesitation requires interpreting context-dependent behaviors that may co-occur in conversation. Existing affective computing benchmarks rarely evaluate such co-occurring signals, and conventional multi-label F1 overlooks semantic relationships and annotator disagreement. We introduce Social Signal Bench, a 47-hour densely annotated benchmark for the evaluation of social signal recognition and engagement, comprising two datasets: Social Signal Bench Video (25 hours), covering ten social signals in audiovisual recordings, and Social Signal Bench Audio (22 hours), covering six signals in audio-only recordings. Each dataset pairs a public training set of online conversational video, of which 10 hours are expert-annotated and the remainder pseudo-labeled, with a private expert-labeled test set spanning four conversational domains. We also propose Evidence-Weighted F1 (EW-F1), which weights reference labels by annotator evidence and assigns graded credit to semantically related predictions through optimal per-clip matching. Controlled perturbations demonstrate that EW-F1 distinguishes semantically related errors from unrelated ones, unlike conventional F1. Under a shared evaluation protocol, 7B open models post-trained on Social Signal Bench outperform general-purpose frontier models on video and match them on audio.

papers.intro:
Social signals are states such as hesitation or skepticism that observers infer from nonverbal and paralinguistic cues, such as pauses and changes of tone [62, 47]. Reading these signals from video and audio is a long-standing goal of affective computing and social signal processing [45, 65, 61], and omni-modal foundation models now take both streams as input [63]. Listeners form several such judgments about the same moment at once [61, 2]. Video and omni-modal language models describe what is visible and audible well and lead general audio-visual benchmarks [66, 12, 20, 43, 19, 35, 25], but reading social signals also requires reasoning about interpersonal dynamics, where current models remain limited [40, 27].

Video and omni-modal language models describe what is visible and audible well and lead general audio-visual benchmarks [66, 12, 20, 43, 19, 35, 25], but reading social signals also requires reasoning about interpersonal dynamics, where current models remain limited [40, 27].

Measuring this ability is difficult in two ways. On the signal side, cues and signals map many-to-many: one cue can support several interpretations, and one signal can be expressed through different cues [8, 21]. Interpretation also depends on the interactional setting and on preceding and, when available, subsequent behavior [21, 68], and culture and speaker style change how behavior is expressed and read [34, 16, 1]. Signals co-occur, so the task is multi-label [60]. On the observer side, trained raters can reasonably disagree, and such disagreement often reflects genuine ambiguity rather than annotation noise [55, 18, 32].

Multi-label recognition is commonly scored with variants of the F1 score [67]. Multi-label F1 treats all classes as orthogonal, and predicting related or close signals costs as much as predicting unrelated or distant ones. It also treats the reference as certain. A label that every rater marked with high confidence and a label that only one rater inferred carry the same recall mass. Under the standard F1 scoring, a model that omits a label it is unsure of can therefore score higher than a model that predicts a closely related one (Figure 6). Exact F1 thus favors omission over a near miss, and F1-optimal decision thresholds are known to favor abstention on rare labels [39].

papers.title: Quantum-classical dynamical density functional theory for solvation dynamics
papers.abstract: We provide a unified modeling framework for thermalization and non-equilibrium spectroscopy in overdamped polar environments. This framework extends dynamical density functional theory to describe the coupled quantum-classical evolution of a molecular electronic subsystem and an overdamped polar solvent represented by a reaction-field coordinate. The nonadiabatic dynamics is formulated in terms of an operator-valued distribution obeying a quantum-classical Ehrenfest--Smoluchowski equation which exhibits nonlinear classical diffusion and non-increasing free energy, thereby retaining detailed balance. In contrast, a quantum-classical Liouville--Smoluchowski model with quantum-classical linear diffusion develops unstable long-time behavior and fails to reach a stationary thermal state. The method is applied to a two-level model of a polar dye in three different solvents: chloroform, dichloromethane, and dimethyl sulfoxide, each differing in polarity and dielectric relaxation time. Absorption and time-resolved emission spectra are obtained from dipole-dipole correlation functions, capturing the solvent-induced spectral broadening, the dynamic Stokes shift, and the time evolution of the emission bandwidth. The calculated solvent spectral response agrees well with the experimental relaxation trends of the three solvents.

papers.intro:
Solvent environments can considerably reshape the energetics, dynamics, and optical response of molecular systems in solution. These effects arise because the solute and solvent continuously influence one another: the molecular charge distribution polarizes the surrounding medium, while fluctuations and relaxation of the solvent modify the effective energetic landscape experienced by the solute. This interplay is relevant both at equilibrium, where the solvent samples a thermal distribution of configurations around the solute, and under non-equilibrium conditions, where the environment relaxes in response to a change in the molecular state.Maroncelli et al. (1989); Rosspeintner et al. (2013); Venkatraman and Orr-Ewing (2021)

(1989); Rosspeintner et al. (2013); Venkatraman and Orr-Ewing (2021)

For polar solutes, the response of the surrounding medium to the molecular charge distribution can be conveniently described within a dielectric continuum picture. In this framework, the polarization of the solvent is represented through the reaction field acting on the solute.Tomasi et al. (2005); Terenziani and Painelli (2003); Burghardt and Bagchi (2006) Two contributions to this field are usually distinguished: a fast component associated with the electronic polarization of the solvent and a nuclear component related primarily to molecular reorientation. The latter can itself display distinct dynamical regimes. At very short times, the solvent response may contain an inertial component associated with collective librational motion, whereas at longer times it evolves toward predominantly diffusive relaxation.Maroncelli et al. (1989); Rosspeintner et al. (2013); Venkatraman and Orr-Ewing (2021); Bolzonello et al. (2018) The present work focuses on this latter regime, where the nuclear solvent response can be described in terms of overdamped dynamics. Dipolar donor-acceptor dyes are particularly sensitive to solvent polarization because their ground and excited electronic states can differ markedly in charge distribution and permanent dipole moment, leading to pronounced solvatochromic effects.Reichardt (1994); Terenziani and Painelli (2003); Bardi et al. (2023)

If the solvent distribution is initially out of equilibrium with a given electronic state, dissipative dynamics drives the coupled system toward the corresponding stationary state. Following photoexcitation, the non-equilibrium character of the problem becomes especially apparent: the electronic charge distribution changes before the nuclear solvent polarization can reorganize, so that the solvent initially retains the configuration associated with the ground state of the dye and subsequently relaxes in response to the excited state charge distribution.Maroncelli et al. (2013); Venkatraman and Orr-Ewing (2021) This reorganization changes the stabilization of the electronic states and is directly reflected in time-dependent optical observables. In particular, solvent relaxation produces the dynamic Stokes shift, while thermal fluctuations of the reaction field contribute to the inhomogeneous broadening of optical spectra.Maroncelli et al. (1989); Horng et al. (1995); Bardi et al. (2023)

Recent experiments have provided increasingly direct access to this coupled solute-solvent dynamics. Ultrafast optical spectroscopy has resolved the initial stages of solvent relaxation, while time-resolved X-ray scattering has revealed structural rearrangements of the surrounding solvent driven by photoinduced charge redistribution and electron transfer.Bolzonello et al. (2018); Biasin et al. (2021); Winte et al. (2025); Mitterer et al. (2026) These observations reinforce the view of the solvent as a dynamical component of the relaxation process and motivate theoretical descriptions able to treat the electronic dynamics of the solute together with the dissipative response of the environment.

To describe this dissipative regime, the collective dielectric response can be mapped onto an effective reaction-field coordinate. Within the linear-response regime, the corresponding free-energy surfaces are quadratic functions of this coordinate, while the solvent state is described by a probability distribution over reaction-field values. The dynamics of this distribution is conventionally described by a Smoluchowski equation.Chernyak and Mukamel (1996); Terenziani and Painelli (2003); Di Maiolo and Painelli (2020); Bardi et al. (2023) Its characteristic timescale is related to the longitudinal relaxation time of the solvent, τL\tau_{L}. This effective coordinate framework provides a compact description of the dissipative solvent response and connects solvent relaxation with the time-dependent evolution of optical spectra.Terenziani and Painelli (2003); Terenziani and Painelli (2015); Di Maiolo and Painelli (2020) The situation becomes more subtle when the electronic subsystem is allowed to evolve dynamically rather than being represented only through state-specific free-energy surfaces. The instantaneous reaction field modifies the electronic Hamiltonian, while the electronic state determines, in turn, the forces driving the solvent coordinate. Here, we develop a mixed quantum-classical (MQC) description that retains the quantum evolution of the electronic subsystem together with the overdamped, dissipative relaxation of the classical environment.

Despite this difference from the standard approach, the thermodynamic free energy F=E−T​SF=E-TS remains a natural quantity for describing the solvent dynamics. As usual, here EE denotes the total energy, while SS is the entropy and TT the reference equilibrium temperature.

papers.title: A Transformer-Derived Iterative Preconditioner
papers.abstract:
Transformers trained on in-context prediction problems can learn known numerical algorithms, e.g., gradient descent. We go further, showing that their internal computations can reveal new algorithms with provable guarantees. A softmax-attention transformer trained to solve linear systems $Xw=y$ implicitly improves matrix conditioning. Tracing $XX^\top$ reveals an iterative preconditioning primitive, which we develop into RAPID, a standalone algorithm requiring no learned components.
  RAPID is an anytime preconditioner for symmetric positive definite (SPD) matrices, using randomized mixing and sparse local corrections to improve conditioning. Proof-of-concept experiments on synthetic and real-world problems consistently improve conditioning and reduce conjugate gradient iterations needed to reach a target accuracy. For a Haar-mixing idealization, we prove convergence to any fixed target condition number regardless of spectral distribution, with only logarithmic dependence on initial conditioning. Together, these results show how a transformer can discover a broadly applicable numerical algorithm.

papers.intro:
Transformers can learn from examples in their input at test time without updating their parameters, a capability known as in-context learning (Brown et al., 2020; Garg et al., 2022). Studies of in-context linear regression have shown that transformers can implement familiar numerical algorithms, including gradient descent, preconditioned gradient descent, and Newton-like methods (Akyürek et al., 2023; Von Oswald et al., 2023; Ahn et al., 2023; Fu et al., 2024). We ask: Can studying learned transformer computations lead to new, general-purpose numerical algorithms that work independently of the transformer and beyond its training distribution? We answer affirmatively by uncovering a new preconditioning primitive in a trained transformer’s computations and developing it into a standalone numerical algorithm.

The resulting algorithm: RAPID. Preconditioning is often crucial for efficiently solving symmetric positive definite (SPD) systems A​x=bAx=b. Conjugate gradient (CG) avoids direct factorization, but its convergence depends strongly on the spectrum of AA (Hestenes and Stiefel, 1952; Saad, 2003). Preconditioners improve convergence by transforming the system into an equivalent, better-conditioned one (Benzi, 2002; Wathen, 2015). Classical approaches often construct approximate factorizations, inverses, or surrogate operators (Meijerink and van der Vorst, 1981; Benzi et al., 1996).

We introduce RAPID (Randomized Anytime Preconditioning by Iterative Dynamics), which improves global conditioning through simple local corrections. Its key idea is to repeatedly randomize the coordinate system, exposing different matrix interactions that can be corrected locally. Specifically, RAPID alternates two steps. First, random orthogonal mixing redistributes matrix interactions without changing the spectrum. Second, each row selects its smallest off-diagonal entry and applies a sparse correction that acts to weaken the selected coupling. Repeating these steps allows local corrections to progressively improve global conditioning without explicitly computing eigenvectors or matrix inverses.

papers.title: Modeling of basic physics issues in toroidal pinches and tools for performance control
papers.abstract: Nonlinear modelling has improved significantly in dealing with physics issues encountered in magnetically confined toroidal pinches, such as the Reversed Field Pinch and Tokamak configurations. Here, recent results relevant to the understanding of helical self-organization processes are presented: formation of internal transport barriers, temporary loss of operational point, relaxation-reconnection events, excitation of Alfv\`en waves, and a possible fundamental mechanism for ion heating in plasmas. Starting from physics processes in Reversed Field Pinch plasmas, several similarities with Tokamaks are presented. In addition, data analysis tools, machine learning autoencoding techniques, are here trained for the first time on a RFP data analysis case.

papers.title: Testyard Benchmarks: a Dynamic RISC-V-based Benchmark Framework including DfT insertion, Structural and Functional Test Flows
papers.abstract: The main challenge of modern computing manufacturing is to produce silicon products capable of operating under the worst possible conditions, both in data centers and under stringent functional safety constraints. These requirements impose exceptionally high quality standards on silicon vendors, while testing costs keep escalating as transistors continue to shrink. Evaluating new testing strategies, however, presents a dual challenge for researchers. Standard academic benchmarks, such as the ITC-99 suite, remain valuable for fast test prototyping, but they lack the structural complexity of modern VLSI devices. Assessing the true computational effort of academic methodologies on industrial scale designs is equally difficult without accessible and scalable models. A further obstacle is the absence of a unified framework able to abstract the commands imposed by each EDA tool and the configurations tied to each technology library, forcing researchers to spend time adapting and debugging fragile scripts. This work addresses both needs by proposing the Testyard framework, built on top of the Chipyard framework, to derive a set of open-source, industrial scale benchmarks. It also extends the Hammer VLSI flow abstraction framework with hardware testing capabilities. Three new functionalities are introduced into Hammer: Design-for-Testability (DfT) insertion, ATPG, and functional tests fault simulation. Each functionality is driven by high-level descriptions, while the framework translates these inputs into the commands required by each EDA tool. Consequently, over the years, many suites of benchmark circuits have been proposed, such as ISCAS-85 [1], ISCAS-89 [2], ITC-99 [3], and IWLS-05 [4], to enable researchers to work on complex, open-source circuits while simultaneously providing valuable methodologies for the industry.

As the complexity of modern silicon devices increases exponentially, the evaluation of new testing strategies requires benchmarks that closely mirror industrial designs, enabling direct assessment of computational effort and methodology scalability on realistic circuits. At the same time, benchmarks must also remain manageable for fully open-source academic tools since some features that may be needed to support a research direction are only accessible when the source code is available. Both requirements serve different research models: large, complex benchmarks ensure that results are predictive of actual silicon behavior, while smaller, manageable configurations support research that requires access to the internal functions or data structures of a testing tool. To support both models, there is a critical need for flexible, open-source benchmark suites capable of scaling seamlessly from smaller, manageable configurations up to high-complexity, industry-standard architectures [5].

papers.title: Flip Combinatorial Invariance for flipclasses with small residues
papers.abstract: We establish (Normal) Flip Combinatorial Invariance for flipclasses with no residues longer than 8. Actually, we show more generally that all flipclasses of finite type with no residues longer than 8 have only one increasing path. For flipclasses of Weyl type, these are precisely the flipclasses having only one increasing path. This marks a refinement of the classical Combinatorial Invariance of Kazhdan--Lusztig polynomials.

papers.title: The Cooperstein conjecture and additive alternating $d$-codes
papers.abstract:
Let $\bigwedge^2 V$ be the second exterior power of a vector space $V$ over a finite field. The Cooperstein conjecture asserts a dimension bound for flats external to varieties consisting of points of bounded rank in $\mathrm{PG}(\bigwedge^2 V)$. This geometric problem can be translated into a question about linear spaces of alternating matrices whose nonzero elements have rank at least a prescribed value. For matrices of odd order, the sharp cardinality bound was already established by Delsarte and Goethals (1975).
  In this paper, we prove the Cooperstein conjecture for matrices of even order and, more generally, we prove its additive analogue by determining, for all admissible parameters, the maximum size of an additive subgroup of alternating matrices in which every nonzero matrix has at least the prescribed rank. Our proof uses Pfaffian equations to characterize alternating matrices of rank below the prescribed minimum. We study the minimal graded free resolutions of the corresponding Pfaffian rings. The Cohen--Macaulay property and the $a$-invariant of each Pfaffian ring determine the largest shift in its resolution. We use trace functions on evaluation quotients to construct polynomial indicators for the matrices of small rank in an additive subgroup. The largest shift controls their degrees, yielding the upper bound by a counting argument. Finally, we give explicit trace constructions attaining the bound.

papers.title: Thermal radiation of nanowires and near-field interaction with substrates: exact computation and proximity approximation
papers.abstract: Radiative heat transfer involving complex nano-objects is difficult to evaluate due to their sub-wavelength size, which induces deviation to macroscopic Planck's opaque surface-to-surface formalism, and due to the small distances involved, which lead to near-field radiative (photon tunneling) effects. As a result, thermal radiation has mostly been neglected in analyses of thermal transport in nanowires. Here, we report on calculations of thermal emission by single nanowires and on the radiative interaction between suspended silicon nanowires and flat substrates. We observe that metallic nanowires can be particularly emissive in comparison to wires made of other materials. While thermal emission from an isolated silicon nanowire is lower than Stefan-Boltzmann's prediction, the radiative exchange with a substrate can be larger by one order of magnitude. The considered configurations also allow benchmarking various levels of common or original approximations, including, in near field, the proximity approximation, the thickness-dependent PA, the electrostatic approach, and the effective emissivity in the far field.

papers.title: Photon condensation driven by scalar spin chirality
papers.abstract: Gauge invariance forbids equilibrium photon condensation for spatially uniform electric-dipole coupling, motivating alternative routes based on orbital magnetic response. We show that triangular molecular magnets coupled to a cavity support photon condensation driven by emergent scalar spin chirality. Starting from the half-filled Hubbard model in the Mott regime, we derive an effective Hamiltonian in which virtual ring exchange couples the cavity flux directly to scalar spin chirality. Mean-field theory, collective-fluctuation calculations, and finite-size exact diagonalization reveal a phase with spontaneous chirality ordering and a macroscopic cavity displacement, together with hybrid chirality-photon excitations. The condensation threshold can be tuned electrically through the molecular chirality splitting. Our results establish emergent orbital degrees of freedom in frustrated magnets as a route to equilibrium light-matter ordering beyond conventional dipolar cavity quantum electrodynamics.

papers.title: Multiple Field-Induced Transitions, Magnetocaloric Response and Anisotropic Magnetotransport in Orthorhombic RAlGe (R = Dy, Ho)
papers.abstract: We present a comprehensive study of the magnetic, thermodynamic, and magnetocaloric properties of single-crystalline DyAlGe and HoAlGe, both members of the RAlGe Weyl semimetal family. Magnetization, heat capacity and transport measurements reveal multiple magnetic phase transitions associated with the evolution of complex magnetic structures. For DyAlGe, the primary magnetic ordering occurs at \textit{$T_{N1}$}= 30.5 K , while HoAlGe orders at a much lower temperature of \textit{$T_{N1}$}= 11.5 K, followed by additional first-order magnetic transitions at 6.6 K and 8 K, respectively. The magnetization isotherms display pronounced anisotropy for the B $\parallel$ a, consistent with competing exchange and crystal-field interactions. The magnetic entropy change ($\Delta S_M$) derived from isothermal magnetization demonstrates a significant magnetocaloric effect (MCE) with sign change in both systems, with a maximum $\Delta S_M$ of $\approx$ 5$-$23 J/kg-K along B $\parallel$ a for a field change of 0$-$7 T. The sign reversal of $\Delta S_M$ across field-induced transitions highlights the complex field-tuned spin configurations. The moderate MCE and magnetic anisotropy suggest that these materials may serve as model systems for studying magnetocaloric effects in topologically nontrivial intermetallics with interplay between localized 4\textit{f} magnetism and crystal symmetry.

papers.intro:
Weyl semimetals exhibit a variety of remarkable physical properties, including topologically protected electronic states that coexist with conventional metallic conduction, giving rise to unconventional transport phenomena. Recently, magnetic topological materials in the family of strongly correlated f-electrons intermetallics have attracted much attention as they provide rich physical properties due to the interplay between correlated-electron phenomena and topological electronic bands [1], which make them valuable for both fundamental research and technological applications [4, 36]. More recently, the rare-earth based RAlGe (R = rare earth) intermetallics have attracted considerable attention as potential Weyl semimetal candidates [3, 5, 30, 34, 13]. The RAlGe family provides a platform for investigating the interplay between rare-earth magnetism and nontrivial electronic structures. While the electronic and magnetic properties of several members have been explored, the magnetic phase diagrams and anisotropic transport responses of the heavy rare-earth compounds remain comparatively less understood. In particular, a systematic investigation of single-crystalline DyAlGe and HoAlGe is important for establishing how rare-earth-dependent magnetic interactions and crystal-electric-field effects influence their field-induced transitions and magnetocaloric properties.

Most compounds in the RAlGe family exhibit intriguing magnetic and transport properties arising from their diverse electronic structures and complex magnetic ordering. The light rare-earth-based RAlGe (R = La-Eu) crystallize in a disordered centrosymmetric body-centered tetragonal structure [13, 37]; however, their structural model is corrected as the ordered noncentrosymmetric I41md type structure in recent studies [18]. The Ce- and Pr-based members of the RAlGe family exhibit intriguing magnetic and electrical properties [14, 37, 11, 45, 43, 33, 7, 42, 53]. Single-crystalline NdAlGe, in particular, displays a field-induced metamagnetic transition, a large anomalous Hall effect, and a helical magnetic structure[54, 8, 52]. Recent studies show that the heavy rare-earth-based compounds RAlGe (R = Y-Lu) crystallize in the YAlGe-type structure with space group C​m​c​mCmcm [49, 50], where the Al atoms occupy the 4a(0, 0, 0) site and R and Ge atoms occupy two kinds of inequivalent 4c (0, y, 0.25) sites, respectively. Relatively little attention has been devoted to the heavy rare-earth members of the RAlGe family. Until recently, most of these compounds had been investigated primarily in polycrystalline form [48, 49, 50]. More recently, studies of single-crystalline GdAlGe and TbAlGe have begun to shed light on their structural, magnetic, and electronic properties. Orthorhombic GdAlGe has been reported to exhibit Dirac-like linear band dispersion [27], while high-field measurements on TbAlGe have revealed complex magnetic-field-induced magnetotransport behavior[19]. These studies, together with recent investigations of the heavy rare-earth RAlGe series[44], provide a basis for exploring the magnetic anisotropy, field-induced transitions, magnetocaloric and magnetotransport properties of DyAlGe and HoAlGe.

In this study, we present the comprehensive investigation of the magnetic, magnetocaloric, and high-field magnetotransport properties of single-crystalline orthorhombic DyAlGe and HoAlGe, including measurements in magnetic fields up to 35 T. Through detailed characterization of these single crystals, we investigate the evolution of the two antiferromagnetic (AFM) states, which emerge below TN​1T_{N1} = 30.5 K and TN​2T_{N2} = 6.6 K in DyAlGe and TN​1T_{N1} = 11.5 K and TN​2T_{N2} = 8 K in HoAlGe (Fig. 1), and track their evolution under applied magnetic fields, revealing a rich landscape of field-induced metamagnetic transitions. We further elucidate the pronounced magnetic anisotropy of these orthorhombic compounds and discuss the possible roles of anisotropic exchange interactions, crystal-electric-field effects, and spin–orbit coupling in shaping their complex magnetic structures. In addition, the substantial magnetocaloric response highlights the potential of these materials for magnetic-refrigeration applications. Together, these findings deepen our understanding of the interplay between localized rare-earth magnetism and electronic transport in the RAlGe family, a class of materials associated with Weyl-semimetal physics.

papers.title: Memory kernel and closure for systems driven by intermittent forcing with power-law waiting times
papers.abstract: Many systems are controlled by intermittent control variables that take on a random value for a random time interval. In the presence of such noise at update steps, the main equation for the controlled variables has a memory kernel whose coefficients are the cumulants, also known as $G$-cumulants, of the noise, which are fully ordered in time. In the case of Poisson switching, these correspond to the Boolean cumulants of the jump distribution, and the kernel can be summed exactly. We derive an exact decomposition of these coefficients for any waiting-time distribution with independent amplitudes and durations, which separates the jump statistics from the renewal statistics. In the case of waiting times that follow a power-law distribution with a finite mean, it is highly probable that a long time interval will be covered by a single period, and we have shown that, as a result, the coefficients for long delays intersect in all orders, from Boolean cumulants to the usual moments of the jump law. The long-lag kernel thus becomes a superposition of frozen deterministic flux kernels, weighted by the expression $\xi^2p(\xi)$, and from this the corresponding main equation in closed form follows. For $2<\mu<3$, where the noise correlation time is infinite, the second-order closure retains a finite error even in the presence of slow dynamics, whereas the main equation of the frozen flows in this limit yields an exact stationary mean value. The telegraphic process is the only case of noise with renewal steps for which second-order conclusions are exact. An exactly solvable model with additive and correlated multiplicative noise confirms these predictions.

papers.intro:
Many systems in physics, the geosciences, biology, and the social sciences are governed by an intermittent driving force. Rather than fluctuating continuously, this driver remains approximately constant for a random time interval before jumping abruptly to a new value. Examples of this phenomenon include the stochastic velocity of a Lévy walk [1, 2], the on/off states of a nanoscale blinking emitter [3, 4], the laminar and turbulent phases of an intermittent flow [5, 6], and episodic atmospheric forcing, such as bursts of westerly winds that influence the El Niño-Southern Oscillation (ENSO) [7, 8].

For certain Markov processes, specifically, dichotomous Markov noise [26, 27, 28, 29] and so-called ”kangaroo processes” [30], exact higher-order results are available. In the case of non-exponential renewal processes, however, the driving force is non-Markovian; its higher-order correlations generally cannot be factorized and, prior to reaching the steady state, depend on the age of the process [31, 32]. For non-exponential renewal processes, researchers have investigated generalized master equations, linear response theory, and stochastic resonance [32, 33, 34, 35, 36, 37]; furthermore, within the framework of the Kubo-Anderson line-shape theory, studies have examined residence times characterized by a power-law distribution [38, 39]. Analogous kinetic descriptions are found in ”continuous-time random walks” (CTRWs) [40, 41, 42] and Lévy walks [2]. What has been missing thus far is a general theoretical framework that, at all orders, separates jump statistics from renewal statistics by operating at the level of the memory kernel—specifically, through what are known as GG-cumulants. Such a theoretical framework would make it possible to evaluate the accuracy of a lower-order approximation, rather than simply taking it for granted.

For non-exponential renewal processes, researchers have investigated generalized master equations, linear response theory, and stochastic resonance [32, 33, 34, 35, 36, 37]; furthermore, within the framework of the Kubo-Anderson line-shape theory, studies have examined residence times characterized by a power-law distribution [38, 39]. Analogous kinetic descriptions are found in ”continuous-time random walks” (CTRWs) [40, 41, 42] and Lévy walks [2]. What has been missing thus far is a general theoretical framework that, at all orders, separates jump statistics from renewal statistics by operating at the level of the memory kernel—specifically, through what are known as GG-cumulants. Such a theoretical framework would make it possible to evaluate the accuracy of a lower-order approximation, rather than simply taking it for granted.

The theoretical framework developed here is based on the formalism of generalized cumulants (or MM-cumulants), which was introduced in the works [43, 44, 45]. In this context, total time ordering defines the GG-cumulants that appear in the memory kernel, whereas partial time ordering leads to a temporally local equation. Renewal processes provide a natural application for this: in [46], exact and asymptotic results were obtained for a continuous-time random walk with drift and position-dependent noise intensity; meanwhile, in [9, 47], universal correlation structures for two or more time points were derived. These include a representation of correlation functions based on a partitioning of time intervals, as well as a simplification for extreme time points in cases where waiting times follow a power law and possess a finite mean.

papers.title: JointGV: Structure-Aware Correction of Visual World Models with Parallel Graph Dynamics for Long-Horizon Modeling
papers.abstract: Visual world models predict future visual states conditioned on actions, but recursive errors in entity poses and spatial relations limit their long-horizon prediction for robot planning and control. We ask whether a separately predicted relational state can correct this drift without restructuring the visual model. This is challenging because graph nodes and visual states share neither elements nor a feature space. We propose Joint Graph--Visual Dynamics Correction (JointGV), a plug-in based on a cross-granularity dynamics hypothesis: despite their different representations, graph-node and visual-state changes describe the same physical transition. JointGV rolls out a task-conditioned scene graph alongside the visual world model, couples their predicted changes, and combines the resulting graph-motion context with graph-predicted node positions to compute a bounded residual. Graph-learning and correction gradients do not propagate into the original visual dynamics. We attach JointGV to DINO-WM (spatial tokens) and DreamerV3 (a global latent state), evaluating both on DMC Cheetah Run and Walker Walk across three seeds and extending the evaluation to contact-rich manipulation with DMC Finger Turn Hard. Across 32-step rollouts, JointGV improves structural and visual-prediction accuracy, reducing joint-position error by 11--28\%. For spatial tokens, learned graph--visual change coupling gives lower error than broadcasting the same mean graph-motion context to every token, particularly when non-adjacent parts appear close together in the image. On real-robot inverted-pendulum sequences, JointGV reduces DINO-WM's 32-step pole-angle error from $12.56^\circ$ to $6.69^\circ$ and improves DreamerV3 and LeWorldModel as well. In simulated inverted-pendulum control, an actor trained with JointGV-corrected rollouts completes 46 of 50 episodes, compared with none using the original rollouts.

papers.title: Online Inference for Dynamic Categorical Regression
papers.abstract: The multinomial probit is a widely used model for categorical data in many applications, especially in econometrics and the discrete-choice literature. The computational challenges encountered when fitting this model still motivate ongoing research from the frequentist and Bayesian viewpoints. We consider a dynamic formulation based on a state-space model, where at each time one observes a sample from a multinomial probit whose parameter evolves according to Markovian dynamics, thereby inducing dependence across time. We show that the filtering and predictive distributions of the latent parameter belong to the unified skew-normal family, developing an associated i.i.d.\ sampler to approximate quantities of interest via Monte Carlo. Motivated by the computational bottlenecks of the sampler encountered for larger sample sizes, we also develop approximate methods for online inference based on assumed density filtering and expectation propagation. This gives more scalable, yet accurate, algorithms for online inference about the latent state and prediction of future observations. Finally, we derive a novel expectation maximization procedure to learn from the data the covariance matrix underlying the latent-utility representation of the multinomial probit. We investigate the performance of the proposed methods on simulated data and on a real dataset of reservations from an online booking platform.

papers.intro:
Discrete-choice models represent a popular and widely used tool to study preferences of agents. Among them, the multinomial probit (MNP) model (Hausman and Wise, 1978; Daganzo, 1979) has gained widespread popularity across many fields, extending the original range of the social sciences and economics applications also to machine learning and related fields (Girolami and Rogers, 2006; Riihimäki et al., 2013; Kindo et al., 2016; Fasano and Durante, 2022; Loaiza-Maya and Nibbering, 2023). One of the most appreciated benefits of the MNP is its enhanced interpretability, arising from the latent covariate-dependent Gaussian utilities employed in the construction of the model. This comes together with great flexibility, since the aforementioned latent Gaussian utilities can be correlated, avoiding the restrictive assumption of independence of irrelevant alternatives (IIA) (Hausman and Wise, 1978). See also Greene (2017) and Agresti (2012) for more details on the MNP and discrete-choice models in general. When preferences of individuals are observed at different time instants, classical MNP constructions would fail to capture the time-dependence of the samples. Using such a construction in this case would translate into the strong assumption that the effect of the predictors remains constant in time, which may be too restrictive. We thus focus on dynamic formulations of the MNP, leveraging state-space models, where dependence across time is driven by some latent parameter evolving according to Markovian dynamics. In the considered construction, at each time one observes a sample from an MNP model with time-specific parameter 𝜷t\mbox{\boldmath$\beta$}_{t}, which is allowed to vary across time to consider possible variations of the effect of predictors on the class-probabilities for the output. A key task is the ability to perform efficiently online inference, namely filtering and prediction, which boils down to the study of the conditional distributions p(𝜷t∣𝐲1:t)p(\mbox{\boldmath$\beta$}_{t}\mid{\mathbf{y}}_{1:t}) and p(𝜷t+1∣𝐲1:t)p(\mbox{\boldmath$\beta$}_{t+1}\mid{\mathbf{y}}_{1:t}), where 𝐲1:t{\mathbf{y}}_{1:t} represents the set of all observed samples 𝐲1,…,𝐲t{\mathbf{y}}_{1},\ldots,{\mathbf{y}}_{t} from time 11 to tt and 𝐲s=(ys,1,…,ys,ms){\mathbf{y}}_{s}=(y_{s,1},\ldots,y_{s,m_{s}}) represents the sample of observations for time s=1,…,ts=1,\ldots,t. We then first show that the aforementioned distributions belong to the unified skew-normal (SUN) family (Arellano-Valle and Azzalini, 2006; Azzalini and Capitanio, 2014), developing an associated i.i.d. Monte Carlo sampler. However, due to the form of the SUN distribution characterizing the filtering and predictive densities, such an approach becomes computationally unfeasible when the number of observations and/or possible choices, or classes, increases. The form of the likelihood poses severe computational challenges also to classical particle filter approaches, as they would require the computation of a multivariate Gaussian cumulative distribution function (cdf) of size equal to the number of alternatives reduced by one, for each particle. papers.title: WebAgents: Unbundling Agent Creation, Hosting, and Execution for an Agent-Native Web
papers.abstract: Large language models are moving from isolated assistants toward autonomous agents that can plan, use tools, and coordinate with others, motivating an emerging Agentic Web of independently developed agents and services. Realizing this vision requires agent behavior to move across creators, hosts, and runtimes without coupling publication to a particular execution environment or transferring authority over user resources. We introduce WebAgents, which unbundles these roles through a signed agent.pkg that carries portable workflows, skills, schemas, and resource requirements. An OpenClaw-based agent-native browser/runtime verifies the package, obtains authorization, and binds it at run time to user-controlled models, tools, permissions, and budgets, while hosts distribute the public program and may retain private services server-side. We demonstrate this contract with three unrelated workflows executed unchanged under local and API-backed models, including literature review with live services and a website-published travel agent using semantic tools and user-selected personal resources. In a controlled suite, WebAgents explicitly blocks all 716 injected contract violations while accepting all 295 matched benign controls, with median automated pre-execution processing below 0.5 s for all three packages. We conclude by outlining a path toward NANDA-based discovery and interoperable package ecosystems while retaining execution authority in the user's runtime.

Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly moving beyond passive content generation toward autonomous agents that can plan, invoke tools, maintain state, and coordinate with others. These capabilities are already being explored across domains ranging from scientific discovery to enterprise automation, suggesting a shift from isolated AI applications toward ecosystems of interacting agents [1, 2, 3]. As these systems mature, the Web can become a substrate not only for humans accessing pages and services, but also for agents discovering capabilities, delegating tasks, and acting across organizational boundaries. We refer to this emerging setting as the Agentic Web: an open environment where independently developed agents, tools, and services can be discovered, composed, and executed [4]. Realizing this vision, however, requires more than increasingly capable models. It requires infrastructure that allows agent behavior to move across creators, hosts, and runtimes without coupling publication to a particular execution environment or transferring authority over user resources.

papers.title: The system of length sets of transfer Krull monoids over $C_3 \oplus C_3 \oplus C_3$
papers.abstract: Let $H$ be a Krull monoid with class group $G$ and suppose that each class contains a prime divisor. There are precisely nine groups (up to isomorphism) for which the set of distances of $H$ is contained in $\{1, 2\}$. For all these groups, except for $C_3 \oplus C_3 \oplus C_3$, the system of length sets has been written down explicitly. In this paper we close this gap and determine the system of length sets when the class group is isomorphic to $C_3 \oplus C_3 \oplus C_3$.

papers.title: Supersaturation and reconfiguration diameter of independent transversals
papers.abstract: Consider the collection of independent transversals of a vertex-partitioned graph of maximum degree $\Delta$. It is a classic result that when all parts have size at least $2\Delta$, the collection is nonempty. Recently, it was found that if the parts have size at least $2\Delta+1$, then every pair of independent transversals is connected, within the collection, by a sequence of one-vertex reconfigurations. We prove, among other results, that there are exponentially many independent transversals when the parts have size at least $2\Delta$, and that the reconfiguration diameter is at most linear in the number of parts when the parts have size at least $4\Delta$.

papers.title: Fair Bubble Sort: Provably Optimal Fair Ranking with Continuous Sensitive Attributes
papers.abstract: Most fair-ranking methods assume categorical protected attributes, requiring continuous attributes such as age or income to be discretized into groups. This introduces arbitrary thresholds, loses fine-grained information, and ignores the natural ordering of the attribute. In this paper, we study the problem of fair ranking with continuous protected attributes without relying on thresholding. We introduce Continuous Pairwise Parity (CPP), a fairness notion based on Kendall correlation between ranking positions and the protected attribute, and seek rankings that satisfy a prescribed CPP constraint while minimizing their Kemeny distance from an initial score-based ranking. To solve this problem, we propose Fair Bubble Sort (FBS), an efficient post-processing algorithm based on targeted adjacent swaps. We prove that FBS is exactly optimal for the unweighted Kemeny distance and provide approximation guarantees for the score-weighted setting. FBS is output-sensitive, with running time determined by the number of swaps required to meet the fairness constraint. Experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets show that FBS is scalable and consistently outperforms discretization-based baselines, achieving a superior fairness-accuracy Pareto front.

papers.intro:
Algorithmic ranking systems increasingly influence decisions in high-stakes domains ranging from hiring to criminal justice, from credit scoring to college admission. As a consequence, fairness aspects in algorithmic ranking have attracted growing attention Jagadish et al. (2019); Mitchell et al. (2021); Pitoura et al. (2022); Zehlike et al. (2022); Patro et al. (2022). Much of such literature deals with group fairness along the lines of demographic parity Dwork et al. (2012) or equal opportunity Hardt et al. (2016), i.e., requiring the same chances of a positive outcome for different demographic groups, as defined by protected attributes, such as gender or race. In the case of ranking, this is typically cast as the problem of maximizing utility under a group-fairness constraint, which requires a minimum fraction of individuals from each group to be included in the top-kk positions Zehlike et al. (2017); Celis et al. (2018); Singh and Joachims (2018). The very notion of groups implies an underlying categorical attribute. However, in many real-world scenarios, sensitive attributes are inherently continuous, such as age, income, or health scores. When dealing with such variables, the standard practice of discretizing them into groups introduces arbitrary thresholds, discards fine-grain information about the population (individuals falling into the same bucket are treated equivalently), and destroys the natural ordinality of the data (e.g., the fact that the bucket of age [20,30) comes after the bucket [13,20) and before the [30,45) one). Despite recent progress on continuous sensitive attributes in classification and regression, fair ranking with continuous attributes remains largely unexplored. The core challenge lies in the combinatorial nature of rankings: standard continuous fairness regularizers cannot be trivially applied to listwise utility metrics or discrete ranking permutations.

When dealing with such variables, the standard practice of discretizing them into groups introduces arbitrary thresholds, discards fine-grain information about the population (individuals falling into the same bucket are treated equivalently), and destroys the natural ordinality of the data (e.g., the fact that the bucket of age [20,30) comes after the bucket [13,20) and before the [30,45) one). Despite recent progress on continuous sensitive attributes in classification and regression, fair ranking with continuous attributes remains largely unexplored. The core challenge lies in the combinatorial nature of rankings: standard continuous fairness regularizers cannot be trivially applied to listwise utility metrics or discrete ranking permutations.

In this paper, we study the problem of producing a ranking that is as close as possible to a given score-based ranking while satisfying a fairness constraint defined directly on a continuous protected attribute, without any discretization. Our starting point is a pairwise view of fairness: in a fair ranking, an item with a larger protected-attribute value should be no more likely to rank above another item than below it. We capture this principle through Continuous Pairwise Parity (CPP), defined using the Kendall correlation between ranking positions and the protected attribute. CPP requires no discretization, preserves the ordinal information in the attribute, and reduces to pairwise statistical parity for binary protected attributes.

In this paper, we study the problem of producing a ranking that is as close as possible to a given score-based ranking while satisfying a fairness constraint defined directly on a continuous protected attribute, without any discretization. Our starting point is a pairwise view of fairness: in a fair ranking, an item with a larger protected-attribute value should be no more likely to rank above another item than below it. We capture this principle through Continuous Pairwise Parity (CPP), defined using the Kendall correlation between ranking positions and the protected attribute. CPP requires no discretization, preserves the ordinal information in the attribute, and reduces to pairwise statistical parity for binary protected attributes.

Given a score-based ranking, our objective is to find the closest ranking satisfying a prescribed CPP constraint. We measure distortion using the Kemeny distance, as it mirrors the pairwise structure of the fairness notion, decomposing the utility loss as a sum over pairs of items whose order in the produced ranking disagrees with the score-based ranking. Weighting each pair by their difference in score further captures the intuition that swapping items of near-identical merit is essentially costless, while swapping items of very different scores is expensive. This shared pairwise decomposition of cost and fairness is precisely what allows a single algorithmic primitive – the adjacent swap – to navigate both quantities, and is the structural feature on which our theoretical guarantees rest (see Appendix B for an extended discussion motivating Continuous Pairwise Parity).

papers.title: Agent Trajectories as Evidence for Software Quality Assurance
papers.abstract: Autonomous software agents increasingly plan, implement, and test software with limited human oversight. Their decisions may introduce implicit assumptions that final code and passing tests do not adequately expose. We propose analyzing observable agent trajectories alongside software and agent specifications and AI generated artifacts as evidence for targeted quality assurance. The aim is to prioritize consequential decisions for scrutiny, investigate their possible contribution to software problems, and inform improvements to specifications and development practices. Industrial experience motivates the idea; available execution records and preliminary analysis methods make it plausible. However, trajectories alone do not establish that decisions are justified, outcomes acceptable, or corrective changes effective. We ask how this evidence can support review, diagnosis, and continuous quality improvement, and when simpler QA approaches suffice. Perspectives from requirements engineering, verification and validation, agent systems, causal inference, empirical software engineering, and human factors could help develop and evaluate the idea.

papers.title: tmol: a GPU-accelerated implementation of the Rosetta energy function for machine learning
papers.abstract: Physics-inspired forcefields complement generative machine learning models, showing better generalization beyond the training distribution. However, these forcefields are typically slow to evaluate, and their derivatives are difficult to integrate into ML frameworks. We introduce tmol, a GPU-native PyTorch library implementing the state-of-the-art RosettaGenFF forcefield. tmol supports efficient batched differentiable scoring and whole-structure refinement with up to 362-fold throughput increase (batched). Used as a reward in generative protein design, tmol increases hydrogen bonds and water bridges at designed interfaces.

papers.intro:
Generative machine learning (ML) models have led to dramatic improvements in our ability to predict and design biomolecular structures1, 2, 3. However, such models generalize poorly to underrepresented chemistry: ligand-docking accuracy falls for unfamiliar pockets and ligands, where generated models often show poor stereochemistry4, 5, 6; and RNA structure prediction degrades sharply on novel folds7. These limitations make physical forcefields appealing as priors, identifying physically implausible conformations that generative models may miss. Unfortunately, integrating such forcefields has been difficult, as they are often too slow to incorporate into an ML pipeline, and incompatible interfaces makes efforts to do so laborious. GPU-accelerated forcefields10, 11 address part of this, accelerating molecular-mechanics simulations, but the Rosetta energy function and its sampling algorithms, including discrete side-chain optimization and torsion-space minimization, have had no differentiable, GPU-native counterpart.

Here we introduce tmol, an open-source PyTorch library that addresses both of these issues by reimplementing the RosettaGenFF forcefield12, 13 as highly efficient batched tensor operations. Building on the successful Rosetta software package8, 9, we also implement a set of “core algorithms,” including whole-structure and residue-pair scoring, discrete side-chain optimization (packing), Cartesian and torsion-space minimization 14, and a general-purpose refinement protocol (relax) 15. Scoring, packing and minimization are all native PyTorch operations returning coordinate or torsion derivatives through autograd16, so energies and refinement may compose directly into ML model training and inference.

papers.title: Constitutive-fibre mechanics: mechanics-directed uncertainty in constitutive function space
papers.abstract: A structural prediction rests on constitutive functions that are known only through a finite number of tests. The tests fix the response along the states they visit; together with a declared regularity bound they leave a set of admissible constitutive functions, which we call the constitutive fibre. Constitutive-fibre mechanics (CFM) computes the range of a quantity of interest over this set. Adjoint solves of the mechanical problem represent the test observations and the quantity of interest as elements of the constitutive function space. The part of the sensitivity of the quantity of interest that is orthogonal to all observation sensitivities is hidden from the tests; for exact data it alone determines the half-width of the prediction, and for data with tolerance the half-width is a finite convex problem in the span of the adjoint representers. Comparing the two values shows whether a new type of test or a more precise test is needed, and a rank-one update ranks candidate tests before they are performed. A learned constitutive class can only under-represent the range; the deficit is computable. Beyond the linear range, an optimality system with state-dependent representers gives the extreme constitutive functions. The same set decides whether the prediction is defined for every admissible constitutive function, which is a different question from its precision. For a phase-field bar with unknown degradation function, 3% of the sensitivity of the stability eigenvalue is hidden and produces 70% of its uncertainty. For an open-hole composite lamina, the coupon that sharpens the compliance most is not the one that makes the prediction valid; validity is proved on a declared cell by a certificate accepted in exact arithmetic.

papers.intro:
Every structural analysis uses constitutive functions: a strain-energy density, a degradation function, a yield surface. None of them is measured as a function. A test programme records a finite number of forces, strains or displacements, each with a tolerance, on specimens that visit a limited set of constitutive states. Between and beyond those states the constitutive function is fixed by the chosen model form and not by the data. A prediction for a structure that visits other states, at a hole edge, near a crack tip or close to a stability limit, therefore depends on constitutive information that the tests did not supply. This paper asks how large that dependence is for a given quantity of interest, which tests would reduce it, and whether the prediction is defined at all for every constitutive function that the tests admit.

The classical route selects a parametric model and identifies its parameters, from homogeneous tests or from full-field data with finite-element model updating and the virtual fields method [1]. Bayesian calibration turns measurement noise into a posterior on the parameters [2, 3], and sampling-based sensitivity analysis with surrogate models propagates parameter uncertainty to structural responses, including fracture properties computed with phase-field models [4, 5]. In both cases the uncertainty is conditional on the model form. Recent work removes part of this restriction. Model discovery selects a sparse law from a large library [6], with a hierarchical Bayesian version that carries uncertainty over the library coefficients [7]. Constitutive neural networks build physical constraints such as objectivity and polyconvexity into the architecture [8, 9], and Bayesian variants attach credible intervals to the learned response [10, 11]. Neural networks are also used to solve the variational problem of the mechanics itself, with the energy as loss function [12], including phase-field fracture [13]; in CFM they enter as constitutive representations, and Section 5 states what their spread can and cannot show. Constitutive relations are also learned from indirect observations by optimisation constrained by the balance laws, with adjoint sensitivities [14]. In all these approaches the uncertainty lives on the parameters of one representation. A direction of the constitutive function that the representation cannot express carries no uncertainty, whether or not the data determine it.
