Whether indirect observations determine a constitutive function is the question of identifiability. Ju [15] shows for scalar state-dependent constitutive functions of several classes of field equations that sparse indirect observations of one type leave the posterior dominated by the prior however many are collected, and that a few direct measurements at well-placed states are decisive. Bayesian optimal experimental design chooses tests by expected information gain [16, 17, 18]; it has been applied to the load path of a cruciform specimen [19] and to history-dependent constitutive laws [20]. These criteria measure information about parameters. A structural prediction usually depends on a few specific combinations of the constitutive unknowns, and information that does not reach those combinations does not improve it.

Bayesian optimal experimental design chooses tests by expected information gain [16, 17, 18]; it has been applied to the load path of a cruciform specimen [19] and to history-dependent constitutive laws [20]. These criteria measure information about parameters. A structural prediction usually depends on a few specific combinations of the constitutive unknowns, and information that does not reach those combinations does not improve it.

A different line of work describes what is known by a set. Model-free data-driven mechanics replaces the constitutive law by the material data set and solves for the state closest to it [21, 22]; it does not extrapolate beyond the data. Convex and interval models propagate bounded uncertainties through a structural analysis [23, 24]. Optimal uncertainty quantification computes extreme values of a quantity of interest over all models consistent with stated assumptions and information [25]. In approximation theory, optimal recovery and information-based complexity determine the smallest worst-case error with which a functional can be estimated from finitely many, possibly inaccurate, linear measurements of an element of a known class [26, 27, 28, 29, 30, 31, 32]. Our companion work on constitutive-set mechanics (CSM) [33] follows the set-based view for the potential energy: the constitutive function ranges over an admissible set, and the extreme values of the minimum potential energy over that set are bounded and certified with a small number of finite-element solves.

CSM answers how far the energy can move over a given admissible set. It does not say why the set is as large as it is, and it is tied to the energy as the quantity of interest. The present paper starts from the tests. Given the observations of a test programme with their tolerances, a reference law and a declared bound on the regularity of the deviation from it, the set of admissible constitutive functions that reproduce the observations is fixed. We call it the constitutive fibre, since it is the preimage of the data under the observation map, and we call the resulting method constitutive-fibre mechanics (CFM). The object of the method is the range of a quantity of interest over the fibre. The quantity of interest is arbitrary: an energy, a reaction, a local strain, a stiffness or a stability eigenvalue.

papers.title: OpenPINN/PINO: An Extensible Open-Source Framework for Agent-Assisted Physics-Informed Neural Networks and Neural Operators
papers.abstract: Substantial challenges in physics-informed learning have motivated many improvements, but fragmented implementations hinder systematic organization, integration, and comparison. We propose OpenPINN/PINO, an extensible open-source PyTorch framework for physics-informed neural networks and neural operators. Two shared specifications connect problem setup, local computation, and evaluation. Agents support problem formulation, solver planning, and diagnosis. ProblemSpec defines geometry, governing equations, constitutive relations, parameters, initial and boundary conditions, and optional data. MethodSpec configures the model, sampling, loss, optimization, and differentiation. Researchers can register new problem templates and method components, then combine or compare strategies such as Fourier features, residual-adaptive sampling, and self-adaptive loss weighting for a fixed problem. Agents translate natural-language descriptions into specifications, flag missing information, and propose solver plans. The framework validates these specifications and deterministically generates local training and testing code. A diagnostic agent reviews training logs and evaluation results to identify problems and suggest revisions. Three examples show how method choices and agent diagnostics affect accuracy. For viscous Burgers, Fourier features and residual-adaptive sampling each reduced relative $L^2$ error by about $75\%$ from a shared baseline. For periodic Poisson, spectral differentiation reduced mean-free relative $L^2$ error by about $68\%$ across 16 held-out forcings. For a plate with a hole, successive agent diagnoses guided nondimensionalization and optimization. After initial training failure, all three runs met the $10\%$ target, with relative $L^2$ displacement errors of $3.51\%$--$6.31\%$.

papers.title: On the multiplicity of crossing limit cycles of double diagonalizable piecewise linear vector fields
papers.abstract: We consider planar piecewise linear vector fields with two zones separated by a straight line and having two diagonalizable components, which we call the \emph{double diagonalizable configuration}. In this configuration, the Poincar\'{e} half-maps correspond to separatrices of saddle points in the foliations of symmetric differential forms $\omega_r(x)-\omega_r(y)$, where $\omega_r$ is a rational $1$-form with exactly three simple poles. Limit cycles correspond to non-diagonal intersections of two such separatrices, and the multiplicity of a limit cycle is precisely the order of contact at the intersection point. We prove that two distinct separatrices which are not nested segments of the same straight line have a contact of order at most $4$ at a diagonal point and at most $2$ at a non-diagonal point. As a consequence, we obtain that the multiplicity of limit cycles in the double diagonalizable configuration is at most two, this bound being sharp.

papers.title: Moral Inversion: Expressive Payoffs and the Reliability of Consensus
papers.abstract: Moral inversion is a public consensus on an account that falsely reverses responsibility for a harm. We study how expressive payoffs affect its emergence in a sequential social-learning model. A larger payoff makes an account more attractive to endorse, but also makes each endorsement of that account weaker evidence in its favor. We show that under a single-peakedness condition on private beliefs a larger payoff both increases the probability of an incorrect consensus on the favored account and reduces its reliability. Without this condition, both comparisons can reverse, and the informativeness of the public record can strictly improve in the Blackwell order. Finally, we show that a sufficiently large increase in the expressive payoff nevertheless restores the benchmark comparative statics.

papers.intro:
Moral inversion occurs when those responsible for a harm receive approval while those who suffered the harm are blamed. For example, during the Dreyfus affair, the innocent Alfred Dreyfus was condemned as a traitor while the actual spy, Ferdinand Esterhazy, was acquitted and publicly applauded (Bredin, 1986; Ministère de la Justice, 2011). Similarly, perpetrators of racial terror lynchings in the United States could receive public acclaim while Black victims were blamed for the violence inflicted on them (Equal Justice Initiative, 2017). How can such an incorrect attribution gain widespread acceptance, even when contrary information is available?

papers.title: NVIDIA Kumo Tabular: Pushing the Accuracy$\unicode{8211}$Efficiency Frontier for Tabular Prediction
papers.abstract: We introduce Kumo Tabular, a family of open tabular foundation models for classification and regression, in three sizes: Kumo Tabular-S (27M parameters), Kumo Tabular-M (61M), and Kumo Tabular-L (214M). Pretrained only on artificial tables from the Kumo prior, they can make predictions on new tables without any training. In our approach, a table encoder compresses each row into an embedding, and an in-context learning transformer predicts the unlabeled rows from the labeled ones. Kumo Tabular introduces architectural innovations that improve both training stability and predictive performance, enabling the model to scale up to 150M cells on modern GPUs. Kumo Tabular-L ranks first on eight benchmarks: TabArena, TALENT, BeyondArena, ScoringBench, STRABLE, MulTaBench, RamanBench, and TabBench-Bio. These cover probabilistic regression, tables with over 1M rows or 100K columns, and tables with strings, text, or images. Accuracy improves with model size in all tested comparisons. All three sizes lie on the accuracy-speed frontiers of TabArena and BeyondArena. Kumo Tabular-L predicts faster than the runners-up, LimiX-2 on TabArena (36 times) and TabPFN-3.5 on BeyondArena (1.7 times). Weights and pretraining code are released under OpenMDW-1.1 and Apache 2.0, respectively.

papers.intro:
Tables are among the most common forms of data in industry and science, from bank transactions, credit histories, and online orders to factory sensor logs, patient records, census data, and laboratory measurements (Benjelloun et al., 2020; Shwartz-Ziv and Armon, 2022; Borisov et al., 2024; van Breugel and van der Schaar, 2024). For two decades, the strongest predictors on such data were gradient-boosted decision trees (Friedman, 2001; Chen and Guestrin, 2016; Ke et al., 2017; Prokhorenkova et al., 2018), tuned for each task and often ensembled by AutoML systems (Erickson et al., 2020). Tabular foundation models (TFMs) have changed this picture. They can make predictions on a new table without training or tuning on it. Pretrained on a large number of predictive tasks, they read the labeled train rows of the table as context and predict the labels of its test rows in one forward pass (Müller et al., 2022; Hollmann et al., 2023). The strongest TFMs now rank well ahead of tuned and ensembled gradient-boosted trees and deep tabular networks on TabArena (Erickson et al., 2025) and BeyondArena (Purucker et al., 2026), two broad benchmarks of real-world tabular datasets (Figure 1).

papers.title: Constraints on the volume enclosed by Fermi surfaces
papers.abstract: A fundamental property of a Fermi liquid (FL) is that the volume enclosed by the Fermi surface is determined by $\rho$, the total density of electrons. In a fractionalized Fermi liquid (FL*), the volume enclosed by the Fermi surface is determined by the same expression after $\rho$ has been shifted by a quantized amount, most commonly to $\rho -1$ (we assume spin rotation invariance, for simplicity). The FL* shift is related to the quantized symmetry fractionalization data of a quantum spin liquid, whose fractionalized spinon excitations are present alongside the Fermi surface quasiparticles. In this review article, we establish the FL* Fermi volume by generalizing the original Luttinger proof for FL to parton gauge theories of the quantum spin liquid and FL*. We also discuss Oshikawa's flux insertion arguments for FL, and their extension to FL*, including a discussion of gapless spin liquids.

papers.title: Collecting Infrastructure-Level Measures for Energy Analysis in Modern Computing Infrastructures
papers.abstract: Modern HPC facilities are complex environments in which all components are tightly coupled; consequently, precisely modeling and accounting for energy consumption requires approaches that go beyond instrumenting individual compute nodes. Aiming for a cluster-wide vision, we designed a scalable data collection pipeline that aggregates fine-grained measurements from multiple subsystems-spanning component loads, software and hardware counters, sensors and energy-ensuring consistent sampling frequencies and synchronized data acquisition across the infrastructure. We present a dataset of comprehensive metrics collected at 1 Hz over one month from a production research data center supporting heterogeneous workloads, including HPC, Kubernetes services, and distributed storage. To illustrate what this approach makes possible in practice, we analyze two case studies-distributed I/O and large-language-model inference-showing how cluster-wide measurement reveals system-level dynamics missed by localized instrumentation. The proposed dataset and collection methodology provide a foundation for future work on predictive modeling, energy-aware resource management, and more efficient computing infrastructures.

papers.intro:
Despite a massive surge in computational demand, global data-center energy consumption remained effectively flat between 2010 and 2022, at approximately 200 TWh, thanks to substantial gains in hardware and infrastructure efficiency—the latter commonly tracked through the Power Usage Effectiveness (PUE) metric [1, 2]. The explosive growth of artificial intelligence and cloud services has now broken this trend: global data-center demand reached 400 TWh in 2024—a 2×2\times increase over 2020, about 1.5% of worldwide electricity consumption—and is projected to reach 800 TWh by 2030 [3].

A further, more subtle obstacle is the nature of the data that facilities typically collect. Operational monitoring stacks are designed for dashboards and alerting: they scrape metrics on a best-effort basis, at sparse or adaptive intervals, downsample aggressively as data ages, and treat occasional gaps as acceptable. Data of this kind cannot support quantitative energy analysis, where power series must be integrated over time, cross-correlated across subsystems, and joined at fine granularity with application events. What is needed instead is measurement: fixed-frequency sampling, synchronized timestamps across the whole infrastructure, lossless collection, and validated completeness.

In this work we report the design, deployment, and validation of a measurement pipeline covering an entire production research data center—compute, storage, network, cloud services, and facility-level power—and we release the resulting dataset. Our contributions are twofold:

1. A reproducible measurement pipeline. We describe a collection architecture assembled exclusively from open-source components. The pipeline samples at a fixed frequency with cross-node timestamp alignment, and we quantify its collection overhead, its vertical and horizontal scaling headroom (Section III). Any center can replicate the setup with commodity components and produce its own dataset; we distribute the deployment configurations alongside the data. 2. A public, high-quality dataset. We release 28 days of continuous 1 Hz telemetry measuring from a production facility running heterogeneous workloads (HPC jobs, Kubernetes services, distributed storage): more than 2.4×10102.4\times 10^{10} rows across 11 telemetry tables, complemented by the Slurm job database table and by the token-level billing records of a production LLM inference service (Section IV). Unlike existing job-centric datasets, ours consists of raw, non-aggregated time series spanning every infrastructure layer, whose completeness (i.e., absence of gaps) and temporal alignment (i.e., timestamp synchronization across sources) are explicitly assessed.

papers.title: Discovery of new antiviral agents through artificial intelligence: in vitro and in vivo results
papers.abstract: In this research, we employed a deep reinforcement learning (RL)-based molecule design platform to generate a diverse set of compounds targeting the neuraminidase (NA) of influenza A and B viruses. A total of 60291 compounds were generated, of which 86.5% displayed superior physicochemical properties compared to oseltamivir. After narrowing down the selection through computational filters, nine compounds with non-sialic acid-like structures were selected for in vitro experiments. We identified two compounds, DS-22-inf-009 and DS-22-inf-021 that effectively inhibited the NAs of both influenza A and B viruses (IAV and IBV), including H275Y mutant strains at low micromolar concentrations. Molecular dynamics simulations revealed a similar pattern of interaction with amino acid residues as oseltamivir. In cell-based assays, DS-22-inf-009 and DS-22-inf-021 inhibited IAV and IBV in a dose-dependent manner with EC50 values ranging from 0.29 uM to 2.31 uM. Furthermore, animal experiments showed that both DS-22-inf-009 and DS-22-inf-021 exerted antiviral activity in mice, conferring 65% and 85% protection from IAV (H1N1 pdm09), and 65% and 100% protection from IBV (Yamagata lineage), respectively. Thus, these findings demonstrate the potential of RL to generate compounds with promising antiviral properties.

papers.title: From nonlocal correlations to local symmetry breaking: Asymmetry dynamics of crosscap states
papers.abstract: Under unitary dynamics preserving a global symmetry, bipartite entanglement typically grows while an initially broken symmetry is locally restored. Here, we show that this conventional scenario can be reversed when symmetry-breaking coherence is initially encoded in long-range entanglement. We investigate this phenomenon in a family of charge deformed crosscap states, characterized by antipodal entangled pairs with tunable entanglement and symmetry breaking. We first characterize their static properties, finding a Page-like entanglement profile and an entanglement asymmetry that vanishes for subsystems smaller than half the system size, but grows logarithmically for larger subsystems. For symmetric subsystems, we also analyze the symmetry-resolved entanglement and investigate how it evolves as the subsystem is continuously deformed away from a symmetric partition. Following a quench to a free-fermion tight-binding chain, we uncover an unconventional dynamics in which the entanglement entropy decreases whereas the entanglement asymmetry increases, so that initially symmetric subsystems dynamically develop local symmetry breaking. This behavior is quantitatively captured by a quasiparticle picture describing the propagation of antipodal correlations. Our results reveal how symmetry-preserving dynamics can redistribute globally encoded symmetry-breaking coherence, making it locally accessible, and establish the initial entanglement structure as a key ingredient in determining the fate of local symmetries out of equilibrium.

papers.intro:
Bipartite entanglement entropy is one of the most widely used tools to investigate and characterize pure states of many-body quantum systems. In equilibrium, it exhibits universal scaling with subsystem size for ground states of local Hamiltonians [106, 86, 5, 60, 21, 39, 23, 69]. Out of equilibrium, it also displays universal behaviour: typically showing linear in time increase and eventual saturation, indicating local relaxation in quenches from lowly entangled states [22, 2, 25]. Discovering these universal behaviours and how they might be avoided has led to a far greater understanding of quantum matter. Going beyond this and exploring the interplay between entanglement and other system properties can then give a more refined picture of the structure of many-body quantum states. A natural candidate for this is to consider the relationship between the symmetries of a system and its entanglement and ask how the entanglement of a state is reshaped when it respects, or breaks, a certain symmetry or how does the presence of entanglement affect symmetry restoration and breaking.

papers.title: Parametric and Universal Thouless Invariants in Matrix Product States
papers.abstract: We investigate the classification of continuous families of translation-invariant injective matrix product states on an infinite chain, parametrized by a paracompact Hausdorff space $X$ and subject to a compact Hausdorff symmetry $G$. We construct an invariant for phases of such families, valued in $\check{H}^1(X;\widehat{G})$, that generalizes the known $\widehat{G}$ phase invariant for $G$-symmetric Thouless pumps. The phase invariant is constructed as the pullback to $X$ of a single universal \v{C}ech cohomology class on a classifying space of $G$-symmetric translation-invariant injective matrix product states. Several examples are given over various parameter spaces where this invariant is nontrivial.

papers.intro:
Thouless pumps are a well-known class of periodic processes in the study of topological phases of quantum matter. In a typical Thouless pump, a many-body quantum system in one spatial dimension with a U⁡(1)\mathrm{U}(1) symmetry undergoes a periodic and adiabatic evolution in which charge is transported along the spatial dimension. In the original work of Thouless [Tho83], it is shown that for certain infinitely extended systems, the amount of charge transported in one period is quantized and has a topological interpretation.

Our interest in studying parametrized systems largely stems from Kitaev’s conjecture [Kit13, Kit15, Kit19]. Roughly, his conjecture states that in each spatial dimension dd there should be a space 𝒬d\mathcal{Q}_{d} of gapped bosonic invertible quantum states, and that there should be weak homotopy equivalences 𝒬d→Ω​𝒬d+1\mathcal{Q}_{d}\to\Omega\mathcal{Q}_{d+1}, where Ω​𝒬d+1\Omega\mathcal{Q}_{d+1} is the loop space of 𝒬d+1\mathcal{Q}_{d+1}. A parametrized family of such states in dd spatial dimensions could then be realizable as a continuous function X→𝒬dX\to\mathcal{Q}_{d}, whereas a phase could be identified as a homotopy class of maps X→𝒬dX\to\mathcal{Q}_{d}. The topology of 𝒬d\mathcal{Q}_{d} determines what kinds of invariants distinguish the different phases of parametrized systems. We note that Kitaev also made the analogous conjecture for fermionic systems, but we will restrict our attention to bosonic systems here.

papers.title: On the volume growth assumption in the Eulerian definition of RCD spaces
papers.abstract: We prove that every infinitesimally Hilbertian metric measure space whose reference measure is a Radon measure, and which satisfies the Sobolev-to-Lipschitz property and the weak Bochner inequality with a lower Ricci bound, has Gaussian volume growth; in particular, balls have finite measure. Hence, in the Eulerian definition of $\mathsf{RCD}(K,\infty)$ spaces, both the volume growth assumption and the finiteness of the measure of balls are redundant. The proof combines the self-improvement of the Bakry--\'Emery gradient estimate, obtained without using the conservation of mass of the heat flow, with a dimension-free Harnack inequality derived from the Sobolev-to-Lipschitz property.

papers.intro:
Lower bounds on the Ricci curvature of metric measure spaces were introduced, in a synthetic form based on optimal transport, by Sturm [Stu06a, Stu06b] and Lott–Villani [LV09], through the curvature-dimension condition 𝖢𝖣⁡(K,N)\mathsf{CD}(K,N); see also [BS10, CM21] for the reduced condition 𝖢𝖣∗​(K,N)\mathsf{CD}^{*}(K,N) and its globalisation. The first-order calculus underlying the theory goes back to Cheeger [Che99] and was developed, in the form used here, by Ambrosio, Gigli and Savaré [AGS13, AGS14a], who also identified the heat flow as the L2L^{2}-gradient flow of the Cheeger energy and as the Wasserstein gradient flow of the entropy (see also [Gig10]). Requiring in addition that the Cheeger energy be a quadratic form, that is, that the space be infinitesimally Hilbertian [Gig15], singles out the class of 𝖱𝖢𝖣⁡(K,∞)\mathsf{RCD}(K,\infty) spaces [AGS14b], extended to σ\sigma-finite reference measures in [AGMR15]; the finite-dimensional class 𝖱𝖢𝖣⁡(K,N)\mathsf{RCD}(K,N) was introduced in [Gig15] and studied in [EKS15, AMS19, CM21]. The Eulerian characterisation of these classes, via the weak Bochner inequality and the Sobolev-to-Lipschitz property, was obtained in [AGS15] for N=∞N=\infty and in [EKS15, AMS19] for N<∞N<\infty; the classes are stable under (pointed) measured Gromov–Hausdorff convergence [AGS14b, GMS15]. For the second-order calculus on these spaces we refer to [Gig18] and to the monograph [GP20], whose notation we follow, and to the survey [Amb18] for a general account of the theory.

papers.title: What's in a Tree ? Hierarchical $n$-gram models as controlled approximators of language
papers.abstract: Hierarchical models have been proposed as synthetic settings for studying language. However, their relevance to realistic language corpora remains underexplored. In this work, we introduce tree-grams, autoregressive generative $n$-gram models that build the conditional probability tensor $p(x_n \mid x_{1:n-1})$ through a hierarchical composition of order-2 and order-3 tensors. $n$ controls the maximal context window, whereas a rank hyperparameter $d$ controls model capacity, yielding an interpretable and systematically scalable family of approximators of language. We show how tree-grams outperform existing $n$-gram baselines, while remaining competitive with deep transformer-based language models. We demonstrate the utility of such controlled approximations by using tree-grams as generative models. In particular, we show that hyperparameter transfer under $\mu$P can be made more robust when narrower models are tuned on simpler data, generated by tree-grams with moderate $n$ and $d$. In addition, we show that entropy and effective range of correlations control performance gap after fine-tuning. This is because tree-grams allow us to explicitly control horizon and capacity. When allowed to route across candidate topologies, we observe emergent sparsity in tree-grams. Such concentrated routing permits pruning upto 95\% of topologies without significant change in performance.

papers.intro:
Language is hypothesized to be hierarchically structured (Chomsky, 1956; Chomsky, 1957; Everaert et al., 2015; Hauser et al., 2002; Goodfellow et al., 2016). Its statistical structure has been studied using classical and modern language models, including Markov-chain and nn-gram models (Shannon, 1951; Brown et al., 1992; Bengio et al., 2003a). Synthetic datasets inspired by context-free gramars (Chomsky, 1956; Hopcroft and Ullman, 1979; Klein and Manning, 2004; Kim et al., 2019) have also been proposed as tractable testbeds to understand language modeling. In particular, (Cagnetta et al., 2024) propose a family of tree-like generative models where a hierarchy of latent nodes determines the probability distribution of the leaves. Tree-like generative models can successfully represent compositional dependencies and improve language modeling (Dyer et al., 2016; Kuncoro et al., 2018); however, learning linguistically meaningful tree structures directly from data remains difficult (Klein and Manning, 2004; Kim et al., 2019; Hewitt and Manning, 2019). It is also important to understand what tree-like properties are present in real data, which can be accomplished by creating trainable versions of such models.

• We present tree-grams as generative models for controlled approximation of language. The approximation is controlled through a horizon parameter nn and a rank parameter dd. In contrast with context-free grammars, tree-grams learn the latent features from data. In particular, we show that HP transfer is more robust when the smaller proxy is trained on lower-complexity synthetic data. We also investigate the effect of alignment between pre-training and finetuning data, where we show that performance has a stronger dependence on the finetuning distribution. • We observe concentrated topology-routing distributions when tree-grams are allowed to choose topologies at each layer through linear routers. Thus the focus in this work was to set up a basic version of tree-like models that scale better than existing nn-gram baselines.

Hierarchical models have been used to study synthetic datasets resembling language. (Chomsky, 1956; Chomsky and Schützenberger, 1963; Yao et al., 2021; Cagnetta et al., 2024). Justification for such hierarchical modelling comes from statistical property analysis (Thurner et al., 2015), information theory (Futrell and Hahn, 2026; Yang et al., 2026) and cognitive representations (Crain and Nakayama, 1987; Pallier et al., 2011; Ding et al., 2016; Hale et al., 2018). However, all such models fix hidden features based on semantic or syntactic structures. Tree-grams are introduced as generative models where the hidden node features are directly learnt from data. In addition, it is useful to have independent knobs that control the complexity of the full corpus. Such an approximation can be made by either controlling the capacity or the horizon of the generative model (Cagnetta et al., 2026). Such approximations have been made by using traditional and smoothed nn-gram counts (Chen and Goodman, 1996; Parikh et al., 2014a; Liu et al., 2025), hidden Markov models (Balle et al., 2014) or tensor-trains (Miller et al., 2021; Su et al., 2024). However, these methods are difficult to scale beyond few words. On the other hand, the effect of various architectural hyper-parameters in transformers on model capacity is poorly understood. We introduce tree-grams in light of the above considerations. Detailed background and related works are presented in Appendix B.

papers.title: Copula-Based Synthetic Data Generation: A Use-Inspired Perspective on Trade-offs
papers.abstract: The generation of synthetic data offers a promising way to address challenges related to data scarcity and privacy concerns. While many approaches have been developed, tabular synthetic data generation methods often require complex models and extensive training data, while lacking interpretability. In this work, we investigate versatile probabilistic approaches using copulas, and leverage in particular the Gaussian Mixture Copula Model, to model the joint distribution of multivariate data, with a main focus on moderate-dimensional data sets. Taking a use-inspired perspective, we examine key trade-offs inherent to synthetic data evaluation, spanning fidelity, utility, and privacy, and demonstrate that copula-based methods achieve a sound balance across all three dimensions while remaining interpretable and providing an explicit probabilistic model. We illustrate and highlight the potential benefits of the method on a test case focusing on systematic missing values in a cardiovascular risk calculator and develop specific evaluation metrics for this application.

papers.intro:
In medical research, clinicians work with valuable patient data that could be instrumental for tackling important research questions. However, privacy concerns often delay or restrict data sharing with other researchers. Synthetic data generation offers a compelling compromise by creating datasets that mirror the statistical properties of the original data while enhancing privacy. Researchers can then conduct statistical analyses on resulting synthetic data, allowing for developing reproducible models that may eventually be applied to patient data once conditions are met.

The field of synthetic data generation has expanded rapidly in recent years, leading to the development of numerous machine learning methods for tabular data synthesis [50, 26, 49]. These models offer significant potential but may often be challenging to interpret and require large training datasets. Furthermore, they are susceptible to overfitting, which can compromise privacy by inadvertently replicating specific patient details instead of capturing general patterns.

While increasing the complexity of generators usually enhances synthetic data fidelity - how closely the synthetic data statistically resembles the real data - and utility - the usefulness of synthetic data for a downstream application - it tends to deteriorate privacy - how much information the synthetic data discloses about the original data. Managing this trade-off is central to the challenge of synthetic data generation.

In the present work, we consider machine learning and probabilistic approaches to synthetic data generation and how they compare in terms of classical and original criteria reflecting the latter dimensions of interest (fidelity, utility, privacy). We focus in particular on probabilistic approaches that model the joint distribution of moderate-dimensional multivariate data via disentangling marginal and flexible dependence modeling. Our experimental results demonstrate in particular that copula-based methods achieve a sound balance across all three dimensions while remaining interpretable and providing an explicit probabilistic model. In turn, the original evaluation criteria pave the way for future research.

One classical approach to address privacy concern explores differentially private variations of these complex methods [4, 26], typically by introducing noise into the learning process. This approach provides mathematical guarantees that the information gained about an individual included in the data set remains negligible [12]. However, a lot of noise must typically be added to achieve a strong privacy guarantee, which results in insufficient synthetic data utility [18]. We approach this trade-off differently by using conceptually simple statistical models, which are less prone to overfitting, to generate synthetic data without having to add noise. We empirically evaluate if the generated synthetic datasets maintain sufficient privacy for our applications while guaranteeing high statistical utility.

We present a comprehensive framework for synthetic data generation using copulas. The approach is particularly valuable for datasets of moderate dimensions and a limited number of observations, a common scenario in medical research. While the framework is primarily aimed at continuous variables, it can also be used in the case of discrete and mixed variables. We consider the GMCM as our main proposal, alongside vine copulas and the Gaussian copula as competitors. As main example, we consider a dataset from the Department of Obstetrics and Gynecology of the University Hospital (Inselspital) in Bern, containing both personal and clinical information for 359 female patients aged 40 to 69. This dataset has been collected in the framework of the CIMBOLIC study [16] and is publicly available on Zenodo [15]. As shown in Figure 1, our method using GMCM is able to generate realistic synthetic samples which preserve marginal distributions as well as bi-variate dependence measures.

This main example focuses more specifically on an application of synthetic patient data generation to the problem of systematically missing inputs in medical risk calculators. We argue that metrics for synthetic data evaluation should be tailored to each specific situation and especially the intended applications of synthetic data generation. We recall the main evaluation objectives — fidelity, utility, and privacy — and for each category we consider metrics adapted to our main example. In particular, for utility we evaluate how useful our synthetic data is for risk prediction with systematically missing inputs. For privacy, we adapt a metric simulating an attack scenario where the attacker aims to derive the cardiovascular risk of a patient, and we develop a new permutation test that compares the closest distances within real datasets to those between real and synthetic datasets — the premise being that if both datasets originate from the same distribution, these distance vectors should share similar distributions, otherwise there may be a lack of privacy protection.

papers.title: When a Larger Guidance Scale Repairs Text-to-Video Failures and When It Does Not
papers.abstract: When a text-to-video diffusion model ignores part of a prompt, the usual first fix is to raise the classifier-free guidance scale. This paper is a measurement study of when that fix works. On Mochi, the same increase repairs failures on rare compositions ("a snowy beach") beyond what generating again does, does not repair negations ("a highway with no vehicles"), where it fixes fewer failures than generating again does, and changes nothing for events that must happen late in a clip ("a sandcastle that a wave washes flat"). Which of these happens can be known in advance, from the prompt and one inexpensive score. The score, which we call demand, measures how strongly the denoiser reacts to the part of the prompt that the failed video leaves out, and it is read from the first quarter of denoising, before any video exists. Our main finding is a condition: raising the scale is effective only when the prompt contains no negation and no event tied to a specific time, and when demand is sufficiently high, with recovery clearly higher above a fitted threshold than below it. Published corrections for the three failure types, used as fixed probes, behave as this account predicts. A short decision rule follows: before generating again, a user can tell whether the most common fix is worth trying, and what to use when it is not.

A user gives a text-to-video model the prompt “A tall sandcastle standing on a beach where a wave rushes in and washes it completely flat leaving only wet sand behind.” The model returns a well-rendered beach, a well-rendered castle, and no wave (Fig. 2, top). We use this prompt as a running example and call it the sandcastle prompt. The usual next step is to raise the classifier-free guidance scale. In many cases the video that comes back is no better: the wave is still missing. This paper asks in which cases a larger scale does repair the video and in which it does not.

We use this prompt as a running example and call it the sandcastle prompt. The usual next step is to raise the classifier-free guidance scale. Whether raising the scale helps depends on the kind of failure (Table 1). On Mochi, it lowers the failure rate on rare compositions such as a snowy beach from 47.2% to 29.7%. On negations such as a highway with no vehicles it repairs 17.1% of the failures, fewer than the 25.0% that generating again with a new seed repairs. For the sandcastle, whose wave must arrive late in the clip, it changes nothing (49.5% to 52.7%, p=.32p=.32). Many inference-time methods modify the guidance update to repair such failures [18, 19, 20, 4, 6, 24, 43]. Each of these methods was built to repair one particular kind of failure, for example only negations, and its authors tested it only on prompts of that kind. The plain scale, which is what a user reaches for first, has not been examined in the same way. Our answer has two parts. First, raising the scale repairs some failures and not others. Second, a user does not have to try it to find out which will happen: reading the prompt, and computing one number from the model at a fraction of the cost of one generation, is enough to tell beforehand.

Demand separates two ways of failing, and they account for the three outcomes. Negation prompts that fail have higher demand than negation prompts that succeed: the model reacts strongly to no vehicles, but toward the vehicles, a reaction that raising the scale cannot turn around. For rare-composition and temporal prompts it is the other way round: those that fail have lower demand than those that succeed. Low demand means that the model’s prediction hardly changes when the difficult part is added, that is, the model almost ignores it. A larger scale multiplies the influence of the text, so it can strengthen this weak reaction until the difficult part appears in the video, which is why the scale helps rare compositions. That each correction repairs the failure type it was designed for is expected and is not a result of this paper. The new information is in the other cells, where a method meets a failure type it was not designed for, and in the rows for the raised scale: on Mochi the raised scale repairs few negation failures where the directional correction repairs half, and demand relates to failure in opposite ways in negation and in the other two failure types, so no single scalar fix can serve all three.

Our contributions are the following. (1) The main finding. On Mochi, raising the guidance scale repairs failures only under three conditions: the prompt contains no negation; it does not require something to happen at a particular time in the clip; and the model’s demand score for the prompt is high enough. Above a threshold that we fit to the data, the scale repairs about 1.7 times as large a share of failures as below it. (2) An explanation. A failed video is the video of the default prompt, which we confirm by generating from the default prompt directly. (3) A measurement. The demand score, read from the model before any video is generated. It predicts which rare-composition prompts will fail, whereas three predictors computed from the prompt text alone (its length, a rating of how rare the scene is, and the distance between the two prompts in the text encoder) do no better than random guessing on two of the three models. (4) A practical implication. The decision rule of Fig. 1. Two of its branches send negations and temporal prompts to the corrections that were designed for them, which is not new; what is new is the branch for the plain scale, which says when to raise it and when to leave it alone. The conditions are measured on Mochi, and on a second model they come out differently (Appendix J), so they are re-measured, not assumed, on the model in use.

papers.title: Remarks on Fourier--Mukai invariances
papers.abstract: This note proves that smoothness and Gorensteinness are Fourier--Mukai invariants for proper flat families of Noetherian algebraic spaces. Moreover, a kernel realizing such a partnership is perfect if, and only if, the families are smooth.

The relationship with diagonal morphisms with smoothness is classical: for a finite type morphism of locally Noetherian schemes, smoothness is equivalent to flatness and perfectness of the diagonal [15, Tag 0FDP]. papers.title: Deciding Without Pointing: A Case Study of Whether a Decision Model Localizes the Anomalies It Detects
papers.abstract: Decision models can answer a typed question about an image with a probability per option, without generating text. In our case study of Clef-flash (post-trained Qwen3.5-9B backbone) on industrial inspection benchmarks, we ask whether it localizes the anomalies it detects. We obtained uneven results with zero-shot detection: per-category image AUROC 0.924 on MVTec AD and 0.668 on MVTec AD 2. On the former, the decision head's routing attention produces 0.391 mean per-image pixel AUROC, and hiding the image tokens from it leaves detection unchanged. The multimodal LLM's backbone attention does point at the defect, however it falls below a center prior when we change question. It falls below chance if we remove textual context in the question, partly due to backbone attention leaving the object, while the head's map hardly changes. The backbone's states carry the location when probed with normal images, on the test-split images, however, the decision depends on the defect region. A larger model, Clef, that comes with a post-trained Qwen3.8-27B backbone, gives no useful map in the decision head either. We found that it's possible to recover anomaly location by asking question specifically on an image region, retraining the head or reading the backbone, but none matches dedicated few-shot localizers.

papers.title: Exotic cluster structures on $Sp_{2n}$
papers.abstract: We modify the seeds of Berenstein, Fomin and Zelevinsky attached to reduced words for~$(w_0,w_0)$, for any simply connected simple complex algebraic group and any aperiodic Belavin--Drinfeld pair. In every type, moves of words act on the resulting seeds by mutations. After a change of coordinates introduced by Gekhtman, Shapiro and Vainshtein, the seeds are, for $SL_N$, seeds of the cluster structures of these authors, and for $Sp_{2n}$ they define regular complete cluster structures with the expected properties. This proves the aperiodic version of their conjecture for $Sp_{2n}$, with its uniqueness part in a refined form.

papers.title: Lord/Egg of the LRDs: One geometry for its many faces
papers.abstract: Little red dots (LRDs) combine V-shaped ultraviolet-optical continua, broad Balmer emission, and weak X-rays. The nearby analog SDSS J102530.29+140207.3, known as Lord/Egg, offers detailed spectroscopy and polarimetry. We test one active galactic nucleus (AGN) geometry by fitting its ultraviolet-to-infrared continuum with an inclination-dependent accretion-disk spectral energy distribution (SED), young stars, and a clumpy dusty screen. The same SED is used in Cloudy calculations of a radially stratified, virialized broad-line region (BLR). The fit favors log10(M_BH/M_sun) about 7.4, highly super-Eddington accretion, inclination above 70 degrees, and line-of-sight cloud extinction of about 3 mag. It also predicts a 2 keV luminosity below the Chandra limit. A BLR whose density rises from 10^9 to 10^11 cm^-3 near the sublimation radius reproduces the broad H-alpha profile without a separate intermediate-width Gaussian. For cloud columns near 10^23 cm^-2, it also matches the different Balmer-line widths, exponential-like wings, and Balmer decrement without electron scattering. The redshifted H-beta-H-delta absorber lacks an H-alpha counterpart, requiring velocity-coherent H-alpha re-emission into the absorption trough. Cool outer clumps explain K I and saturated Na I absorption, while the geometry recovers the continuum and H-alpha polarization and their position-angle offset. Ca II triplet absorption requires localized, non-radiatively heated, warm dust-poor zones near the sublimation front. He I absorption traces a fast, about 500 km s^-1, low-column ionized BLR skin. All projected absorber velocities remain below the local escape speeds, consistent with a bound failed BLR wind. Thus, a dusty, high-inclination accretion system can explain Lord/Egg within one connected geometry.

The James Webb Space Telescope has uncovered many compact, high-redshift broad-line sources with red rest-optical colors, blue ultraviolet continua, large Balmer equivalent widths (EWs), and weak X-rays. These “little red dots” (LRDs) may signal rapid black-hole growth, but differ from ordinary unobscured quasars (Greene et al., 2024; Matthee et al., 2024; Juodžbalis et al., 2024; Kocevski et al., 2025; Geris et al., 2026, e.g.). Proposed explanations include reddened active galactic nuclei (AGNs), super-Eddington flows, and dense reprocessing envelopes, usually tested against only part of the available data.

The nearby source SDSS J102530.29+140207.3 (z=0.1006z=0.1006; J1025) provides a stringent test. Initially identified as a metal-poor dwarf with persistent broad Hα\alpha (Izotov and Thuan, 2008), it is X-ray underluminous and shows a narrow blueshifted Hα\alpha absorber against its broad-line region (BLR) (64; Burke et al., 2021). Ji et al. (2026a) named it “Lord,” and Lin et al. (2026) called it “the Egg”; we use Lord/Egg. Its V-shaped continuum, broad Balmer and Paschen lines, Balmer and He i absorption, exceptionally strong Na i, K i, and Ca ii absorption, weak X-rays, and mid-infrared emission closely reproduce the LRD phenomenology. The smooth turnover near the Balmer limit shows no secure discontinuity and is interpreted here as the crossover between young stars and a reddened disk.

papers.title: Strong Transitivity of Group Cellular Automata: Characterization and Decidability
papers.abstract: A discrete-time dynamical system is strongly transitive if every point can be reached, in finitely many steps, from every non-empty open set. We study this property for group cellular automata, \ie cellular automata over a finite group alphabet whose global map is a group endomorphism, in every dimension $d\geq1$. We prove that no group cellular automaton over a non-abelian group is strongly transitive, and we develop a decomposition of group cellular automata over abelian groups, via quotients by power subgroups, which preserves strong transitivity. For linear cellular automata over $(\mathbb Z/p\mathbb Z)^n$ we use Pontryagin duality to characterize strong transitivity in terms of the characteristic polynomial $\chi_A$ of the associated matrix $A$ of Laurent polynomials: the automaton is strongly transitive if and only if $\det(A)\neq0$ and no irreducible factor of $\chi_A$ has an invertible constant term. Combining these results, we obtain that strong transitivity is decidable for group cellular automata in every dimension. For every fixed dimension $d$, we give an explicit decision procedure whose running time is polynomial in the group size $N$, the number $k$ of neighbours, and the neighbourhood radius $\varrho$.

papers.intro:
Cellular automata (CAs) are discrete-time dynamical systems defined by the synchronous application of a local rule on a regular lattice ℤd{\mathbb{Z}^{d}} of cells, each of which takes values in a finite alphabet. Despite their simple definition, they exhibit a wide range of dynamical behaviors, and many of their dynamical properties are undecidable in general [20]. This motivates the search for natural classes of CAs in which such properties become decidable and admit explicit characterizations.

papers.title: VoxelSBFL: Voxel-Level Spectrum-Based Failure Prediction for Vision-Language-Action Models
papers.abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models integrate visual perception, language understanding, and action generation to control robots. Testing these systems produces trajectories and task outcomes, but existing approaches provide limited guidance on using these recorded trajectories to assess subsequent executions or inform policy repair. We conjecture that, for a given policy and task, traversing certain workspace regions is associated with a higher likelihood of failure. To investigate this conjecture, we propose VoxelSBFL, a black-box adaptation of Spectrum-Based Fault Localization (SBFL) in which workspace voxels replace program elements as units of analysis. Recorded tool-center-point (TCP) trajectories provide binary voxel coverage, which is combined with execution outcomes to construct suspiciousness maps using established SBFL formulas. These maps identify failure-associated regions and score unseen trajectories without requiring internal model access. We evaluate 34 spectrum-based techniques across four VLA models using 96,000 Pick-Up trajectories in simulation and compare the leading techniques against eight action- and trajectory-based metrics. VoxelSBFL obtains an overall macro ROC-AUC of 0.704, significantly outperforming state-of-the art baselines. Sensitivity analyses show that performance varies with spatial granularity and training-set size. These findings support spatial spectra for VLA execution assessment and motivate future research on runtime monitoring, self-healing and targeted policy improvement.

papers.intro:
Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models (Zhong et al., 2025) integrate visual perception, language understanding, and action generation to control robots that follow users’ instructions. Models such as the GR00T-N1 VLA family (Bjorck et al., 2025) and π0\pi_{0} (Black et al., 2024) translate visual observations and natural-language instructions into robotic actions. Within the complete robotic stack, these actions are executed by low-level controllers, producing trajectories through the physical workspace. Therefore, assessing the reliability of VLA-enabled robots requires understanding when and under which conditions their executions fail. To support this assessment, recent approaches have proposed different testing methods, including test generation approaches (Wang et al., 2025; Kanwal et al., 2026a) or methods that aim to deal with the test oracle problem (Valle et al., 2026b; Valle et al., 2026a). However, once these tests have been executed and their outcomes determined, existing testing approaches offer limited guidance on how to use the recorded trajectories to predict failures in subsequent executions or inform policy repair. Certain approaches aim at predicting failures during VLA executions. For instance, Valle et al. (Valle et al., 2025) propose both white-box and black-box approaches to distinguish successful and failed executions or high, medium or low quality task executions. SAFE (Gu et al., 2026) and VLA-Tug (Podolinsky et al., 2026) rely on internal VLA representations, restricting their use to policies that expose those representations. VLA-Tug also uses annotated failure onsets during training. Nevertheless, these approaches have certain limitations. From the debugging perspective, the scores and alerts produced by these methods give developers limited guidance and explainability of under what circumstances the VLA fails. From the practical perspectives, some of such approaches require internal access to the VLA policy (e.g., white-box uncertainty metrics from (Valle et al., 2025), internal VLA activations at each policy step for obtaining training data (Podolinsky et al., 2026)), which is not always easy to obtain.

Figure 1 shows the robot’s end-effector trajectories in three dimensions (left) and projected onto the 2D X-Y plane (right), with failed executions shown in red and successful ones in green for the π0\pi_{0} model. The 2D projection makes the spatial pattern particularly clear. Failed trajectories predominate in the upper region outlined in red, while successful trajectories predominate in the right-hand region outlined in green. We therefore conjecture that, in VLA-enabled robots, traversing certain regions of the workspace is associated with a higher likelihood of task failure. This conjecture draws on an analogy with conventional software. A test that executes a faulty statement may be more likely to fail because certain inputs or program states can trigger the fault. Similarly, a robot execution may be more likely to fail when the end effector passes through a problematic region of the workspace. This analogy motivates treating the regions visited by a robot as a form of coverage, much like the statements executed by a software test.

Figure 1 shows the robot’s end-effector trajectories in three dimensions (left) and projected onto the 2D X-Y plane (right), with failed executions shown in red and successful ones in green for the π0\pi_{0} model. The 2D projection makes the spatial pattern particularly clear. Failed trajectories predominate in the upper region outlined in red, while successful trajectories predominate in the right-hand region outlined in green. We therefore conjecture that, in VLA-enabled robots, traversing certain regions of the workspace is associated with a higher likelihood of task failure. This conjecture draws on an analogy with conventional software. A test that executes a faulty statement may be more likely to fail because certain inputs or program states can trigger the fault. Similarly, a robot execution may be more likely to fail when the end effector passes through a problematic region of the workspace. This analogy motivates treating the regions visited by a robot as a form of coverage, much like the statements executed by a software test.

Building on this intuition, we propose VoxelSBFL, which recasts failure prediction for VLA-enabled robots as a spatial adaptation of spectrum-based fault localization (SBFL) (Jones et al., 2002). We partition the robot’s three-dimensional workspace into voxels and use these voxels in place of program elements. Just as a software test covers a statement by executing it, a robot trajectory covers a voxel if at least one recorded position of the end effector’s tool center point falls within it. We combine this voxel coverage information with the success or failure outcome of each execution and apply standard SBFL formulas to quantify how strongly coverage of each voxel is associated with failure. The resulting suspiciousness map highlights workspace regions that warrant closer inspection. Developers can use it to identify segments of failed trajectories to examine, including the actions and observations that preceded entry into a highly suspicious voxel. The same map could guide the generation of new trajectories that exercise these regions and the collection of successful demonstrations for targeted repair (e.g., through policy fine-tuning). In this study, we evaluate how well the map distinguishes successful from failed executions, as a proof to determine whether spectrum-based techniques can be employed in this context.

papers.title: Perturbation results for the Choquard equation in the sublinear case
papers.abstract: We study perturbations of the positive ground state of the Choquard equation $$ -\Delta u+u=(I_\alpha*|u|^p)|u|^{p-2}u\qquad\text{in }\mathbb R^N $$ by means of a Lyapunov--Schmidt reduction. For $p\ge2$ the energy is $C^2$ on $H^1$ and a standard machinery applies. The case $\alpha=2$, $1+2/N<p<2$ is different: the ground state has an algebraic decay and the energy is not twice differentiable on $H^1$. We introduce a weighted space adapted to the tail and we perform a finite-dimensional reduction on it. The outcome is a positive solution of a localized perturbation problem near every critical point of the first-order interaction functional with nonzero local degree. For the singularly perturbed problem with potential $V$ we obtain, under a small relative oscillation assumption, solutions concentrating near every critical point of $V$ with nonzero local degree, and a Lusternik--Schnirelman lower bound near compact sets of local minima. We also consider the variant in which $V$ multiplies both the linear and nonlocal terms, and we construct solutions that concentrate near isolated critical points of nonzero degree.

is a nonlocal equation that arises afrom the coupling of a (linear) Schrödinger equation and a Poisson equation. The nonlinearity couples the value of uu at a point to the Riesz potential generated by |u|p|u|^{p}.

The equation has a classical physical origin in the Hartree-type description of a quantum particle interacting with its own induced field. In the case α=2\alpha=2, it is closely related to the pioneering work of Pekar on the polaron and to the Choquard model for an electron trapped in a polar crystal; in the same spirit, the equation appears in the description of one-component plasmas and other mean-field models with long-range interactions. Mathematically, this is the Euler–Lagrange equation of a nonlocal energy where the potential generated by the density |u|p|u|^{p} is represented by a Riesz convolution kernel. For the physical background we refer to [25, 9, 16, 18] and, for the modern mathematical development, to [19, 21, 22].

The existence theory for Choquard-type equations has developed through a series of fundamental contributions. In the classical Hartree setting, Lieb proved the existence of a minimizer for the corresponding variational problem, and Lions developed the concentration-compactness framework that underlies the existence of ground states in the nonlocal setting; see [16, 19]. For the Choquard equation with general exponents, existence and qualitative properties of positive solutions were later established in the works of Moroz and Van Schaftingen, together with the systematic study of regularity, decay, and radial symmetry; see [21, 22]. In the sublinear regime considered here, the recent analysis of decay and nondegeneracy in [30, 31] is essential, and it is the starting point for the perturbation theory developed in the present paper.

papers.title: TANGO: Real-World Unregistered RGB-Guided Hyperspectral Super-Resolution with Two-Camera Acquisitions
papers.abstract: Unregistered hyperspectral image super-resolution aims to recover a high-resolution HSI from a low-resolution hyperspectral observation and an unregistered high-resolution RGB reference. Although recent methods have begun to address the geometric misalignment between the two modalities, their evaluation is still constrained by the lack of a large-scale public benchmark based on real two-camera RGB--HSI acquisitions with a high-resolution HSI reference. To address this gap, we introduce DUET, the first large-scale public dataset for unregistered RGB-guided hyperspectral super-resolution, comprising 403 indoor and outdoor scenes captured with two separate RGB and hyperspectral cameras. We further propose TANGO (Two-camera AligNment with Gated Occlusions), which first compensates for the dominant cross-camera displacement through end-to-end global alignment and then refines the remaining inconsistencies with a coarse-to-fine local feature alignment. A learned gating mechanism further attenuates the RGB guidance where the two views cannot be consistently matched. Experimental results show that TANGO achieves state-of-the-art performance on both DUET and REAL across all evaluated scale factors, outperforming the strongest competitor on DUET by up to 2.29 dB in PSNR while requiring 2.5$\times$ fewer FLOPs. The code and dataset will be available at https://github.com/FagiolottoConSombrero/TANGO-DUET

papers.intro:
Hyperspectral imaging provides dense spectral measurements across tens or hundreds of contiguous wavelength bands, enabling fine-grained analysis of materials and scene properties beyond the capabilities of conventional RGB imaging. This rich spectral representation has made hyperspectral imaging valuable in a wide range of applications [13, 32, 26, 4, 24, 35]. However, hyperspectral acquisition is inherently affected by a trade-off between spatial resolution, spectral resolution, and signal-to-noise ratio. Consequently, hyperspectral images often provide detailed spectral information at the cost of limited spatial detail, making hyperspectral image super-resolution (HSI-SR) an important problem. A first line of research addresses this limitation by relying exclusively on the low-resolution HSI, exploiting the intrinsic spatial and spectral correlations of the hyperspectral cube to infer the missing high-frequency spatial information through increasingly effective spectral-spatial processing, attention mechanisms, and efficient feature extraction [15, 40, 19]. Nevertheless, single-image methods remain fundamentally constrained by the spatial information available in the low-resolution observation itself. To overcome this limitation, RGB-guided HSI super-resolution introduces an auxiliary high-resolution RGB image that provides complementary high-frequency spatial information. Several methods have demonstrated that combining the spectral content of the HSI with the spatial detail of an RGB reference can substantially improve reconstruction quality [10, 23, 20]. However, most RGB-guided methods assume that the RGB and hyperspectral observations are spatially registered before fusion.

This assumption becomes problematic when the two modalities are acquired with independent cameras. Differences in viewpoint, focal length, sensor geometry, and scene depth introduce global displacement, perspective changes, depth-dependent parallax, local geometric inconsistencies, and occlusions. Under these conditions, directly injecting RGB features into the hyperspectral reconstruction may transfer spatial information to incorrect locations and introduce reconstruction artifacts.

As a result, no existing benchmark combines real two-camera RGB–HSI acquisitions with the scale, scene diversity, and range of scale factors required to train and evaluate learning-based methods.

papers.title: Operator Precedence Tree Automata
papers.abstract: Operator-precedence tree automata (OPTA) separate the construction of a word's syntactic structure from its recognition: an operator-precedence (OP) matrix determines a canonical tree, which is evaluated by a finite bottom-up automaton with regular horizontal transition languages. OPTA define exactly the operator-precedence languages. For a fixed matrix and language, a tree-context congruence yields an effectively constructible canonical complete deterministic exact recognizer, minimal in the number of vertical states and unique up to isomorphism. For acyclic OP matrices, we characterize balanced non-counting by aperiodicity of the context transition monoid of the canonical minimal ranked tree recognizer. Combined with existing characterizations of OP languages, this gives an equivalence with first-order definability over OP words, definability in Precedence-Oriented Temporal Logic (POTL), and star-free operator-precedence expressions for acyclic matrices.
papers.intro:
Operator-precedence languages (OPLs) originated in Floyd’s work on deterministic parsing of programming languages [10]. Their defining feature is a finite matrix of precedence relations between terminal symbols, which determines how a word is decomposed into nested syntactic units. Beyond their original application, OPLs form a family of deterministic context-free languages, properly containing Input Driven or Visibly Pushdown languages [17, 1] and retaining many of the properties that make regular languages useful. These include Boolean and concatenation closure under compatible precedence assumptions [7], and automata-theoretic and logical characterizations [13, 15]. Their local parsability also supports the analysis of separate input fragments, providing a basis for parallel parsing [2, 5].

papers.title: A Reidemeister-type theorem for vineyards
papers.abstract: Closed vineyards record how persistent homology changes along a periodic family of filtrations. Their topology can be surprisingly complicated, with recent work showing that vines may exhibit nontrivial monodromy even in very simple settings, and more generally that every link can occur in a closed vineyard. In this paper, we study how the global topology and structure of a vineyard change when the periodic family of functions changes. We study radial persistence for a generic planar curve $\mathcal{M}$, where an observation point $x\in\mathbb{R}^2$ defines the squared-distance function $d_\mathbb{E}^2 (\cdot ,x)|_\mathcal{M}$. Moving the point $x$ along a closed observation loop $\gamma$ produces a closed vineyard. Utilizing tools from singularity theory, we show that the topology of this vineyard is controlled by the interaction of $\gamma$ with the generalized symmetry set of $\mathcal{M}$, the geometric discriminant formed by the union of focal and symmetry sets. We establish a Reidemeister-type theorem: under a generic deformation of $\gamma$, every topological change in the vineyard is generated by a finite collection of elementary local moves occurring when $\gamma$ passes codimension-two singularities of the generalized symmetry set. Thus, despite the potentially unbounded global complexity of closed vineyards, their evolution is governed by a finite collection of local geometric events. We classify these events and determine the corresponding changes to the vineyard, giving a complete local description of how radial vineyards evolve under generic deformation. In addition, we derive sufficient geometric conditions under which the resulting vineyard has no monodromy and trivial topology. The 2D case already exhibits very rich behaviour, and we conjecture that in fact it captures all possible generic changes in vineyards.

papers.title: Correcting Flows with Marginal Matching
papers.abstract: Flow matching models, ODE-based generative models, generate samples by gradually morphing a simple source distribution into a target distribution. However, these models still face challenges in optimally balancing computational efficiency with generation fidelity. While predictor-corrector schemes have been proven to help address this issue in diffusion models effectively, their application to flow matching models remains under-explored. In this work we present a novel training-based predictor-corrector framework for flow matching, which exploits the fact that the ODE can be easily reversed. Our key idea, termed Marginal Matching, is to correct samples at a particular time step in the forward ODE towards a matching marginal distribution of the backward ODE. This scheme proves to reduce a bound on the distance between the data distribution and the learned distribution, motivating two different implementations for the correction function. We show that our proposed method improves sample quality on CIFAR-10 and ImageNet-64, with minimal overhead in computation time.

papers.intro:
Flow-based generative models have emerged as a promising alternative to diffusion models, offering faster sampling while maintaining high generation quality (Lipman et al., 2023; Liu et al., 2023a; Tong et al., 2024). While these models require fewer sampling steps than diffusion probabilistic models (DPMs), they still face challenges in balancing computational efficiency with generation quality. This trade-off is crucial, as applications like image synthesis and audio generation require real-time performance, while protein design and robotics demand efficient resource utilization for complex tasks (Yan et al., 2024; Liu et al., 2023b; Le et al., 2024; Irwin et al., 2024; Hu et al., 2023).

In DPMs, predictor-corrector schemes have proven effective at improving sample quality. These schemes combine prediction steps, which estimate the next time step’s sample, with correction steps that refine samples to better match the current time-step distribution. Previous work include both training-free methods (Song et al., 2021b; Zhao et al., 2023; Zhao et al., 2024), which do not require additional model training, and training-based techniques (Lezama et al., 2022), which involve training a model specifically tailored to the task. However, applying these schemes to flow matching models remained relatively unexplored until recently. Song & Lai (2024) demonstrated the viability of implementing a predictor-corrector scheme for flow matching models without requiring additional training.

Traditional predictor-corrector frameworks aim to refine a sample at time step tt of the generation towards the marginal distribution of the learned diffusion process at time tt. For flow matching, the marginal distribution at time tt is the push-forward of the initial Gaussian distribution by the ODE up to time tt. However, due to limitations of the neural network training, a learned flow does not exactly map Gaussian noise to perfect images, even with perfect integration. Here, we introduce a novel training-based predictor-corrector approach specifically tailored for flow matching models that leverages known marginal distributions to provably yield the exact data distribution. Our method exploits time reversibility, which has been explored in diffusion models (Wallace et al., 2023; Mokady et al., 2023), but is arguably less involved in flow matching models as it only requires solving the ODE in reverse time (Liu et al., 2023a).

Consider a reverse ODE, starting from the data samples and flowing back in time according to the learned flow model. Our main insight is that starting the generation from samples on this trajectory will generate perfect images. Building on this, we enhance generation quality through a predictor-corrector scheme that alternates between ODE solver steps (predictor) and learned correction steps, reducing the discrepancy between generated samples and the time-reversal ODE solution. We provide theoretical guarantees that such a correction function minimizes a bound on the Wasserstein distance (Kantorovich, 1942) between the target approximation and the true target distribution, as a function of the error reduction of the corrections at different time steps. We hypothesize that for practical flow models, the forward and backward ODEs will be relatively aligned, making the correction easy to learn and apply with minimal overhead.

papers.title: Assessment of electric-field-induced forces for bulk solids within the projector-augmented wave method
papers.abstract: We assess the performance of electric-field-induced forces for bulk solids within the projector-augmented wave method. This capability allows for first-principles structural relaxations of bulk semiconductors and insulators under external electric fields, thereby enabling the calculation of linear and nonlinear responses to electric fields as well as properties associated with electric-field-driven structural changes. The approach is first validated by presenting calculated ion-clamped and unclamped dielectric and piezoelectric constants, quadratic dielectric susceptibilities, and Born effective charges for semiconductors AlX (X=P, As and Sb), showing good agreement with density functional perturbation theory calculations as well as with available experimental and theoretical data. As a further demonstration, we examine the electric-field-driven antiferroelectric-to-ferroelectric phase transition in AgNbO$_3$, for which our computed polarization versus electric field hysteresis loop aligns with previous calculations.

papers.intro:
Electric fields are commonly used in experiments for manipulating a variety of properties, e.g., magnetic interactions [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6] (see reviews in Refs. [7, 8, 9]), exchange bias [10, 11], metal-insulator transition [12], superconductivity [13, 14], optical absorption [15], and structural distortions [16, 17, 18]. However, the nonperiodic nature of the electric-field potential makes its treatment nontrivial within first-principles methods based on periodic boundary conditions [19]. In addition, the unboundedness of the electric field potential can always lower the energy of an insulating system by transferring charge from valence bands of one region to conduction bands in another distant region, resulting in a dielectric breakdown [19, 20]. Nevertheless, under a small finite-electric-field when the Zener tunneling is not severe, it turned out that the density matrix remains periodic under translation by a lattice vector [21] and the long-lived field-polarized states can be obtained by minimizing the electric enthalpy functional [22, 21, 23, 24] with the electronic polarization calculated using the modern theory of polarization [25, 26].

[7, 8, 9]), exchange bias [10, 11], metal-insulator transition [12], superconductivity [13, 14], optical absorption [15], and structural distortions [16, 17, 18]. However, the nonperiodic nature of the electric-field potential makes its treatment nontrivial within first-principles methods based on periodic boundary conditions [19]. [28]. With the growing use of electric fields as a versatile tool for tuning material properties in both experiments and simulations, robust and efficient approaches for treating finite-electric-fields in bulk solids are increasingly valuable for the ab initio community. A recent review of first-principles modeling of ferroelectric oxide perovskites discusses the modern theory of polarization, explicit finite-electric-field methods, and the calculation of functional and electromechanical responses [48]. While several well-known packages, such as ABINIT [49, 21, 28], Quantum ESPRESSO [50, 23], and CASTEP [51], already incorporate finite-electric-field capabilities, the present work provides a systematic assessment of the electric-field-induced forces for bulk solids within the PAW formalism as implemented in the Vienna Ab initio Simulation Package (VASP) [52, 53]. Specifically, we benchmark the accuracy and reliability of the finite-electric-field response by evaluating ion-clamped and relaxed-ion dielectric and piezoelectric constants, quadratic dielectric susceptibility, and Born effective charges for the prototypical semiconductors AlX (X=P, As, and Sb). As a further validation, we reproduce the electric-field-driven antiferroelectric-to-ferroelectric phase transition in AgNbO3 [37]. The paper is organized as follows. In Section II, we detail the methodology underlying the finite-electric-field treatment as implemented in VASP. Computational details are provided in Section III. The benchmark results are presented and discussed in Section IV, and a summary is given in Section V.

papers.title: Stochastic Modeling of the Mean Time Between Software Failures: A review
papers.abstract: A review of several models for the software failure detection stochastic process is per- formed. We focus on how the Mean Time Between Failures is obtained from those models and present a comparative study. The models considered involve some of the well known based on non- homogeneous Poisson processes and a recently proposed model based on contagion. Our main target is to evaluate the models performance when they are applied to modern software projects developed under Agile methodologies. Recently developed Software Engineering practices (TDD, Scrum, etc.), propose an iterative procedure be- tween development, testing and debugging, introducing this way, particular challenges to Software Reliability modeling. As opposed to the non-homogeneous Poisson processes, the failure rate of the contagion model depends not just on time but also on the number of previously detected failures. All the considered models are particular cases of non- homogeneous Birth Processes, a general fundamental theory on how to obtain time to failure and time between failures expectations is also shown.

papers.title: Beyond Reconstruction: A Unified Framework for Trustworthy and Explainable EEG Artifact Removal Evaluation
papers.abstract: Deep-learning methods have achieved strong performance in EEG artifact removal, but evaluation remains dominated by reconstruction metrics such as error, correlation, and signal-to-noise ratio. Although these metrics assess similarity to clean EEG, they do not establish whether models effectively suppress artifacts, preserve neural activity, or provide reliable explanations. To address these limitations, we propose TriX-EEG, a three-level framework for trustworthy and explainable EEG artifact removal. Level 1, Signal Validity (SV), evaluates reconstruction quality and neural band-power preservation. Level 2, Removal Faithfulness (RF), assesses the removed component through artifact error and residual artifact/neural leakage. Level 3, Explanation Reliability (ER), examines model behavior through temporal alignment, causal relevance, and stability. We evaluate TriX-EEG using nine published neural denoisers across three public benchmarks derived from EEGDenoiseNet and the PhysioNet Motion Artifact Contaminated EEG Dataset, covering EOG, EMG, and motion artifacts. Results show that reconstruction metrics alone are insufficient for trustworthy denoiser assessment: RF complements it by revealing whether errors stem from residual artifact or suppressed neural activity, while ER captures distinct aspects of explanation behavior, supporting joint evaluation of three aspects within a unified framework rather than reliance on any single factor. External validation on an independent EEG/EOG dataset and the BCI Competition IV-2a motor-imagery dataset further demonstrates broadly consistent rankings under dataset shift. Higher-ranked denoisers generally preserve more task-relevant information or cause less downstream performance degradation. Overall, TriX-EEG provides a comprehensive basis for EEG denoiser assessment, encouraging models that are not only accurate but also faithful and explainable.
