papers.intro:
Electroencephalography (EEG) provides a non-invasive measurement of neural activity with high temporal resolution, but it is highly susceptible to artifacts from eye movements (electrooculography, EOG), muscle activity (electromyography, EMG), and motion. These artifacts can distort neural rhythms and reduce the reliability of downstream analysis [17, 13]. Removing these artifacts is challenging. Indeed, insufficient suppression leaves contamination in the signal, whereas excessive correction may attenuate neural activity relevant to downstream analysis [6]. These challenges highlight the need to evaluate artifact removal not only by its apparent effectiveness, but also by the information it preserves.

These artifacts can distort neural rhythms and reduce the reliability of downstream analysis [17, 13]. Removing these artifacts is challenging. Indeed, insufficient suppression leaves contamination in the signal, whereas excessive correction may attenuate neural activity relevant to downstream analysis [6]. These challenges highlight the need to evaluate artifact removal not only by its apparent effectiveness, but also by the information it preserves.

Deep neural networks have become increasingly popular for EEG artifact removal because they can learn nonlinear mappings from contaminated EEG to clean EEG and often achieve strong reconstruction performance [25]. The introduction of EEGDenoiseNet [41] has facilitated systematic comparisons under controlled EOG and EMG contamination, with performance commonly quantified using temporal and spectral relative root-mean-square errors (RRMSE), correlation coefficient (CC), and signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) improvement. These metrics provide essential measures of reconstruction quality, but primarily summarize the overall agreement between denoised and reference signals. Consequently, they do not explicitly describe the structure of the remaining error, including its relationship to residual artifact, unintended neural attenuation, or frequency-specific distortion. Moreover, a favorable reconstruction may still suppress neural activity or retain part of the artifact, and does not necessarily establish that the denoised signal retains the information required by downstream EEG applications [6], and therefore may not represent trustworthy artifact removal.

Moreover, a favorable reconstruction may still suppress neural activity or retain part of the artifact, and does not necessarily establish that the denoised signal retains the information required by downstream EEG applications [6], and therefore may not represent trustworthy artifact removal.

In short, standard reconstruction metrics primarily quantify the discrepancy between the denoised output and the clean EEG reference [41], providing an overall measure of reconstruction fidelity without explicitly distinguishing residual artifact from unintended neural-signal suppression. A more informative evaluation should therefore examine not only the reconstructed EEG, but also the signal removed by the denoiser. Although reconstruction and removal errors are coupled, evaluating the removed component against the paired artifact and clean EEG references provides a complementary perspective on denoising behavior. For instance, denoisers with similar reconstruction errors may differ in their relative artifact suppression and neural-signal preservation. Thus, examining the removed component against paired neural and artifact references can provide additional diagnostic information about the nature of denoising errors, complementing conventional output-based metrics. This distinction is particularly relevant when neural activity and artifacts overlap in frequency or when subtle signal distortions may affect subsequent analysis [29, 33, 14].

Beyond signal quality, the interpretability of learned denoising operations raises a further evaluation challenge. Explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) methods are increasingly applied to EEG models to identify influential temporal, spectral, or spatial features [19, 23]. However, visually plausible attribution maps do not necessarily provide faithful explanations of model behavior. Some saliency methods can be insensitive to model parameters or data relationships, while attribution quality may vary substantially across time-series models [1, 10]. Existing quantitative XAI evaluations have primarily focused on classification tasks [35], where explanations are typically associated with a specific class prediction. In contrast, EEG denoising maps a contaminated waveform to a reconstructed waveform, so the model operation being explained should be defined explicitly. Even with a well-defined target, highlighting influential input regions does not establish that a denoiser attends to the artifact rather than to neural activity, nor that the attribution actually drives its behavior. A reliable explanation of a denoiser should therefore satisfy complementary properties. It should be temporally aligned with the true artifact. The model’s spectral sensitivity should be consistent with the artifact spectrum. Also, removing the highlighted inputs should causally change the denoising operation. Finally, the attribution should remain stable under small, non-semantic input perturbations.

Motivated by these limitations, we propose TriX-EEG, a three-level evaluation framework that systematically assesses EEG artifact removal from complementary perspectives. Level 1 (Signal Validity, SV) evaluates how accurately clean EEG is reconstructed, considering temporal and spectral reconstruction quality and neural band-power preservation. Level 2 (Removal Faithfulness, RF) characterizes the removed component and its errors relative to neural and artifact references through artifact similarity, energy agreement, reconstruction error, and conditional estimates of artifact gain and neural leakage. Level 3 (Explanation Reliability, ER) assesses whether explanations of the model operation exhibit temporal alignment with artifact activity, spectral sensitivity consistent with the artifact spectrum, intervention-based relevance, and stability under small input perturbations. The three levels are retained as diagnostic profiles and integrated into an overall TriX-EEG Denoising Score (TDS) using a geometric mean. Together, they extend conventional reconstruction-based evaluation by examining not only the quality of the denoised signal, but also the characteristics of the removed component and the reliability of explanations of the denoising operation.

papers.title: Operating an Agent-Driven Dataset Factory: Discovery, Construction, and Public Release
papers.abstract: Turning public data into prediction datasets requires connecting source discovery, task definition, construction, and distribution. We deployed Dataset Factory to perform these steps continuously under a standing release policy. Bounded language-model tasks interpret sources, write construction code, and review task meaning; deterministic software manages state, workers, retries, and publication. Over 81.53 hours, the factory published 14 datasets at an estimated recurring operating expenditure of about \$2.74 per publication. The accounting includes failed attempts, inference, workers, and hosting. Separate agents completed prediction experiments on all twelve evaluated releases. Source review nevertheless identified a task whose construction filters contradicted its population declaration. The original reviewer accepted later-record exclusions without reconciling them with the published selection rule. This experience documents an operating source-to-release workflow and shows why successful execution and consumer use need separate checks of task meaning.

papers.title: Asymptotic enumeration of histories and limit laws in two random graph evolution models
papers.abstract:
We study growth models for random graphs where the growth is established by vertex or edge creations and where there is no dependence between vertices and edges. Creations are logged by time stamps such that the history of the resulting graph can be reconstructed. We investigate two prototypical models, an undirected and a directed one, called undirected independent growth model (UIG-model) and directed independent growth model (DIG-model). The generating functions for the number of histories have radius of convergence equal to zero. In the UIG-model, we express the asymptotic number of histories as a sum that is amenable to the discrete Laplace method. We derive the asymptotic number of histories, study the number of vertices of a random history, and prove a central limit theorem.
  In the DIG-model we use a rescaled Borel transform to get an entire function. Then we show that this function is Hayman admissible, which enables us to derive the asymptotic number of histories in this model. The counting sequence is closely related to the framework of generalized Legendre-Stirling numbers. To determine the number of vertices in a random history, we prove that the bivariate generating function is e-admissible and infer that again a normal limit law holds. Finally, we discuss a correspondence to set partitions with even block sizes and present an algorithm based on Boltzmann samplers that generates such graphs uniformly at random.

papers.intro:
Dynamic graph models have emerged as useful tools for modeling systems whose interaction structure changes over time. Examples include social networks, where the times at which interactions occur form an essential part of the data [6], and stochastic graph-rewriting models for biochemical systems [5]. More broadly, random graph theory contains a wide variety of static and evolving models. It started with the classical Erdős–Rényi random graph process [20], which has been extensively studied and is nowadays well-covered by [8, 26] and ranges to more recent models for social networks like the preferential attachment model surveyed by Albert and Barabási [1].

In the classical dynamic models there is typically no or no strict separation between the growth in the number of vertices and the growth in the number of edges, see [1, 13]. For instance, in the Erdős–Rényi models the number of vertices, say nn, is fixed and the number of edges grows. Then one lets nn tend to infinity and studies asymptotic properties, where a dependence on nn for the number of edges is usually imposed on the model. In [22] a new random graph growth model is suggested where the size as well as the order of a graph may grow according to the inherent structure of the graph process itself. Classical accounts on dynamic random graphs focus on the study of several popular models such as the copying model, the small-world graph, and the preferential attachment model as well as variations in [9], power law graphs and duplication models (static and dynamic) in [11] and the treatment largely based branching processes in [19].

The evolution is accomplished through one of two operations at each discrete time step: the creation of a new vertex or the addition of an edge between two existing vertices. There are several ways to do that and in this work we consider two particular models: the undirected independent growth model (UIG-model) with undirected edges and where no loops are allowed, and the directed independent growth model (DIG-model) with directed edges and where loops are allowed.

The counting sequence for the UIG-model is, up to a one-step shift, OEIS A124373, while the DIG-model gives the sequence of generalized Bell numbers, OEIS A135920. These sequences belong to a broader algebraic framework of polynomial base changes that traces back to Carlitz [10] and arises naturally in spectral analysis [21]. It was later systematically extended to the Legendre–Stirling framework by Andrews and Littlejohn [3, 2], who also gave a combinatorial interpretation in terms of certain set partitions over sets of integers present in two colors. Across these families, the counting sequences satisfy analogous recurrence relations, and the functional equations for their generating functions differ only by a single parameter. Furthermore, they all admit natural graph-theoretic interpretations as special instances of the diagram families studied in [7].

papers.title: Python Code Generation for Isabelle/HOL
papers.abstract: The Isabelle theorem prover provides an environment for formalising mathematics and reasoning about programs. To make verified implementations practically usable, its code generator translates functions expressed in the executable fragment of its logic into conventional programming languages. Its targets have traditionally been functional languages (Standard ML, OCaml, Haskell, and Scala), recently joined by Go. Python, which is becoming the dominant language of scientific computing, data science, and education, has remained out of reach. In this work, we close this gap with a Python backend for Isabelle's code generator. This generator enables verified algorithms to be used in Python applications, or to serve as verified references against which established Python libraries can be differentially tested, without leaving the Python ecosystem. We validate the backend on regression suites covering large parts of the HOL library and by testing six verified data structures and algorithms against established Python libraries. The generated code is slower than hand-written libraries, but well suited as a verified reference.
papers.intro:
Isabelle/HOL [27] is an interactive theorem prover (ITP) based on higher-order logic (HOL), a typed λ\lambda-calculus with polymorphism and type classes. The user of Isabelle/HOL creates theory files, which can include datatype and type class declarations, inductive definitions, and functions. A fragment of HOL is executable, which means that it can be evaluated inside Isabelle, and also translated into programs in conventional programming languages. Isabelle’s code generation framework was reimplemented by Florian Haftmann in his PhD thesis [12, 13], replacing an earlier design [3], and has since featured a more modular setup, in which parts of the generator can be shared by different language backends. Traditionally, these backends covered functional programming languages, such as Standard ML, OCaml, Haskell, and Scala, as their evaluation schemes are also (at least loosely) based on the λ\lambda-calculus. Recently, another backend [32] for the programming language Go has been added, which for the first time allowed generating code in an imperative programming language.

Its usage covers almost all areas of computing, and includes scientific computing, data science, machine learning and AI, scripting, automation, testing, and web backends. Several of Python’s design choices simplify code generation from HOL. Its integers have arbitrary precision, matching HOL’s int, and its match statement expresses most of HOL’s patterns directly. Since Python is dynamically typed, polymorphism and type classes need not be fitted into a static type system. Python, however, raises obstacles of its own: CPython, the reference implementation of the Python language [29], limits recursion depth and does not eliminate tail calls, closures capture variables rather than values, and if/else and pattern matching are statements, not expressions. section 3 describes how the backend addresses these issues.

papers.title: Another Variant of the Neoclassical Inequality
papers.abstract: The neoclassical inequality is an inequality related to the binomial theorem, involving fractional powers. It naturally gives rise to four other similar inequalities, by varying the inequality sign and the range of the fractional parameter. Three of these statements are known, and the remaining one was conjectured in the literature, based on numerical evidence. It is proved in the present note. The method we use yields short proofs for two of the known related inequalities.

papers.title: Surrogate-assisted beam distribution shaping at the CERN Proton Synchrotron and Super Proton Synchrotron
papers.abstract: The Super Proton Synchrotron at CERN delivers protons to the North Area experimental facility at 400 GeV/c. The extracted beam is split twice vertically in the transfer line with Lambertson septa to serve three fixed-target experiments simultaneously. A significant fraction of the beam is lost during these splitting processes, driving radioactive activation of the Lambertson septa. This contribution investigates reducing the splitting losses by optimising the vertical beam distribution before extraction. The developed method relies on resonant excitation with the transverse damper, reshaping the Gaussian vertical profile into a uniform and ultimately bimodal distribution, with the excitation amplitude acting as a single continuous control knob. A loss reduction of up to 23.5 % was measured. In simulations, the vertical amplitude detuning is established as a second knob that reduces the resulting beam envelope. This technique was verified with measurements at the CERN Proton Synchrotron. Surrogate models based on generative deep learning were developed for efficient real-time validation and Bayesian system identification.

papers.title: On Green's Conjecture for Curves on Anticanonical Surfaces
papers.abstract: We prove Green's conjecture for smooth curves $C$ on rational surfaces $X$ such that $-K_X|_C$ is effective on $C$. In addition, on birationally ruled surfaces $X$ of irregularity $q \geq 1$ carrying an effective anticanonical divisor, we show that Green's conjecture holds for all smooth curves $C$ on $X$ covering the base curve with degree at least $2$, provided the latter has only finitely many gonal pencils or the gonality of $C$ is special with respect to the ruling.

papers.title: Tropicalization and slow manifolds: A case study of the Michaelis--Menten reaction
papers.abstract: We present a case study of a recently developed approach to multiple-scale systems based on exponential scaling and tropicalization (Kristiansen and Sarantaris, \emph{On a tropicalization of planar polynomial ODEs}). Parameters and variables are scaled exponentially with respect to a small parameter $\epsilon$, so that orders of magnitude become a genuine non-smooth singular limit $\epsilon\to 0$. Tropical geometry, via subdivisions of the Newton polygon, classifies the asymptotic regimes and locates the candidates for slow manifolds on all scales of the variables simultaneously. Here we combine this framework with blow-up and geometric singular perturbation theory. {In particular,} the non-smooth singular limit is resolved by spherical and cylindrical blow-ups, and degeneracies caused by exponentially small terms with flat contact are treated by adding the exponential quantities as new variables {(following Kristiansen, \emph{Blowup for flat slow manifolds})}. As the case study, we take the Michaelis--Menten reaction. The tropical classification yields three asymptotic regimes of parameters. In two of these, we find a sequence of blowups and desingularizations where the system has a {global} normally hyperbolic critical manifold on the blown up space. In the remaining case, we obtain a similar result, but only for a subcase. In particular, there is an asymptotic regime of parameters where there is no global slow manifold of the Michaelis--Menten reaction.

papers.intro:
Polynomial systems of ordinary differential equations (ODEs) occur in many different areas of science, perhaps most notably as models of chemical reaction networks [12]. Frequently, dependent variables and parameters vary on vastly different scales, leading to multiscale behaviour of solutions. In suitably scaled forms of the equations, dimension reduction methods can be used to obtain qualitative insight. A prime example is dimension reduction by Quasi-Steady-State-Assumption (QSSA), which is based on the assumption that certain concentrations (involved in fast reactions) are equilibrated for an extended (slow) time [42]. One way of making QSSA precise is through the concept of slow manifolds from Geometric Singular Perturbation Theory (GSPT). These objects are locally invariant manifolds capturing the essential dynamics after initial transients [13]. GSPT, in combination with the technical tool of blowup, is by now a well-developed toolbox for systems depending singularly on a distinguished small parameter [29, 46]. In different regions of phase space and parameter space, different types of slow manifolds can exist in separate scales. However, finding the relevant scales is often challenging [35].

Recently, concepts from tropical geometry have been used to find the governing scales in a systematic and algorithmic way, see [5, 35, 44]. The basic idea is to scale all parameters and variables according to certain weights and then determine the weights such that dominant terms of opposite signs cancel. This gives candidates for dimension reduction (in the spirit of slow manifolds). In [24] this approach was formalized for planar systems by writing the parameters and variables in suitable logarithmic coordinates. In a singular limit, one obtains a piecewise smooth system with tropical curves as discontinuity sets. Sliding along suitable tropical curves is a proxy for motion on slow manifolds, see also [24, 39].

papers.title: Atomic-scale Imaging of Time Reversal Breaking Supercurrents in $\mathrm{Bi_2Sr_2CaCu_2O_8}$
papers.abstract: A persistent mystery of CuO_2-based high temperature superconductivity has been the mechanism and consequences of time reversal ($\mathcal{T}$)-symmetry breaking. Although theoretical hypotheses focus upon persistent electronic currents as a potential cause, these have been invisible to direct experimental probes. That impasse has recently been removed by development of techniques for atomic-scale supercurrent visualization. Here, by imaging the energy-resolved density of electronic states $N(r,E)$ in $\mathrm{Bi_2Sr_2CaCu_2O_8}$, we search for the specific signatures of flowing supercurrents in a disordered $d$-wave superconductor. Employing the strategy of artificial neural networks (ANN) for complex quantum matter visualization, we designed a dual-ANN (VMAP) to efficiently implement $d$-wave supercurrent visualization, achieving imaging of supercurrent speeds $V(r)$ at magnetic fields $|B| \leq \mu T$ in $\mathrm{Bi_2Sr_2CaCu_2O_8}$. Correspondence between specific characteristics of $N(r,E)$ around each supercurrent loop and a quantum "Rosetta Stone" which translates $N(r,E)$ to $V(r)$, emphasizes the validity of $V(r)$ detection and visualization. Then, for hole-densities 0.17 $\leq p \leq$ 0.22 we observe statistically repeatable networks of supercurrent flows. Crucially, these supercurrents satisfy Kirchhoff's law at junctions within each network. Further, theoretical predictions for supercurrent speeds $V$ in disordered $d$-wave superconductors are consistent with measured 1250 m/s $< V <$ 4000 m/s, and with reported magnetic field amplitudes $|B| \approx$ 0.1 mT Thus, detection and visualization of these supercurrent loop networks provides unique perspectives on $\mathcal{T}$-symmetry breaking in cuprates. It also emphasizes the accelerating utility of ANN techniques for physics discovery from high data volume quantum matter research.

papers.title: PersonaHate: A Scalable Persona-Based Data Synthesis Pipeline for Hate Speech Analysis
papers.abstract: Hate speech remains a persistent and evolving threat on online platforms. The widespread use of large language models (LLMs) further intensifies this problem by making hateful content easier and cheaper to generate at scale. Although stronger hate speech detectors continue to be proposed, their performance remains uneven across target identity groups and different forms of hateful expression, partly because existing training data provides only limited coverage of these cases. Thus, we introduce PersonaHate, a scalable persona-driven data synthesis pipeline for constructing diverse hate speech datasets. PersonaHate begins with a large persona pool of 457K personas drawn from two real-world sources. Conditioned on selected personas from this pool, it prompts eight LLMs to generate hate speech across 34 identity groups and performs multi-judge annotation to obtain reliable labels. The resulting corpus contains 791K samples, from which we curate a 67K group-balanced training set. Our modular design also supports extension to new identity groups, generators, and emerging hate targets. Built upon this dataset, we evaluate two detector training strategies: training from scratch and further fine-tuning. Results show that all trained models achieve competitive performance across four widely used external benchmarks. Notably, a 184M-parameter DeBERTa-v3 model trained on PersonaHate reaches 77.5% average F1 and 79.4% average accuracy, outperforming OpenAI's Moderation API on HateBenchSet and MHS. Furthermore, fine-tuning Llama-3.1-8B raises its average F1 from 70.7% to 78.4%, a gain of 7.7 percentage points, surpassing LlamaGuard-3, Meta's official safety model based on the same Llama-3.1-8B architecture, on three of four benchmarks. These results show that PersonaHate can substantially improve the robustness and cross-dataset generalization of hate speech detectors.

Our results show that persona conditioning improves semantic and lexical diversity over direct prompting, that persona diversity transfers to output diversity, and that hateful personas from 4chan and general-purpose personas provide complementary signals. papers.title: Provable Mixing Properties of Parallel Mixnets Revisited
papers.abstract: A mix-network (mixnet) is a routing network that breaks source-to-destination message trackability by indistinguishably mixing the routes of concurrently transmitted messages, thus providing anonymity to senders, receivers and sender-receiver pairs. Given their potential use in high-stakes scenarios like protecting whistleblowers, one would like to prove formally that sender anonymity holds in a mixnet, even against strong adversaries that can compromise subsets of mixnet servers. However, existing work on anonymity in mixnets is either limited to linear mixnets (which do not scale horizontally), relies on special provisions such as additional noise or chaff messages, or is empirical -- typically based on entropy, which does not provide strong guarantees if the adversary has auxiliary information. In this paper, we present a new analysis of parallel mixnets which scale horizontally, showing that these networks can provide strong indistinguishability for messages even without additional noise messages. Our analysis works by bounding the statistical variance of the adversary's posterior likelihood of where a message of interest is at a given point in time. Using concentration bounds on this distribution, we show that parallel mixnets satisfy $(\varepsilon, \delta)$-differential indistinguishability for messages routed through the mixnet (similar to $(\varepsilon, \delta)$-differential privacy) with very small failure probabilities $\delta$ and small privacy parameters $\varepsilon$ under reasonable operating conditions. Our model also enables an examination of the quantitative trade-off between anonymity, latency and per-router bandwidth in parallel mixnets.

papers.intro:
Mix-networks or mixnets are a fundamental building block of anonymous communication [13, 24, 23, 21, 5, 26, 27, 22, 19, 14, 3, 25, 30, 11, 4, 28, 6, 12, 2, 7, 17, 18, 29]. Mixnets provide anonymity by routing all messages through a set of servers; each server indistinguishably mixes all messages it receives within a round, a fixed duration of time. The ideal mixnet consists of a single server that collects messages from senders in each round, shuffles them, and forwards them to recipients with reencryption. Assuming that NN senders send messages in a round, the adversary’s posterior distribution over possible senders of a given message exiting the network is uniform with probability mass 1/N1/N, i.e., the ideal mixnet provides perfect anonymity. However, the ideal mixnet has two shortcomings: (1) it has a single point of failure — its only server — and (2) its throughput is limited to that of one server.

Mixnets provide anonymity by routing all messages through a set of servers; each server indistinguishably mixes all messages it receives within a round, a fixed duration of time. The ideal mixnet consists of a single server that collects messages from senders in each round, shuffles them, and forwards them to recipients with reencryption. Assuming that NN senders send messages in a round, the adversary’s posterior distribution over possible senders of a given message exiting the network is uniform with probability mass 1/N1/N, i.e., the ideal mixnet provides perfect anonymity. However, the ideal mixnet has two shortcomings: (1) it has a single point of failure — its only server — and (2) its throughput is limited to that of one server.

These shortcomings are addressed by a simple generalization called a parallel mixnet, which consists of ww servers that can communicate with each other pairwise. To send a message, the sender selects a random sequence of ℓ\ell servers from this set and sends its message to the first server in this sequence in the next available round.11 1 The discussion here also applies to a parallel mixnet that is structurally separated into ℓ\ell layers, each with ww distinct servers. Our analysis assumes this layered structure (section 2.1). At the end of each round, every server uniformly mixes the messages it has received in that round, and forwards each message to the next server on the message’s chosen path, after re-encryption (the last server on a message’s path delivers the message to the intended recipient). A parallel mixnet scales horizontally with the number of servers because the average steady-state load on a server is N/wN/w, which reduces with ww, and a parallel mixnet’s anonymity degrades gracefully with the fraction of servers the adversary can compromise. At the same time, because each message mixes indistinguishably with only a subset of other messages in each round (exactly the subset that share the router in that round), the anonymity provided by a parallel mixnet is probabilistic and not as high as that provided by the ideal mixnet.

A pioneering, foundational baseline is a quantitative tradeoff between strong anonymity, low bandwidth and low latency due to Das et al. [9], who establish an upper bound (not a lower bound) on the anonymity that a mixnet can provide for any fixed values of bandwidth and latency. This bound is quite loose as it is derived from general arguments, not a specific analysis of parallel mixnets, and it is orders of magnitude away from empirically estimated anonymity (see [22, Table 2]). At the other extreme, there are principled methods to estimate the degree of anonymity afforded by a parallel mixnet very precisely using empirical simulations, even with confidence intervals [22, 13], but these methods do not yield provable bounds.

Karaoke [19] and systems related to it such as Yodel [20], Groove [2] and Stadium [29] are highly scalable parallel mixnets that rely on additional noise (chaff) messages between pairs of servers to create specific “gadgets” (patterns of message flows) with high probability. Analyzing the probability with which such gadgets exist and relying on a relational argument, Karaoke proves that any two sent messages become indistinguishable to an adversary with very high probability after a few rounds of mixing. The property, which we call (ε,δ)(\varepsilon,\delta)-message indistinguishability, works as follows. Suppose that a rational adversary wants to determine where a specific entering message exits the mixnet in a specific run of the mixnet. Based on its observation of message routing during the run, the adversary can assign posterior odds to each message in the network, representing its a posteriori belief that this message is the message it is tracking. Figure 1 illustrates how the adversary calculates these odds after observing the full routing in a run of the system (a posteriori): At each routing step on a server, the adversary adds all the incoming odds on the server and divides them evenly among the outgoing messages.

papers.title: Indentation of pre-tensioned cortex-like fibre networks: tension, local stretching and the signature of defect architecture
papers.abstract: Indentation is widely used to infer the mechanical state of biological materials like the actomyosin cortex. It reduces a single force-indentation curve to an apparent modulus. The cortex, however, is a pre-tensioned, heterogeneous fibre network. We show that this inference is ambiguous. The same amount of weakening can leave the indentation force unchanged or lower it tenfold, depending on where it lies relative to the probe. The force reflects how the probe couples to the tensioned, load-bearing structure, not the amount of weakening. We combine molecular dynamics simulations of a pressure-loaded, crosslinked fibre network indented by a rigid sphere with a continuum membrane solution. We represent the simulated force-depth response by a two-term fit, $F\propto a\delta+b\delta^{3/2}$, with $a$ reflecting the global tension, and $b$ the stiffening with depth. At a fixed fraction of weakened bonds, diffuse weakening lowers the force by a factor of about 1.5. A weak cluster beneath the probe lowers it 8-12-fold, because the slack cluster decouples the probe from the tension. When the clusters are displaced from the contact, the force returns to within 15% of the healthy value. Two opposite effects cancel. The clusters soften the whole layer, which lowers its tension and the force. But they also channel the load through the intact network beneath the probe, which stiffens it locally and raises the force. The shape of the curve retains what the force level hides. The coefficient $a$ reflects the softened layer when clusters beside the probe keep the force near the healthy value. The local exponent $\alpha=\mathrm{d}\ln F/\mathrm{d}\ln\delta$ increases with depth in every configuration except when a cluster lies beneath the probe, where the two-term form no longer applies. Detecting localised weakening requires spatial sampling and analysis of the curve shape, not a single fitted modulus.

papers.title: Fragmented Markers, Mixed Results: A Systematic Review of AI Coding Assistants and Developer Productivity
papers.abstract:
AI coding assistants are increasingly embedded in software engineering practice, yet the literature still offers no cumulative, easily interpretable picture of their effects on software developer productivity. The central problem is not a lack of studies, but a lack of comparability: prior work operationalizes productivity through heterogeneous markers, settings, and reporting styles, making cross-study conclusions difficult. To address this, we conduct a staged systematic literature review. In the first stage, we synthesize studies that explicitly examine developer productivity. In the second, we extend the scope to productivity-related developer outcomes using SPACE as a theory-informed lens, capturing human-centered evidence that explicit productivity studies often omit. Across both stages, we analyze how productivity is operationalized, which confounding factors are discussed, and how reported effects are distributed.
  We identify 187 unique productivity and productivity-related markers, while individual studies typically only use five, revealing a broad but highly fragmented evidence base. Explicit productivity research is dominated by time-, output-, and artifact-oriented proxies, whereas the broader SPACE-aligned corpus makes satisfaction, psychological aspects, and well-being substantially more visible. Reported effects are often positive, but this pattern is stronger in perceived and tendency-based findings than in objective or statistically evaluated ones. Overall, the literature suggests that AI coding assistants can support productivity, but current evidence does not yet support simple, context-independent conclusions. The key contribution of this review is therefore a structured basis for making productivity evidence more interpretable, multidimensional, and comparable across studies.

Despite the growing number of studies on AI coding assistants, the evidence on developer productivity remains difficult to interpret. Reported effects vary substantially across studies: some find large time savings when completing a task(Peng et al., 2023), no statistically significant time savings in some phases(Borg et al., 2025), and some even slower task completion(Becker et al., 2025). These differences are not surprising: studies examine different kinds of tasks (researcher-designed exercises(Peng et al., 2023), realistic maintenance tasks(Borg et al., 2025), and real repository issues(Becker et al., 2025)) and use highly heterogeneous productivity measures. This comparability problem is not merely a methodological inconvenience, but directly affects the conclusions that researchers and practitioners draw from the literature. When results from fundamentally different study settings are interpreted side by side as if they were equivalent, the field risks overgeneralizing effects that may depend on task type, population, study environment, or unreported contextual factors. The consequences are twofold: practitioners may base adoption decisions on evidence from study designs that do not reflect realistic software engineering work, and researchers may repeatedly reproduce similar weaknesses because the literature lacks a structured overview of which findings are comparable, under what conditions, and with which confounders in mind. The key question for a review is therefore not only what effects have been reported, but whether existing syntheses make those effects interpretable and comparable in the first place.

We address this gap with a staged systematic literature review (SLR) designed to improve the interpretability and comparability of evidence on AI coding assistants’ effects on software developers’ productivity. The staged design reflects two analytically distinct synthesis objectives. Explicit productivity studies provide the clearest basis for analyzing how productivity is defined, measured, reported, and under which conditions effects emerge. At the same time, productivity is widely understood as multidimensional, and prior work does not consistently label all developer-centered, productivity-relevant outcomes as productivity. papers.title: Language Models Can Rewrite Their Own Weights
papers.abstract: Language models are trained once, frozen and deployed: improving one again takes another training run, and a prompt, a scaffold or extra computation at inference is gone once the task ends. A frontier model has been shown to edit the weights of a much smaller one. We ask whether a model can rewrite its own weights to make itself better, and find that it can, by its own reasoning, with no gradients and no training; we call this self-rewriting. Given its weights, graded answers and the ability to run itself, a 27B model diagnoses its failure and edits the weights behind it. It surpasses itself: its own edit makes it 6.6 points more accurate on 490 problems it never saw, in a test fixed in advance, and another session's edit also makes it significantly better. It keeps getting better: it submits an edit only when its own tests support it, each edit replacing the last, and over its first eight such sessions its accuracy only rises. Unlike test-time scaling, the gain persists in its weights and adds no cost per answer; unlike training, it needs no pre- or post-training infrastructure, only an open model and hours on one GPU. It repairs a damaged copy of itself: it locates the corrupted matrix and rewrites it with values of its own, never reading the undamaged weights; found on text math problems alone, the repair lifts the copy on six image benchmarks it never saw from 7% to 70% accuracy, 83% of the undamaged model's. And the ability emerges with scale: across four sizes of one family, the 2B model makes no edit and the 4B and 9B models break themselves; only the 27B model works on itself as a human would, comparing its hidden states on answers that finish and on answers that run out of tokens, weakening the direction that separates them. Like a human, a model need not separate training from inference; improving a language model may come to take a conversation rather than a training run.

A language model can rewrite its own weights to make itself better, by its own reasoning and in one conversation, and this ability emerges with scale. A language model is trained once, frozen and deployed. Improving it again takes people who know pre-training and post-training, large clusters and a training pipeline; what a user can change by talking to it is its prompt, and a prompt is gone once the task changes. A human does not separate the two: the same brain that does the work changes itself, from each success and failure, with no separate training run. The edited model needs no new prompt, no scaffold around it and no extra computation per answer: the improvement lives in its weights.

Given its own weights and the ability to run itself, the model edits itself; the edit it keeps is checked once on practice problems it cannot otherwise use, and the model decides itself whether to submit it. Over the first eight such sessions, the model in use only gets better (figure 1): two of the three edits it submits make it significantly more accurate on new problems than the model it started as, fewer of its answers run out of tokens, and in five more sessions it withdraws and stays as it was (table 13). The model surpasses itself, with no pre-training or post-training. Given a copy of itself in which one block of weights is overwritten with noise, so that it solves almost nothing, it locates the corrupted matrix and repairs it: like an injured animal that recovers without being raised anew, the copy regains what it lost with no retraining, by a fix the model finds itself. It never reads its undamaged weights and does not restore them: the values it writes in the corrupted rows are its own (Sec. E.3). Like a physician who falls ill and treats themself, the model that fails is the one that examines the failure and changes what produces it, and the change stays in its weights.

papers.title: From Human Videos to Bimanual Dexterous Manipulation Data: Confidence-Guided RL Refinement of Video Priors
papers.abstract: Collecting demonstrations for bimanual dexterous manipulation is costly, motivating the use of human videos as a source of robot training data. However, uncertainty in video-derived motion estimates and differences between human and robot embodiments make direct motion transfer challenging. In this work, we introduce PriDex, a framework that transforms human-video Priors into executable robot Dexterous manipulation demonstrations through reinforcement learning in simulation. PriDex preserves task-relevant interaction structure while allowing embodiment-specific behavior to be regenerated for the robot. Human-object interactions provide affordance cues for selecting task-relevant, robot-specific grasps from geometry-based candidates. For motion refinement, object trajectories provide a task-level reference, while relative bimanual wrist trajectories offer complementary guidance for coordinated motion. Since object-motion estimates can become unreliable under occlusion or visual ambiguity, PriDex uses object-motion confidence to adaptively balance these two priors, emphasizing object-level guidance when confidence is high and increasing the contribution of wrist-level guidance as confidence decreases. Reinforcement learning refines these video-derived priors under the robot's kinematic and physical constraints, and the resulting policies are rolled out to generate robot demonstrations for training a vision-based diffusion policy. We evaluate PriDex on four bimanual dexterous manipulation tasks, including pouring, sweeping into a dustpan, bottle-cap unscrewing, and plate cleaning, assessing both simulation-based robot data generation and downstream visuomotor policy learning.

papers.intro:
Learning bimanual dexterous manipulation requires large amounts of high-quality robot interaction data. Collecting such data directly on robots is particularly demanding for high-dimensional dexterous systems, where demonstrations must coordinate two arms, multiple fingers, and contact-rich object interactions over extended horizons. Human manipulation videos provide an appealing alternative: they are abundant, naturally capture coordinated bimanual behavior, and contain rich cues about where and how objects are manipulated [1, 2]. However, these videos do not directly provide supervision that can be readily transferred to robots. Human and robot hands differ substantially in morphology and kinematics, while object and hand motions recovered from video can be inaccurate due to occlusion, partial observability, and reconstruction uncertainty.

Collecting such data directly on robots is particularly demanding for high-dimensional dexterous systems, where demonstrations must coordinate two arms, multiple fingers, and contact-rich object interactions over extended horizons. However, these videos do not directly provide supervision that can be readily transferred to robots. Human and robot hands differ substantially in morphology and kinematics, while object and hand motions recovered from video can be inaccurate due to occlusion, partial observability, and reconstruction uncertainty.

To extract more actionable supervision from human videos, recent approaches reconstruct 3D hand and object motions and use the resulting trajectories for retargeting, reinforcement learning, or simulation-based skill acquisition [3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8]. However, reconstructed motions remain only approximate proxies for robot behavior. Their quality can vary due to partial observability and reconstruction uncertainty, while even accurately recovered human motions may not transfer directly to a robot because of differences in kinematics and collision constraints. Consequently, video-derived motion should not be treated as uniformly reliable or directly executable robot supervision. The key challenge is therefore not simply how faithfully to reproduce reconstructed human motion, but which cues from the video should guide robot learning and when.

Our key insight is to separate transferable interaction structure from embodiment-specific motion when transferring human demonstrations to robots. Human videos provide useful cues about where interaction occurs and how the manipulated object evolves, whereas exact human grasp configurations and hand motions are strongly embodiment-dependent and therefore need not be reproduced by the target robot. We therefore preserve interaction cues that transfer more naturally across embodiments, while allowing grasping and motion details to be regenerated and refined for the robot. This reframes human-video transfer from reproducing human motion to preserving the interaction structure most relevant to successful execution.

For motion learning, object trajectories provide the primary reference for the desired evolution of the manipulated object. PriDex then uses object-motion confidence to adaptively balance the two guidance signals, emphasizing object-level supervision when confidence is high and placing greater weight on wrist-level guidance as confidence decreases. Reinforcement learning refines these video-derived priors under the robot’s kinematic and physical constraints, producing coordinated behaviors without requiring exact reproduction of the demonstrated human motion. Finally, the learned policies are rolled out in simulation to generate bimanual dexterous robot demonstrations, which are subsequently distilled into a vision-based diffusion policy [11] for downstream visuomotor control.

We evaluate PriDex on four bimanual dexterous manipulation tasks from the EgoDex dataset [1], including sweeping, pouring, bottle-cap unscrewing, and plate cleaning. Starting from only three human videos per task, PriDex performs reinforcement learning in Isaac Sim [12] to expand these demonstrations into hundreds of robot trajectories for downstream policy learning. We evaluate the resulting data-generation pipeline through simulation RL and downstream visuomotor policy learning, examining both skill acquisition and the utility of the generated demonstrations.

papers.title: The metric theory of tracial matrix algebras does not converge
papers.abstract: We show that the theories of tracial matrix algebras and metric unitary groups do not converge with the dimension. In the main argument, we recover the canonical diagonal using spectral gap and internality. Uniform definability of the diagonal and its normalizer then transfers the distinct theories of universal sofic groups to matrix ultraproducts. The same methods show that isomorphisms preserve every internal subalgebra and give fixed finite distance formulas over six unitaries. Finally, we construct an explicit continuum family of matrix ultraproducts with distinct theories and trivial first-order fundamental groups.

papers.title: The Bessis Moussa Villani conjecture in finite von Neumann algebras
papers.abstract: We prove the Bessis--Moussa--Villani conjecture, which is known for matrix algebras, for bounded operators in a finite von Neumann algebra with a faithful normal tracial state. Following the approach of Heinavaara, for a pair of positive operators, we construct a tracial joint spectral measure on the punctured plane whose moments are the traces of symmetrized words. We construct a scalar measure by holomorphic spectral selection and a Lyapunov identity. An integral identity for its moments then gives positivity of two coordinate-weighted distributions. From these we obtain the planar measure and the Laplace representation of the trace exponential.

Hillar established descent results for the two letter counts; in particular, validity in one degree implies validity in every smaller degree [7, Theorem 1.7 and Corollary 1.8]. papers.title: Competing Magnetic Orders and Continuously Varying Exponents in $U(1)$ Spin Liquids
papers.abstract: Unequal couplings to a common emergent gauge field provide a continuous way to tune competing magnetic instabilities in an effective description of $U(1)$ spin-liquid mixtures. We study this mechanism in quantum electrodynamics in 2+1 dimensions with two families of four-component Dirac fermions. Combining a leading large-$N$ treatment with Schwinger--Dyson equations, we obtain chiral condensates representing N\'eel order in the two sectors. At fixed fermion number, the coupling ratio $\kappa=e_2^2/e_1^2$ controls which condensates develop. Depending on $N$, the phases with a single condensate are connected through either coexistence or a finite interval in which both fermion families remain gapless. The mass-generation thresholds are reciprocal, and the fermion gaps close with Miransky essential singularities. The renormalization group flow has a circular line of fixed points parametrized by the invariant ratio $\kappa$. At the calculated order, gauge-invariant staggered magnetization correlations have continuously varying exponents in the gapless regime, while the exponent for correlations between the two sectors is independent of $\kappa$. These results connect the competition between magnetic orders to a continuous family of critical theories and identify magnetic correlation signatures of the intervening gapless regime.

papers.title: A comparative exploration of Steinerberger curvature and resistance curvature in model and real-world complex networks
papers.abstract: Discrete curvature extends the concept of curvature from continuous spaces to discrete structures such as graphs and networks. It provides a mathematical framework for characterising local and global network geometry, that offers insights into structural properties such as connectivity and clustering. In this study, we investigate Steinerberger curvature (SBC) and resistance curvature (RC) and examine their relationships with established graph curvature measures, namely Forman-Ricci, Augmented Forman-Ricci, and Ollivier-Ricci curvatures, a notion of scalar sectional curvature, as well as conventional vertex-based measures. A systematic comparative analysis is conducted across various synthetic network models and real-world networks, focusing on curvature distributions, correlations with structural measures, and the identification of structurally important vertices through network disintegration experiments based on global efficiency. Our results show that SBC generally exhibits weaker correlations with other measures. On the other hand, RC is strongly positively correlated with established discrete Ricci curvature measures, whereas it is predominantly negatively correlated with conventional vertex-based measures like degree and centrality-based measures. Furthermore, RC achieves a reduction in communication efficiency comparable to or faster than established Ricci curvature measures. These findings suggest that SBC captures structural characteristics that are largely distinct from those reflected by other measures, while RC exhibits distinct structural associations and shows significant potential for identifying vertices critical to network connectivity.

papers.intro:
Curvature is a fundamental concept in differential geometry that describes the intrinsic and extrinsic geometric properties of spaces and their deviation from flat Euclidean geometry. In the classical setting, several notions of curvature have been developed to capture different aspects of geometry, including Gaussian curvature, mean curvature, sectional curvature, Ricci curvature, and scalar curvature [1, 2, 3]. With the development of discrete and combinatorial approaches to geometry, researchers have extended the concept of curvature beyond smooth manifolds to discrete structures such as graphs, simplicial complexes, and CW complexes [4]. These extensions aim to capture geometric information from combinatorial, metric, and topological properties without necessarily requiring an underlying smooth structure. Consequently, a variety of discrete curvature notions have emerged, each motivated by a different aspect of classical curvature or by a distinct mathematical framework. For example, Forman’s discretization is based on a combinatorial analogue of the classical Bochner Weitzenböck formula in differential geometry [5], Ollivier’s coarse Ricci curvature for metric spaces equipped with a measure or random walk [6, 7], and Bakry-Émery’s notion originated from a so called Bochner identity [2], as well as a notion of sectional curvature that provides a global perspective on geometry [8]. Also, a notion of resistance curvature was introduced by Devriendt and Lambiotte, based on effective resistance inspired by electrical circuit theory in [9].

First, these notions have been investigated primarily from a theoretical perspective and have later been applied to the analysis of complex networks and other discrete structures [10, 11, 12, 13]. Network science investigates the structural properties and organizational principles of networks composed of interconnected nodes and edges, with the aim of identifying common patterns as well as features that distinguish different classes of networks [14]. Networks provide a natural framework for representing complex systems arising in diverse fields, including biology, transportation, communication, and social sciences [15, 16, 17, 18]. To characterize the structure and organization of such systems, researchers have increasingly employed geometry-inspired measures that capture different aspects of network structure [10, 11, 19, 17, 18, 20].

To characterize the structure and organization of such systems, researchers have increasingly employed geometry-inspired measures that capture different aspects of network structure [10, 11, 19, 17, 18, 20].

In particular, discrete notions of curvature have attracted considerable attention as tools for investigating the local and global structural properties of complex networks [10, 11, 12, 13, 15]. By assigning curvature values commonly to vertices or edges, these approaches provide geometric perspectives on network structure and can help identify features such as bottlenecks, clustering, and community detection. Consequently, researchers have studied and applied several discrete curvature notions in network analysis, although their mathematical foundations and the structural characteristics they capture vary by definition; for details, see [21].

Consequently, researchers have studied and applied several discrete curvature notions in network analysis, although their mathematical foundations and the structural characteristics they capture vary by definition; for details, see [21].

In this study, we investigate Steinerberger curvature [22] and resistance curvature. The notion of resistance curvature was initially introduced by Devriendt and Lambiotte [9]. Subsequently, building on that work and connecting it to Steinerberger curvature [22], Devriendt, Ottolini, and Steinerberger [23] proposed a related formulation based on the effective resistance matrix. In the present work, we adopt the latter formulation and refer to it simply as resistance curvature throughout the article. Both notions provide ways to characterize the structural properties of networks through distance-based information. Unlike conventional graph measures, such as degree and centrality, which primarily describe local connectivity or a vertex’s position within the network, these curvatures incorporate global information [22, 23]. This makes them potentially useful tools for investigating structural patterns across different network topologies. We examine their behavior across different synthetic network models and real-world networks to understand how they vary with network topology. We also investigate their relationships with commonly used graph measures and established discrete Ricci curvature measures [14], including Forman–Ricci [5, 11] and Ollivier–Ricci curvature [6]. Additionally, we compare Steinerberger curvature and resistance curvature with scalar sectional curvature to identify similarities and differences in the structural information captured by these measures. Through these comparisons, we aim to determine whether Steinerberger curvature and resistance curvature capture structural characteristics that are not fully reflected by existing measures and to assess their potential as complementary tools for network analysis. It is worth clarifying that the resistance curvature introduced by Devriendt and Lambiotte [9] and the curvature defined by Devriendt, Ottolini, and Steinerberger [23] are essentially equivalent, differing only by a scalar factor at each vertex. The resistance curvature introduced by Devriendt and Lambiotte has also been used to establish theoretical relationships with Forman–Ricci and Ollivier–Ricci curvatures. However, subsequent studies have primarily focused on specific applications, such as graph neural networks (GNNs), hyperuniformity, and particular classes of graphs [24, 25, 26, 27]. Here, we undertake a systematic comparative study of these curvature measures across a range of synthetic network models and real-world networks, with the aim of providing a comprehensive understanding of their behaviour.

papers.title: A Universal $8$-Vertex Origami Torus Triangulation
papers.abstract:
An origami torus is a piecewise affine isometric embedding of a flat
  torus into $\R^3$. We prove that every flat torus is realized
  as an $8$-vertex origami torus based on the triangulation
  with degree sequence $4,6,6,6,6,6,7,7$. This provides an
  $8$-vertex universal triangulation for origami tori.

The Universality Theorem says that there is a single 88-vertex combinatorial type out of which you can build an origami torus of any shape you like. Our construction yields 22 continuous families of 88-vertex origami tori based on 𝒯⁡(46666677){\cal T\/}(46666677) which together realize all shapes. We do not know if a single continuous family suffices, but see Remark 3.3. Here 88 is as good as it gets: In [S1] it is proved that 77-vertex origami tori do not exist. See also [S2]. The Universality Theorem is the culmination of a series of results about origami tori, some quite recent. ∙\bullet In 1960, Y. Burago and V. Zalgaller [BZ1] give the first construction of origami tori. ∙\bullet In 1995, Y. Burago and V. Zalgaller [BZ2] prove that every lattice is realized by some combinatorial type. ∙\bullet In 2020, T. Tsuboi [T] gives explicit constructions which realize every lattice as an origami torus called a diplotorus (For the rectangular lattices one needs a modified construction.) P. Arnoux, S. Lelièvre, and A. Málaga [ALM] give an independent proof of the same result. The construction requires infinitely many combinatorial types. Diplotori were discovered by U. Brehm [Br] in 1978. See also [Se, §6]. ∙\bullet In 2023, F. Lazarus and F. Tallerie [LT] give a universal triangulation having 12171217 vertices. Their paper also has an excellent discussion of the various attempts made to realize all lattices as origami tori. ∙\bullet In 2025, R.E.S. [S1] constructs an 88-vertex origami torus and proves that a 77-vertex origami torus does not exist. See also [S2]. The 88-vertex origami tori in [S1] and [S2], called pup tents, have combinatorial type 𝒯⁡(66666666){\cal T\/}(66666666) and are symmetric with respect to order 22 rotation about the ZZ-axis. ∙\bullet In 2025, P.G.D. and R.E.S. [DS] prove that a lattice is realized by a pup tent provided that it is neither rectangular nor sharp rhombic. A lattice is rectangular if it is generated by a pair of perpendicular vectors and sharp rhombic if it is generated by a pair of equal-length vectors which make an angle of at most π/3\pi/3 with each other. When the angle is π/3\pi/3 you get the famous hexagonal lattice. Thus, almost every lattice is realized by a pup tent. In [DS] the authors speculate that perhaps the remaining lattices can be realized by 88-vertex origami tori without 22-fold symmetry. ∙\bullet In 2026, F. Lander [L] proves that the square lattice is realized by 𝒯⁡(66666666){\cal T\/}(66666666) and the hex lattice is realized by 𝒯⁡(46666677){\cal T\/}(46666677). These origami tori have no symmetries.

Writing down explicit origami tori seems quite difficult, partly because there are too many choices to make. The idea that emerged in [DS], and was used again in [L], is to work instead on the boundary of the space of origami tori, where faces collapse together and so make some of these choices for us. The most collapsed examples lie entirely in a plane; we find these first and then push them back inside. Here we carry this out for 𝒯⁡(46666677){\cal T\/}(46666677) and every lattice. papers.title: Second-class particle in ASEP. Rarefaction fan
papers.abstract: We study the asymptotic behavior of a second class particle in ASEP on the integer lattice. We prove a general formula for the distribution of its position at any fixed time for arbitrary initial conditions. As a first application, we obtain its limiting distribution for arbitrary initial conditions in the rarefaction fan case, generalizing the result of Cator--Pimentel from TASEP to ASEP.

papers.title: Probing Lorentz-violating electrodynamics with CMB polarization. II. Updated constraints and forecasts for the Simons Observatory and LiteBIRD
papers.abstract: We update the constraints on Lorentz-violating electrodynamics from the polarization of the cosmic microwave background (CMB). Within the minimal Standard Model Extension, we consider the renormalizable CPT-odd and CPT-even operators of the photon sector, which source cosmic birefringence and circular polarization, respectively. Combining Planck, Atacama Cosmology Telescope (ACT) and South Pole Telescope (SPT) temperature and $E$-mode data with $B$-mode measurements from BICEP/Keck, SPT-3G D1 and SPTpol, we constrain the CPT-odd coefficients to $|k^{(3)}_{(V)00}|<7.75\times10^{-45}$ GeV and $|\mathbf{k_{AF}}|<3.82\times10^{-45}$ GeV at 95% credible level. These are the strongest bounds to date from any probe, and are driven by the SPT-3G D1 $B$-mode data. For the first time in this type of analysis, we also include the Planck PR4 $EB$ spectrum, which yields a mild preference for a non-zero $|k^{(3)}_{(V)00}|$. For the CPT-even coefficient, we find $k_{F,E+B}<5.99\times10^{-32}$. Including the latest circular polarization measurements from the Cosmology Large Angular Scale Surveyor (CLASS) tightens this bound by about 7%. This is the first time that CMB circular polarization data contribute to constraining this coefficient. Finally, we forecast the sensitivity of the Simons Observatory (SO) and LiteBIRD. With linear polarization only, the two experiments are complementary, with SO tightening the CPT-even bound by about 30% and LiteBIRD the CPT-odd ones by 40 to 45%. Exploiting the sensitivity to circular polarization provided by the non-idealities of its half-wave plate, LiteBIRD could also improve the CPT-even bound by more than an order of magnitude.

papers.intro:
Lorentz invariance is one of the fundamental symmetries of modern physics, underlying both the Standard Model of particle physics and general relativity. Several approaches to quantum gravity nonetheless suggest that this symmetry might be violated at very high energies, with residual violations potentially surviving down to observable scales Mattingly (2005); Amelino-Camelia (2013); Addazi and others (2022). Searching for such violations is therefore a powerful way to probe physics beyond the Standard Model.

Lorentz invariance is one of the fundamental symmetries of modern physics, underlying both the Standard Model of particle physics and general relativity. Several approaches to quantum gravity nonetheless suggest that this symmetry might be violated at very high energies, with residual violations potentially surviving down to observable scales Mattingly (2005); Amelino-Camelia (2013); Addazi and others (2022). Searching for such violations is therefore a powerful way to probe physics beyond the Standard Model.

A general and widely used framework for parametrizing possible deviations from exact Lorentz invariance is the Standard Model Extension (SME) Colladay and Kostelecký (1998); Kostelecký and Mewes (2002), an effective field theory that extends the Standard Model by adding all Lorentz-violating (LV) operators consistent with the underlying gauge symmetries, organized by their mass dimension. In the photon sector, the leading renormalizable operators are a CPT-odd, dimension-3 term and a CPT-even, dimension-4 term. Both modify the propagation of photons, with an effect that grows with the distance they travel, making astrophysical and cosmological sources particularly sensitive probes. Among these, the cosmic microwave background (CMB) is the most distant source of electromagnetic radiation available in nature and is linearly polarized by Thomson scattering at recombination and reionization Hu and Dodelson (2002). Any modification of its polarization induced by these operators is therefore integrated over the longest possible path, so that even tiny Lorentz violations can leave a measurable imprint Kostelecký and Mewes (2007); Caloni et al. (2023). Concretely, the CPT-odd operator induces a rotation of the linear polarization plane of CMB photons, an effect known as cosmic birefringence; its time component sources an isotropic rotation, while its space components source an anisotropic one. The isotropic rotation gives rise to parity-violating E​BEB and T​BTB correlations, absent in the standard cosmological model, while both induce a leakage of EE- into BB-mode polarization. Isotropic birefringence is particularly relevant today, since analyses of Planck and Wilkinson Microwave Anisotropy Probe (WMAP) data have found hints of a non-zero rotation angle Minami and Komatsu (2020); Eskilt and Komatsu (2022); Diego-Palazuelos and others (2022), recently supported by a consistent measurement from the sixth data release (DR6) of the Atacama Cosmology Telescope (ACT) Diego-Palazuelos and Komatsu (2026). If confirmed to be of cosmological origin, and not due to a residual miscalibration of the detector polarization angles, such a signal would be evidence of parity-violating physics beyond the Standard Model. Proposed mechanisms include a pseudoscalar coupling between photons and an axion-like field Carroll et al. (1990); Carroll (1998); Li and Zhang (2008); Pospelov et al. (2009), which may constitute dark energy or dark matter Fujita et al. (2021); Obata (2022); Gasparotto and Obata (2022); Murai et al. (2023); Gasparotto and Sfakianakis (2023) or form networks of domain walls and cosmic strings Takahashi and Yin (2021); Kitajima et al. (2022); Jain et al. (2021); Ferreira et al. (2024), a vector Chern-Simons coupling between photons and the neutrino current in the presence of a large lepton asymmetry Geng et al. (2007); Zhou et al. (2023); Kasai and Obata (2026), and the LV electrodynamics considered in this work. The CPT-even operator, instead, converts linear into circular polarization, sourcing a non-zero V​VVV spectrum. Circular polarization is not generated by scattering at recombination, and the mechanisms that can produce it within the standard cosmological model yield a negligible signal Montero-Camacho and Hirata (2018); King and Lubin (2016). A detection of VV modes in the CMB would therefore be a signature of beyond-Λ\LambdaCDM physics Alexander et al. (2009); Ejlli (2018); Tizchang et al. (2016); Ejlli (2017); Inomata and Kamionkowski (2019); Bartolo et al. (2019); Hoseinpour et al. (2020); Bavarsad et al. (2010); Kushwaha and Jain (2026), including Lorentz violation.

(2021), we mapped the LV operators onto phenomenological parameters that source isotropic and anisotropic birefringence and circular polarization in the CMB, and constrained them with data from Planck 2018 Aghanim and others (2020c), BICEP/Keck 2018 Ade and others (2021) and ACT DR4 Aiola and others (2020). papers.title: Oblique incidence and non-commuting limits: a remark on the convergence of Fresnel integrals
papers.abstract: The Gaussian integrals of quantum mechanics and of paraxial optics are oscillatory and only conditionally convergent. Textbooks usually make them converge by adding a small imaginary part to the time or by analytic continuation. We point out that the one-dimensional Fresnel integral converges by itself, while in two dimensions the result depends on the shape of the expanding domain: over squares it converges, over discs it oscillates for ever. The second case is the field of a uniformly excited plane of dipoles, which Feynman uses to explain the refractive index. Lai, Lau and Wong showed that at oblique incidence the integral converges and that normal incidence is recovered in the limit; we note that the two limits do not commute, and that this provides a transparent introduction to the regularization of the time-sliced path integral, where the ordering of the integrations in time plays the role of the physical prescription.

papers.title: Potential theory for double phase equations with measure data
papers.abstract: We develop a potential theory for elliptic equations with double phase growth and signed measure data. We establish existence of solutions obtained by approximation, pointwise bounds for the flux in terms of linear Riesz potentials, and nonlinear potential estimates for the solution in terms of generalized Wolff potentials; a quantitative decay estimate for the flux excess is the main ingredient and also yields a potential criterion for gradient continuity. The results cover both singular and degenerate equations, including the range $p>n$.

papers.title: A PhEW Good Simulations: I. Galaxy Properties
papers.abstract: Although galactic outflows driven by stellar feedback are widely implemented in modern cosmological simulations, the interactions between them and the circumgalactic medium (CGM) remains poorly resolved. To overcome this limitation, we conduct a suite of cosmological simulations that use the PhEW (Physically Evolved Winds) subgrid model, which analytically tracks the exchange of mass, metals, momentum, and energy by winds with the ambient CGM using an algorithm based on high-resolution cloud-crushing simulations. Our results show that even without AGN feedback, our simulations are able to accurately reproduce the observed galactic stellar mass functions (GSMFs) and stellar mass-halo mass (SMHM) relations at $z\gtrsim 1$, after which the massive galaxies in our simulations start to overproduce stars. Our simulations also match the observed relations of $M_{\mathrm{HI}}-M_*$, $M_{\mathrm{H_2}}-M_*$, $Z_*-M_*$ and $Z_{\mathrm{ISM}}-M_*$. Taken together these results suggest that AGN feedback is much less important for galaxy formation and evolution than previously believed. However, like found in many previous simulations, the specific star formation rates (sSFRs) of our galaxies are significantly lower than those observed at $z\gtrsim1$ at all stellar masses. Significantly, we find that our results are robust against changes in the resolution and volume of our simulations, without the need to retune our wind parameters.

papers.intro:
Simulations have found that the baryon cycle dominates the formation and evolution of galaxies [1, 90]. The major ways that a galaxy can accrete gas, the fuel for star formation, are through cold-mode and hot-mode accretion of pristine gas, and through the re-accretion of gas previously expelled by the galaxy [40, 39, 59, 35]. Gas can be expelled by winds driven by supernovae or by supermassive black holes (AGN). Simulations find that wind re-accretion dominates for much of a galaxy’s later life while cold-mode accretion dominates at earlier times [59, 35]. In addition, the energy from supernova and AGN can prevent gas from accreting that would otherwise accrete [71, 84]. Hence, even the most basic properties of galaxies, e.g. their stellar mass, depend on a delicate balance between incoming and outflowing gas [61, 68], and this balance depends sensitively on how the ejected gas interacts with the gas in the halo of the galaxy, the CGM [83]. And any interactions with the CGM, e.g. exchanges of momentum, will determine exactly where the gas re-accretes, thus determining the structure of galaxies. Unfortunately, all of these processes occur on scales much smaller than those resolved by simulations of galaxy formation. This will be true for the foreseeable future.

Galactic outflows connect galaxies with the circumgalactic medium (CGM) and play a critical role in regulating star formation. There are two main sources that are believed to drive these outflows: stellar feedback, in which supernovae produced by star formation drive galactic winds (e.g. Oort and Spitzer 58, Chevalier and Clegg 12, Dekel and Silk 19, Heckman et al. 33, Geen et al. 27, Zhang 92), and active galactic nucleus feedback, in which supermassive black holes at the centers of galaxies can eject gas and energy into their surroundings (e.g. Scannapieco and Oh 72, Di Matteo et al. 20, Fabian 22, King and Pounds 42). This can be in the form of quasar winds (quasar mode), usually tied to high Eddington ratio accretion, or radio jets (radio mode), usually tied to low Eddington ratio accretion [22, 54, 32].

This can be in the form of quasar winds (quasar mode), usually tied to high Eddington ratio accretion, or radio jets (radio mode), usually tied to low Eddington ratio accretion [22, 54, 32].

On a galactic scale, outflows affect the star formation activities of galaxies in several ways. First, they can deplete galaxies of their cold gas, although this gas can return to fuel future star formation (e.g. Oppenheimer et al. 59). Second, they can heat up the CGM and make it harder for the central galaxies to accrete gas (e.g. Scannapieco et al. 71, van de Voort et al. 84). Third, they can also carry metals synthesized by the stars, which, when mixed into the CGM, increase the cooling rate of its gas (e.g. Scannapieco and Broadhurst 69, Thacker et al. 81). The enriched gas may then be accreted by the galaxies at higher rates, thereby enhancing their star formation.

The enriched gas may then be accreted by the galaxies at higher rates, thereby enhancing their star formation.

While the first effect is direct, the other two, and the return of ejected cold gas, all involve interactions between the outflows and the CGM. Understanding these interactions is, therefore, vital to our understanding of the self-regulation of star formation and the baryon cycle of galaxies. However, they are very complicated in nature. Galactic outflows are widely observed to be clumpy, multiphase, and turbulent [65, 85]. To look into their interactions with the CGM, a number of small-scale cloud-crushing simulations have been conducted [45, 70, 7, 74, 53, 29, 5, 3, 4, 8], which hydrodynamically evolve a single, cool cloud moving supersonically relative to a hot ambient gas. These simulations found that the clouds develop complex internal structures as they gradually mix with the ambient gas. A wide range of physical processes, including radiative cooling, thermal conduction, magnetic fields and non-equilibrium chemistry, can significantly affect the evolution of the cloud. Moreover, they demonstrate that extreme resolution, down to sub-parsec levels [53], is needed to fully resolve the fragmentation of the clouds.

Moreover, they demonstrate that extreme resolution, down to sub-parsec levels [53], is needed to fully resolve the fragmentation of the clouds.

This poses a significant challenge to cosmological and galaxy formation simulations. Even in zoom-in simulations that focus on the CGM, such as the FOGGIE project [51], the spatial resolution in the CGM is much coarser than the sub-parsec scales needed. The situation is worse in cosmological simulations, such as EAGLE [73], IllustrisTNG [62], and SIMBA [14], which have even poorer resolution. In these simulations, a number of sophisticated subgrid models have been implemented to track the feedback processes that drive galactic outflows. However, none of these simulations include models that evolve these outflows after they are launched. Instead, the outbound winds are temporarily decoupled from the surrounding medium and, once they reach the CGM, are simply treated as regular gas particles and evolved by the hydrodynamic code. This causes the evolution of the outflows to be very poorly resolved, which in turn makes some of the properties of galaxies in these simulations sensitive to changes in the resolution. For example, Pillepich et al. [62] found that the galaxy stellar mass function (GSMF) of IllustrisTNG shifts significantly with resolution. Likewise, in the SIMBA simulation suite, the wind launch parameters have to be retuned for different resolutions to match the GSMF [14].
