To overcome these limitations, we have developed the PhEW (Physically Evolved Winds) model (Huang et al. 37, Huang et al. 36, 37 and 36 hereafter), a subgrid model for cosmological hydrodynamic simulations that tracks galactic outflows from stellar feedback. In this model, when an outbound wind particle reaches the CGM, it is treated as a collection of identical clouds (cloudlets) that are going through a cloud-crushing process. Instead of letting the hydrodynamic code handle their evolution, we evolve them analytically using a routine that is calibrated against high-resolution cloud-crushing simulations conducted by Scannapieco and Brüggen [70] and Brüggen and Scannapieco [7]. As these cloudlets travel through the CGM, we track the exchange of mass, metals, momentum, and energy between them and their neighboring CGM gas particles, as well as the evolution of their velocities. This enables us to model the interactions between the outflows and the CGM, and the role they play in regulating the star-forming activities of galaxies, in a physical way that is based on the results of small-scale cloud-crushing simulations. In addition, as long as the hot, ambient gas in the CGM is itself well-resolved, the PhEW model evolves the winds independently of the resolution of the simulation. Since the development of the PhEW model, several other groups have proposed other subgrid wind evolution models that are based on similar principles (e.g. Weinberger and Hernquist 87, Smith et al. 77).

papers.title: Abelian varieties with homotheties
papers.abstract: In 1980, Bogomolov proved that the $\ell$-adic Galois image of an Abelian variety over a number field contains an open subgroup of the homotheties. In 1986, Serre refined that result, showing that the homotheties coming from the Galois side were uniformly bounded in $\ell$ inside the homotheties of the codomain of the representation. In a 2007 paper, Zarhin shows that Bogomolov's conclusion can fail in non-trivial cases for global function fields. We prove a suitable analogue of Serre's results over finitely generated fields of positive characteristic. As a consequence, we prove a new case of the 1978 conjecture by Geyer and Jarden.

papers.title: MI-Hyper: Generating Multiple Instance Models for Weight Space Transfer Learning in Histopathology via Mixed Tasks Pretrained HyperNetwork
papers.abstract: Zero-shot whole-slide image (WSI) prediction aims to generalize to new pathology tasks without parameter updates at deployment. MI-Zero makes these predictions by pooling patch-text similarities. Conditional weight generation, combined with supervision from diverse pathology tasks, offers an alternative: learning to construct predictive rules from task descriptions. We introduce MI-Hyper, a hypernetwork pretrained across mixed tasks to generate the aggregation and classification weights of multiple instance learning (MIL) models. We first train the generator and a shared MIL basis jointly using source labels. We then freeze the basis and refine the generator. The generated task weights are reused across cases. Across 308 tasks from 52 pathology datasets, MI-Hyper improves mean AUC, balanced accuracy and macro-F1 over MI-Zero by 1.85, 1.17 and 0.57 percentage points, respectively. On some molecular prediction tasks, both AUC and balanced accuracy improve by more than 20 points. These results support task-conditioned weight generation as a promising approach to weight-space transfer for long-sequence modeling.

Zero-shot whole-slide image (WSI) prediction seeks to reuse a trained system for new pathology tasks without task-specific optimization at deployment. Because the same slide can support subtyping, grading and molecular prediction, the relevant tissue evidence depends on the endpoint. A zero-shot predictor must therefore select and combine patterns across long patch sequences according to the task.

Pathology foundation models provide a common starting point through reusable representations at the patch and whole-slide levels [30, 11]. For patch-based prediction, multiple instance learning (MIL) converts a bag of representations into a slide-level output through aggregation and classification [18, 32]. Aggregation and classification parameters determine how tissue features contribute to a particular endpoint. The remaining question is how to obtain these parameters for a new task without additional target-task optimization.

This language interface also suggests a complementary route: generating the parameters that govern MIL aggregation and classification from the descriptions.

papers.title: Second-Order Polarization Propagator Approximation to the Quadratic Unitary Coupled Cluster Framework I: First-Order Properties
papers.abstract: We have developed a new formulation for calculating first-order properties in the quadratic unitary coupled-cluster singles and doubles (qUCCSD) method, using a second-order polarizable propagator approximation. The accuracy and reliability of this new framework of the proposed approach have been assessed through the calculation of ground- and excited-state dipole moments and oscillator strengths for a set of small molecules. The Hermiticity of the UCC similarity-transformed Hamiltonian allows molecular properties to be evaluated without introducing left-hand eigenvectors, thereby simplifying the theoretical formulation and computational procedure. Furthermore, the proposed formulation preserves the size-intensivity of transition moments, a property that is not generally guaranteed within the conventional non-Hermitian equation-of-motion coupled-cluster framework. To assess the performance of the proposed method, we have benchmarked both ground- and excited-state properties for 11 small molecules against the extrapolated full configuration interaction (exFCI) reference values and compared with the conventional coupled cluster singles and doubles (CCSD) and third-order algebraic diagrammatic construction (ADC(3)) results. The qUCCSD method yields average errors comparable to those of CCSD while demonstrating significantly improved accuracy over the ADC(3) method.

papers.intro: Excited-state properties such as dipole moments, transition intensities etc. play a central role in understanding spectroscopic phenomena, photochemical processes, and energy transfer mechanisms, making their accurate theoretical prediction is essential for the characterization of electronically excited states.[12, 27, 57, 84, 59, 36, 33, 19, 25] Wave-function-based many-body methods can be improved systematically, but excited states are harder to describe than the ground state: they are more sensitive to electron correlation and near-degeneracies, and several electronic configurations often have to be treated on an equal footing. The first-order properties corresponding to a particular state can be evaluated in two different ways: either as expectation values of the corresponding operators or as energy derivatives with respect to an external perturbation associated with the observable. These two formulations are equivalent when the Hellmann-Feynman [28, 24] theorem is satisfied; however, they may differ, particularly for approximate wave functions. The accuracy of the calculated first-order properties depends upon the underlying electronic structure method. Coupled cluster theory (CC) [14, 56, 4, 3, 16, 76] has long been regarded as the gold standard for ground-state electronic structure calculations due to its size extensivity, systematic improvability, and favorable accuracy–cost balance. Extensions of CC theory to excited states, such as equation-of-motion coupled cluster (EOM-CC)[67, 77, 23, 15] and linear response coupled cluster (LR-CC)[38, 54, 55, 11] formalisms, have been very successful for single-reference systems. However, these approaches rely on a linear parameterization of excitation operators and are based on the non-Hermitian similarity-transformed Hamiltonian. [22, 70] The non-Hermitian nature of the CC ansatz makes the first-order property calculations using analytic derivatives at least twice as expensive as that of the energy calculation. In the expectation-value coupled-cluster (XCC) formalism, the energy functional gives rise to a nonterminating expansion that requires an appropriate truncation scheme. Moreover, owing to the nonvariational nature of conventional truncated coupled-cluster theory, first-order properties evaluated using a perturbatively truncated expectation-value expression generally differ from those obtained through analytic energy derivatives.[6] In addition, evaluating excited-state expectation values requires solving the corresponding left and right eigenvalue problems. This approach is commonly used in equation-of-motion coupled-cluster (EOM-CC) theory, where additional sets of amplitudes are required, especially in derivative-based formulations. One of the formal problems of the EOM-CC expectation value approach is that the transition properties are not size-intensive.[37] In recent years, unitary coupled cluster (UCC)[43, 62, 31, 6] theory has emerged as an attractive alternative to conventional CC formulations. By employing an anti-Hermitian cluster operator, UCC leads to a Hermitian similarity-transformed Hamiltonian, which can be advantageous in situations where conventional CC has difficulties. [49, 81, 26, 40, 35] Also, UCC has been extensively explored in recent years due to its application in quantum simulation and variational quantum algorithms;[53, 9, 8] however, its application on classical computers remains rather limited. A major problem of the UCC ansatz in classical computers is that the similarity-transformed Hamiltonian does not terminate naturally. As a result, practical implementations require an explicit truncation of the expansion, which can compromise the size extensivity of the resulting energy. [61] To overcome this issue, Bartlett and co-workers proposed a perturbative truncation of the UCC energy functional denoted as UCC(n)(n), where nn specifies the perturbation order. [5] This scheme retains the size extensivity of the energy and can be systematically extended to include triple and quadruple excitation operators.[7] However, this approximation often fails due to the poor convergence behavior of the underlying low-order Møller-Plesset (MP) perturbation, particularly for larger and complex molecular systems. [63] Recent developments introduced a truncation of the UCC expansion by limiting the rank of the nested commutators using the Bernoulli expansion of the similarity-transformed Hamiltonian.[46] This has demonstrated improved performance in systems where the MP series exhibits poor convergence.[63] Recently, Liu et al. proposed an alternative to UCC(n) based on a perturbative truncation of the Bernoulli expansion, referred to as UCCn, which is closely related to the ADC hierarchy.[46, 29, 45] Despite these attractive features, reports of property calculations with UCC-based methods remain limited. Bartlett and co-workers have reported an analytical gradient technique for the UCC(4) method. [83] Dreuw and co-workers have recently reported the ground and excited-state dipole moments using the UCC3 method. [30] Although UCC3 can be used for property calculations, it often gives less accurate results than the standard CCSD method[51]. DePrince and co-workers found that the commutator-based truncation approach of UCC reaches the full configuration interaction (FCI) limit more quickly and produces more accurate results than methods that rely on perturbative truncation.[63] Cheng and co-workers introduced a commutator-based, non-perturbative quadratic unitary coupled cluster method with single and double excitations (qUCCSD), demonstrating accuracy comparable to the conventional CC approach for energy calculations.[47] We have extended this formalism to the relativistic regime and computed ground-state correlation energies and properties using both UCC3 and qUCCSD [50, 51]. The qUCCSD method has shown significant improvement over UCC3 for ground-state property calculations owing to a more complete treatment of single excitations[51]. Perturbative triples corrections to the unitary coupled cluster method have also been developed.[85, 52] The qUCCSD method extends the standard UCC framework by explicitly retaining terms quadratic in the cluster operator in the amplitude equations. Although qUCCSD has shown promising performance for ground-state energies and properties,[48, 50] excited-state properties have not yet been studied within this framework. In addition to the analytic derivative and expectation value approaches, there exists a third approach for property calculation using the polarization propagator approximation.[58, 60, 1] The second-order polarization propagator approximation (SOPPA) has been successfully used in the literature for property calculation[32, 69, 34]. The use of coupled cluster-based propagators, where coupled cluster amplitudes and eigenvectors are used with the second (or higher) order approximation, has been found to be an accurate and inexpensive approach for the calculation of properties[41]. The algebraic diagrammatic construction (ADC)[72, 82, 74, 20] can be derived as a propagator approximation to unitary coupled cluster[65]. Using the same analogy as the coupled cluster propagator, the qUCCSD method can be combined with the second-order intermediate state representation (ISR)[73, 71, 74, 20] as a simple way to calculate ground- and excited-state properties. The aim of this paper is to calculate the ground and excited-state first-order properties using the second-order polarization propagator approximation of the qUCCSD method. The paper is organized as follows: Section II provides the theoretical description of the method, Section III presents the computational details, and Section IV provides the results and discussion for the selected systems. Finally, conclusions are summarized in Section V.

papers.title: ROSMonitoring in Action: Runtime Monitoring and Enforcement for ROS 2 Actions
papers.abstract: Robotic applications often rely on long-running operations, such as navigation, manipulation, and inspection, which in ROS~2 are commonly implemented as actions. Unlike topics and services, actions involve a structured lifecycle comprising goal submission and acceptance, feedback, status updates, result retrieval, and cancellation. Existing versions of ROSMonitoring support topics and services, but do not reconstruct this lifecycle or expose action-level events to a runtime-verification oracle. In this paper, we extend ROSMonitoring with runtime monitoring and enforcement for ROS~2 actions. Actions are declared directly in the monitoring configuration and automatically instrumented through the underlying ROS~2 communication endpoints. The generated monitor reconstructs action-level events, correlates them through goal identifiers, maintains the state of active goals, and translates violations into protocol-aware enforcement operations. These include goal rejection, cancellation, message suppression, and protocol-compliant responses generated directly by the monitor when the original communication cannot be forwarded. We evaluate the implementation through controlled stress tests that vary the number of action invocations, workload size, and clientâ€“server topology. The results show approximately linear growth in monitoring cost with repeated action invocations under a fixed workload, while larger action workloads and a greater number of configured clientâ€“server pairs introduce additional overhead. These results characterise the scaling behaviour of the current implementation under the tested sequential workloads while highlighting the main performance limitations of the current synchronous implementation.

papers.title: Holomorphic Vector Bundles on the Quantum Projective Line
papers.abstract: We study Birkhoff--Grothendieck splitting for holomorphic vector bundles on the quantum projective line in the Dolbeault-module framework. We prove that every polynomial holomorphic bundle admitting a finite filtration by standard line objects is a direct sum of standard lines, with uniquely determined splitting integers. The proof uses a Dolbeault differential graded category and the two-arrow Kronecker quiver. For a three-parameter rank-two extension family, we determine the splitting types and distinguish the nonzero splitting strata by the determinant of a quantum connecting map. For general non-diagonal rank-two connections, we derive noncommutative Riccati equations for invariant graph submodules and formulate the global splitting problem in terms of holomorphic projectors. We also discuss twisted positive Hochschild cocycles and formulate a variational principle and a conformal-stability conjecture. On the algebraic side, we explain why both the bare sheaf category of the quantum projective line and the Artin--Zhang category of the quantum plane inherit classical Birkhoff--Grothendieck splitting. We distinguish these results from unrestricted standard-line splitting, which fails for polynomial gauges, and outline a differential quantum GAGA programme with explicit attention to regularity and equivariance.

papers.intro:
The Birkhoff–Grothendieck theorem classifies holomorphic vector bundles on the Riemann sphere: every bundle EE of rank rr admits a decomposition E≃𝒪⁡(k1)⊕⋯⊕𝒪⁡(kr),k1≥⋯≥kr,E\simeq\mathcal{O}(k_{1})\oplus\cdots\oplus\mathcal{O}(k_{r}),\qquad k_{1}\geq\cdots\geq k_{r}, (1.1) with uniquely determined integers k1,…,krk_{1},\ldots,k_{r} [Bir09, Gro57, HM82]. By GAGA, its algebraic and holomorphic formulations agree [Ser56]. The theorem can therefore be expressed in terms of ∂¯\bar{\partial}-operators, locally free sheaves, or factorization of transition matrices over ℂ⁡[z,z−1]\mathbb{C}[z,z^{-1}]. In noncommutative geometry these descriptions need not agree. A quantum Birkhoff–Grothendieck problem must first specify the underlying geometry, the category of bundles, and the allowed isomorphisms.

This paper studies the splitting problem from differential and sheaf-theoretic viewpoints. On the differential side, we work with the holomorphic structures of Khalkhali, Landi and van Suijlekom (KLvS) on the standard Podleś sphere [KLvS11]. We prove splitting for polynomial holomorphic bundles admitting a finite filtration by standard line objects, and determine explicit rank-two splitting strata using the Kronecker quiver. For general non-diagonal connections, we formulate the search for invariant line summands as a noncommutative Riccati problem. We distinguish holomorphic splitting into possibly nonstandard line objects from splitting into standard lines, and explain why retaining arbitrary equivariance can obstruct the latter. papers.title: TeleChat to Xing4: Advancing Frontier Agentic Models on Domestic Chips and Frameworks
papers.abstract: We present Xing 4, a series of large language models that extends the TeleChat lineage through coordinated advances in model architecture and training infrastructure on Ascend. This report describes the design principles and systems engineering behind the series, spanning architecture selection, large-scale pretraining, and reasoning and agentic post-training. We study how sparse activation, attention design, model depth and width, and speculative decoding balance model capacity with computation, memory access, and execution overhead. Our pretraining infrastructure builds on MindSpore HyperParallel, combining topology-aware hybrid sharding, efficient distributed optimizer execution, and coordinated management of long-sequence workloads and activation memory. CPU affinity and core isolation further reduce host scheduling interference. Together, these mechanisms support the pretraining of a 285B-parameter model on 8,192 Ascend 910C cards, providing a concrete setting for the architectural and systems studies. For post-training, we introduce TeleGym, a unified agent execution platform that connects execution, evaluation, and trajectory construction to policy optimization. Disaggregated asynchronous execution, bounded oversampling, and partial rollout accommodate heterogeneous task durations while preserving trajectory continuity across policy updates. Together, these advances establish an Ascend-oriented training foundation for the continued development of Xing 4 across model scales and increasingly demanding reasoning and agent workloads.

papers.title: Search for UHE photon sources using direction-time clustering algorithms with a BDT particle discriminant
papers.abstract: Direction-time clustering methods for neutral particle searches are motivated by the possibility that ultra-high-energy (UHE) neutral particles are produced during flaring periods of various astrophysical sources. In this scenario, clusters of events correlated in both arrival direction and time would be generated, which, when observed, would indicate a neutral-particle flare, and a non-observation would provide upper limits on fluxes for point-like sources. Focusing on UHE photon searches, an improvement of the sensitivity of direction-time clustering methods by the application of different photon tags, such as the depth of the extensive air shower maximum (X_max), the lateral distribution of the total signal across an array of detectors (S_b), or a cumulative signal trace-based discriminant variable (C_t), is investigated. A Boosted Decision Tree (BDT) is used to combine multiple observables, by which photon tagging is optimized and photon/hadron separation is improved. The number of events required to identify a photon flare is thereby further reduced compared to using individual photon tags, across a range of flare durations. The possibility of extending the known and assumed PeVatron photon sources into the UHE regime by applying these clustering methods to existing and future observatory data is also discussed. The discovery of UHE neutral particles would mark the next milestone in multimessenger astrophysics, by which a new window onto the non-thermal universe would be opened.

papers.intro:
Ultra-high-energy cosmic rays (UHECRs; E>1017​e​VE>10^{17}eV) are particles with the highest measured energies; however, associating them with any known astrophysical objects or events has yet to yield positive results[1]. If some of the UHECRs measured from Earth originated from some astrophysical flaring events (point sources), we expect them to be clustered with directional and temporal correlations. Detecting such direction-time clustering will be more probable for UHE neutral particles, like photons, as they will not be deflected by cosmic magnetic fields on their path to Earth. Although no astrophysical photons have been measured with energy above 1016​e​V10^{16}eV, the recent advancements in astronomical detection techniques have rekindled the motivation for developing more sensitive methods for identifying such clustered events.

If some of the UHECRs measured from Earth originated from some astrophysical flaring events (point sources), we expect them to be clustered with directional and temporal correlations. Detecting such direction-time clustering will be more probable for UHE neutral particles, like photons, as they will not be deflected by cosmic magnetic fields on their path to Earth. Although no astrophysical photons have been measured with energy above 1016​e​V10^{16}eV, the recent advancements in astronomical detection techniques have rekindled the motivation for developing more sensitive methods for identifying such clustered events.

In this paper, we present an algorithm for finding direction-time clusters in UHECR data [2, 3], using an unbinned likelihood method. The technique was first developed to investigate correlations between neutrino events recorded by the IceCube Neutrino Observatory [4, 5]. We have incorporated the technique to work with cosmic ray air-shower data and strengthen particle discrimination by including distinct observables, referred to as photon tags. These tags help us differentiate between signal (photon-initiated air showers) and background (hadron-initiated air showers) events, based on different characterizations of the measured air shower events. The technique has been demonstrated to be sensitive in identifying a photon flare by requiring only a few events, spread across a wide range of flaring periods. We extend the application of the technique by searching for photon sources expected to accelerate photons in the UHE regime, using the public UHECR data of the Pierre Auger Collaboration [6].

papers.title: Finite sample guarantees of MPPI: suboptimality, sample complexity and closed-loop guarantees
papers.abstract: This paper considers model predictive path integral (MPPI) control for nonlinear finite-horizon optimal control problems with bounded inputs, allowing nonconvex and nonsmooth costs. We prove theoretical guarantees that quantify the suboptimality caused by positive temperature and finite sampling on MPPI and establish their implications for closed-loop guarantees. Specifically, we derive a suboptimality bound for infinite-sample MPPI that characterizes the effects of temperature and prior coverage, followed by a high-probability finite-sample approximation error bound that reveals the dependence on sample size, temperature, and cost variability. By incorporating these bounds into a terminal-constraint-free MPC framework, we further establish semi-global practical recurrence of the closed-loop system. Numerical examples involving a four-link planar manipulator illustrate the temperature-sampling tradeoff and the influence of prior quality on approximation accuracy and closed-loop performance.

papers.title: Engineering antiferromagnetic (LaVO3)m/(PrVO3)n superlattices
papers.abstract: In this study, we demonstrate the atomic-scale engineering of antiferromagnetic (LaVO3)m/(PrVO3)n superlattices grown by MBE on (001)-oriented SrTiO3 substrates. Our work achieved a precise layer-by-layer control, revealing how interface-driven structural distortions can be systematically tuned. X-ray diffraction and reciprocal space mapping confirm both the epitaxial strain state and the high crystalline quality of the superlattices. High-resolution scanning transmission electron microscopy further uncovers layer-resolved atomic displacements, where La3+ and Pr3+ exhibit antipolar motions modulated by the superlattice periodicity. The alternate stackings of LaVO3 and PrVO3 yield a unique antiferromagnetic transition temperature, which can be tuned by adjusting their relative proportions. This behavior exists despite the distinct spin ordering temperatures observed in the constituent materials. Layer-resolved spectroscopic measurements reveal that the hybridization of La and Pr 5d orbitals with O 2p orbitals is also modulated and directly correlated to the oxygen octahedra rotations. By determining the orbital hybridization and mapping the cation displacements as proxies, we can visualize indirectly the trilinear coupling between oxygen octahedra rotations and antipolar rare earth displacements. Notably, the interfacial oxygen octahedra connectivity between cubic SrTiO3 substrate and orthorhombic vanadate layers significantly influences the structural distortions. These distortions, almost quenched near the interface, relax over few unit cells, demonstrating how strain and interfacial effects propagate through the superlattice. This study illustrates how artificial superlattices can be engineered to control structural distortions at the atomic scale, offering a pathway to tune the magnetic properties through strain-distortion relationships in perovskite oxides.

papers.title: Symmetries of Counterfactuals: Identification and Testability of Counterfactual Maps from Covariate Heterogeneity
papers.abstract: In general, counterfactuals are not identified from data alone, because many causal models produce the same observed distributions but different counterfactuals. A common approach to circumvent this problem is to restrict the mechanism to a class in which it becomes unique, such as triangular monotone maps or optimal transport maps. However, whether the assumed class is correct is usually not examined. In this work, we study what the data can tell us when covariates are available that influence the outcome only through its latent cause. First, we characterise all counterfactual maps that are consistent with the data. They differ from the true map by a group of symmetries that preserve the conditional outcome distributions given the covariates. The more these distributions vary across covariate values, the smaller the group. Second, we show that for the classes above, consistency with the data is equivalent to a single conditional independence, which yields a test of the assumed class. We illustrate both results on synthetic data and on the ACTG 175 HIV trial.

papers.title: Disambiguating Moral Circuits and Moral Features in Language Models: Moral content, normative judgment or cue words? Evidence from 14 models
papers.abstract: Interpretability methods can locate the attention heads and sparse autoencoder (SAE) features that change the answer a language model gives to a moral prompt, e.g., whether "Stealing medicine for a dying child is morally" continues with "justified" or "wrong". Such a component could respond to moral content, to the judgment of conduct by any norm, or to the word "morally" in the prompt. We built 227 minimal pairs of short phrases, validated by five annotators, whose two versions differ in a moral standard, in another kind of norm (prudence, etiquette, aesthetics or evidence) or in a descriptive quality, and showed them to 14 open-weight models (Llama, Gemma and Qwen, 1B to 14B, base and instruction-tuned), with and without the word "morally". In every model, the heads that change the moral answer belong to an evaluation circuit the models use for every kind of normative judgment we tested: these heads carry the same share of the effect for moral as for other normative pairs (pooled ratio 1.00, 97.5% confidence interval [0.92, 1.07], with the word; 0.90, [0.84, 0.96], without it), and the models need them as much for both. The models need these heads also when nothing in the prompt asks for a judgment, and on 400 scenarios of the ETHICS benchmark, where removing them takes away 37 to 39% of the difference between acceptable and unacceptable scenarios, against 1 to 3% for ten random heads. The SAE features we located respond mostly to the word "morally" rather than to what the phrase is about. The models represent the category of a pair (the standard the annotators assigned to it): it can be read from their hidden states, and, in the eight models we tested, removing the direction that carries it weakens the moral verdict by a few percent, and more than the other verdicts in seven of them. We release the pairs, the ratings, the code, the trained SAE dictionaries and the result files.

papers.title: Optimal Network Design under Node Failures
papers.abstract: Networks are frequently constructed before it is determined which nodes will persist. We address the design problem in scenarios where nodes fail independently, links are costly and must be established in advance, and the benefits to surviving nodes diminish with distance. Examples include supplier, interbank, and infrastructure networks. Among all possible networks, the complete, star, and empty configurations are each welfare-optimal within specific ranges of link costs. However, with four or more nodes, failures introduce a range of costs in which every optimal network contains more links than the star but fewer than the complete network. At the lower end of this range, we show that the optimal networks are exactly those obtained by removing a matching from the complete network. We develop an exact algorithm for complete multipartite networks. It finds an optimal network by dynamic programming in a number of operations that grows with the fourth power of the number of nodes, although the class itself grows superpolynomially. For networks with up to six nodes, restricting the design to this class results in no loss under explicit conditions. We also characterize pairwise-stable networks within this class and establish their existence for every level of link cost. Finally, we quantify the cost of misjudging failure risk. Overestimating node survival leads to overbuilding and can yield lower welfare than building nothing, whereas underestimating it never does. Under uncertain failure risk, design should therefore favor conservative reliability estimates.

papers.title: Clicks, Carbon, and Risk: Climate Attention, Persistent Financial Risk, and Real-Sector Activity
papers.abstract: Do shifts in public climate concern alter persistent financial risk and subsequently matter for real activity? We combine daily U.S. sectoral equity returns with a monthly Climate Concern Index (CCI) constructed from internet search intensity and decomposed into adverse and transition-oriented components. GARCH-MIDAS estimates reveal substantial heterogeneity: adverse climate concern raises persistent volatility in carbon-intensive Energy activities, while transition-oriented attention tends to reduce persistent volatility in regulated Utilities, with important differences across sub-sectors. We then construct a persistent-risk differential between Energy and Utilities and examine its predictive content for sectoral real activity using local projections. Innovations associated with adverse climate concern precede declines in Oil and Gas industrial production and employment over the following quarters, while comparable Utilities responses are limited. The production result is preserved when the financial predictor is reconstructed using the more closely matched Oil, Gas, Coal equity sub-sector and remains economically similar across several robustness checks. Overall, the findings establish a link between climate concern, persistent sectoral financial risk, and subsequent real-sector activity.

papers.title: Probabilistic Simple Types for Almost-Sure Termination (Extended Version)
papers.abstract:
We present a type system for almost-sure termination (AST) in higher-order probabilistic computation. Our vehicle is the recent Functional Machine Calculus (FMC), which combines the lambda-calculus with effectful imperative computation. Importantly for our purpose, it models branching and looping computation with sum types and a typed iterator construct. Our key observation is that by replacing sum types with probability distributions, types ensure that iteration has a non-zero chance of exiting, which then gives AST in a simple and natural way.
  Concretely, our type system assigns explicit probability distributions to termination outcomes, allowing probabilistic behaviour to be tracked compositionally at the type level. Types then soundly guarantee almost-sure termination, even in the presence of higher-order functions. The fragment of ground terms, which consists purely of the branching and iteration constructs with probabilistic sampling, is equivalent to finite Markov chains and is positively AST (expected evaluation time is finite). The full calculus is more expressive, which we demonstrate through an example term with infinite expected evaluation time.

papers.title: Magnetic tuning of odd elastic instabilities in chiral active crystals
papers.abstract: We investigate the dynamical properties of an odd active crystal whose elementary units follow an inertial dynamics and experience a Lorentz force induced by an external magnetic field. The continuous injection of energy associated with active chirality gives rise to odd elasticity, manifested through transverse forces between the crystal constituents. We show that the interplay between the magnetic field and these transverse forces produces a distinctive long-wavelength instability at vanishing wavevector, which is absent in both non-magnetic elastic crystals and passive crystals subjected to a magnetic field. Moreover, the magnetic field provides a means of tuning the collective oscillations of the crystal, enabling the emergence of exceptional points and tuning the dynamical instability induced by odd elasticity at finite wavevectors. Our analytical results yield explicit predictions for the displacement spectrum, static structure factor, and intermediate scattering function. These findings suggest that magnetic fields could provide a powerful tool for controlling collective phenomena in high-density systems of granular or colloidal spinners.

papers.title: Bent-tailed radio galaxies as tracers of the intrafilament medium
papers.abstract: Bent-tailed radio galaxies have traditionally been associated with, and used as tracers of, the dense intracluster medium. In recent years, however, such sources have also been identified outside of clusters, with only a few discovered in low-density environments of cosmic filaments. Their occurrence in low-density environments remains rare and is still poorly understood. We announce the discovery of bent-tailed radio galaxies in galaxy cluster filaments. We have identified two bent-tailed radio galaxies, J0020-25 and J0019-26, within a filament at the redshift of $z \sim 0.1273$, and another bent-tailed radio galaxy, J0019-25, in a separate filament at $z \sim 0.1126$. We used MeerKAT observations of these bent-tailed radio galaxies to place constraints on their intrafilament medium (IFM). The effects of the filaments could be seen in the radio morphologies of these galaxies. Using faint regions in each galaxy, we estimate the intrafilament pressure, density, magnetic field strength, and total energy density. We found an IFM density of $\rho_\text{IFM} \approx 3.8\times 10^{-29}$ g cm$^{-3}$ for the surrounding medium of J0020-25 and J0019-26, and $\rho_\text{IFM} \approx (0.2 - 1.1) \times 10^{-26}$ g cm$^{-3}$ around J0019-25. We found that our estimates for the intrafilament environment around J0020-25 and J0019-26 lie within the $\rho_\text{IFM}$ literature estimates, while the density estimate found using J0019-25 is higher than the literature density estimates for the IFM and in agreement with the density of group environments. J0019-25 likely resides in a galaxy group embedded within a filament. These discoveries show the capabilities of using bent-tailed radio galaxies as probes to locate the otherwise invisible large-scale filaments.

papers.title: Cubic graphs with circumference ratio 21/22 and cyclic connectivity 5
papers.abstract: We construct a cyclically $5$-connected cubic graph of order $22m$ and circumference $21m$ for every $m\geq 3$. Consequently, the shortness coefficient of the class of cyclically $5$-connected cubic graphs is at most $21/22$, improving the previously known upper bound of $24/25$. We also demonstrate how I-reductions, which delete an edge and suppress its two end-vertices, can be used to prove cyclic connectivity.

papers.title: Countering Anion Inhibition of Laccase Electron Transfer: Electrostatic Design, Charge-Transfer Dynamics on a Superconducting Quantum Processor, and Its Limits
papers.abstract: Hydroxide at neutral-to-alkaline pH and halides inhibit fungal laccases and limit their use in wastewater treatment. From GFN2-xTB cluster models of Trametes versicolor laccase (PDB 1GYC) we build a four-site Hubbard model of the His454-T3A-T3B-His452 junction of the trinuclear copper cluster and execute its charge-transfer dynamics on the Euro-Q-Exa quantum computer (IQM, 8 qubits, Trotterized circuits with Pauli twirling; 726 jobs). The charge-transfer frequency is measured to 3-5 meV, reproducibly over nine days and across changes of the device qubit map: hydroxide raises the charge-transfer energy of the crystal-geometry model by 92.0 +/- 2.2 meV (exact 87) and exceeds fluoride by 10.1 +/- 1.8 meV. A screen of charged probes in three dielectric models identifies Y116E; in the probe model the hardware resolves a reduction of the hydroxide penalty by 74 +/- 7 meV and of the halide penalty by 64 +/- 5 meV, acting on the site-energy gap rather than on the coupling. A real Glu116 (five conformers) with PROPKA protonation states and the coupled Asp456 gives a realistic reduction of 10-30 meV, with the same sign in 28 of 28 model combinations; the direction and ordering are the prediction, rate factors only an illustration. Scanning the on-site repulsion reverses the sign of the hydroxide effect, and a one-electron Hartree model reproduces the reversal: the measured dynamics is effectively single-particle. On a Fermi-Hubbard benchmark the hardware does not resolve electron correlation; it would need a contrast loss below 0.13 percent per CZ gate instead of the measured 0.34-0.54 percent.

authors.name: Lucia Malickova
authors.institution: Bratislava University of Economics and Business

papers.title: Mechanically induced self-propagating reactions within the realm of mechanochemistry: Fundamentals, overview, in situ monitoring and perspectives
papers.abstract: Mechanically induced self-propagating reaction (MSR) represents a promising but rather underexplored phenomenon within mechanochemistry, a solvent-free alternative to classical solution-based chemistry. In contrast to the gradual mechanochemical reactions, MSRs are sub-second combustive-like processes bringing about substantial benefits such as faster product formation, time efficiency, and lower energy consumption. Despite the fact that the mechanochemical field is in the research spotlight, MSR investigation remains on the periphery. This review aims to catalyze a renaissance in MSR fundamentals investigation by reviewing the current state-of-the-art. This is done via systematically reviewing the reaction systems that were reported to react via a MSR in the past twenty years, such as metal-metalloid ones (carbides, borides, silicides, and carbonitrides), metal chalcogenides, metal oxides, and other specific types of reactions. A couple of case studies are briefly reviewed for each system, and the comprehensive table follows afterward. The review also revisits the factors impacting the MSR course from milling conditions and reagent's properties point of view, showing either a direct or inverse relationship with MSR ignition time. The recent development in the in situ monitoring of mechanochemical reactions allowed to obtain some mechanistic insights into the MSR process, which are summarized in the last chapter.

papers.title: The SymTFT and Quantum Phases of Matter
papers.abstract: The symmetry topological field theory (SymTFT) provides a unified framework for ordinary and generalized symmetries of quantum many-body systems. By encoding symmetry in a topological theory in one higher dimension, it separates symmetry data from the details of a specific quantum system. In this review, we give a pedagogical introduction to this framework and survey its applications to phases of quantum matter. For fusion category symmetries in ${(1+1)}$d, we explain how the SymTFT characterizes anomalies, classifies gapped phases, and organizes the symmetry structure of gapless phases. We also give a broad overview of further developments of this framework, including extensions to symmetries in higher dimensions, continuous symmetries, fermionic systems, mixed states, and spacetime symmetries.

authors.name: Sakura Schafer-Nameki
authors.institution: Mathematical Institute of the Slovak Academy of Sciences

papers.title: Sidorenko Inequalities in Oriented Graphs
papers.abstract: We introduce relative Sidorenko and relative anti-Sidorenko inequalities for oriented graphs, strengthening the corresponding well-studied notions for tournaments by allowing arbitrary host graphs. An orientation $\vec H$ of a graph $H$ is relatively Sidorenko if $\hom(\vec H,\vec G) \ge 2^{-e(H)}\hom(H,G)$ for every oriented graph $\vec G$ with underlying graph $G$, and relatively anti-Sidorenko if the reverse inequality holds. We provide a complete characterisation of the class of connected relatively Sidorenko graphs in terms of weakly norming graphs, and exhibit several families of relatively Sidorenko and relatively anti-Sidorenko oriented graphs. Despite the substantially stronger definitions, many known tournament Sidorenko and anti-Sidorenko examples satisfy the relative inequalities, suggesting a broader theory of these phenomena in arbitrary host graphs and motivating several new structural and classification problems.

authors.name: Veronica Bitonti
authors.institution: Mathematical Institute of the Slovak Academy of Sciences

authors.name: Emma Hogan
authors.institution: Mathematical Institute of the Slovak Academy of Sciences

papers.title: The Nygaard graded piece, the Frobenius--Witt cotangent complex and regularity criteria
papers.abstract: For a $p$-torsionfree $p$-quasisyntomic ring, we construct a fiber sequence relating the $p$-th Nygaard graded piece of absolute prismatic cohomology to the Frobenius--Witt cotangent complex. The latter is an arithmetic analogue of the cotangent complex in which the differential of $p$ need not vanish. We also clarify the relationship between the regularity criterion proved by Mao using the Frobenius--Witt cotangent complex and the regularity criterion established by Bhatt and Mathew using the Nygaard graded piece. This relationship was anticipated by Bhatt and Mathew.

papers.title: Recovering hysteresis in reduced models of plasma turbulence: a Mori--Zwanzig-inspired closure
papers.abstract: Hysteretic transitions between turbulent and strongly zonal-flow-dominated states provide an important test for reduced models of plasma turbulence and a minimal setting for studying dynamics relevant to L-H transitions. The 12-mode truncation of the modified Hasegawa-Wakatani system developed by Guillon and G\"urcan retains this transition but underestimates the hysteresis observed in direct numerical simulations (DNS). Guided by the Mori-Zwanzig framework, we construct a phenomenological closure for the influence of discarded modes. The discarded spectrum is coarse-grained into a reservoir, whose feedback on the retained modes is modeled together with a separate drift-wave damping term. Without increasing the number of retained modes, the closure recovers nearly all of the hysteresis width missing from the unclosed truncation and places both transition thresholds close to their DNS values. To test the model beyond hysteresis, we also examine particle flux. The closed model improves upon the unclosed truncation, agreeing more closely with DNS at low adiabaticity but underestimating transport at high adiabaticity. These results show that a low-dimensional representation of discarded-mode feedback can improve predictions of hysteretic turbulence-flow transitions.

authors.name: Xavier Garbet
authors.institution: Commissariat à l'Énergie Atomique et aux Énergies Alternatives

papers.title: Beyond Episodic Recall: Experience-to-Knowledge Evolution for Lifelong Embodied Navigation
papers.abstract: Lifelong embodied navigation requires agents to accumulate experience through continuous interaction and reuse it for subsequent goal searches. Existing memory-enhanced methods typically retain historical observations or construct structured scene representations. However, storing observations or high-dimensional semantic embeddings incurs growing storage costs. Meanwhile, structured representations support retrieval and semantic reasoning but do not explicitly evolve accumulated experience into environment-specific knowledge. To address these limitations, we propose Experience-Evolving Memory (EvoNav), a novel two-timescale memory framework. It organizes semantic observations, spatial relations, and task-feedback cues into sparse experience atoms. During online operation, experience atoms continually consolidate repeated observations and form dynamic links based on transitions. At the slower timescale, EvoNav distills accumulated category co-occurrences and feedback signals into environment-specific structural knowledge without relying on predefined object--room relations. For each new goal, EvoNav combines direct goal evidence from experience atoms with learned structural knowledge to guide goal-directed search on the current traversability map. Experiments on single-goal, sequential multi-floor, and multimodal navigation demonstrate effective experience reuse and improved path efficiency with compact persistent memory, together with successful transfer to a real robot.

papers.title: Multistage Contextual Optimization for Vehicle Repositioning
papers.abstract: Ride-hailing platforms reposition idle vehicles to improve spatial supply-demand balances. This problem is prediction-driven and multistage: at each stage, the platform forecasts future demand, executes current decisions, and uses the resulting state to initialize the next stage. We formulate a multistage linear program (LP) with a macroscopic fundamental diagram (MFD) linking accumulation to trip completion. We then develop a multistage contextual optimization approach that uses decision performance to train the prediction model. The learning problem combines multiple coupled stages, context that depends on earlier decisions, and predictions that affect the objective, the constraint matrix, and the right-hand side of the LP. We derive the exact gradient, which has three parts: parameters change forecasts and hence decisions; earlier decisions change the current decision through the inherited state; and this state also changes forecasts as context. An equivalent adjoint uses reverse vector-Jacobian products, avoiding full solution and state-parameter Jacobians. Finally, forward propagation solves many stage LPs one after another, which makes training slow. We propose a parallel block evaluation algorithm that solves blocks of consecutive stages in parallel and repeatedly feeds each block output to the next block. We prove that the algorithm recovers the serial trajectory within a finite number of passes and that its gradient error remains bounded when it stops early. On New York City ride-hailing data, multistage contextual optimization yields 7.7% to 9.1% more business benefit than the same predictor trained by mean squared error, outperforms all compared baselines from five paradigms, and even outperforms realized demand fed to the same policy. With eight workers, parallel block evaluation shortens training by a factor of 1.86 without loss of decision performance.

papers.title: Convection--diffusion equations with non-integrable initial data
papers.abstract: We characterize the long-time behaviour of solutions to the convection--diffusion equation $u_t-u_{xx}+(|u|^{q-1}u)_x=0$, $q>1$, with initial data behaving like a non-integrable power at infinity, $|x|^\gamma u_0(x)\to k_\pm$ as $x\to\pm\infty$, $0<\gamma\le1$. The decay rate in time and the asymptotic profile depend on the strength of convection as compared to the size of the solution at infinity, leading either to a convective behaviour or to a diffusive one. When the nonlinear convection dominates, we observe an enhanced dissipation effect: the decay rate in time is faster than for the purely diffusive equation with the same initial datum. For $0<\gamma<1$ we obtain the limit self-similar profile, which, in the convective regime, has one shock, or two when $k_+k_-<0$ and $|k_+|>\eps(\gamma,q)|k_-|$, where $\eps(\gamma,q)\in(0,1)$ is an explicit threshold. For $\gamma=1$ logarithmic corrections appear, and the limit is a multiple of the heat kernel if $q>2$ and an $N$-wave if $1<q\le2$. The convergence takes place in the spaces to which the datum belongs, and not only on expanding sets. The main new ingredients are an Ole\u{\i}nik type estimate of H\"older type valid for $q\geq 2$ and a far-field estimate, uniform in time, showing that beyond the self-similar region the solution is still described by its own datum.

authors.name: Liviu I. Ignat
authors.institution: IMAR - Institutul de Matematică „Simion Stoilow” al Academiei Române

papers.title: An algorithm for solving structured problems involving $L$-infimal convolutions
papers.abstract: We develop an operator-splitting framework for solving structured minimization problems involving linear compositions of $L$-infimal convolutions. We introduce a primal-dual shadow Douglas-Rachford splitting method and establish its convergence. As a result, we derive a fully primal-dual splitting algorithm for the class of the aforementioned minimization problems.

papers.title: A search for optical bursts from the repeating fast radio burst in the M81 globular cluster, FRB 20200120E
papers.abstract: We present a search for optical bursts from the repeating fast radio burst FRB 20200120E, which is located in a globular cluster of M81 and is the closest known extragalactic FRB. We observed FRB 20200120E simultaneously with the high-speed, quintuple-beam optical camera HiPERCAM on the 10.4-m Gran Telescopio Canarias and the Effelsberg 100-m Radio Telescope. We detected one radio burst of fluence $\mathcal{F}_{\rm R} = 0.14\pm0.01$ Jy ms during our observations, but found no evidence for corresponding optical bursts in the 11.98 ms frames. We find 5$\sigma$ upper limits on the optical burst fluence of $\mathcal{F}_{\rm O} < 1.8\times10^{-3}$ Jy ms (combined $u_s g_s r_s i_s z_s$-bands) and the optical burst energy of $E_{\rm O} < 5.4\times10^{36}$ erg ($r_s$-band), corrected for interstellar extinction. We compare our upper limit on the optical-to-radio fluence ratio $\mathcal{F}_{\rm O}/\mathcal{F}_{\rm R} < 0.013$ to various emission models involving inverse-Compton scattering in the magnetosphere or nebula of a highly-magnetised neutron~star.

authors.institution: Max Planck Institute for Radio Astronomy

authors.name: W. J. Page

papers.title: Exploited Before It Was Fixed? Vulnerability Timelines from Open, Machine-Readable Evidence
papers.abstract:

  We introduce an evidence model implemented in Vulnerability-Lookup that selects the earliest evidence for each lifecycle event, distinguishes vulnerability-specific records, preserves date precision, and ensures traceability to original sources.
  Among 3,758 vulnerability identifiers with exploitation evidence, 98% have disclosure dates, while only 15.7% have patch evidence. Vendor-side dates required by VTEM are entirely absent. Most exploitation dates originate from catalog listings, including 1,041 entries associated with bulk catalog imports. After excluding these entries and ambiguous same-day observations, 59 vulnerabilities exhibit patch evidence following exploitation evidence, with a median interval of 7.6 days, predominantly between catalog listings and distributor fixes.
  Evidence traceability also exposes systematic measurement errors: one collector incorrectly classified exploit publications as active exploitation, accounting for 40% of initial exploitation dates, while another catalog assigned vulnerability publication timestamps to 11% of its listings.
  Our findings demonstrate that exploitation-to-patch intervals are computationally measurable, but their reliability depends on the availability, precision, and provenance of published evidence. We identify the additional disclosure, exploitation observation, and patch availability timestamps needed to improve vulnerability lifecycle measurements.

papers.title: Power loss for the local Mizohata--Takeuchi estimate on smooth hypersurfaces
papers.abstract: We prove power-type lower bounds for the local Mizohata--Takeuchi constants for $C^{2,\beta}$ hypersurfaces with $0<\beta\leq1$ whose second fundamental form is nonzero at some point. This result, in particular, disproves the so-called local Mizohata--Takeuchi conjectures for the paraboloid and the sphere and, in turn, presents an obstruction to a general weighted approach to the theory of Fourier restriction of those classical surfaces.

papers.title: Feedback and Resource Competition in Incoherent Feedforward Loops: When Is Cumulative Dose Ordering Preserved?
papers.abstract: Biochemical coupling can change the expression levels and timing predicted by an incoherent feedforward loop (IFFL) model without changing cumulative dose ordering. We derive ordering conditions using shared-production identities and Metzler comparison bounds, with tail guarantees beyond finite computation. A nonlinear example exhibits delayed slope reversal at a fixed dose, on an $O(1/\eta)$ timescale as pathway mismatch $\eta$ vanishes. At one fixed joint fit, validated bounds establish decreasing cumulative output across 20-100 ng nominal burden, from zero to full target loading, at every positive finite observation time for a translation-blocking model and an RNA-decay model. Full loading at 20 ng reduces 48-hour cumulative output by 13.35% and 10.18%, respectively, while endpoint concentration in the first model changes by only +0.15%. Preserved ordering therefore does not ensure quantitative agreement.

papers.title: A polynomial-time decoding algorithm up to half the square-root bound for quadratic residue and generalized quadratic residue codes
papers.abstract: Binary quadratic residue (QR) codes, introduced by Prange in 1958, are cyclic codes of prime length $p\equiv\pm1\pmod 8$ and dimension $(p+1)/2$ whose minimum distance satisfies the square-root bound $d\ge\sqrt p$. They include the Hamming code $[7,4,3]$ and the Golay code $[23,12,7]$, and were generalized by van Lint and MacWilliams to generalized quadratic residue (GQR) codes of prime-power length $q$, for which the bound $d\ge\sqrt q$ still holds and is attained when $q$ is a square. In coding theory, one usually first finds a lower bound on the minimum distance of a family of codes, and then a polynomial-time algorithm decoding up to half of this bound, as for BCH, Reed--Muller or Gabidulin codes. Until now, GQR codes had resisted this approach: no such algorithm was known, apart from individual short lengths. We give a deterministic algorithm which, for every odd prime power $q\equiv\pm1\pmod 8$, corrects every error pattern of weight at most $\lfloor(\sqrt q-1)/2\rfloor$ in the binary GQR code of length $q$, in $O(q^{9/2})$ operations in $\F_q$. We start from a description of QR codes due to Helleseth, which we extend to GQR codes, and in which the syndrome gives the values of the quadratic character of the error-locator polynomial. We then recover this polynomial by adapting to GQR codes the tools that Kopparty developed for recovering polynomials from noisy character values, with the decoding of dual BCH codes as an application. Since the square-root bound is attained when $q$ is a square, this radius is the largest that can be guaranteed uniformly on the class of GQR codes.

papers.title: Multicomponent Adaptive Sampling Configuration Interaction method in openLOWDIN: positronic and quantum nuclear systems
papers.abstract: We present a multicomponent Selective Configuration Interaction (SCI) method based on the deterministic Adaptive Sampling CI (ASCI) algorithm for computing energies and wavefunction properties of molecular systems containing leptons of variable masses, or quantum nuclei. Near-FCI accuracy is achieved by incorporating second-order Epstein-Nesbet perturbation theory or by dressing the Hamiltonian via Davidson's and co-workers shifted-Bk method. We validate the approach through benchmark positronic (e$^+$LiH, e$^+$OH$^-$, e$^+$Mg) and quantum nuclear systems (HCN), establishing a novel protocol for accurate convergence, based on the iterative adaptation of natural orbitals starting from those obtained by considering only cross-particle CISD excitations, to those obtained from SCI variational space, surpassing the accuracy of previous SCI studies. Overall, we show that the present multi-component SCI framework offers a simple, systematically improvable, and cost-effective alternative to traditional CI approaches.

papers.title: Temperature Flips the Sign of the Hydrogen Response in Nanogranular Palladium Networks
papers.abstract: In nanogranular palladium networks, hydrogen uptake has two opposing effects on electrical resistance. Absorbed hydrogen scatters electrons within the particles, raising their resistance, while particle expansion narrows the gaps between them and lowers the junction resistance. Such networks are widely studied as resistive hydrogen sensors, and the sign of their net response is usually treated as a fixed property of the architecture. In networks grown by atomic layer deposition on macroporous silicon, we show that changing the operating temperature can reverse this sign at a fixed hydrogen concentration. A thermodynamic model indicates that scattering contributes less as temperature rises, allowing sub-angstroem changes in gap width to dominate. Where the two effects cancel, the network absorbs hydrogen yet gives the same reading as in hydrogen-free gas, so a leak could escape detection. Between 25 and 40 degrees Celsius, this cancellation point is predicted to rise over tenfold, crossing reported leak-alarm setpoints. At 55 degrees Celsius, the measured response stays negative but passes through a minimum, so a concentration above a setpoint can mimic one below it. Annealing at 200 degrees Celsius alters the calibration and turns the room-temperature response negative at the lowest concentration tested. Quantitative sensing therefore requires a defined thermal pretreatment and an operating temperature giving distinct signals across the intended concentration range. Response polarity becomes an operating parameter rather than a fixed property. More broadly, any nanoparticle network whose particles deform on sorption may show the same temperature-dependent competition between transport within and between particles, with implications for sensors and switches beyond palladium-hydrogen.

papers.title: The Role of Galactic Shear in Regulating Local Star Formation Efficiency: A Combined MaNGA DynPop and ALMaQUEST Study
papers.abstract: We study the local regulation of star formation efficiency (SFE) in star-forming regions of nearby galaxies using spatially resolved data from the Mapping Nearby Galaxies at Apache Point Observatory (MaNGA) and the ALMA-MaNGA QUEnching and STar formation (ALMaQUEST) surveys. We define the local SFE as $\Sigma_{\rm SFE} \equiv \Sigma_{\rm SFR}/\Sigma_{\rm H_2}$, where $\Sigma_{\rm SFR}$ is the star formation rate surface density derived from dust-corrected $\rm H\alpha$ emission, and $\Sigma_{\rm H_2}$ is the molecular hydrogen surface density derived from CO measurements. Combining these data with dynamical properties from the MaNGA DynPop project, we use random forest regression to identify the dominant factors of $\Sigma_{\rm SFE}$. Galactic shear, quantified by the Oort parameter $A_{\rm Oort}$, emerges as the dynamical property most strongly associated with lower SFE on average, exceeding the predictive power of mass surface density (either total or stellar), Toomre stability, and mid-plane pressure. However, these quantities provide only modest predictive power and primarily trace the radial variation of SFE. After removing the shear-related radial trends, only weak correlations remain between SFE and other local galactic properties, implying that the remaining azimuthal variations are likely governed by cloud-scale processes below our resolution limit. Furthermore, the relationship between SFE and shear varies among galaxies and weakens in gas-rich regions, suggesting that gas density may modulate the impact of shear. This behavior is consistent with competition between shear-induced cloud stabilization and shear-driven cloud-cloud collisions. Overall, galactic shear appears to regulate the large-scale radial distribution of SFE, while cloud-scale interstellar medium physics may drive the remaining variation.

authors.name: Lihwai Lin
authors.institution: Institute of Astronomy and Astrophysics, Academia Sinica

papers.title: Dissecting the GPU Load/Store Unit and Exposing Its Security Risks
papers.abstract: GPUs are the main platform for large-scale machine learning and power the largest supercomputers. Their load/store units (LSUs) often determine kernel performance and have been exploited in prior attacks. Yet what is known about the LSU is only a few isolated mechanisms and parameters, and even a single one has been enough for an attack. In particular, it is still unknown what a load costs, where loads contend, and even whether a warp can starve due to contention. Until each is measured, neither its security risk nor a defense is known. We reverse-engineer how the LSU serves load instructions on recent NVIDIA GPUs with microbenchmarks and analyze the security implications. We give a cycle-accurate latency formula for a global L1 hit or shared memory access from the addresses it touches, whose address-dependent terms are bank conflicts and the L1 tag lookup; we show that loads contend at both, and that when the LSU pipeline is full a warp can starve a warp of a later-launched block. We then show that the LSU's attack surface is far broader than prior attacks revealed: through channels never exploited before, it can leak information, communicate covertly, and degrade colocated workloads. Through either global bank conflicts or tag lookups alone, we recover a full AES-128 key under the threat model of prior GPU AES timing attacks. Under NVIDIA's Multi-Process Service (MPS), the bank access and the tag lookup each open a covert channel across processes, whose rate rises with each GPU generation. Also under MPS, this starvation lets one warp slow a colocated cuBLAS matrix multiplication by up to 750x on the A100 and 563x on the H100.

authors.name: Pierre Talbot
authors.institution: Interdisciplinary Centre for Security, Reliability and Trust

papers.title: Forests of Omnitrees: Analysis and Applications to Anisotropic Space--Time Finite Elements
papers.abstract: We prove output-optimal work bounds for omnitree forests, which bisect cells along selected axes. A canonical descriptor characterizes representable partitions independently of split order. Complete one-level cycles, including coarsening, face balance and selected coarse meshes, take sequential work proportional to stored input and output at fixed dimension and key width, with polynomial depth dependence even for unbalanced input. From balanced input, refinement-only balance stays within each request's coordinate slab; this bound is attained. Polynomial trace equations characterize conforming high-order spaces across crossed face partitions. Reconstruction moments bound interpolation errors and capture the logarithmic loss that bilinear nodal interpolation can suffer on balanced meshes. Elements of degree up to four resolve moving heat layers on unstructured 4D space-time and 5D space-time-parameter meshes. Multigrid uses the generated hierarchies.

papers.title: Synchrony, Affect, and Perceived Autonomy in Virtual Robot-Facilitated Anxiety Support Groups
papers.abstract: Socially assistive robots could expand access to group-based mental health support when skilled human facilitators are unavailable. However, their effectiveness will depend on whether they foster productive interactions among participants. We examined dyadic head-movement synchrony among 96 participants across 18 virtual robot-facilitated anxiety support group sessions. A human-controlled virtual robot, via a Wizard-of-Oz (WoZ) system, facilitated all sessions. We found that stronger peak synchrony predicted lower post-session negative affect. In contrast, speakers who more often followed listeners' movements reported higher negative affect and state anxiety, demonstrating that synchrony strength and direction capture distinct interpersonal processes. Participants who believed the robot was autonomous showed more genuine synchrony and stronger peaks than those who believed it was human-operated; more negative attitudes toward robots also predicted greater synchrony. These findings support synchrony as an objective, behaviorally grounded measure for evaluating robot-facilitated groups and a potential signal for guiding future autonomous facilitators.

papers.title: MoE--LoRA Methods for Multilingual Adaptation: A Systematic Empirical Study
papers.abstract: Routed low-rank adapters offer a parameter-efficient means to improve the performance of large language models (LLMs) across tasks. Hence, it is assumed that they can also be used to improve the support of low-resource languages in LLMs, which currently serve English far better than the thousands of other languages spoken worldwide. However, this assumption has never been verified empirically under a shared multilingual evaluation protocol. We address exactly this gap by comparing eight low-rank adaptation (LoRA) methods on a frozen base model using 200 unique languages in more than 9{,}000 evaluation settings. Our results suggest that a reduced-scale search can identify viable configurations of LoRA methods but does not reliably predict their relative performance, as the top-ranking configuration is never best at scale. LoRA reliably improves language-model fit on translation data, consistently degrades reading comprehension, and benefits low-resource languages most. These findings suggest that LoRA methods should be regarded as targeted tools rather than general-purpose means for improving the multilingual capabilities of LLMs.

papers.title: A Unified Choice Model of News Selection: Experimental Evidence on Stance, Rank, and Engagement Cues
papers.abstract: Social media platforms often display visual engagement cues alongside ranked news articles, yet their influence on clicks remains poorly understood when considered jointly with ranking position and users' political preferences. We propose a unified discrete choice framework using a conditional multinomial logit model to jointly estimate and compare the influence of these factors on news selection. We evaluate the model using 1,480 choices from 370 human participants across four news topics in a controlled study with and without visual engagement cues. The framework allows us to assess the incremental contribution of each factor through nested-model likelihood-ratio tests. We find that including visual engagement cues significantly improves model fit across all topics after accounting for rank and stance. Engagement cues alone also predict clicks better than either of these features, although the full model achieves the highest held-out log-likelihood. Finally, we quantify via counterfactual analysis the impact of ranking position and displayed engagement counts on click probabilities. These findings can inform platform owners, researchers, and policymakers evaluating how platform design affects the selection of political news.

papers.title: Limite 1B - Violetto: Technical Report
papers.abstract: We present Limite 1B - Violetto, a one-billion-parameter model designed for high-throughput mathematical reasoning. Limite is trained from scratch on 237 billion tokens from a carefully curated, mathematics-centric corpus and supports context lengths of up to 131k tokens. Its architecture and training recipe were developed together to maximize reasoning capability while keeping training and inference costs low. Post-training combines knowledge distillation, targeted supervised fine-tuning, and RLVR on a curated curriculum. Limite achieves 94.01% on AIME 2026 and 74.25% on BeyondAIME, placing it among models many times its size on our evaluation suite. The model is deliberately only lightly instruction-tuned: it is intended primarily as a single-turn mathematical solver and as a fast, parallel component of larger systems, rather than as a general-purpose assistant. We release the model, its base and value checkpoints, and an optimized serving implementation under the Apache 2.0 license.
papers.intro:
Progress in mathematical reasoning has often come with increases in model size, training compute, and test-time sampling. While this has produced increasingly capable systems, it also makes repeated sampling, long-context inference, and large-scale deployment expensive. Many applications require a different operating point: a model that can solve difficult problems while remaining small enough to run at relatively high throughput and to generate many candidate solutions in parallel. This motivates a complementary question to conventional scaling: how much mathematical capability can we concentrate into a model with approximately one billion parameters?

With one billion parameters, it supports contexts of up to 131k tokens, and is designed to provide high reasoning capability per parameter. The model is only lightly instruction-tuned and is intended primarily as a single-turn mathematical solver, as opposed to a general conversational assistant.

With one billion parameters, it supports contexts of up to 131k tokens, and is designed to provide high reasoning capability per parameter. The model is only lightly instruction-tuned and is intended primarily as a single-turn mathematical solver, as opposed to a general conversational assistant.

Efficiency guides the design of the entire training pipeline. Limite uses a deep architecture with a mixture of local and global attention, allowing it to perform many sequential transformations while limiting the cost of long-context inference. The model is pre-trained on 237 billion tokens drawn from a larger mathematics-centric corpus containing problem-solution pairs, synthetic mathematical material, and carefully filtered STEM-adjacent web text. The resulting base model already exhibits substantial mathematical ability before post-training.

We begin with knowledge distillation from millions of filtered mathematical solutions, then alternate targeted supervised fine-tuning with RL. Rather than repeatedly training on broad, static datasets, each stage focuses on areas where the current checkpoint remains weak. Later RL stages also use a learned value model to improve credit assignment over long reasoning traces.

We evaluate Limite across seven benchmarks covering recent mathematical competitions and research-level problems. It obtains 94.01% on AIME 2026, 83.62% on HMMT February 2026, and 74.25% on BeyondAIME [37, 13, 8]. A more comprehensive evaluation is available in Section 5. These results are competitive with models ranging from several billion to tens of billions of parameters.

We envision Limite’s small size as possibly enabling a broader mode of use, where a controller may delegate mathematical questions to multiple Limite instances, inspect their outputs asynchronously, and combine promising lines of reasoning. This separates high-level coordination from high-frequency mathematical exploration and makes it possible to spend additional test-time compute through parallelism rather than through a single large model. The same specialization that makes Limite effective in this setting is also its principal limitation: outside mathematics, it may misinterpret a request or replace it with a superficially related mathematical task, an example of this is shown in Appendix H. Also within mathematics, Limite works best at mathematical reasoning, while it may struggle with knowledge of the literature or formalization and structured theorem proving.

This separates high-level coordination from high-frequency mathematical exploration and makes it possible to spend additional test-time compute through parallelism rather than through a single large model. The same specialization that makes Limite effective in this setting is also its principal limitation: outside mathematics, it may misinterpret a request or replace it with a superficially related mathematical task, an example of this is shown in Appendix H. Also within mathematics, Limite works best at mathematical reasoning, while it may struggle with knowledge of the literature or formalization and structured theorem proving.

We show that strong mathematical reasoning can be achieved with a restricted parameter count and relatively few steps of training. By jointly designing the architecture, data, optimization, and post-training process around a narrow objective, Limite concentrates substantial reasoning capability into a compact model that can be sampled from and deployed efficiently. We release the final model, its base and value checkpoints, our evaluation suite, and the serving implementation all under the Apache 2.0 license.

papers.title: Cycles of Arbitrary Period in Multidimensional Heterogeneous Hegselmann-Krause Dynamics
papers.abstract: We study periodic behavior in heterogeneous Hegselmann-Krause opinion dynamics with multidimensional opinions and norm-defined confidence neighborhoods. We prove that, for every dimension $d\ge3$, every $\ell_q$ norm with $q\in[1,\infty]\setminus\{2\}$, and every integer $m\ge2$, a system of five agents admits a periodic trajectory of minimal period $m$; moreover, different periods can coexist for fixed confidence radii. Four agents remain stationary, while the fifth moves along a line segment contained in their convex hull. The stationary agents may share a common strictly positive confidence radius, and all confidence inequalities are strict. A geometric criterion underlying the construction extends these results to further classes of norms. However, this criterion cannot be satisfied in dimensions one and two, regardless of the confidence norm. We also prove that no heterogeneous Hegselmann-Krause system with less than five agents admits a nonconstant periodic trajectory, under any norm and in any dimension; every trajectory with at most three agents converges exponentially.

authors.name: Iryna Zabarianska
authors.institution: Moscow Institute of Physics and Technology

papers.title: Where Demand Meets Supply: Spatial Elastic Consensus for Low-Bandwidth Collaborative Perception
papers.abstract: Occlusions and limited sensor range make ego-only 3D perception insufficient for safe driving. Collaborative perception addresses this by enabling connected vehicles to share complementary observations, yet it remains constrained by tight vehicular communication budgets. While spatial selection is more flexible than fixed-rate feature compression, existing selectors remain largely sender-driven and waste scarce bandwidth on ego-visible targets. Furthermore, applying convolutions after masking spreads isolated tokens into their neighborhoods, silently violating low-bandwidth constraints. To address this, we propose Spatial Elastic Consensus (SEC), a bandwidth-adaptive framework centered on bilateral demand-supply consensus. Instead of unilateral token selection, the ego vehicle formulates a content-aware demand prior while each collaborator evaluates its local supply. This single-round consensus allocates the token budget to critical ego-missed evidence rather than ego-visible redundancy, without transmitting dense maps. To guarantee exact budget compliance, an anti-dilation refine-before-mask pipeline refines features prior to discrete token selection, preventing receptive-field leakage. A lightweight deformable sampler then aggregates these sparse messages with learned local offsets, compensating for the spatial context lost to token selection and mitigating inter-agent pose drift. Evaluated at a stringent 64KiB budget, SEC consistently achieves the best AP@0.7 on the simulated OPV2V and V2XSet datasets and the real-world DAIR-V2X dataset. These results demonstrate that combining bilateral consensus with budget-exact transmission is key to efficient low-bandwidth collaborative perception.
