authors.institution: Office National d'Études et de Recherches Aérospatiales

authors.name: Karen Godary
authors.institution: Centre National de la Recherche Scientifique

papers.title: Projection of global daily CO2 emissions in 2026
papers.abstract: Global fossil-fuel combustion and industrial-process CO2 emissions remain close to historical highs, yet the recent slowdown in growth is difficult to assess before conventional inventories become available. We project emissions for 2026 and examine daily departures during major climate and energy disruptions. Carbon Monitor activity-based estimates from 1 January 2019 to 30 September 2026 are combined with Prophet projections for 1 October to 31 December across 47 region-sector series. Global emissions are estimated at 38.1 Gt CO2 in 2026, 36.6 Mt CO2 (+0.10%) above 2025. The reference 68% range for the year-on-year rate is +0.011% to +0.18%. Five September-cutoff hindcasts show lower daily forecast errors for Prophet than for a seasonal-naive benchmark. Regional increases total 0.32 Gt and decreases total 0.29 Gt, so 94.0% of the 0.61 Gt gross movement cancels in the global sum. China contributes the largest reduction (-0.19 Gt), concentrated in industry and ground transport, whereas India contributes the largest increase (+0.19 Gt), led by power and industry. Heat-period power anomalies differ among countries and can be muted by summer averaging, while aviation and shipping show different disruption and recovery profiles. Resolving the near-zero global change reveals where reductions are concentrated and where continued growth offsets them, providing a timely basis for assessing the breadth of mitigation progress.

authors.name: Philippe Ciais
authors.institution: Centre National de la Recherche Scientifique

papers.title: When Neural Collapse Fails to Route: Routing Drift in Continual Learning
papers.abstract: Progressive neural-collapse classifiers can learn strong task-local decision boundaries while failing the global Class-IL decision. We identify the failure as routing drift: under an expanding equiangular tight frame (ETF) classifier, a held-out sample can remain separable within its true task block, yet receive its largest global score from another block. This produces high Task-IL accuracy but low Class-IL accuracy, and small replay buffers can mask the problem because stored samples are optimized repeatedly and often remain well routed. We formalize route accuracy directly from the global class argmax and use it to separate within-task discrimination from cross-task score comparability. This decomposition suggests a classifier-level correction: preserve the global ETF frame, but add class-local reliability evidence when transported class measures deviate from the neural-collapse ideal. We develop Reliability-Calibrated Routing (RCR), a lightweight post-hoc classifier that composes standardized ETF alignment with radial plausibility around transported, NC-shrunk class representatives. Across three datasets and two fixed replay-buffer budgets, this NC-consistent correction gives the best Class-IL FAA on five of six settings and reduces Class-IL forgetting on all six. The largest gains occur in harder routing regimes: up to $+6.75$ FAA over the reported reference, and up to $+8.03$ FAA and $+8.62$ final route accuracy in paired evaluations, while preserving Task-IL performance. These results position routing drift as a measurable failure mode of ETF-based continual learning and show that reliability-calibrated class evidence can repair part of the lost global routing without retraining the representation. Code and evaluation artifacts are available at https://towzeur.github.io/RCR/.

authors.name: Nicolas Larue
authors.institution: Centre National de la Recherche Scientifique

papers.title: Properties of Chromium and Manganese in Tycho's SNR with XRISM/Resolve
papers.abstract: The X-ray emission of young supernova remnants gives access to the composition and spatial distribution of elements ejected in supernovae. The emission from the ejecta provides crucial insights into the explosion mechanism, especially for Fe-group elements formed in the innermost layers of the star. The objective of this paper is to provide constraints on the supernova progenitor and explosion mechanism of Tycho's type Ia supernova remnant by studying the properties of Cr and Mn. The unprecedented spectral resolution of XRISM/Resolve allows us to detect significant emission lines of Cr and Mn in different regions of Tycho's supernova remnant, even at small scale, providing a much more precise spatial distribution of Cr and Mn with respect to previous measurements. Significant Cr and Mn emission lines are observed in the Fe bright northeastern-to-southeastern emitting rim, some in the center region, but none in the southern region. The observed mass ratios of Mn/Fe, Cr/Fe and Mn/Cr, are consistent with 1D delayed detonation models of near-Chandrasekhar-mass Type Ia supernovae and 1D pure-detonation models of 1 Msol sub-Chandrasekhar-mass progenitors. In both cases, the observations imply supersolar zero-age main-sequence progenitor metallicities. Overall the best agreement is found for models with a too high metallicity to be realistic for Tycho's location. This points to additional sources of neutronisation such as carbon simmering for Chandrasekhar mass progenitor. For sub-Chandrasekhar mass, double detonation models with a WD mass lower than 1Msol are suggested.

papers.title: Crowd model with anticipation and interactions: an exclusion process based mean-field game
papers.abstract: Mean-field games (MFG) is a powerful framework to describe competitive optimization processes. A natural field of application is crowd dynamics, where pedestrians are considered to optimize their path, while interacting with the others. Despite its success to incorporate anticipation in describing pedestrian behavior, the mean-field games framework neglects microscopic granular effects, rendering its results less realistic in various applications (bottlenecks, evacuations etc.). In this work, we consider an explicitly interacting microscopic model, namely an asymmetric simple exclusion process and derive the corresponding mean-field game. This mean-field game is applied to an evacuation setting and the differences from the standard MFG based on non-interacting Langevin dynamics, as well as the correlations induced by the granular interactions are discussed.

authors.name: Cecile Appert-Rolland
authors.institution: Centre National de la Recherche Scientifique

authors.name: Denis Ullmo
authors.institution: Centre National de la Recherche Scientifique

papers.title: Classification of Tissues on MALDI-MSI Image Modality for Pancreatic Cancer Studies
papers.abstract: Mass Spectrometry Imaging (MSI) spatially maps molecular distributions in tissue sections. Despite the availability of preprocessing tools for MSI data, building end-to-end workflows suitable for deep learning remains challenging. We have developed a fully automated pipeline for transformation of raw Matrix-Assisted Laser Desorption/Ionization Mass Spectrometry imaging (MALDI-MSI) data into deep-learning-ready image patches for binary pancreatic tissue classification (tumoral vs non-tumoral) and built individual models for recognition of tumoral regions in spectral images. Images resulting from the proposed pipeline and from reference interactive workflow are very close in terms of image quality metric mean squared error (MSE). The proposed pipeline computational time is of 20 min in average compared to a full working day of the reference interactive workflow. The models achieved 0.94 accuracy on high-resolution spectra and a mean accuracy of 0.59 on lower-resolution spectra.

papers.title: Can Verifiable PIR Match the Online Efficiency of SimplePIR?
papers.abstract: Verifiable Private Information Retrieval (vPIR) ensures that a malicious server cannot return tampered database records, but it traditionally incurs significant overhead compared to classical PIR.Recent advancements, notably VeriSimplePIR, approach the online efficiency of SimplePIR by introducing a proof preprocessing phase and requiring only lightweight client-side online verification. However, this scheme relies on an additional Short Integer Solution (SIS) assumption and SIS-based commitments, which only support relaxed range proofs. Consequently, these schemes are forced to adopt significantly weaker parameter choices, resulting in additional online overhead. In this paper, we propose a novel vPIR protocol that employs a newly designed error-correcting code-based commitment scheme as the database digest. This approach (i)supports efficient proofs of linear relations, (ii) achieves precise range proofs and (iii) eliminates the reliance on the SIS assumption. Thus, our scheme successfully adopts parameter choices identical to those of SimplePIR. As a result, our vPIR protocol is the first to achieve exactly the same online communication and server computation costs as SimplePIR, while keeping online client computation nearly identical. Additionally, compared to VeriSimplePIR,our protocol reduces online communication and client-side computation by approximately 20%, and decreases online server-side computation by over 35%.

authors.name: Zirui Wang
authors.institution: Centre National de la Recherche Scientifique

papers.title: Generalized and Convex Poincar\'e Inequalities via Transport-Divergence Inequalities
papers.abstract:
We investigate the relationship between generalized $(q',p')$-Poincar\'e inequalities and transport-divergence inequalities involving $\chi^q$-type divergences. Extending the classical correspondence between the $(2,2)$-Poincar\'e inequality and quadratic transport-$\chi^2$ inequalities, we prove that a $(q',p')$-Poincar\'e inequality is equivalent to a transport-divergence inequality for conjugates $(p,p')$ and $(q,q')$. We then study the convex counterpart of these inequalities. Using weak barycentric optimal transport and convex order, we establish an equivalence between convex $(q',p')$-Poincar\'e inequalities and weak transport-divergence inequalities involving a projected $\chi_q$ divergence. We further characterize the minimizers arising in this projection problem through a geometric condition on the relative density. In dimension one, we analyze the geometric consequences of $(q',p')$-Poincar\'e inequalities by identifying sharp conditions on the behavior of the density both at infinity and near isolated zeros.
  We show that when $q'>p'$, the concentration behavior becomes polynomial rather than exponential at infinity. Finally, we interpret these inequalities through the lens of optimization in Wasserstein space. In particular, the equivalence between transport-divergence and Poincar\'e inequalities appears as an analogue of the equivalence between quadratic growth and Polyak--\L ojasiewicz inequalities in finite-dimensional optimization.

authors.name: Thibaut Le Gouic
authors.institution: Centre National de la Recherche Scientifique

papers.title: SPICE: Sparse Parameter Gossip for LLM Pretraining
papers.abstract: Pretraining language models across geographically distributed resources requires communication-efficient methods that operate under limited and variable internet bandwidth. Decentralized training replaces global collectives with peer exchanges, but full-model messages make larger peer neighborhoods costly. We introduce SPICE, which combines sparse parameter gossip with error feedback through corrected parameter values that remain directly interpretable as peer neighborhoods change. These sparse exchanges make broader neighborhoods affordable, achieving better training quality with less communication than the evaluated dense decentralized baselines. As the replica count grows, SPICEincreases the number of peers contacted while keeping individual messages sparse, limiting the quality degradation observed with dense gossip. Under bandwidth constraints, SPICE achieves higher training throughput than DDP and dense gossip, while sustaining throughput during transient link slowdowns.

authors.name: Edouard Oyallon
authors.institution: Centre National de la Recherche Scientifique

papers.title: Pressure Drop: Gravity Vector Estimation from a Distributed Barometric Pressure Sensor Array
papers.abstract: While gravity is often used in mobile robotics as a global constraint for Simultaneous Localization and Mapping (SLAM) algorithms, most estimation methods rely on indirect observation of the gravity vector. In this paper, we propose the use of altimeter measurements to directly observe the direction of the gravity vector. We provide a theoretical evaluation of the estimation noise and validate it through extensive experimental data, along with an evaluation of the impact of intersensor distance on our gravity vector estimates. Experimental results demonstrate that a median error of $0.87^\circ$ on the tilt estimation can be achieved with our system in semi-static scenarios. Furthermore, we demonstrate the potential of this approach by comparing it with state-of-the-art methods based on Inertial Measurement Units (IMUs). We highlight that we achieve similar performance to that of IMU-based systems in highly dynamic scenarios and even outperform in specific cases of accelerometer measurement saturation. Finally, an additional experiment shows the potential use within a robotic system through the integration into an Iterative Closest Point (ICP) algorithm.

authors.name: Johann Laconte
authors.institution: Institut National de Recherche pour l'Agriculture, l'Alimentation et l'Environnement

papers.title: On the V-toothpick sequence
papers.abstract: We give a generating function for the V-toothpick sequence and an algorithm that computes any term in time polynomial in the number of binary digits of its index. We determine its quadratic growth and periodic fluctuations, and give convergent series for the constants in its asymptotic bounds.

papers.title: Cutoff on abelian groups
papers.abstract: We prove the long-predicted equivalence between the cutoff phenomenon and the product condition along any sequence of abelian random walks whose inverse transition probabilities grow at most logarithmically with the size of the group. Our result does not require reversibility, and comes with a sharp quantitative estimate on the mixing window. Moreover, we show that our sparsity restriction is optimal by constructing abelian Cayley graphs which satisfy the product condition but fail to exhibit cutoff, and whose degrees are arbitrarily close to being logarithmic in the volume.

authors.name: Justin Salez
authors.institution: Centre de Recherche en Mathématiques de la Décision

papers.title: Near Resonance, Less Ordered: Radius and Mass Ordering in Compact Multi-planet Systems
papers.abstract: Compact multi-planet systems exhibit a tendency for planetary radii to follow ordered sequences with orbital position, suggesting that these non-random patterns preserve a fossil record of their formation. Here, we investigate whether ordering of planet radii and masses with orbital period is related to proximity to mean-motion resonances. We compare near-resonant and non-resonant systems using complementary rank- and inversion-based measures of ordering, while accounting for differences in planet multiplicity and uncertainties in the measured planetary properties. We find that radii and masses are less monotonically ordered in near-resonant systems than in non-resonant systems, with the primary radius analysis providing stronger evidence than the mass analysis. This result is opposite to the naive expectation that dynamical instabilities should erase the primordial ordering of initially resonant systems and leave non-resonant systems in a more disordered state.

papers.title: Color Through Time: Distributions, Sparsity and Dominance in Western Painting
papers.abstract: We investigate the evolution of color in Western painting using a large corpus of digitized artworks. Each painting is represented by its distribution over a fixed palette of colors in a perceptually uniform space. We compare the color distributions of historical periods and artistic movements through their Jensen-Shannon distances, and introduce two interpretable descriptors, sparsity and dominance, that quantify how many colors are used and how unevenly they are represented. We find a historical transition from dark, earthy palettes toward a broader and more saturated chromatic range, unfolding through distinct shifts from the nineteenth century onward. Periods evolve smoothly over time, whereas artistic movements display increasingly distinct chromatic signatures beyond chronology. In the sparsity-dominance plane, painting follows a two-stage historical trajectory, first broadening the range of colors used and later increasing color dominance. Comparison with natural images reveals distinct ways in which artistic palettes depart from nature, either through the colors they use or through how broadly and evenly those colors are distributed. Finally, two surveys on generated images show that judgments of harmonious color balance concentrate around two complementary regimes: many colors arranged in a strong hierarchy, or few colors used evenly.

papers.title: Avalanche Sharpness and the Stationary State of the Bak--Sneppen Model on $\mathbb Z^d$
papers.abstract:
We establish the stationary picture for the nearest-neighbour Bak--Sneppen model on $\mathbb Z^d$, for every $d\ge1$. There exists a critical level $t_c$ such that, as $N\to\infty$, every fixed family of stationary fitnesses on the torus $(\mathbb Z/N\mathbb Z)^d$ converges, in exponential coordinates, to independent random variables with law $t_c+\operatorname{Exp}(1)$.
  The proof relies on three estimates for avalanches. For $d\ge2$, these replace the interval structure available in dimension one. We show that the threshold at which the mean avalanche range diverges coincides with the threshold for the appearance of an infinite avalanche, using the hierarchical structure of avalanches and an estimate on the creation of new sites under translation. We then prove that an avalanche reaching a macroscopic distance on the torus can, after any fixed positive increase of the level, be amplified into one covering the whole torus. Finally, below criticality, we obtain exponential integrability of the avalanche range and give a finite--infinite volume comparison.
  These three ingredients allow us to implement the Meester and Znamenski program that connects these avalanche estimates to the stationary law of the finite-volume process.

papers.title: A short proof of the 1-1/e performance of RANKING on the complete upper triangular instance
papers.abstract: The randomized online bipartite matching algorithm RANKING of Karp, Vazirani and Vazirani (1990) matches, asymptotically, a fraction $1-1/e$ of the vertices of the complete upper triangular (CUT) instance. We give a short proof of this fact that looks at the final matching from the offline side. A single observation drives the argument: the first $k$ arrivals can distinguish the offline vertices $v_k,\ldots,v_n$ only through their ranks. As a consequence, whether $v_k$ is matched is decided by a uniform draw among the remaining ranks, and the number of matched vertices among $v_1,\ldots,v_k$ is a Markov chain with explicit transition probabilities. A linear differential equation, solved by hand, gives the limiting profile of this chain, and the constant $1/e$ appears where the matching probability reaches one.

papers.title: Digital Qiang Garden: Artist Residency as Interface for Creativity Under Change
papers.abstract: This research presents Digital Qiang Garden, an artist-led residency situated in Qiang ethnic minority villages in western Sichuan, China, as a practice-based inquiry into creativity for change. Rather than framing creativity as a discrete outcome or individual agency, the project examines how creative practice unfolds through lived conditions under uncertainty. Drawing from three years of residency practice, the pictorial identifies four creative modes of praxis that repeatedly emerged through shared living, material engagement, and cross-media collaboration. Through annotated visuals and project-based case studies, we further trace how these modes generated eight interrelated layers of change, spanning artistic processes, social relations, cultural encounters, ecological awareness, organizational structures, and artists' longer-term trajectories. By framing an artist-led residency as a transferable structure, this work contributes to HCI and creativity research by foregrounding designed conditions, situated action, and relational processes through which change unfolds over time.

papers.title: What Does an Agent Need? Bundle-Aware Agent Resource Composition
papers.abstract: An agent resource's value depends on its backbone and companion resources and is known only after execution. Token-based generators remain tied to their training catalog, while independent resource scoring misses complementarities and reused bundles target other tasks. We formulate Task-Conditioned Agent Resource Composition (AgentComposition): jointly selecting a backbone model and a tool-skill bundle to maximize end-to-end execution utility. Our Retrieval-Grounded Bundle-Aware Agent Generation retrieves candidate resources and past configurations of similar tasks. A fine-tuned generator reads resource descriptions and recombines candidates through constrained beam search, allowing new resources without retraining. A bundle-aware critic ranks complete configurations using a large language model (LLM) teacher and historically successful configurations as execution proxies, and adapts to execution feedback when available. We evaluate reference recovery, offline execution with judged and native rewards, and online recommendation with real execution, building AgentSelect-Exec with 5,060 executed configurations. Our method recovers the complete reference configuration within ten candidates for 67.73% of AgentSelect queries, nearly twice the strongest baseline, and leads all baselines on SkillsBench. The proxy-trained critic raises the top-ranked agent's execution score from 7.58 to 8.37 out of 10; execution feedback increases it to 8.78, above the strongest baselines. Four target-domain queries suffice to adapt the generator to SkillsBench. Agents recommended online outperform the strongest baselines under both an LLM judge and native verifiers. These results support learning and transferring joint resource composition from task experience.

papers.title: Multilevel Filtering on Manifolds with Light Schr\"odinger Bridges
papers.abstract: In this article we consider the filtering of partially observed diffusions when the observations, made at discrete times, are noiseless. Each observation then confines the hidden state to a manifold defined by the data, whose type, for instance a sphere or an affine subspace, may change from one observation time to the next. In practice, the filter is approximated by particle filters, which require the diffusion to be discretized in time. Multilevel Monte Carlo reduces the cost of this discretization only if the particle approximations at consecutive discretization levels stay close, which standard particle filters do not ensure. We develop a new particle filter based on light Schr\"odinger bridges, which works between changing manifolds and can be coupled across discretization levels. A key insight is that the previous state enters the light Schr\"odinger bridge only through a few features, so that the bridge only has to be fitted on the new manifold, regardless of the type of the previous one. We bound the bias of this particle filter and the gap between its approximations at consecutive levels, and show numerically, on spheres and on manifolds that change type, that this gap is much smaller than with standard multilevel particle filters, and that, with the cost of the fits included, a hybrid estimator that uses it at the fine levels reduces the cost at small tolerances.

papers.title: Where Should Physics Enter? Information, Identifiability and Calibration in Probabilistic Sea Surface Temperature Forecasting
papers.abstract: Advection-diffusion priors are a common way to make neural sea surface temperature (SST) forecasts physics-informed. We test where such a prior must enter a heteroscedastic ConvLSTM to help, using daily NOAA OISST v2.1 for the Bay of Bengal (1982-2024) and a synthetic benchmark on the same grid with known currents of controlled strength. (i) On real data, a soft advection-diffusion residual with a learned velocity gives no reliable benefit (lead-15 CRPS -0.007 degrees C, 95% interval [-0.022, +0.008]); a plain temporal-smoothness penalty matches it, and equivalence within 3% is not established either. (ii) Learned velocities do not recover the currents, whether placed in the loss, in an explicit transport step, or in a transport step without neural correction: they correlate with the reference no better than a shuffled-date null, even on synthetic data where knowing the currents would improve day-15 forecasts by 16-23%. (iii) Supplied currents help on synthetic data, but mostly as information: giving them to the network as input channels, without transport, recovers 92% of the transport design's lead-5 gain, and a frozen-current numerical forecast does as well as either. (iv) With GLORYS12 reanalysis currents on real data, the transport design is 6% and 4% worse at leads 1 and 5; reanalysis advection explains essentially none of the daily OISST change (correlation 0.02), and frozen-current transport is worse than persistence. (v) The defect that matters is lead-dependent miscalibration shared by every model. One variance multiplier per lead, fitted on validation data, brings 90% coverage to 0.85-0.91 at all leads and lowers day-1 CRPS by 13-21%; fine-tuning on 15-day rollouts fixes long-lead coverage but costs short-lead skill. This version withdraws an earlier claim of an 81% CRPS reduction that came from an uncontrolled comparison.

papers.title: FMT: Lossless Image Compression in a Fixed Number of Parallel Steps
papers.abstract: Learned lossless codecs make smaller files than common classical codecs, yet the images we archive and train on still use classical codecs. A main reason is time: a learned codec takes seconds to decode a photo that a classical codec opens in milliseconds, and their faster variants give up most of their gain in size. We argue that much of this time is spent waiting, not computing: the network waits for the values it conditions on, and the arithmetic decoder reads them one at a time. We introduce FMT (Fixed-step Multiscale Tree), a lossless image format whose decoding order and entropy coder are designed together so that neither wait grows with the image. FMT stores an image as a coarse-to-fine tree whose steps hold independent values: a GPU predicts each step at once and decodes it in parallel rANS lanes that carry their states from step to step, so an image of any size decodes in a fixed number of sequential steps. On this tree we build a family of bit-exact codecs, from a rule with no network to large networks, and no codec we ran on the same GPU beats any of them on both size and speed. Without a network, FMT beats NVIDIA's HTJ2K on size and speed; with a large one, it decodes Kodak photos 9 to 61X faster than learned codecs we ran on the same A100, at the same size or smaller.

papers.title: SpikWM: Efficient End-to-End Spiking World Modeling for Visual Planning
papers.abstract: Goal-conditioned planning with image observations and goals requires predictions that distinguish visual states and action consequences. Spiking neural networks offer sparse computation, but single-step spikes can obscure motion cues and merge actions with different physical outcomes. We propose the Spiking Latent World Model (SpikWM), an end-to-end joint-embedding predictive architecture (JEPA) with one simulation step per image and one neural update per latent position. Spiking Regional Encoding retains spatial cues through regional pooling. Bi-Spike Action Encoding combines positive and negative binary responses, while Causal Membrane Prediction carries subthreshold evidence across the latent history with learned group-wise time constants. The encoder and predictor are trained jointly on reward-free image--action trajectories using next-embedding prediction and SIGReg. With a common planner, SpikWM achieves mean success rates of $88.67\%$, $97.33\%$, $99.33\%$, and $86.67\%$ on Push-T, Two-Room, Reacher, and OGBench-Cube, respectively, outperforming two spiking baselines. Push-T ablations support each module, and controlled replays examine responses to appearance and physical state changes. Under a matched planning budget, SpikWM reduces estimated arithmetic energy by $75.6\%$ relative to LeWM. Code will be released at https://github.com/ShawnYE618/SpikWM.

papers.title: The profinite shape equivalence
papers.abstract: We show that, for every $\infty$-topos $\mathcal{X}$, the profinite shape induces a canonical equivalence between the $\infty$-category of pro-objects in locally constant constructible sheaves of anima in $\mathcal{X}$ and the slice $\infty$-category of profinite anima over the profinite shape $\widehat{\Pi}_{\infty}(\mathcal{X})$. We deduce this profinite shape equivalence from the monodromy classification theorem by establishing a continuous version of the straightening-unstraightening equivalence for profinite anima. In addition, we explain how the monodromy classification theorem recovers its classical counterparts concerning locally constant sheaves of finite sets and of (abelian) groups.

papers.title: Connecting Calcium Depletion and Dust Evolution in the Rapid Accretor T28
papers.abstract: We present a multi-wavelength case study of the star T28 in the Chamaeleon I star-forming region and investigate the dust evolution of its highly Ca-depleted protoplanetary disk. We combine new observations from the MIKE spectrograph on the Magellan Clay Telescope with archival IRS spectrum and photometry. We constrain the optical extinction using the hydrogen column density of the region, and apply ROTFIT to obtain stellar parameters. We estimate the mass accretion rate by fitting the excess flux above the photosphere with an accretion shock model. We model the line profiles of Ca II K and H$\alpha$ with magnetospheric accretion models to infer Ca/H abundance, while the infrared excess is modeled with irradiated accretion disk models to get disk properties. We find that T28 is a high accretor with significant Ca depletion in its accretion flows. We find that the disk is best fit with a pre-transitional model with a disk mass of 0.12 $M_{\odot}$, where two optically thick disks are separated by a gap filled with optically thin dust extending to 16 au. This gap would not be resolved in the existing observations. T28 follows the trend of increasing depletion with increasing mass accretion rate. This trend can potentially be explained by preferential and early giant planet formation in massive disks, as suggested by recent planet formation simulations, leading to enhanced capture of refractory material in the massive disks of high accretors and thus depletion in the material reaching the star.

papers.title: REEL: Brain-Guided Video Generation and Selection by Reranking Encoder Embeddings with Linear Decoding from fMRI data
papers.abstract: Visual brain decoding from functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) data has made remarkable progress in recent years, driven by increasingly powerful artificial intelligence (AI) models and the growing availability of large-scale public datasets. However, despite the impressive advances achieved in static image decoding, the reconstruction of videos from fMRI signals remains challenging due to the temporal mismatch between rapidly changing video stimuli and the slow dynamics of the blood-oxygen-level-dependent (BOLD) response. We evaluate a Bayesian-inspired proposal-and-rerank strategy on CC2017 and the BOLD Moments Dataset (BMD), using a linear semantic decoder, a pretrained video generator, and three neural encoding streams with ridge readouts and learned pooling in two streams. We refer to this framework as REEL (Reranking Encoder Embeddings with Linear decoding). Compared with a single generated candidate, reranking increases mean Video 50-way accuracy from 0.2359 to 0.2434 across three CC2017 participants and from 0.3653 to 0.3920 across ten BMD participants. These findings suggest an alternative and conceptually simpler strategy for improving video brain decoding, highlighting the potential of our approach as a complementary direction to increasingly complex pipelines.

papers.title: Quantum Born Geometries from Modular Quantization
papers.abstract:
A structural link between quantization and "thermal-doubled" non-commutative Born geometry (with its split-quaternionic structure) is uncovered via Tomita-Takesaki first-quantized modular theory for complexified and polarized ortho-symplectic spaces.
  Implications for the modular algebraic quantum gravity program (arXiv:1007.4094) hint at further deep modifications of the notions of space and geometry (thermal quantum space-time hypothesis) waiting to be further explored.
  Speculative suggestions in the direction of A.Sakharov and L.Boyle-K.Finn-N.Turok CPT-mirror cosmologies will be mentioned, among several others.
  The present work is based on the manuscript "Modular Quantization and Non-commutative Space-time" (now on alphaXiv) that has been shared, with a selected number of researchers, since end of April 2026.

papers.title: Global phase-plane organization of a toxin-mediated plant-herbivore model
papers.abstract: Plant-herbivore interactions with chemical plant defence mechanisms can generate complex population dynamics through the nonlinear interplay between resource availability, herbivore pressure, and defence-induced feedbacks. In this work, we investigate the dynamical organization of a plant-herbivore model characterized by a non-monotone functional response accounting for inhibitory effects on grazing activity. In particular, we perform a qualitative and geometric analysis of the associated homogeneous system, characterizing the dynamical regimes supported by the model and the transitions between them. The results reveal the emergence of oscillatory behaviour through a Hopf bifurcation and the occurrence of stable periodic solutions. We further characterize the global phase-plane organization, providing a complete classification of equilibrium configurations and heteroclinic structures supported by the model. In addition, we identify the conditions under which homoclinic connections may occur and discuss their role in shaping the global dynamics. The analysis provides a unified description of the phase-plane organization and highlights how nonlinear defence feedbacks generate qualitatively distinct ecological outcomes, including extinction, stable coexistence, persistent oscillations, and global bifurcation scenarios organized by heteroclinic and homoclinic structures.

papers.title: From a High-T$\rm_C$ Spin-Gapless Semiconductor to a Spin-Glass: The Role of Disorder in NiMnCrAl
papers.abstract: We combine first-principles calculations with structural, magnetic, and transport measurements to investigate the influence of chemical disorder on the quaternary Heusler alloy NiMnCrAl. For the ordered Y-type structure, density-functional-theory calculations predict a ferrimagnetic spin-gapless-semiconducting state with a total magnetic moment of $1.99\,\mu_{\mathrm{B}}/\mathrm{f.u.}$ and a mean-field ordering temperature of approximately $1300~\mathrm{K}$. Polycrystalline NiMnCrAl forms in a single average cubic phase; however, combined x-ray diffraction, neutron diffraction, and extended x-ray absorption fine-structure measurements reveal substantial antisite disorder, characterized by predominantly B2-like disorder with additional cross-sublattice mixing. No long-range ferrimagnetic transition is observed up to $700~\mathrm{K}$. Instead, the compound exhibits a broad magnetic anomaly near $37~\mathrm{K}$, frequency-dependent ac susceptibility, slow stretched-exponential relaxation, and field-cooled and zero-field-cooled memory effects, establishing a glassy magnetic state. The electrical resistivity is metallic and the Seebeck coefficient is negative, consistent with the loss of the ideal spin-gapless electronic structure. Exchange-interaction calculations show that antisite disorder introduces short Mn--Mn separations and competing antiferromagnetic Mn--Mn and Mn--Cr interactions, providing a microscopic basis for magnetic frustration. These results demonstrate the strong sensitivity to the predicted spin-gapless and ferrimagnetic states of NiMnCrAl to chemical disorder.

papers.title: Who Pays for Byzantine Robustness? Validity, Data-Share Dictatorships, and Fairness When Only a Few Hospitals Collaborate
papers.abstract:
Clinical federated learning (FL) collaborations typically connect only three to six hospitals, yet Byzantine-robust aggregation rules are designed and benchmarked on synthetic partitions across dozens of equal-sized clients. We conduct an empirical audit of eight standard aggregation rules: FedAvg, coordinate-wise median, trimmed mean, Krum, Multi-Krum, Bulyan, geometric median (GeoMed), and Centered Clipping (CC). We evaluate both unweighted and sample-size-weighted variants across three cross-silo medical datasets from the FLamby benchmark: Fed-Heart-Disease ($n = 4$ hospitals), Fed-TCGA-BRCA ($n = 6$ regions), and Fed-ISIC2019 ($n = 6$ centres). We execute 54,214 training runs across enumerated attacker coalitions ($f \in \{1, 2\}$) paired with exact-twin leave-out controls that decompose performance drops into honest data loss versus adversarial attack damage.
  We report three findings. First, client-count validity checks fail to capture breakdown in skewed medical consortia: while $n = 6, f = 1$ satisfies every count condition except Bulyan's, assigning sample-size weights turns median and GeoMed into a clean-model dictatorship whenever a single hospital holds more than half the training data, and causes weighted median, GeoMed, and CC to collapse when that dominant centre attacks. Second, exact-twin leave-out controls reveal that when the largest hospital attacks, the apparent failure of count-based robust rules is predominantly caused by the loss of honest training data (7.5 to 10.4 points on ISIC) rather than adversarial perturbation (2.3 to 3.8 points on ISIC). Conversely, weight-dependent rules suffer large true attack damage (16.1 to 25.1 points on ISIC). Third, unweighted robust rules consistently discount whichever institution generates the most atypical parameter updates, penalizing the smallest hospital on Heart but penalizing larger institutions on TCGA and ISIC.

papers.intro:
Medical institutions rarely possess sufficient local patient volume to train generalizable diagnostic or prognostic models independently, while strict data-governance frameworks prohibit centralizing raw clinical records. Federated learning (FL) addresses this by keeping patient records on local hospital servers and aggregating only parameter updates at a central coordinator [1, 2]. Unlike cross-device consumer applications involving thousands of mobile phones, real-world clinical consortia are small cross-silo networks: across the seven real-world healthcare datasets in the FLamby benchmark, each federation comprises between two and six institutions [3].

Unlike cross-device consumer applications involving thousands of mobile phones, real-world clinical consortia are small cross-silo networks: across the seven real-world healthcare datasets in the FLamby benchmark, each federation comprises between two and six institutions [3].

Decentralized training, however, exposes the global model to corrupted updates. Hardware faults, miscalibrated imaging pipelines, label-mapping errors, or compromised hospital nodes can produce arbitrary parameter shifts, commonly modeled as Byzantine failures [4]. Because standard Federated Averaging (FedAvg) computes a linear combination of client updates, even a single corrupted institution can displace the global parameters arbitrarily far. To mitigate this risk, Byzantine-robust aggregation rules replace linear averaging with outlier-resistant operators, including coordinate-wise medians and trimmed means [5], nearest-neighbour distance selection such as Krum and Bulyan [4, 6], Weiszfeld geometric medians [7], and norm-bounded Centered Clipping [8].
